The parish's leading benefactor, Samuel Wyman, bought the Homewood estate in 1839; Homewood is the corridor's most-documented slavery site — but its documented enslaved history (Johns Hopkins' 'Enslaved at Homewood') is the CARROLL era through 1836, BEFORE Wyman, and Wyman-era slaveholding is not established by available sources. The poet Lizette Woodworth Reese, buried in this same churchyard, portrayed Waverly's Black domestic community in her memoir 'A Victorian Village' (1929) — 'Daddy Black and Others,' 'old black Eli... the butler' — but did not tie them to these graves. The Episcopal Diocese of Maryland's 'Trail of Souls' slavery-reckoning project (2014; a ~$1.39M reparations fund) invites every parish founded before 1864 to research its ties to slavery; St. John's qualifies (founded 1843) but has NOT participated — it is absent from the project and the diocesan history. So these servants remain, for now, real stakeholders in this ground whose story has not been told: the honest next step is the primary research St. John's has not done — burial registers, vestry minutes, and a physical survey of the rear section — that would let them be counted and, where possible, named.

Robertson Taylor (1840–1924), coffee-and-sugar importer of the clipper-ship era who organized the firm Taylor & Levering and was later with the U.S. Fidelity & Guaranty Co. A native of Norfolk, Va., he came to Baltimore in 1865 just after Appomattox, having served throughout the Civil War in the Confederate Army — enlisting as a private, promoted (per the obituary) to colonel, and wounded at the Battle of the Wilderness. He helped organize and establish the Protestant Episcopal Church of St. Michael and All Angels (the parish St. John's, Waverly, had spawned), and donated the houses at Charles and Twentieth Streets that became a hospital for crippled children — later the Kernan Hospital and Industrial School. Died Oct. 15, 1924 at his summer home in Carroll County, age 84; interred in St. John's churchyard (Find A Grave #30939895). Note: his Find A Grave record lists him as Adjutant, 6th Virginia Infantry — a rank discrepancy with the obituary's 'colonel.'

Oliver Perry Baldwin (d. July 17, 1878), of the editorial staff of The Baltimore Sun (earlier a Richmond newspaper editor). On July 29, 1878 the Sun ran a front-page memorial tribute written — anonymously, at his own wish — by Professor George Frederick Holmes of the University of Virginia, opening with Hamlet's line for Yorick ('Alas, poor Yorick! I knew him, Horatio; a fellow of infinite jest') and praising his wit, learning, and 'unstinted generosity which embraced all conditions.' Interred in St. John's churchyard, Waverly (Find A Grave #32287331).

Nathaniel Chew (c.1834–1905), of the Chew family, early Huntingdon/Waverly gentry. Son of Washington P. and Mary Hall Chew of Havre de Grace (a Chew–Hall marriage tie; his mother shares the name of the Mary Hall Chew, d.1837, among the churchyard's earliest stones). Brother of James W. Chew, longtime clerk of the U.S. District Court. He lived in retirement at 1431 Madison Avenue, where he died Nov. 14, 1905 at age 71; his funeral was held from St. John's Protestant Episcopal Church, Waverly (Find A Grave #32289322).

James White Chew (d. Jan. 9, 1907), for more than 50 years Clerk of the United States Circuit Court and District Courts of Baltimore. Brother of Nathaniel Chew; the two shared the family home at 1431 Madison Avenue, where he died of Bright's disease. His funeral was held from St. George's Protestant Episcopal Church (Pressman and Division Streets), conducted by Rev. Thomas Atkinson, rector of St. Barnabas', with burial in St. John's churchyard, Waverly (Find A Grave #32289346).

New York Times obituary (June 21, 1932): Oliver Perry Baldwin Jr., ~50 years on the editorial staff of The Baltimore Sun and its managing editor during the 1904 Baltimore fire, died at his Baltimore home June 20, 1932, aged 82. Born Richmond 1850, son of Sun editor O.P. Baldwin; UVA law, Maryland legislator, late-life anti-Prohibition leader. Survived by widow Caroline Frances Sutton, daughters Anna Lee and Dorothy, and son Hanson W. Baldwin of The New York Times (later Pulitzer-winning military editor). Buried St. John's, Waverly.

The Maryland General Assembly passed 'An act to divorce Elizabeth Blakeley, and her husband John Blakeley, of Baltimore county' (reported passing in the Maryland Gazette, Annapolis, Jan. 25, 1827) — a legislative divorce, decades before Maryland's courts could grant one. This John Blakeley appears to be the one buried at St. John's (1803-1860): he would have been about 24 in 1827, and his churchyard wife Maria Elizabeth Robinson (b.1820) was far too young to be the 'Elizabeth' of the act — consistent with Elizabeth being a divorced first wife and Maria a later marriage. Identification is a strong lead, not yet confirmed against the session-law text (Laws of Maryland, Dec. 1826 session) or Meyer's 'Divorces and Names Changed in Maryland by Act of the Legislature, 1634-1867'.

Charles B. Baker bought the old City school property at Greenmount Avenue & 33rd Street at public auction for $75,400, subject to an irredeemable $50 ground rent — the origin of what became the 'Baker Block.' The lot fronted 193 feet on 33rd St and 143 feet on Greenmount and held a schoolhouse of the first school district; contents (books, desks, furniture) had been removed before the sale. The city had tried the previous winter to sell the site to the American Oil Company for $48,700 for a drive-in filling station, but the City Council refused to ratify that deal after opposition (there were already filling stations at the SW and NE corners of Greenmount & 33rd). Reoffered at auction (Meyers & Meyers, auctioneers), bidding opened with New York's Morris Schapiro at $70,000, climbed past a Board of Estimates-appraised value of $47,500, and came down to a final duel between Schapiro ($75,350) and Baker, who topped him at $75,400. Other bidders included Lester L. Smith ($45,500), Thomas J. McDonald ($37,000) and William A. Harris ($50,000); American Oil's Louis Blaustein — the company's founder — had made an unsuccessful individual offer of $50,000 to the Board of Estimates before the auction. The sale proceeds were earmarked to help pay off the mortgage the city took to buy the Hoen Building (A. Hoen & Co.'s former lithography plant) as a City Hall annex under the Broening administration — directly tying the Baker Block's origin to the corridor's other marquee 19th-century name, August Hoen.

Nov 1, 1924: the Mayor and City Council formally conveyed title to the school property (southwest corner of 33rd & Greenmount) to C. B. Baker, about a month after the Sept 1924 auction. Baker immediately reconveyed a 40x95 ft portion at the southeast corner of Talbott & 33rd Streets to George M. Doebereiner — a confectioner who ran a business on the 33rd St side of the emerging block — for $20,000, through the Maryland Title Guarantee Company, calling it an investment.

Jul 29, 1926: construction announced for the Baker Block — 'Business Structure To Rise On Site Of Old School At Waverly.' A one-story-and-basement stucco building, architects Smith & May, ~140 ft frontage on Greenmount Ave and ~150 ft on 33rd St, containing EIGHT stores on Greenmount and FOUR on 33rd Street; the $100,000 contract was to be awarded that day, with completion expected by late October 1926. This CORRECTS the National Register/CHAP dating of the Baker Block to 'ca. 1925' — construction was actually contracted and built in 1926. Lee E. Hartman & Co. were the leasing agents for the property (the same firm that brokered Woolworth's 1927 lease here).

Jul 31, 1926: the construction contract for the Baker Block (SW corner of 33rd & Greenmount, on the recently-demolished school site) was awarded to Thomas Hicks & Sons, builders, for the ~$100,000 stucco commercial building.

May 6, 1927: F. W. Woolworth Company signed a 20-year lease for the storefront building at 3228-3230 Greenmount Avenue, near 33rd St, from C. B. Baker — one of three long-term leases the chain closed that day (also 2102-4-6 E. Monument St and a Westminster, Md. store), all through broker Lee E. Hartman & Co. This confirms the exact Woolworth address within the Baker Block.

Feb 1928: C. B. Baker leased the stores at 423 and 425 East Thirty-third Street to W. H. Wiley for automobile-showroom purposes, for two years with a three-year option, through brokers F. N. Iglehart & Co. — likely two of the four 33rd St-facing storefronts in the newly-built Baker Block (which had ~150 ft of 33rd St frontage), though canon does not yet have separate Property rows for these two addresses, so this is pinned to the Baker Block anchor parcel pending that split.

May 7, 2025: a Substitute Trustees' Sale was scheduled at the Clarence M. Mitchell Courthouse to foreclose on QT HAU, LLC's Dec 10, 2021 Purchase Money Deed of Trust (Liber 24654, Folio 362) covering the whole combined tax lot -- Tax ID 12-20-3882-012, described by the auction house as '3226-3240 Greenmount Ave., includes 419-427 E. 33rd St.,' ~22,910 sq ft (0.526 ac), ~19,000 sq ft of retail building in 8 rental units. The auction was POSTPONED. This is a separate, private-lender foreclosure running in parallel with the tax-sale-certificate foreclosure already in canon (ATCF IJ Maryland, Case C-24-CV-25-000132, Feb 2025) -- both converging on the same distressed 2021 QT Hau purchase. IMPORTANT CONFIRMATION: this listing is direct, official evidence that 3226 Greenmount (this Property, #769) and 3240 Greenmount (Property #2310) are ONE physical tax lot, not two -- resolving the parcel-duplication question flagged 2026-07-16.

City of Baltimore Department of Public Works property plat of Block 3882 (Ward 12, Section 20; scale 1in=50ft; dated May 1930) shows lots 12 and 13 already combined into one parcel ("12/13") fronting Greenmount Ave between Merryman Lane and E 33rd St -- the Baker Block footprint -- alongside the triangular lot arrangement along Merryman Lane/Brentwood Ave to the north. Confirms the combined 12/13 lot (now assessed as lot 012) is not a modern artifact of a later consolidation but was already unified by 1930, within a few years of the Baker Block's 1926 construction. Corroborates the 2025 Alex Cooper auction listing's framing of 3226-3240 Greenmount + 419-427 E 33rd St as one tax lot.

May 14, 1976: '13-7, Inc.' filed a UCC-1 financing statement with First Maryland Leasecorp for a full restaurant equipment package at 3236 Greenmount Ave -- Custom Keating electric griddle, three-section roll warmer, refrigerated worktable, Scotsman ice flaker, six-foot compartment sink, Jet Spray drink dispenser, stainless steel worktables/hand sinks, Plexiglass display sign and menu board, coffeemaker, exhaust hood/duct/fan, table and chairs. Confirms a diner/restaurant operator ('13-7, Inc.') at 3236 Greenmount -- a middle storefront in the Baker Block strip -- continuing the corner's long restaurant-succession pattern (Hasslinger 1927-28, Boulevard/Anderson family 1945, Godfrey's Steer and Beer 1970). Financing statement continued Dec 30, 1980 (Liber WA 3995 Page 720).

Jan 9, 1986: shortly after acquiring the Baker Block corner (Dec 26, 1985, PropertyIncident #18788), Greenmount Avenue Limited Partnership financed the purchase through Centrabank, Inc. with a Deed of Trust/Mortgage recorded in Liber 759, Folio 477. The SAME DAY, Ira Adler and Lucille Adler (owners of the neighboring 3220/3222 Greenmount parcels) also gave Centrabank a Deed of Trust/Mortgage recorded in Liber 759, Folio 500, likewise referencing '3226-3240 Greenmount Avenue (Block 3882)' -- an unresolved research thread on the exact nature of the Adlers' interest in this lot (co-financing, a cross-collateralized package loan across adjoining Baker-strip parcels, or a boilerplate address reuse by the bank). Both loans were satisfied on the same day, Oct 5, 1999, by Bank of America N.A. (successor to Centrabank) -- Certificates of Satisfaction recorded Liber FMC 103, Pages 5-6 and 7-8.

Sept 15, 1999: Greenmount Avenue Limited Partnership refinanced the Baker Block corner (address on this instrument: 3228-3232 Greenmount Ave) with a $1,755,000 loan from Morgan Guaranty Trust Company of New York, trustee Stuart A. Kruger, recorded Sept 16, 1999 (Book 8844, Pages 248 and 314 -- Deed of Trust and Assignment of Leases and Rents). The old 1986 Centrabank mortgages were satisfied three weeks later (Oct 5, 1999), a routine refinance sequence. The Morgan Guaranty loan was itself securitized: assigned effective Jan 25, 2000 to Norwest Bank Minnesota, N.A. as trustee for the J.P. Morgan Commercial Mortgage Finance Corp. Mortgage Pass-Through Certificates, Series 2000-C9 (recorded Feb 16, 2001, Book 1094 Pages 378-385) -- an early example of this parcel's debt entering the commercial mortgage-backed securities market.

May 13, 2016: as part of JAPAK LLC's sale of the Baker corner to Samuel S. Ha and Mie Young Ha (PropertyIncident #18790), JAPAK (Sung K. Pak, managing member) extended the Has a $650,000 purchase-money Deed of Trust (Liber 18198, Folio 264). Satisfied a year later, May 16, 2017 (Book MB 19225, Pages 50-54) -- the Has paid off their purchase note to JAPAK within twelve months.

Feb 5, 2015: Subway Real Estate, LLC signed a lease for store #126 at 3232 Greenmount Ave (5-year term, three 5-year renewal options) -- the Memorandum of Lease was acknowledged by the landlord on June 30, 2016, six weeks after JAPAK LLC's sale to Samuel & Mie Young Ha, with Samuel Ha signing as 'President' of an entity recorded as 'Greenmount Avenue, Inc.' (the printed 'Japak LLC' was struck through) -- a landlord-entity name not otherwise seen in this parcel's chain, possibly a Ha-family holding entity or a scrivener's reuse of the historic 'Greenmount Avenue Limited Partnership' name; flagged as an open thread, not merged with either.

March 13, 2026: Open Bank satisfied QT Hau LLC's Dec 10, 2021 purchase-money Deed of Trust ($2,975,000, Book 24654 Page 362) -- recorded March 17, 2026 (Book XAC 28869, Page 105) -- clearing the debt shortly before the property's final conveyance to NSR OF MD LLC. Concurrently, NSR OF MD LLC obtained its own financing: a Commercial Real Estate Deed of Trust dated March 9, 2026 (recorded ~April 1, 2026, Book 29047, Page 399) from Atlantic Union Bank, Grantor NSR OF MD LLC (14404 Big Bear Court, Silver Spring, MD), maximum principal $1,641,500 -- against a purchase price of $2,188,750, implying meaningful buyer cash equity in the deal. This completes the chain of title from the 1985 Baker Jr. sale through the 2026 NSR OF MD LLC purchase with no remaining gaps.

June 3, 1935: Charles B. Baker, by then 'of Shadwell, Albemarle County, Virginia, formerly of Baltimore County,' executed a Declaration of Trust (recorded amongst the Land Records of Baltimore City in Liber M.L.P. No. 6102, folio 614, 'as well as elsewhere') declaring that he held certain property -- including the Waverly/Greenmount & 33rd corner he'd bought at the 1924 city auction -- as Trustee for the benefit of members of his family. This resolves the apparent 61-year title-chain gap between the 1924 purchase and the 1985 sale to Greenmount Avenue LP: no intervening SALE ever occurred because Baker simply declared his own existing property held in trust for his family -- a self-declaration requires no new deed. Directly corroborated in Baker's own words by a Dec 15, 1949 resignation instrument (Liber M.L.P. No. 7962, folio 5) he personally signed -- see PropertyIncident for that instrument. The 'as well as elsewhere' phrase suggests the 1935 declaration was recorded across more than one jurisdiction (Baker was a Virginia resident by then), which is likely why the Baltimore City folio 614 citation, jumped to directly, showed an unrelated 1940 mortgage instrument rather than the trust text -- probably a cross-reference stub rather than the full declaration.

Feb 22, 1983 (recorded Jun 24, 1983; Book 70, pp. 800-806): Robert M. Goldman, Charles B. Baker Jr., and The First National Bank of Maryland -- Substituted Trustees of 'the Trust U/D of Charles B. Baker' (the 1935 self-declared family trust) -- conveyed the Waverly corner out of the trust to Charles B. Baker Jr. and Rachel Anne Fleet jointly. The deed recites the trust's succession history: Fred Metzger had renounced serving as Substituted Co-Trustee by notices dated Mar 19, 1951 and Jul 8, 1955 (Liber M.L.P. 8394 folio 18 and M.L.P. 10120 folio 172), after which Charles B. Baker Jr. was appointed Substituted Co-Trustee, and Carrie S. Baker (the elder Baker's widow) was appointed Co-Trustee upon and after Charles B. Baker's death. This 1983 distribution -- splitting the property between Baker Jr. and Rachel Anne Fleet -- directly explains why the Dec 1985 deed to Greenmount Avenue LP (PropertyIncident #18788) conveyed only a ONE-HALF interest for $312,500: Baker Jr. held exactly half, with Fleet (presumably a sibling) holding the other half via a probably-companion deed not yet located.

Dec 15, 1949 (recorded Jan 4, 1950; Liber M.L.P. No. 7962, folio 5): Charles B. Baker, in his own hand and words ('of Shadwell, Albemarle County, Virginia, and formerly of Baltimore County, State of Maryland'), resigned as Trustee of the 1935 family trust and appointed the First National Bank of Baltimore and Raphael Walter of Baltimore City as successor trustees -- exercising a right he'd reserved under paragraph 9 of the original 1935 Declaration of Trust. This is the first of two successor-trustee appointments recited in the 1983 distribution deed (PropertyIncident, source mdlandrec/mdlandrec-baker-trust-1983-distribution): Fred Metzger (who must have succeeded Raphael Walter or First National Bank at some point) later renounced serving as Substituted Co-Trustee in 1951 and 1955, after which Charles B. Baker Jr. was appointed in his place.

William T. Datcher, 18, of 3205 Barclay St, drowned in the Jones Falls below the old Cedar Avenue bridge (the Timanus dam; the site is now Round Falls, under Wyman Park Drive) on July 16, 1930. Two coroners' juries ruled the death accidental; ten days later the community alleged that white boys had chased and shoved him and that his body surfaced fully clothed. Accident and allegation both stay open in the record.

Baker Jr.'s half (PropertyIncident #18788, Dec 26, 1985), same grantee, same legal description. This closes the loop the 1983 trust distribution opened: the trust split the property between Baker Jr. and Fleet (Feb 1983), and each sibling sold their half to Greenmount Avenue LP SEPARATELY, eleven months apart -- Fleet first (Jan 1985), Baker Jr. eleven months later (Dec 1985) -- fully assembling the parcel under single ownership by the end of 1985. On the 1937 HOLC Residential Security Map, the Oriole Park (V) ground at 30th & Greenmount lies within the ONLY place in Baltimore where all four grades converge: C (yellow, the ballpark block), D (red, across Greenmount into Better Waverly and in the Abell wedge), B (blue, ~four blocks west toward Charles/Guilford), and A (green, north in Oakenshawe). Insight first named by Dr. Lawrence Brown (2026-07-23). VERIFIED 2026-07-24 by computation against the full national Mapping Inequality polygon set (10,154 areas / 314 surveys / 197 all-four-grade cities): Baltimore has a single connected four-grade convergence region citywide (convergence radius R*=81m, ~one block) — so "the only such place in Baltimore" is TRUE. The tightest junction is actually two triple-points ~200m apart (A-B-D and A-C-D). Measured from the ballpark's 30th St edge: the southern junction (A-C-D, on Greenmount just above E 32nd) is ~340 m - about 2.5 blocks - due north; the 81 m ring's center ~3.5 blocks. The ballpark parcel sits INSIDE zone C4, with the D6 wedge passing ~101 m east of it. NOTE: the national-rarity claim is NOT supported — Baltimore ranks 37/197 (five cities have a mathematically perfect single-point four-corners Baltimore lacks). Grant framing: lead with the only-in-Baltimore fact + the density of story on this ground; drop any "one of the only in the country" claim.

The Federal Home Loan Bank Board, through HOLC, launched the Waverly Community Conservation Test — a WPA field survey (Mar 15–Aug 15, 1939) using a 132-item schedule and at least two photographs of each of the 1,629 buildings in the 39-block, ~163-acre Waverly area (33rd to 42nd Streets, Greenmount Avenue to Ellerslie Avenue/Argonne Drive). The Baltimore Housing Authority sponsored it; the U.S. Housing Authority and HOLC supplied technical services.

The FHLBB published *Waverly: A Study in Neighborhood Conservation* (1940), prepared by economist Arthur Goodwillie under HOLC Deputy General Manager Donald H. McNeal, making the Waverly neighborhood the federal government's national demonstration project for 'neighborhood conservation' — the preventive alternative to slum demolition and a direct ancestor of postwar urban renewal. The 107-page book was offered 'for the inspiration and guidance of other urban communities... throughout the United States.' Waverly was chosen as the 'almost ideal' setting for 'an experimental study in scientific neighborhood conservation.'

The 1940 study defined 'Waverly' as the white residential area north of 33rd Street; it described the district to its south — which includes the Oriole Park (V) ground at 29th–30th & Greenmount — as 'a fully developed... slum district' where 'occupancy is being gradually relinquished to an economically needy and racially mixed residential type,' and which was 'definitely threatening the Area — by its contiguity and by actual infiltration.' The two were separated only by 'a wedge-shaped tract, improved with modern homes... narrow at the west and continuously widening toward the east,' and 'the slum's pressure to cross this sharply defined barrier... [had] been successfully resisted hitherto only by means of the high neighborhood standards.'

The report's summary Table No. 24, 'Dominant Factors in Waverly,' listed under Social conditions the very first factor — 'Race' — with the Favorable entry 'All white.' The study coded its central danger as 'the infiltration of families having more limited earning capacity and lower living and civic standards than their own,' and its Drawing No. 4 mapped 'areas of white and colored occupancy.' A 'well-maintained Negro settlement' of Morgan College teaching staff on Arlington Avenue, land held by 'a group of Negro bankers,' and St. Elizabeth's Home for Female Colored Orphans are named among the Area's environs.

The study documented the federal mortgage apparatus at work in Waverly: the Federal Housing Administration had graded the neighborhood from 58 ('eligible but poor') to 84 ('good') for mortgage-insurance eligibility, refusing Title II insurance anywhere rated below 50; and the Home Owners' Loan Corporation held 122 mortgages and owned 20 properties in the Area — 'the largest single property holder in the Area.'

To make the conservation program permanent, the study established the Waverly Conservation League, incorporated June 13, 1940, with organizing personnel supplied by HOLC: an Advisory Committee of 25 (including the executive heads of the four local improvement associations), an Operating Committee with a chairman from each of the Area's six districts, and 'block captains' for each block. It prescribed 'beneficial restrictions' — deed covenants limiting land to single-family residential use, which it framed as 'effective protection against undesirable infiltration' — and proposed a municipal Department of Conservation to run 'clean-up, paint-up, fix-up' campaigns and enforce restrictions.

The study's Appendix C proposed model legislation drawn from the Waverly experiment — a 'Neighborhood Improvement Act' and an 'Urban Redevelopment Corporations Act' — as templates for other jurisdictions, and the FHLBB explicitly offered the whole formula for 'the treatment of similarly threatened small-home neighborhoods everywhere... increasingly great urban districts throughout the United States.' The Waverly Test thus fed the legal and administrative machinery that became postwar urban renewal.

Before the corridor was built up, Charles Hamilton kept hothouses and flower gardens on York Road 'a little below the tollgate' (Gilmore Lane & York Road = today's Vineyard Lane & Greenmount Ave). He ran gardener want-ads through the 1870s, opened the Waverly Hotel in 1870, held the county contract to supply the courthouse park with flowers, and by 1890 his daughter Ella ran for Waverly postmistress — a horticultural village on the ground the ballpark and stores would later cover.

Polk's 1903 directory listed 'Colored School No. 115' at Merryman Lane near York Road (branch at Barclay near Merryman Lane) and the white 'School No. 51' separately nearby — segregated public education mapped block by block a short walk from the ballground, three decades before the 1937 HOLC map drew the same lines in color.

When the city extended its limits and renamed the old York Road 'Greenmount Avenue,' Waverly residents fought it, arguing the name was coined 'to boom the Greenmount Cemetery' and fearing 'the York road will be unknown.' The spine of the whole wedge had its very name contested — erasure by relabeling.

A Sun kitchen-column recipe submitted by Mrs. J. Merryman of 608 Homestead St., Waverly (blocks from the ballpark): a marble cake with a 'White Portion' (egg whites, white sugar) and a 'Dark Portion' (yolks, molasses, brown sugar), 'each part in turn in a cake pan' — two batters marbled in one tin but never blended, signed with the surname of the 1688 co-grantees of the wedge, a documented Baltimore County enslaving family. (Surname resonance; direct descent not established — the power is the echo.)

When Terrapin Park opened, the city met it with force: 75 officers under Capt. Moxley at the park, 50 more at Oriole Park across the corner, a uniformed man 'at practically every corner' out the York Road, and a mounted squad. Traffic was scripted — 'all vehicles must enter Twenty-ninth street from the York road and go on through to Guilford avenue.' From day one the wedge was a place the police surrounded, choreographed, and controlled.

Before the pennant and the fire, a vast wooden revival tabernacle for evangelist Billy Sunday stood at the wedge — York Road & 29th, the exact corner — drawing crowds past the streetcar barns, an 'Oriole Park' sign already visible in the background. Mass religion and mass transit on the same corner the ballpark, the boycott, and the fire would each claim in turn. The photo also confirms the York Rd→Greenmount / 10th→29th renaming.

A decade before the federal map, the Afro reported that in Waverly, 'where colored people have long lived, and built up churches,' white community associations were pressing Black residents to give up their homes and churches for the northwest section — while across town white residents blocked a Black congregation from buying a church. The private 'improvement-association' machinery the HOLC would later formalize in ink.

For 1937 booking agent Douglass O. Smith secured Oriole Park for the Elite Giants' night games, opening a park 'shut to colored teams for years.' Then it closed again: owner Tom Wilson wanted the park but balked at Smith's fee, and white residents complained to park officials about 'the noise and fanfare' of the night games. For 1938 the Elites were pushed to Bugle Field. The line was undone not by a rule but by a fee and a neighborhood's noise complaint — the same pretext used to evict the Elites for good in 1942.

The 1939 Elite Giants — with championship-series games played on this ground during the season — clinched the Negro National League title over the Homestead Grays. In the deciding game at Yankee Stadium, Sept 24, 1939, Jonas 'Lefty' Gaines shut out the Grays for seven innings and Baltimore won 2–0, taking the NNL championship and the Ruppert Cup — the best season in the franchise's Baltimore run, by a club shut out of the white ballpark's gate.

When Black world featherweight champion Chalky Wright defended his title at the park (stopping Baltimore's Harry Jeffra by TKO, Jun 19, 1942, before ~6,000), he carried a lineage: his grandfather, Caleb Baines Martin, was a runaway from a Natchez plantation who became a Buffalo Soldier and the first African-American ranch owner in southwest Arizona. The site's clearest world-championship night ran a bloodline from bondage to a title belt onto this ground.

Eighty-six years before the ballpark burned, another fire took the same corner. St. John's Episcopal — standing 'at the first toll-gate on the York road,' the exact spot where home plate would sit — was deliberately torched at 2 a.m.; the sacramental vessels stolen, the building gone before the companies arrived. 'The walls are of stone, and they are still good' — and the stone church survives today. Two fires, 86 years apart, on one tollgate corner (1858 arson; the July 4, 1944 ballpark blaze).

At Shiloh AME on E. 28th St., Richard L. Steiner of the Baltimore Redevelopment Commission told ~100 families they'd get 'a good price' for homes the city had claimed. The Waverly site — 17 acres bounded by Greenmount Ave., Reese St., 27th and 30th (taking in the ballpark parcel's own blocks) — was one of Baltimore's first two blighted-area clearance projects. Residents formed the interracial Waverly Area Association to protect themselves. The graded corridor 'cleared' acre by acre — the through-line from the 1937 map to the bulldozer.

A library due-date card from 'Young Actors' Workbook,' Roland Park Middle School: 'Tupac Shakur, class 8-15,' stamped Feb 20 & 27, 1985. Tupac spent his early years in Baltimore — Roland Park Middle, then the Baltimore School for the Arts, a short walk from the wedge — before the family left for California. Years before the voice, the artifact: a kid checking out an acting book a mile from the ballpark's ashes, the ground's Black-excellence lineage running from the Elite Giants and Chalky Wright into hip-hop's Baltimore roots.

The DHCD folder 'Waverly Harry's Facade + Logo' holds the program's most thorough work for a single merchant: about two dozen facade studies for Harry's Liquors at 3113 Greenmount Avenue, in pencil, ink and color, and about forty studies for a bottle-silhouette logo. The facade studies try a horizontal 'HARRY'S LIQUORS' sign band, an awning, a new storefront and brick, pebble or tile in place of the aluminum siding ('alum siding, would you like something better?' reads one note); staff planned color xeroxes with interchangeable parts so the owner could compare them. A page from a wine book showing bottle shapes was clipped in as reference for the logo. The owner was Alan (Allan) Orman, who sat on the 1976 merchants' steering committee and chaired the 1978 fall art show. A phone slip records his call asking for a list of contractors, a cost estimate from Bob Quilter and help with the storefront, and a note in the file carries figures of $8,500 and $6,000. Architect Steve Broache wrote to him enclosing a sheet on the city's REAL rehabilitation loan program and asking him to call Bob Klepper, who ran it. Design, contractor lists, cost estimates and loan referral were one service. The Harry's pages are undated; Broache's letter is on the 1976-77 All-America City letterhead and the related notes date from 1977, so the work was probably done in 1977-79. The one 1982 document in the folder, a sign proposal, belongs to the Golden Star Restaurant. A Harry's Liquors trades at the address today on an active licence, in a building whose retail lineage runs from Knoblock Brothers' grocery in the 1920s through leather goods by 1937 to liquor thereafter. The file documents the Harry.s Liquors name and its owner in the late 1970s, filling part of the gap before the continuous record that begins in 2013; the original Harry is still unidentified. City Archives BRG48-43-10-16, 85 scans.

The revitalization program resurfaced, striped, landscaped and lit the Waverly Shop & Park Lot at 3201 Barclay Street (Block 3881A, Lot 001), with design work in 1979-80 and construction in 1980-81, plus a dedicated expenditures file in 1980. The lot has a merchants' prehistory: a June 1958 'Park Free While You Shop' co-operative announcement listed some thirty-five participating stores and a new 32nd Street parking lot. The ground itself carries a buried history, having been the site of segregated Public School No. 115, in operation from 1889 until the 1950s and demolished in 1960. A deed recorded 30 November 1979 (WA 3844/396) falls inside the rebuild window and may record a city acquisition rather than an internal transfer. The lot remains city-owned and is operated today as the 'Waverly Lot.' Box 10 folders 24-26, 36; Box 10B folder 41. The 'Waverly Parking Lot' folder (BRG48-43-10-12) confirms the rebuild: Hurst-Rosche designed it in 1979, R. Marcantoni & Sons built it under Bureau of Highways Contract 2611 from June 19 to November 22, 1980, and the city accepted it on March 3, 1981.

The 32nd Street Farmers Market opened on 30 May 1980, conceived the previous year by a city housing employee who walked past the Waverly Shop & Park Lot while the revitalization program was rebuilding it. The market has operated continuously ever since, outlasting the Waverly Merchants Association, the urban renewal plan that authorised the lot's reconstruction, and every other institution involved in the 1976-1983 program. It is the most durable thing the Waverly System produced, and it was not in the plan.

George J. Bluso (1920-2009, buried Dulaney Valley Memorial Gardens, Timonium; wife Angelina 1924-2004) purchased 3223 Greenmount Avenue on 16 March 1977 and signed the July 1978 Waverly Merchants Association newsletter as president sixteen months later, announcing the city's commercial revitalization program and its capital schedule. He held the property into the 1990s. Newspaper research records a George J. Bluso of the same city with a 1953 gambling conviction (given as age 34, of the 5600 block Purdue Avenue), a September 1960 federal arrest for bookmaking without a federal gambling stamp, a May 1961 appearance in reporting on a case connected to an East Baltimore Street club (given as age 42, same Purdue Avenue address), a Baltimore Sun description in 1970 as 'a major gambling figure in the area' who served a year in 1964, and a reported federal decision vacating a wagering-tax conviction (Bluso v. United States, 375 F. Supp. 1085, D. Md. 1974). CAUTION: the two newspaper ages agree with each other at a birth of about 1918-19, while the memorial gives 1920; year-only memorial dates are frequently approximate, but the identification is NOT yet confirmed. The decisive test is the grantee clause of the 16 March 1977 deed (RHB 3457/824-830): if it names a grantee residing in the 5600 block of Purdue Avenue, the merchants' president and the gambling defendant are the same man.

Preservation documentation was not performed decades after the revitalization program as an unrelated exercise; it was intertwined with it. The Commission for Historical and Architectural Preservation's City of Baltimore Neighborhood Survey covered Waverly in 1977, surveyed by Michelle Belco, generating Maryland Inventory of Historic Properties forms in a wave running roughly B-2776 to B-2817, with the Greenmount corridor's forms at B-2785 through B-2791. The DHCD program kept its own 'Waverly Historic Survey 1977-1978' folder holding Maryland Historical Trust inventory forms for 3021-3031 Greenmount, the Waverly Town Hall (then the Northside Bar), the row from Harry's Liquors at 3113 to the firehouse, the 1902 Waverly firehouse, the Waverly Theatre (then a Goodwill store), the Boulevard Theatre, and a house in the 600 block of Homestead Street. It filed them with the July 1978 merchants' newsletter, and the Boulevard form records the community's petition against a Burger King in the theatre lobby. The buildings' architectural character was becoming part of the district's economic strategy thirty-six years before the National Register district was listed. City Archives BRG48-43-10-6, 28 scans.

The revitalization program's lending arm is documented on this block: in January 1980 the Mayor and City Council of Baltimore, through the Department of Housing and Community Development, lent the Adlers $67,000 against 3220 Greenmount Avenue as a city rehabilitation loan, mid-program. A comparable stack appears one block north in December 1981, where a $75,000 City of Baltimore / DHCD loan combined with a $125,000 SBA loan was expressly 'applied to the rehabilitation of properties known as Nos. 3202-05-07-09 Greenmount Avenue' for the retail tenant The Princess Shops. Together these establish that the Commercial Revitalization Division's public money was rebuilding Greenmount retail blocks, not merely drawing them.

Every HOLC zone at the Waverly four-corners - A1 (Guilford), B16, C9, D6, and the ballpark's own C4 - was appraised by the same man on the same day: Louis Kroner, property review appraiser, H.O.L.C., May 4, 1937. His sheets (verbatim, Mapping Inequality transcriptions) span a sevenfold income gradient across ~150 m: A1 "Executives, Professional men," income "Over $5,000," Negro "No," trend upward, favorable influence "Close to business area on Greenmount Ave."; D6 "Laborers," income "$700-1,000," "Negro: Yes, 35" (35% foreign-born), "Houses in very bad condition. Many alley properties"; remarks "Vandalism in this section" - and, as D6's listed FAVORABLE influence: "Near desirable properties." C4 (the Oriole Park V ground): population "Mixture," income $2,000, favorable "Goucher college located in the section. Desirable location," detrimental "Industrial plants. Continuing obsolescence of old property," trend static. The four-corners was not four judgments that collided; it was one administrative act - executed three weeks after the ballpark's Negro National League opening day (April 10, 1937).

The Waverly study Survey Influence section quantified the survey itself as a market intervention, in the year ending June 1, 1940: HOLC loans repaid in full nearly doubled; borrowers in default dropped by more than half; for-sale signs fell about 50 percent and for-rent signs over 90 percent; HOLC sales of foreclosed Waverly properties jumped from 24 percent (prior three years) to 57 percent in one year - while Maryland overall FELL from 37 to 34 percent. The measurement was the medicine. The same chapter found definite evidence of overzoning on Greenmount Avenue between Thirty-fifth and Forty-second Streets (also Old York Rd 34th-35th and 33rd St), and recorded early Master Plan wins: the old junk yard and unsightly frame tabernacle at the NW corner of Venable Ave and Old York Rd removed and the lot paved; the first of 12 planned interior play areas (block 3903-A) approved by the Park Commission at 1,286.25 dollars - an assessment of 36.75 dollars per property.

Polk's 1904 Laundries: "Sing Lee, 1116 York rd, 513 Bloom, 2705 Pa av, 1302 Edmondson av, 1442 Eastern av, 2829 O'Donnell and 1133 Greenm't av." Seven-store Chinese laundry chain; 1116 York Road is this building under its pre-renumbering address. Earliest documented commercial use of 3224 Greenmount. Also at 1116: Wm. A. Sanders, carpenter.

Polk's 1906: "Sam Lee, 616 s Bdway, 2108 Canton av, 1044 Greenm't av, 500 n Caroline, 2218 Fdk av, 1200 n Bond and 1116 York rd." Sam Lee has succeeded Sing Lee at this address between 1904 and 1906; 513 Bloom appears in both operators' chains, suggesting acquisition rather than coincidence. Resident: John C. Deckert, oiler.
Polk's 1909: "Sam Lee, 1116 York rd, 2218 Fdk av, 1103 Guilford av and 2707 Huntingdon av." Four locations. Resident at 1116: John C. Deckert, oiler (h = head of household).
Polk's 1912 Laundries: "Sam Lee. 513 Bloom, 2108 Fleet, 2208 Fdk av, 713 Light, 1116 York rd and 728 s Bdway." Last directory year this building is listed under its York Road number.

Polk's 1915: "Sam Lee laund 513 Bloom, 728 s Bdway, 201 s Chester, 2110 Fleet, 2218 Fdk av, 1044 and 3224 Greenmt av, 13 Patapsco av, 129 s Robinson." Nine stores. 1116 York Road has dropped out of the chain and 3224 Greenmount has appeared in its place — the business continuity that proves 3224 = 1116 York Rd across the renumbering. Resident: Mrs. Virginia Hickman (listed at 1114 York rd in 1909).

Polk's 1917: "Sam Lee laund 513 Bloom, 728 s Bdway, 900 w Fayette, 2110 Fleet, 2218 Fdk av, 245 n Gilmor, 1044 and 3224 Greenmt av, 13 e Patapsco av and 415 s Washington." Ten locations, the documented peak. Resident: J. Roger Swartz, clerk. Neighbours that year: Venable Building & Savings Assn at 3220, Garonzik at 3223. NOTE: the 1917 street guide still reads "GREENMOUNT AV ... 3101 31st n ... For continuation see York rd" while the alphabetical section already uses 3224 — the renumbering rolled through unevenly.

Polk's 1920 Laundries: "Sam Lee. 1044 Greenmt av, 513 and 522 Bloom, 900 w Fayette, 415 s Washington and 3224 Greenmt av." Six stores, down from ten in 1917. Residents above the shop: Mrs. Eureth Wheatley; Edward S. Pick, laborer (boarding). A second Chinese laundry on the block that year: Sing Lee at 3242 Greenmount.

3000–3200 blocks Greenmount Ave in 1915 — brick/frame footprints, uses, and street numbers. KEY FINDING: this sheet was drawn during the York Road to Greenmount renumbering and prints BOTH numbers on every building. East frontage reads 3200/1102 (saloon, triangular corner), 3204/1104 (store), 3220/1112 and 3222/1114 (dwellings, THREE stories), and 3224/1116 labelled "Chine Laundry" (two stories, storefront). This establishes that 3224 Greenmount Avenue was 1116 York Road, NOT 1112 York Road, and that the three-story dwelling at 1112 York Rd was still standing in 1915 at what is now 3220.

The arms-length 2013 sale that SDAT records; ANARM LLC holds until 2025.

Full-page "Waverly Park and Shop" cooperative advertisement listing member merchants with addresses in clean type. JASON SHOES, 3224 Greenmount Avenue. ANDERSON'S RESTAURANT, 3226 Greenmount Avenue. The two are separate businesses at separate addresses in the same list. This settles the address of Anderson's Restaurant, which the 3224 white paper (Rev.09, S14) places at 3224 on the strength of 1967 and 1968 clippings whose final digit is destroyed by a column-rule ink blot. There was no restaurant at 3224 in this period; the food-service precedent belongs to 3226, next door. Also listed on the block: Kibler's Jewelers 3222, White Coffee Pot 3200, Adler's House of Fashion 3240, Frank's Dunhills 3212, Charlie Der Laundry 421 E 33rd.

On the same page, the Frank-Dunhills advertisement is signed "Ted Frank & Len Frank" and gives the address 3212-14 Greenmount Avenue, phone BE. 5-7575. THEODORE FRANK and Sylvia Lee Frank bought 3224 Greenmount on Aug. 4, 1955 for $41,000 (MLP 9873/248) and the family held it until 2008. Ted is the ordinary diminutive of Theodore; same surname, same block-face, same years. So the 1955 buyer was not an outside investor but a Waverly men's-wear merchant six doors down the same side of the street, buying the storefront the Wyman estate was selling. Corroborating: the 1963 deed (JFC 1619/451) shows the Franks holding four corridor parcels (3224 and 2950 Greenmount, 2737 and 2745 Maryland Ave), and their holding company was named "Fransue Properties, Inc." LIKELY BUT NOT PROVEN: test with the SDAT charter record for Frank-Dunhills.

George T. Drechsler and Anna E. Drechsler his wife convey to WILLIAM F. LUDWIG and MARY L. LUDWIG his wife, for SEVEN HUNDRED DOLLARS, three lots, of which the SECOND is this parcel: "on the west side of the York Turnpike Road distant northerly one hundred and eighty one feet from the intersection of the northeast side of Merrymans Lane ... thence along said alley and parallel with said Road northerly sixteen feet." The other two lots are on Amity Street in west Baltimore. Ludwig holds 3224 for twenty years, until the 1918 sale to Gee Quong. The deed recites the David Stewart to Sarah E. Sinclair sublease of 1 February 1888, Baltimore COUNTY Liber J.W.S. No. 167 folio 402, as the southern boundary — the same recital that runs unbroken to 1978, eighty years.

THE INSTRUMENT THE WHITE PAPER MISCITES. Rev.09 cites this conveyance as MSA CE 168-13931 pp.00020-22, which is a 1978 deed. The real citation is Liber S.C.L. No. 3217, folio 44 (MSA CE 168-3225), dated 1 June 1918 and recorded 5 June 1918. William F. Ludwig and Mary L. Ludwig his wife convey, for $5 and other considerations, "unto GEE QUONG and GEE QU YING their personal representatives and assigns all that lot of ground in Baltimore City KNOWN AS 3224 GREENMOUNT AVENUE." TWO findings: (1) there were TWO Chinese grantees — the Baltimore Sun of 6 June 1918 printed "William F. Ludwig and wife to George Quong, etc." and the "etc." was a second named person, GEE QU YING, who has never appeared in any account of this building; the records also spell the first grantee Gee Quong, not George. (2) The deed itself says "known as 3224 Greenmount Avenue" in June 1918, so the Greenmount number was in official land-record use by then. Description: 181 feet northerly from Merrymans Lane, thence NORTHERLY sixteen feet, 100 feet deep to a 3-foot alley, bounded south by the 1888 Stewart to Sinclair sublease lot.

Lester S. Levy, Henry E. Wyman, Reuben and Selma L. Oppenheimer, Lester S. Levy as Trustee, and — newly named — ELEANOR K. LEVY and CARRIE K. WYMAN, mortgage the property to PENN MUTUAL LIFE INSURANCE CO OF PENNSYLVANIA. "Ws Greenmount 181 N Merrymans La, 16 x irreg." Carrie K. Wyman is the same person who appears in 1949 as Committee of the Estate of Stella E. Wyman. Found in the Block Book index; the instrument itself is not yet pulled.

The Baltimore City Block Books (MSA CE 9) index every recorded instrument by block. Volume MSA CE 9-651 covers 1936-1942; references to Block 3882 begin on p.83. The complete 1941 record for this parcel is two instruments: the 17 February deed (MLP 6129/439) and the 7 April Penn Mutual mortgage (MLP 6140/545). There is NO lease. The index demonstrably does carry leases — the same pages show "Rental Lease, Waverly Corporation to F W Woolworth Co of N Y" (11 Apr 1938, MLP 5813/143) and an "Asst Lease" for 3218 Greenmount (5 Jul 1938, MLP 5836/383). A five-year shop lease of this period was normally not recorded, and this one was not. Any description of a "recorded 1941 five-year lease" at 3224 is unsupported.

3224 and 3222 both begin 181 feet north of Merrymans Lane and run in OPPOSITE directions. The Block Book entries make it explicit: the 1918 Ludwig to Gee Quong deed reads "W 100 x N 16" while the Burnham parcel reads "W 100 x S 16" in 1915, 1916 and 1920. They are adjacent lots sharing a boundary at the 181-foot mark, and the modern index remarks simply dropped the N/S. With 3220 at "165 N Merrymans, S 21 1/2," the block face resolves with no overlap and no gap: 3220 = 143.5-165 ft, 3222 = 165-181 ft, 3224 = 181-197 ft. This confirms the 1116 York Road identification by metes and bounds, independently of the Sanborn plate. The 3222 chain also surfaces here: Eben B. Hunting releases to William D. and Annie Burnham and Virginia Hickman (Aug 1915), and on 3 June 1920 the Burnhams assign to RAYMOND B. and EMMA L. KIBLER (SCL 3596/17) — Kibler's Jewelers is still at 3222 in the 1958 Evening Sun ad. The white paper's Burnham family sources belong to 3222, and the Burnhams owned it as well as lived in it.

Block Book MSA CE 9-417, Block 3882, p.91: "February 2 — Gee Qu Ying to Gee Quong — Asst — Ws York Rd 181 N Merrymans La W 100 x N 16 — SCL 3965/93." This answers the question the 1918 deed opened: the property was bought by TWO Chinese grantees in 1918, and Gee Qu Ying assigned their interest to Gee Quong on 2 February 1923, which is why every later recital names Gee Quong alone. Same day, Gee Quong and a third name, GEE OTT, mortgaged the lot to the American National Building & Loan Association; that mortgage was released in April 1923 (SCL 3898/621). Gee Ott is unidentified.

READ IN FULL. Helen S. Ridgely, unmarried, conveys to DEA BING YOUNG "his heirs and assigns IN FEE SIMPLE," for $5 and other valuable considerations, together with "the reversion thereof and especially the clear and separate annual rent issuing and payable thereout," and expressly "TO HAVE AND TO HOLD ... TO THE END AND INTENT THAT THE LEASEHOLD ESTATE MAY BE MERGED IN THE FEE AND THE AFORESAID ANNUAL RENT FOREVER EXTINGUISHED." The deed recites both halves: the 1890 Legg-to-Drechsler ground lease that created the $48 rent, the 1896 conveyance vesting the reversion in Ridgely, and "THE leasehold title to said property having been acquired by the said Dea Bing Young by deed dated December 26th and recorded ... in Liber S C L No 4317 folio 338 from Dea Shue Hong." Recorded 8 October 1926 at 2:30 PM, Stephen C. Little, Clerk. Notarised in Prince George's County; witness Elizabeth H. S. Boss; notary Sylvia Caplan. A Chinese laundry proprietor bought the freehold reversion from one of Maryland's oldest landed families and extinguished a ground rent that had run since 1890.

"MRS. EISEMAN GETS $40,000 FROM ESTATE." The will of GERSON EISEMAN, of the firm of EISEMAN BROTHERS, filed for probate. Bequests to the Hebrew Benevolent Society, the Hebrew Hospital and Asylum Association and the Hebrew Orphan Asylum. Widow Rosa Eiseman takes $40,000 in cash plus the personal property. "The residue of the estate is left in trust to Mrs. Eiseman and Mr. Eiseman's three sons-in-law, ISAAC S. HESS, MAURICE WYMAN and SYDNEY STRAUSS, for the benefit of Mrs. Eiseman. At her death the estate is to be divided among the children, SELMA E. HESS, STELLA E. WYMAN and ERNESTINE E. STRAUSS." Will dated 10 June 1912. So Stella E. Wyman, who held a one-third interest in 3224 Greenmount from 1941 and whose estate sold it in 1955, was a daughter of Gerson Eiseman and an heir to the Eiseman Brothers fortune. Reasonable inference, not proven: Eiseman capital is what stood behind the 1941 purchase.

"MAURICE WYMAN, SHOE DEALER, DIES." Maurice Wyman, shoe merchant, died 20 October 1927 aged 64 at the Emersonian Apartments, Eutaw Place and Park Drive, after a six-year illness; apoplexy. "Mr. Wyman ... had conducted a store at 19 WEST LEXINGTON STREET since January 1, 1891, and, in addition, for the last few years had operated a branch store at 111 East Baltimore street." Born in Alexandria, Va.; came to Baltimore as a boy; began at Posner's Department Store and became buyer in the shoe department; left late in 1900 to take over the business of J. Pels & Son at the Lexington Street address "now occupied by the Wyman store." Buried Baltimore Hebrew Cemetery. "Mr. Wyman is survived by his widow, MRS. STELLA E. WYMAN; a son, HENRY E. WYMAN, and three brothers, Julius, Simon and Samuel Wyman. Mrs. Wyman was Miss Stella E. Eiseman." THIS CLOSES THE WYMAN QUESTION. 19 West Lexington Street is location 1 in the white paper's own 1941 Wyman Young Moderns advertisement (S103) and the "Wyman LEXINGTON STREET" of the 1950 shoe advertisement (S104). Stella E. Wyman and Henry E. Wyman are the same two people who took one-third interests in 3224 Greenmount in the February 1941 deed (MLP 6129/439). So the family that owned a third of the building IS the family that founded and ran Wyman Shoe Co., the tenant. The paper's ca.1935-1955 tenancy and the 1941-1955 ownership are one family, and both ended in the same month of 1955.

Death notice, verbatim: "FRIEDLAND. On January 10, 1957, BELLE (nee Frank) beloved wife of the late Harry Friedland of 301 Eighty-sixth street, Miami Beach, Fla., mother of Janet Sue Friedland, DAUGHTER OF EVA AND THE LATE EPHRAIM FRANK and SISTER OF THEODORE AND LEONARD FRANK and the late Charles B. Frank. Services at the Jack Lewis Home, 2100-02 Eutaw place, on Sunday precisely at 11 A.M. Interment B'nai Jacob Lodge Cemetery, Herring Run." This closes the Frank identification the same way the Maurice Wyman obituary closed the Wyman one. Ephraim and Eva Frank held 3212-3214 Greenmount from 1923; the Frank-Dunhills advertisement in the Evening Sun of 11 June 1958 is signed "Ted Frank & Len Frank" at 3212-14 Greenmount; and THEODORE FRANK bought 3224 Greenmount on 4 August 1955 for $41,000 (MLP 9873/248). Theodore and Leonard are Ephraim and Eva's sons. So the 1955 purchase of 3224 was a second-generation Waverly merchant family buying the storefront six doors from the store their parents had held for thirty-two years. Four siblings named: Belle (Friedland), Theodore, Leonard, and Charles B. Frank (deceased by 1957). The family buried at B'nai Jacob Lodge Cemetery. Notice ran in the Sun 11, 12 and 13 January and the Evening Sun 11 and 12 January 1957.

Block Book MSA CE 9-417, Block 3882, p.92, 1923 section, read at 200 dpi from the scan: "Frank, Ephraim to Charles D. Harris, asst, 3212-3214 Greenmount ave, 4121/573" and "Harris, Charles D. to Ephraim / Eva Frank, asst, 3212-3214 Greenmount ave, 4121/574." A same-day straw conveyance through Charles D. Harris to vest the property in EPHRAIM AND EVA FRANK jointly, the tenancy-by-entireties device the family used again in 1983 through Lee Klavans. CORRECTS AN EARLIER STATEMENT IN THIS RECORD: the Franks held 3212-3214 from 1923, not from 1937. The 1937 instruments are later refinancing, not the acquisition. 3212-14 is the Frank-Dunhills address, so the family was established on this block THIRTY-TWO YEARS before Theodore Frank bought 3224 in 1955.

"O.E.S., Kerchoff Ray Chapter, No. 90 - Tuesday, 8 P.M., meeting at Odd Fellows Hall. Initiation of new members. MRS. SYLVIA LEE FRANK, worthy matron." Sylvia Lee Frank was the presiding officer of an Order of the Eastern Star chapter three years before she and Theodore Frank bought 3224 Greenmount. Fills out the civic standing of the family that held this building from 1955 to 2008.

"FRANK, Sylvia Lee. On September 3, 2001, SYLVIA LEE FRANK (nee HYMAN), mother of FRANCES F. KATZ of Owings Mills, MD and SUE SCHWARTZ of Silver Spring, MD, mother-in-law of Robert H. Katz and Sidney L. Schwartz, sister of Henry H. Hyman (Ethel), grandmother of Cheryl L. Katz, Debra Sapcariu (Val), Jeffrey Schwartz (Jamie McElrath), Barry Schwartz (Jennifer) and Lauren Kaufman (Jason), great-grandmother of Sara Kaufman. Funeral Services and Interment at Beth Tfiloh Congregation Cemetery." THREE CONSEQUENCES. (1) CORRECTS AN EARLIER INFERENCE IN THIS RECORD: I had read the change from Sylvia Lee Frank (1955, 1978 deeds) to Mildred A. Frank (1983 deed) as remarriage after Sylvia's death. Sylvia died in 2001, not before 1983, so that reading is wrong. Divorce and remarriage is now the leading explanation, supported by the obituary's conspicuous omission of any "wife of" or "widow of" formula, but two Theodore Franks remains possible. The two 1983 Klavans deeds, Book 146 pp.730-731 and 732-735, would settle it. (2) CONFIRMS THE DAUGHTERS: Frances F. Katz and Sue Schwartz are the two remaindermen named in the 1978 deed as "Frances F. Katz and Harriet F. Schwartz" and in the 2008 land record as "SCHWARTZ, HARRIET S" - so Harriet Sue Schwartz went by Sue. (3) EXPLAINS FRANSUE PROPERTIES: the Franks' holding company, incorporated by 1959, is FRAN plus SUE, named for their two daughters Frances and Sue. Not Frank plus Sue. Sylvia's maiden name was Hyman.

READ IN FULL. SEB 146/730 (MSA CE 164-146). $5, "there being no actual consideration for this transaction"; transfer tax not required. Theodore Frank, "in exercise of the powers conferred upon him in the Deed hereinafter mentioned," conveys to LEE KLAVANS in fee simple. Recites: "BEING the same lot of ground which by Deed dated April 13, 1978, and recorded ... in Liber R.H.B. No. 3611, folio 20, was granted and conveyed by THEODORE FRANK AND WIFE unto the grantor herein, FOR AND DURING HIS NATURAL LIFE, WITH POWERS OF DISPOSITION." And: "It is the intention of the said grantor herein to execute these presents in exercise of the powers conferred upon him in the aforesaid Deed and convey the entire fee simple interest, INCLUDING THE REMAINDER, unto the party of the second part herein." SETTLES THE TWO-THEODORES QUESTION: there is ONE Theodore Frank. This deed identifies its own grantor as the life tenant created by the 1978 instrument, so the man who bought in 1955, granted himself the life estate in 1978, and re-took with Mildred in 1983 are the same person. Signed by Theodore Frank alone; witness Timothy J. Higgins; notary Lois L. Airey; recorded 1 December 1983, Saundra E. Banes, Clerk. Attorneys Edelstein & Stahl, P.A., 233 St. Paul Place.

READ IN FULL. SEB 146/732-735. Lee Klavans conveys to "THEODORE FRANK and MILDRED A. FRANK, HIS WIFE ... joint parties of the second part," for and during their natural lives, with full powers to sell, mortgage, lease or convey the whole fee (except by will). Then the remainder, verbatim: "...then unto and to the use of MILDRED A. FRANK, FOR AND DURING HER NATURAL LIFE OR SO LONG AS SHE SHALL REMAIN UNMARRIED AFTER THE DEATH OF THEODORE FRANK, and immediately after the death or remarriage of the said Mildred A. Frank, then unto FRANCES F. KATZ and HARRIET F. SCHWARTZ, their personal representatives and assigns, IN FEE SIMPLE FOREVER." TWO FINDINGS. (1) DIVORCE, NOT DEATH: Mildred is called Theodore's WIFE in December 1983 while Sylvia Lee Frank was still living (she died 3 September 2001), so Theodore and Sylvia divorced between April 1978 and December 1983. (2) THE DAUGHTERS' REMAINDER WAS NOT EXTINGUISHED, IT WAS RE-CREATED behind a second-wife life estate with the classic until-remarriage limitation. That is why Frances F. Katz and Harriet S. Schwartz are back on title in June 2008 (10788/504): Theodore died, then Mildred died or remarried, and the remainder fell in. The whole Frank arc is one estate plan running fifty-three years: buy 1955, life estate with remainder to the daughters 1978, restructure for the second wife in 1983 with the daughters preserved behind her, daughters take 2008.

Recited in the 1888 sublease: "a lease from W. HALL HARRIS and wife to JAMES E. SINCLAIR dated June 11th 1884 A.D. and recorded among the land records of Baltimore County in Liber W.M.I. No. 141, folio 407." Two lots, whose whole area the four 1888 lots cover. Ground rents of $80 and $80.84, payable 11 June and 11 December, redeemable at six per cent on and after 11 June 1889. This is now the earliest known instrument touching 3224 Greenmount, and it puts James E. Sinclair on this ground from 1884. Not yet pulled.

Recited in the 1888 sublease: the four lots "having been conveyed and assigned subject to said Lease by SARAH E. and JAMES E. SINCLAIR to DAVID STEWART by writing dated on or about January 3rd A.D. 1888 and duly recorded among the land records of Baltimore County prior hereto." Four weeks before Stewart leased them straight back. Not yet pulled; the recital gives no liber. Update Oct. 14, 2026: not at J.W.S. 167/397 to 401 (768:negative-jws167-397-401-no-sinclair-stewart-assignment).

Baltimore County Liber J.W.S. No. 167, folio 402 (MSA CE 62-167), read in full. "This Sub-Lease made this first day of February A.D. 1888 by DAVID STEWART of Baltimore City of the first part to SARAH E. SINCLAIR and JAMES E. SINCLAIR her husband, of Baltimore County, of the second part ... does hereby lease unto the said Sarah E. Sinclair ... ALL THOSE FOUR LOTS of ground lying in Baltimore County on the west side of the York Turnpike Road north of Merryman's Lane." The four lots, measured from Merryman's Lane: FIRST 132 ft 8 in, running north 12 ft (about 3218); SECOND 144 ft 8 in, north 20 ft, through the centre of a partition wall (about 3220); THIRD 164 ft 8 in (3222); and FOURTH, verbatim: "Beginning for the fourth thereof at a point on the west side of the York Turnpike Road distant NORTHERLY ONE HUNDRED AND EIGHTY ONE FEET from the intersection of the northeast side of Merryman's Lane ... and along the northern boundary of the lot thirdly above described one hundred feet to an alley three feet wide ... NORTHERLY SIXTEEN FEET ..." THAT IS 3224 GREENMOUNT, word for word the description carried in every deed for this parcel from 1890 to 1978. SO 3224 WAS THE FOURTH LOT IN THE SINCLAIR SUBLEASE. This reverses the Round 0 finding that the Sinclair material is only block context: it is this parcel's own chain of title. What was wrong was the street number, not the connection. The deed also recites that the four lots cover the whole area of the two lots in the 1884 W. Hall Harris to James E. Sinclair lease, that the Sinclairs had assigned them to Stewart on 3 January 1888, and that lots first and second carry an $80 annual rent while lots thirdly and fourthly carry $80.84, payable 11 June and 11 December, redeemable at six per cent from 11 June 1889.

Recited on the face of the 1890 lease: "For title see deed in fee from DAVID STEWART AND WIFE to the said John N. C. Legg dated the 23rd day of April A.D. 1890 and duly recorded at or before the sealing and delivery hereof." Stewart conveyed the fee one day before Legg created the ground rent. This is the hinge between the Sinclair era and the ground-rent era, and it ties 3224 directly to David Stewart as owner rather than as a neighbouring reference. Not yet pulled; the recital gives no liber. Update Oct. 14, 2026: not at J.B. 1289/563 to 567 (768:negative-jb1289-563-567-no-stewart-legg-deeds); probably in J.B. 1299 before folio 406, beside the Drechsler lease (an inference). Update Oct. 14, 2026: not at J.B. 1299/398 to 405 either (768:negative-jb1299-398-405-no-stewart-legg-deeds); next, the City grantor index under Stewart, David, April to June 1890.

Baltimore City Liber J.B. No. 1299, folio 406 (MSA CE 168-1307), read in full. NOTE THE CITATION CORRECTION: the 1926 Ridgely deed cites this as "J B No 129 folio 406," dropping a digit; the true liber is 1299, which is why it would not resolve. The 1896 deed gives it correctly. "This Lease made this twenty fourth day of April in the year one thousand eight hundred and ninety between JOHN N. C. LEGG of Baltimore City of the first part and GEORGE T. DRECHSLER of the same place of the other part" — note N. C., not the H. C. the 1926 typist wrote. Same metes and bounds: 181 feet northerly from Merryman's Lane, north sixteen feet, 100 feet to the three-foot alley, bounded south by "the lot thirdly described in a Sub-lease dated the first day of February 1888 ... in Liber J.W.S. No. 167 folio 402 &c from David Stewart to Sarah E. Sinclair." So the recital that runs through every later deed to 1978 originates here, in 1890 — an unbroken chain of the same sentence for eighty-eight years.

Baltimore City Liber J.B. 1289, folios 565-566 (MSA CE 168-1297), read in full. Deed dated April 24, 1890, recorded April 26, 1890 at 3:30 p.m. (Jas Bond, Clerk): John H. C. Legg (so written in the margin, body, signature line and acknowledgment) conveys to Helen Stewart Ridgely, wife of John Ridgely of Hampton, Baltimore County, for $800, the reversion in fee of the lot on the west side of the York Turnpike Road beginning 181 feet north of Merryman's Lane and running north 16 feet by east 100 feet, 'especially the right to collect the aforesaid ground rent', being the lot leased by Legg to George T. Drechsler by deed dated April 24, 1890 (J.B. 1299/406), creating an annual ground rent of $48 payable May and November 1st. Its title recital cites the two deeds David Stewart and wife to Legg of April 23, 1890, 'recorded prior hereto'. Witness Robert A. Thursby, J.P. So on the same day Legg created the ground rent and sold the reversion. The 1896 deed (R.O. 1617/161) recites this deed at 1289/565. Legg's initials are H. C. here and N. C. on the lease (J.B. 1299/406); settle them from the 1890 grantor index.

Baltimore City Liber R.O. No. 1617, folio 161 (MSA CE 168-1625), read in full. "This Deed made this twenty ninth day of April A.D. 1896 by HELEN S. RIDGELY and JOHN RIDGELY OF H. her husband to HELEN S. RIDGELY THEIR DAUGHTER ... in consideration of $800." CORRECTS AN EARLIER READING IN THIS RECORD: this is not a husband-and-wife-to-wife conveyance but parents to daughter, so there are TWO Helen S. Ridgelys. The deed conveys the lot "in the annexed district" together with "especially the right to collect the annual rent of $48 payable May and November issuing out of said lot and created by said lease," and gives the correct citations for both 1890 instruments: the Legg to Drechsler lease at J.B. 1299 folio 406 and the reversion at J.B. 1289 folio 565. Witness Anthony S. Bonn, Justice of the Peace; recorded 5 May 1896 at 10:45 a.m. per Robt Ogle, Clerk — the clerk whose initials give the RO series.

Baltimore Sun, 17 October 1904, p.12, in a year-end list of fatal burn cases: "July 7 - MRS. SALLIE SANDERS, 1116 York road, horribly burned, presumably as the result of filling a lighted stove at the home of her mother, Mrs. Thomas Dowery, 103 Reese street, Waverly; died two days later." 1116 York Road is 3224 Greenmount. The 1904 Polk puts "Sanders Wm A. carp. 1116 York rd" at this address, so Sallie was almost certainly the wife of William A. Sanders, carpenter. She died 9 July 1904. This is the earliest named death connected to the building, and it places a family upstairs in the same year Sing Lee's laundry was working the ground floor. Her mother lived at 103 Reese Street in Waverly.

"WOMAN to wash and iron for laundry. CHAS. DIER, 3224 Greenmount ave." A previously unknown workforce advertisement, and it names an operator the record did not have. October 1926 is the same month Dea Bing Young took the fee reversion (deed 20 Sep, recorded 8 Oct 1926), so Dier was running or managing the laundry at the moment the ground rent was extinguished. NOTE: the surname could be an OCR-adjacent reading of a name in the Dea family, but the print reads DIER. The ad sits in a column of situations-wanted notices from Black women - "WOMAN (COLORED), WORK AT HOME"; "WOMAN (colored) wants half-time place"; "WOMAN (COLORED), PART TIME WORK, ANY KIND"; "WOMAN (colored) desires steady position, working daily" - which is the labour market this hiring sat inside.

"GIRL (colored), experienced ironer in laundry. 3224 GREENMOUNT AVENUE." The white paper holds this as a single Evening Sun advertisement of 13 April 1937 (S09). It ran far wider: Evening Sun 13 and 14 April, and Baltimore Sun 14, 15 and 16 April 1937. Five insertions over four days in both city dailies. A campaign of that size for one ironer's position indicates either urgent need or high turnover, and it is much stronger evidence of an operating workforce than a single notice.

"GIRL (colored) to work in laundry. Apply 3224 Greenmount ave." A previously unknown 1937 advertisement, sitting between the April campaign and the 10 August notice the paper already holds. So 3224 was hiring laundry workers in at least three separate rounds in 1937 alone: April, June and August. On the same page: "GIRL (colored), work in laundry. 3312 Ayrdale ave."; "GIRL (colored) to work in a Chinese laundry; experienced. 3633 Park Heights avenue"; "HAND IRONERS and press operators (colored). SANITARY LAUNDRY, 501 E. Preston." The trade was a recognised category of Black women's employment in Baltimore, advertised as such.

Consolidated from the advertisements. The people who worked inside 3224 Greenmount are recoverable, and they were overwhelmingly Black women. Documented hiring rounds: JANUARY 1921, four insertions across both dailies over two days - "COLORED Woman to Wash and Iron. Apply SAM LEE LAUNDRY, 3224 Greenmount ave." phone Madison 6853 (Evening Sun 12 and 13 Jan, Baltimore Sun 12 and 13 Jan). OCTOBER 1926 - "WOMAN to wash and iron for laundry. CHAS. DIER, 3224 Greenmount ave." APRIL 1937, five insertions over four days in both papers - "GIRL (colored), experienced ironer in laundry." JUNE 1937 - "GIRL (colored) to work in laundry." AUGUST 1937 - "GIRL (colored) to work in laundry." That is at least eleven separate insertions across five hiring rounds spanning sixteen years. None of the women is named; Baltimore employers did not name them. But the trade, the race, the sex and the address are all on the record, repeatedly, in the employers' own words. NEGATIVE FINDING WORTH STATING: none of these advertisements appears in the Baltimore Afro-American. Employers placed them in the Sun and the Evening Sun, the white dailies, which is itself a fact about how this labour market was organised.

Baltimore Sun, 26 May 1891, p.2: "JONES. - On May 25, 1891, at the residence of her grandson, GEORGE DRECHSLER, No. 1116 York road, Waverly, MARY M. JONES, in the 78th year of her age. The funeral will take place Wednesday afternoon, May 27, at two o'clock." Ran again 27 May. This is the earliest human record at 3224 Greenmount, thirteen years before the Sallie Sanders death. It also establishes that GEORGE T. DRECHSLER LIVED IN THE BUILDING: he took the 99-year lease from John N. C. Legg on 24 April 1890, and by May 1891 was in residence with his grandmother, who was born about 1813. He was not an absentee ground-rent speculator.

Baltimore Sun, 19 April 1893, p.4: "DRECHSLER. - On April 18, 1893, after a brief illness, ERNA MARIE, youngest daughter of GEORGE T. and A. ESTELLE DRECHSLER. Her funeral will take place from the residence of her parents, No. 1116 York road, Waverly, on this (Wednesday) afternoon, April 19, at two o'clock." Confirms the Drechslers were a resident family, not merely leaseholders, and gives the wife's name: A. Estelle, the "Anna E. Drechsler" who signs the 1898 deed to Ludwig. The family lost a grandmother here in 1891 and a daughter in 1893.

Baltimore Sun, 11 July 1893, p.3, an advertisement placed from this address: "STORE AND DWELLING, on line of electric road, good opening for a Confectionery and Notion Store; county taxes, city water, &c.; 16x100; g. r. $48. [and a second property at] 203 Clinton, (Canton,) STORE and DWELLING, now occupied by a saloon; 19.2x100 feet; ground rent $28. Address 1116 YORK ROAD, Waverly." THIS IS THE EARLIEST DESCRIPTION OF THE BUILDING'S FORM, and it matches this parcel on every measurable point: 16 by 100 feet, ground rent $48, on the electric streetcar line, at 1116 York Road. FOUR CONSEQUENCES. (1) The building was a STORE WITH A DWELLING ABOVE in 1893 - the second floor was residential from the start, which bears directly on the Upper Front Room and the second-floor occupancy question. (2) It independently confirms the 16x100 lot and the $48 ground rent created by the 1890 Legg-to-Drechsler lease. (3) IT COMPLICATES THE ca. 1910 CONSTRUCTION DATE: a store-and-dwelling of exactly these dimensions with exactly this ground rent stood on this lot in July 1893, and the Drechsler family had been living in it since at least May 1891. That does not prove the current building is the 1891 one, but any construction-date claim must now account for a documented building here eighteen years earlier. (4) Drechsler was trying to let or sell it three years after taking the lease.

Same $48 ground rent and the same 'w.s. York road turnpike, nr. Merryman's lane' description as the April 1923 and December 1924 entries.

The April 1923 sale of this parcel, reported in the Sun's real-estate transfer column. The December 1924 conveyance of this parcel to Dea Bing Young, who would hold it until 1941. Again identified only as 'YORK, w.s., nr. Merryman' with the $48 ground rent — a decade after the street was renamed Greenmount Avenue.

Sinclair conveys the ground in fee to Alice P. Harris, wife of W. Hall Harris. Recorded 11 June 1884 at 4:00 p.m., the same day as the lease-back below. Title recited from Elizabeth Huff (E.H.A. 74/321), Thomas J. Wilson and others (J.B. 84/387), and Oliver P. Merryman. Update Oct. 14, 2026: two of its three sources are read: Huff to Sinclair, Mar. 6, 1872, $2,500, a 'Huntington' leasehold at the fork, 10 perches on the road, from Andrew Brown (1866) (768:mdlr-eha74-321-huff-sinclair-huntington-1872); and the Wilson trustees to Sinclair, Oct. 24, 1873, $800, the reversion of the Oct. 1, 1872 lease (E.H.A. 77/361), a lot 44 1/2 ft on the turnpike just north of 'Brown's lot' (768:mdlr-jb84-387-wilson-trustees-sinclair-reversion-1873). 3224 probably lies in the Wilson lot. The Merryman deed is still unfound. Update Oct. 14, 2026: a lead for the unfound Merryman deed: John Litzinger's 1866 lease to John H. White (737:mdlr-jhl48-502-litzinger-white-lease-1866) recites land between the turnpike and the Old York Road that a P. Merryman (the first name reads like 'Olivr', probably Oliver) and wife deeded Litzinger on June 27, 1865 (J.H.L. 46/149). Whether that is the Merryman deed recited here is not shown. Update Oct. 14, 2026: the 1865 Oliver P. Merryman deed is read (737:mdlr-jhl46-149-oliver-merryman-litzinger-brown-lease-fee-1865): it is a different parcel (the Jesse Brown lease ground, from Charles R. Carroll, 1859), so it is not the deed this 1884 deed recites, but it shows Oliver P. Merryman held Carroll reversions on the turnpike. Update Oct. 14, 2026: Oliver P. Merryman bought the reversion of the whole 11-acre Jesse Brown lease from Charles R. Carroll in 1859 (768:mdlr-ghc27-45-charles-carroll-oliver-merryman-brown-lease-reversion-1859), and the 1801 Brown-to-Wheetley and 1811 Whitely-to-Wilson assignments filed here are parts of that lease: so the 'deed from Oliver P. Merryman' this 1884 deed recites is very probably his conveyance of the reversion of Sinclair's part (inference).

The oldest instrument in this parcel's chain, read in full for the first time. W. Hall Harris — PROVEN to be William Hall Harris (1852-1938), President of the Maryland Historical Society 1920-1935 — and his wife Alice P. (Patterson) Harris lease three lots on the westernmost side of the York turnpike road back to Sinclair the same day she took the fee. 3224 lies in the northern half of the second lot (164 ft 8 in to 197 ft). The descriptions run off party walls, proving houses already stood on this block face in June 1884. Update Oct. 17, 2026 (R.O. 1661, R.O. 1715 and S.C.L. 2610/548 read): the lease had a third lot. R.O. 1715/35 (Jan. 18, 1898; 768:mdlr-ro1715-35-harris-alice-gerry-stewart-third-lot-1898) recites 'the same lot of ground thirdly described in a lease from W. Hall Harris and Alice P. Harris his wife to James E. Sinclair dated June 11, 1884 ... W.M.I. No 141 folio 407', 'creating a redeemable ground rent of one hundred and fifty dollars ($150.) per annum': 60 ft of frontage from 36 ft 1/2 in to 96 ft 1/2 in north of Merryman's Lane, the lot just north of the apex. The first two lots are 3224's; the $150 rent would be on folio 409, which is not on disk. The Harrises sold the fee in the third lot to Alice Gerry Stewart for $2,500 on Jan. 18, 1898. Update Oct. 17, 2026 (end of the lease): folios 409 and 410 are read (768:mdlr-wmi141-409-410-harris-sinclair-lease-last-folios-1884): rents $80, $80.84 and $150, each lot liable for its own rent only, redeemable after five years at six per cent, renewable forever, recorded June 11, 1884 at 4:10 P.M.

The Waverly Main Street Historic District nomination's building inventory records that a storefront originally addressed 3212 Greenmount Avenue (part of the building now combined with 3210 and 3214) was occupied by a Men's Furnishings shop operated by Eva Frank in both the 1928 and 1937 city directories — 33 years before Eva Frank and her husband acquired the building outright by deed in 1961.

The NRHP nomination's building inventory records 3222 Greenmount Avenue's historical use — per city directories — as William Wiley's jewelry shop in 1928 and later Raymond Kibler's jewelry shop in 1937. The NRHP nomination's building inventory for the four-story Second Empire building at 3204-06 Greenmount (now Magic Menswear) records that the portion addressed 3206 Greenmount Avenue was a candy company in 1928 and later John Brandau's Men's Furnishings shop in 1937.
