Louis Stoler assigned his interest in the west-side Greenmount lot 62.5 ft north of Merryman's Lane (a 15'6" wide storefront lot -- the future 3208 Greenmount) to Sam Stoler on July 19, 1922, who simultaneously mortgaged it to the Waverly Building & Loan Association of Baltimore County. Nine days later, on July 28, both the Reliance Loan & Savings Association and the American Savings & Loan Association released their own prior mortgages on the same lot to Louis Stoler, clearing the way for the transfer.

Henrietta B. Condon conveyed the west-side York Road lot 77.5 ft north of Merryman's Lane (a 13-ft-wide storefront lot -- the future 3210 Greenmount) to Ernest J. Condon by deed dated October 23, 1922 -- 40 years before Ernest J. and Erna F. Condon sold the same building in 1962 (already on file).

Gee Zu Ying, Gee Quong, and Gee Ott assigned their interest in the west-side York Road lot 181 ft north of Merryman's Lane to Gee Quong, who simultaneously mortgaged it to the American National Building & Loan Association, on February 2, 1923 -- roughly a year before Raymond and Emma Kibler appear in an ownership position at the identical address (below). The exact relationship between the two families' tenure (sale vs. release of a prior interest) is not established from this entry alone.

Raymond B. and Emma L. Kibler received a mortgage release from the Locust Point Building & Loan Association No. 2 and simultaneously took a new mortgage from Ella B. Heckman on the west-side York Road lot 181 ft north of Merryman's Lane -- the future 3222 Greenmount -- on July 9, 1924. This places the Kiblers in an ownership position 13 years before the 1937 city-directory listing of 'Raymond Kibler's jewelry shop' already on file (added this session from the NRHP nomination), meaning Kibler was the long-standing owner-operator, not a late-1930s newcomer.

Philip Cohen and Louis Greenfeld leased the combined storefront building at '3204-3206 Greenmount' to J.W. Crook (through James R. Crook, attorney) by rental lease dated July 1, 1924 -- 25 years before the earliest deed previously on file for this address (the 1949 Gralan Company conveyance).

Edward N. Rich, trustee, together with the Safe Deposit & Trust Co., the Church Home & Infirmary, the Union Memorial Hospital, the Hospital for the Woman of Maryland, and Louis C. Lehr, conveyed the 'SW corner Greenmount & 33rd' -- a 33-ft-wide, 191'2"-deep lot -- to Charles B. Baker by deed dated August 4, 1925. This coalition of Baltimore hospitals and charities had held the parcel as trust property since at least September 7, 1922, when the same group first appears as grantee under trustee Rich. The purchase runs alongside Baker's already-documented September 1924 acquisition of the adjoining former Public School No. 63 property from the Mayor and City Council -- meaning Baker assembled the Baker Block site from two distinct sources within about a year of each other.

John J. Milligan and Richard H. & Marie R. Pleasants conveyed a corner lot at 'the NE side of Merryman's Lane and the west side of York Road' to Frederick H. and Ruth E. Samstag by deed dated June 4, 1924 (Superior Court block book, Block 3882, p. 93; Liber S.C.L. 4206, folio 512; the liber reads 4206 on the book page, last digit a 6, and this entry earlier gave 4204, so try both when pulling the deed). An earlier version of this entry took it for a second corner lot on the block. It is not: the intersection of the northeast side of Merryman's Lane with the west side of York Road is the beginning point of the 3200 lot in every deed from 1976 to 2026. The Samstags had held the corner since 1911 subject to a $120 ground rent, so this deed is most likely their purchase of the reversion, which would have ended the rent. That is an inference from the block-book line; the deed itself has not been read. The reversion line before it, from the same block books: Alice G. Griswold to Mary M. Drischman, Trustee, 1915 (S.C.L. 2996/308); Griswold and Drischman to Title Guarantee and Trust Co., 1916 (S.C.L. 3073/433); Title Guarantee and Trust Co. to John J. Milligan and Richard H. Pleasants, 1920 (S.C.L. 3583/257).

Ephraim Frank assigned a mortgage interest at '3212-3214 Greenmount' to Charles D. Harris, and Charles D. Harris in turn assigned an interest at the same address to Ephraim and Eva Frank jointly, both entries recorded around May 1924 in the Baltimore City Superior Court block book -- 37 years before Eva Frank (by then widowed) and her husband are shown formally purchasing the building by deed in 1961 (already on file).

The Baltimore Sun's daily real-estate transfers column reported 'Louis Stoler to Sam Stoler, 3208 Greenmount ave., g.r. $75' on July 20, 1922 -- independent newspaper confirmation of the block-book assignment dated the day before, and the only source to give the ground rent's dollar value ($75/year).

The Baltimore Sun's real-estate transfers column reported 'Gee Qu Ying to Gee Quong, w.s. York road turnpike, nr. Merryman's lane, g.r. $48' on February 3, 1923 -- independent newspaper confirmation of the block-book assignment dated the day before (Liber 3965/93), with the $48 annual ground rent the deed citation alone didn't give a dollar value for.

Capt. Berkie C. Hardy of the British steamer Cheswick, arriving from Cuba, pleaded guilty in U.S. Court to negligently permitting Gee Quong -- described in the article as 'a prohibited alien' -- to land in Baltimore on March 6, 1917, and was fined $100. This is the earliest documented appearance of Gee Quong in Baltimore, six years before he and Gee Zu Ying appear together in the Feb 1923 property transaction on this block.

FindAGrave memorials confirm Louis Stoler (1886-1943) and Samuel 'Sam' Stoler (1897-1952) as brothers: both are buried in the Neisen Congregation Cemetery in Rosedale, Baltimore County, in adjacent plot sections (D-18-207 and D-17-198), with sequential memorial IDs indicating they were recorded together from the same family plot survey. Louis's headstone is inscribed 'Father'; Sam's is inscribed 'Brother.' This confirms the July 1922 transfer of the 3208 Greenmount shoe-shop property from Louis to Sam (already on file) was a transfer within the family, not a sale to an unrelated party.

FindAGrave identifies Ernest J. Condon (1897-1984) as the son of George H. Condon (1851-1921) and Henrietta Brune Buschmann Condon (1875-1922) -- confirming 'Henrietta B. Condon,' the grantor of the October 1922 deed already on file, and that she died in 1922, the same year she deeded 3210 Greenmount to Ernest. His father George had died the year before, in 1921. Ernest's wife is listed as Erna F. Helmig Condon (1893-1971), matching 'Erna F. Condon' exactly as the co-grantor of the building's 1962 sale (already on file). Ernest died in 1984 and is buried at Immanuel Lutheran Cemetery, Baltimore -- a German Lutheran family, distinct from the Jewish families (Stoler, Kibler) elsewhere on this block.

FindAGrave and an accompanying 1959 Baltimore Sun obituary identify 'Raymond B.' of the 1924 deed as Dr. Raymond Broaddus Kibler (1879-1959), a Baltimore physician born in Luray, Virginia, and 'Emma L.' as his wife Emma Lunetta Hershberger Kibler (1881-1957), whom he married in 1904. The obituary names their son, Edward Grand Kibler (1907-1982), and gives Dr. Kibler's late-life address as 3717 Ednor Road -- meaning by the 1950s the family had moved well away from the Greenmount corridor property they held since 1924, consistent with Raymond having been a landlord/investor rather than the jewelry shop's own operator.

MyHeritage historical records give Ernest J. Condon's full name as Ernest Julius Condon, born July 3, 1897 in Baltimore (his 1917-18 WWI draft card names his mother as 'H. B. Condon' -- Henrietta Brune Condon, the 1922 grantor already on file). His WWII draft card (filed under an OCR-garbled 'Gondon') gives his residence as 615 Regester Ave., Anneslie, Baltimore -- confirming he had moved well away from the Greenmount corridor property by the 1940s, decades before the 1962 sale deed already on file. The Social Security Death Index confirms death March 1984, last residence Baltimore 21212 (the Anneslie/Idlewylde area). Note: FindAGrave gives his birthdate as July 9, 1897; these draft-card and SSDI sources consistently give July 3, 1897 -- a minor discrepancy between sources, recorded here rather than resolved.

MyHeritage's FamilySearch Family Tree record for Raymond Broaddus Kibler (1879-1959) confirms his Luray, Virginia origins and names two children -- Edward Grand Kibler (already on file from his 1959 obituary) and a daughter, Dorothy Melvina Kibler, not named in the obituary. Also lists six siblings (William Booten, Elizabeth, Joseph Franklin, Annie Lee, Mary Elizabeth, Helen D. Kibler), consistent with the Kibler family of Page County, Virginia already identified via FindAGrave.

The Baltimore Museum of Industry's BG&E Print & Negative Collection holds at least seven dated photographs of Baltimore Gas & Electric advertising billboards at the intersection of Greenmount Avenue and 33rd Street between 1957 and 1964 ('White Christmas' 12/12/1957; 'Gas Heat' 3/18/1957, 5/13/1957, and 1/9/1964; 'Hot water' 8/19/1957; 'Housepower' 2/3/1959; a sales-rep signboard 9/1961). The Baker Block (3226-3240 Greenmount, the SW corner) is the most prominent commercial building at this intersection and a plausible host for one or more of these billboards, but the BMI catalog does not name a specific building or address, so this is recorded as a corner-level candidate, not a confirmed Baker Block fact.

Brandau's appears by name in Baltimore Sun holiday shopping-guide advertisements at '3206 Greenmount' in November 1939, November 1940, and again as 'Brandau's Men's Shop, 3206 Greenmount Ave.' in a May 1953 Waverly neighborhood shopping directory -- confirming the business (already on file from the NRHP's 1937 city-directory snapshot) operated continuously under that name for at least 16 years, listed alongside major downtown department stores as a retail outlet.

Louis Stoler (already documented as the shoe-repair proprietor who assigned the property to his brother Sam in 1922) died January 18, 1943, at age 56-57. His obituary gives his home address as 3208 Greenmount Avenue itself -- the family lived at the shop -- and names his wife as Lena Stoler and his son as Meyer Stoler, neither previously documented. He was interred at 'Anshei Nesin Congregational Cemetery, Rosedale' -- almost certainly the same Baltimore-area Jewish cemetery FindAGrave records (garbled there as 'Neisen Congregation Cemetery') as the burial site for both Louis and his brother Sam. Louis living and apparently still present at 3208 as late as 1943, 21 years after the 1922 assignment to Sam, suggests that transfer was a financial/legal restructuring within the family rather than a full handoff of the business.

A display advertisement in a Baltimore Evening Sun feature on 'The Complete Shopping Center for North Baltimore ... where 33rd St. meets Greenmount' names the store at 3212-14 Greenmount Avenue as 'Frank's-Dunhill's,' Waverly's exclusive agent for Arrow shirts, ties, handkerchiefs and underwear, phone Belmont 7575, described as 'the store with the sloping glass front.' This is the same trade name as the 1958 'Frank-Dunhills' ad already on file (signed by Ted Frank) but 11 years earlier, and predates Eva Frank's formal 1961 purchase deed by 14 years -- consistent with the family operating as tenants for decades before acquiring the building outright.

A Baltimore Sun real-estate column reported the sale of the storefront property at 3216 Greenmount Avenue (subject to a $72 ground rent) from Norman and Mae Liebling to an undisclosed investor, reported November 2, 1934 as part of a wave of 'activity in the retail shopping section at Greenmount avenue and Thirty-third street.' The buyer is not named in the article. This fills a previously undocumented ownership gap between the 1913-1921 occupant record (a florist) already on file and the modern deed chain (which does not pick up until 1971+).

FindAGrave records Sol Swerdloff's burial at Mikro Kodesh Beth Israel Cemetery, Baltimore, with a death date of October 2, 1966 -- resolving the date conflict already flagged in this property's own deed history, where the 1978 mortgage states 'October 6, 1966' but five later instruments (1981-1996) all state 'on or about October 2, 1965.' The cemetery record's day (Oct 2) matches the later instruments exactly; only the year was apparently mistranscribed across those five documents, off by one year from the true 1966 death.

A 1977-78 Department of Housing and Community Development file follows the conversion of the former Waverly Theatre building at 3211 Greenmount Avenue from a variety store into a Shoe World shoe store. In December 1977 Finglass Construction filed for owner Grand Company (5436 Harford Road) to change the use from variety store to shoe store, alter the storefront, rebuild the toilet room and add partitions, an estimated $5,000; DHCD architect Steve Broache approved the work December 14-15. A January 1978 application named the owner as F. H. Durkee Enterprises at the same Harford Road address and the lessee as Shoe World, Inc. of Washington, D.C., for a new glass and aluminum storefront, partitions, an acoustical ceiling, lighting and a packaged heating and air-conditioning unit, an estimated $10,000. Broache approved it February 3, 1978, noting the sign needed its own permit. Shoe World's store plan titles the job 'Waverly Theatre, 3211 Greenmount Ave.' On January 9, 1978, Commercial Revitalization Coordinator Paul Gilbert wrote to Jack Himelfarb of Trout and Fox real estate about 'the status of the former Waverly Theatre building', reminding him that under the urban renewal ordinances the owner, not a lessee, answers to the city for compliance. Phone notes name C. Elmer Nolte Jr. for the owner, contractor Sidney Finglass, a Mr. Gusson of Shoe World, and Roger Garfink of the law firm Weinberg & Green, with Nolte to call back 're: lease'. The permits carry the designation 'R54 Waverly Business Area'. City Archives BRG48-43-10-2, 16 scans.

A second set of four drawings shows a different, unidentified corner with a 'RESTAURANT' canopy proposed over its stair entrance. A 1970s survey photo in the same folder, looking west along Gorsuch toward Greenmount, still shows the 'Gorsuch House Restaurant' hanging sign next to the Mr. Nifty cleaners sign. The folder's title matches the land records, where Garonzik conveyed 511 Gorsuch to Mr. Nifty Cleaners in 1977 (Liber 3457/827). Brodie, thanking DHCD for clearing trash from the alley beside her building and asking for an iron gate. The 1977 Maryland Historical Trust survey form for the Waverly Theatre, filed in the city's Waverly Historic Survey folder, gives its common name as 'The Goodwill': the building was a Goodwill store. It describes a two-story front with a Dutch-gable parapet, a black plastic and aluminum second story and a triangular marquee, and gives the history: the Waverly Amusement Company bought the land in 1909 and opened in 1910 with pictures and vaudeville; a roughly $100,000 enlargement in 1920-21 turned the old theatre into the entrance to a new 750-seat auditorium; Durkee Enterprises took it over and reopened it in 1929 and kept it until it closed in spring 1969. The survey photo shows the theatre front still lettered 'WAVERLY' above a triangular marquee, with Rabai's Bakery to the north and a 'Kings Court' store and the Princess Shops to the south. By December 1977 the city was permitting its conversion from a variety store to Shoe World. City Archives BRG48-43-10-6, pages 16-18.

The July 1978 Waverly Merchants Association newsletter reported that Seven-Eleven had contracted to acquire the old Gulf station at 33rd Street and Merryman Lane, across from the library, and would settle within weeks. A convenience store and a lending institution were the Waverly Development Committee's two top business priorities. City revitalization architects were working with Seven-Eleven so the new building would meet the proposed design standards, the franchise was offered to local applicants, and the store was expected to open in fall 1978. City Archives BRG48-43-10-6, page 4.

In July 1978 the Gorsuch House was Bob Moore Jr.'s. The Waverly Merchants Association newsletter carried his sanitation column signed 'Bob Moore, Jr., Gorsuch House' and called the Waverly Development Committee's monthly meeting for Thursday, July 27, 1978 at 8 P.M. at 'Bob Moore's Gorsuch House', with the fall promotion, a community wall mural, the logo and merchant insignia on the agenda. This fits the land records, where Mr. Nifty Cleaners conveyed 511 Gorsuch to Moore in 1978. City Archives BRG48-43-10-6, pages 4-5.

Permit applications for 3211 Greenmount in December 1977 name the owner as Grand Company, and one in January 1978 names F. H. Durkee Enterprises, both at 5436 Harford Road. The Durkee organization had run the Waverly Theatre from 1929 until it closed in 1969 and also owned the Boulevard. DHCD's notes give C. Elmer Nolte Jr. as the owner's contact, at the same phone number Frank Durkee III listed for the Boulevard Theatre in 1976, and Trout and Fox real estate (Jack Himelfarb) as the agent handling the Shoe World lease. City Archives BRG48-43-10-2.

A city survey photo from about 1977, in DHCD's 'Waverly Streetscapes' envelope, shows the big 'Zepp Photo Centers' sign projecting over the Greenmount sidewalk here, with the Northside Bar ahead and Vinson's Animal Hospital, a Sample Store and Beneficial loans across the street. It places the Zepp business at 3040 in the late 1970s. City Archives BRG48-43-10-1, page 24.

Two city survey photos from about 1977 show the 'Vinson's Animal Hospital' sign hanging over the sidewalk at 3015, one looking north toward the old Waverly Town Hall (then the Northside Bar) and one taken from across the street by the Zepp Photo sign. City Archives BRG48-43-10-1, pages 23-24.

A city survey photo from about 1977 shows the attendant booth of the merchants' free-parking lot, probably this Shop & Park lot, with a board reading 'These stores make your free parking possible'. Legible sponsors include Adler's, Becker's, Harry's Liquors, The Oriental House, Provident Savings Bank, Thomas Beauty Salon, Boulevard Hardware, the Boulevard Theatre, Kitty's Lounge, Mr. Nifty Cleaners and the White Coffee Pot. The lot was rebuilt by the city in 1980-81. City Archives BRG48-43-10-1, page 18.

A March 1976 roster of the Waverly Shopping District Steering Committee lists Jack Brandau of Brandau's Men's Shop at 3219 Greenmount, a number now part of this parcel. City Archives BRG48-43-10-5, page 7.

A March 1976 roster of the Waverly Shopping District Steering Committee lists Ms. Tommy Cohen of the Bruce Insurance Co. at 3104 Greenmount, a number now part of this parcel. City Archives BRG48-43-10-5, page 7.

A March 1976 roster of the Waverly Shopping District Steering Committee lists Alvin Miller of the Princess Shops at '3205/3212 Greenmount'; 3205 is now part of this parcel. City Archives BRG48-43-10-5, page 7.

The 1977 Maryland Historical Trust survey form for 3021-3031 Greenmount describes 3021 as a shingled, center-gable, two-story, three-bay house whose first story had been altered to hold a barber shop and a shoe repair. The form dates the row to 1875-99 and calls this stretch from 31st to 33rd the center of Waverly's business district. City Archives BRG48-43-10-6, pages 6-8.

The 1977 Maryland Historical Trust survey form for 3021-3031 Greenmount describes the building next to 3021 as a simple two-story, two-bay stuccoed building with a projecting boxed cornice and decorated frieze, with an addition whose aluminum-siding front continued across a first-story bar. City Archives BRG48-43-10-6, pages 6-8.

The 1977 Maryland Historical Trust survey form for 3021-3031 Greenmount lists, north of the barber shop and the bar, a larger two-story, three-bay building with a renovated first story used by the Beneficial Financial System, its upper windows under a radiating voussoir and keystone; 'The Sample Store', a simple box-like one-story building; and 'The Red Shed', a two-story building covered in vertical planking and shingles with only its parapet and cornice left. The form does not give a house number for each. City Archives BRG48-43-10-6, pages 6-8.

The 1977 Maryland Historical Trust survey form for 3021-3031 Greenmount lists, north of the barber shop and the bar, a two-story building used by the Beneficial Financial System, 'The Sample Store', a box-like one-story building, and 'The Red Shed', a two-story building covered in vertical planking and shingles. The form does not give a house number for each, so which one stood at 3031 is not stated. City Archives BRG48-43-10-6, pages 6-8.

The 1977 survey form for the row from 3113 to the firehouse describes 'Harry's Liquors' at 3113 as a two-story, three-bay painted brick building with a first story refaced in aluminum siding and plate glass, second-story windows boarded over, and a dentilled cornice and frieze, its store spreading into a smaller two-story neighbor of the same design. Allen Orman ran Harry's and sat on the 1976 merchants' steering committee. City Archives BRG48-43-10-6, pages 12-13.

The 1977 survey form for the row from Harry's Liquors to the firehouse describes 'Moses Zalis' as occupying a two-story, six-bay brick building with a Dutch-gabled parapet, its first story turned into a windowed shopfront and its six second-story windows sharing a continuous sill. The form dates the row to 1875-99 and finds it close to its original design. City Archives BRG48-43-10-6, pages 12-13.

The Sun's July 1988 feature reported that Mr. Nifty had retired and the business was now just Nifty Cleaners, run by Gary Wah, who had taken it over about five years earlier. Wah told the paper that daytime foot traffic south of 33rd was about 90 percent Black and that it was wrong for people to label the area high-crime for that reason. City Archives BRG48-43-10-6.

The Sun's July 1988 feature described the People's Community Health Center as one of the last vestiges of the neighborhood's more militant era, a former free clinic now charging on a sliding scale, with more than 80 percent of patients subsidized and about 500 people a month coming through the door. Executive director Pat Cassatt backed removing the benches at 32nd and Greenmount that year, saying people were afraid of those sleeping on them. City Archives BRG48-43-10-6.

Ten years after it opened in the old Gulf station, the Sun's July 1988 feature described the 7-Eleven here as having a money machine with a line day and night, and quoted regulars who insisted it must be the world's busiest 7-Eleven with the world's smallest parking lot. City Archives BRG48-43-10-6.

The Sun's July 1988 feature described the Saturday farmers' market spread over the parking lot behind the 7-Eleven, with local raspberries and vendors marking down wilting flowers by late morning, eight years after the 32nd Street Farmers Market opened on this lot. City Archives BRG48-43-10-6.

The Sun's July 1988 feature on Greenmount and 33rd listed the Butter Crisp bakery, with an oldies record store, among the businesses whose passing people 'quietly mourn', so the bakery had closed by mid-1988. City Archives BRG48-43-10-6.

The Property Acquisition map (Exhibit 2, dated February 2, 1979) of the Waverly Business Area Urban Renewal Plan marks only one block in the district for the city to buy: all of block 3881A, lots 1/12, 13/15, 16, 17, 18 and 23, labeled with house numbers 3201 and 3223 Barclay, 415 and 419 Merrymans Lane and 410 E 32nd Street. The Land Disposition map (Exhibit 3) shows the block as a single disposition lot for public parking of about 46,829 square feet, and the land use map labels it 'Pkg'. This supports reading the deed recorded 30 November 1979 (WA 3844/396) as the city's acquisition, ahead of the 1980-81 rebuild of the Shop & Park lot. City Archives BRG48-43-10-8, pages 24-26.

Appendix A of the final Waverly Business Area Urban Renewal Plan (exhibits dated February 2, 1979) lists 3015 Greenmount Avenue as a non-conforming use: 'Animal Hospital'. Under the plan such uses either became non-conforming with its proposed zoning changes or already were, and were allowed to continue subject to the zoning ordinance's rules on non-conforming uses. The animal hospital was Vinson's, whose sign appears in the city's survey photos of about 1977. Only five properties in the district were listed. City Archives BRG48-43-10-8, pages 23 and 49.

Appendix A of the final Waverly Business Area Urban Renewal Plan (exhibits dated February 2, 1979) lists 420 Merrymans Lane as a non-conforming use: 'Auto Service'. Michelle Belco's 1977 history for the city's neighborhood survey says the Aull family's shoemaker shop was one of Waverly's earliest businesses, and that Henry Jacob Aull, a Bavarian immigrant, bought a gravel pit 'at, what is now, 3116 Greenmount Avenue' and built there a rambling Virginia Colonial house of bricks brought over as ballast on an English sailing ship. She credits his sons Jacob and Louis with building most of the village's cottages after 1866. This is the only source so far that gives the site a modern house number; 3116 is now part of this parcel. Corridor's other record names the founder Jacob Aull (1804-1876), so 'Henry Jacob' may be Belco's error or a fuller name. City Archives BRG48-43-10-11, pages 14 and 16.

Michelle Belco's 1977 history says the Waverly Merchants Parking Lot at the southeast corner of 32nd and Barclay was the site of School No. 115, the Waverly school for Black children: a one-story frame building of four classrooms, probably first an elementary school, listed in 1903 school records as the Colored High and Training School, with an all-Black faculty and 150 to 200 pupils. She notes the Mount Zion Baptist Church, a small stone and shingle building of the late nineteenth century, across the street, perhaps the Black counterpart of the Huntingdon Baptist church a block away. City Archives BRG48-43-10-11, page 21.

Michelle Belco's 1977 history says School No. 51, one of the area's earliest schools, had its first building at 33rd and Greenmount, 'where Adler's is today', before moving to the four-story brick building of 1910 on 34th Street at Ellerslie. In 1976 Stanley Adler listed Adler's at 3240 Greenmount on the merchants' steering committee roster; this corner parcel's Baker Block is the other record placing the school here. City Archives BRG48-43-10-11, page 22.

Michelle Belco's 1977 history says the Waverly Methodist Episcopal congregation began meeting around 1870 over J. E. Sinclair's store, 'then at the corner of Merryman's Lane and Greenmount Avenue', before laying the cornerstone of its first church on Greenmount between 31st and 33rd in 1872. Corridor's deed records put James E. Sinclair's store and tinshop at the York Turnpike corner of Merryman's Lane. City Archives BRG48-43-10-11, page 18.

Before the city rebuilt the Waverly Parking Lot, it cleared the block it had acquired. Housing and Community Development's property management section collected rent from the remaining occupants as a relocation account. Margie Fields of 419 Merryman Lane (front), relocation account 180-40, received a vacate notice dated December 31, 1979, and her tenancy ended March 31, 1980, with keys to be surrendered at the Sharp-Leadenhall relocation site office. The existing lot at 3201-3221 Barclay Street had 28 active parking accounts, among them Mary Lambert's. The city kept them going past March 1980 but told every account to stop using the lot on June 1, 1980. Patricia Massey set the schedule on April 2, 1980: bid advertisement April 18, dwelling vacate date May 1, notice to proceed June 1. David Hunter added three small sheds to the demolition, and a May 16 note reports the houses vacant, BG&E coming to cut services and demolition to follow. The 1953 Sanborn map in the folder already labels most of the block 'Park'g', with houses along Merryman Lane; those houses were the ones cleared. A February 7, 1980 memo describes the last occupied building as 'a wood frame duplex residence at the N.E. corner of the proposed lot which has been acquired by the City but is still occupied', due to be vacated by April 15; property management confirmed it would enforce the March 31 vacate date for residents under Relocation Project No. 180 (BRG48-43-10-14). City Archives BRG48-43-10-12, pages 2, 7-9, 14, 23, 64.

Hurst-Rosche Engineers of Timonium designed the lot for DHCD. After a May 16, 1979 review, David F. Paduch put the revised plan at $120,000 and warned that meeting David Hunter's $100,000 target would mean dropping all curbs and laying only an inch of asphalt. Their preliminary plan went out for utility review on July 13, 1979, and the tight budget ruled out $11,400 of conduit for the lighting cable in favor of $2,850 of direct burial. A landscape plan went to Recreation and Parks on October 3, 1979. The first Hurst-Rosche sketch, on May 11, 1979, came in at about $160,000, including $24,000 of lighting and 106 parking meters at $100 each; someone at DHCD wrote 'Too high - too fat!' across the letter. On June 20, 1979 Hunter set the meter posts 64 feet apart on double-loaded aisles of 22-foot stalls and a 20-foot aisle, and sent the plan to Transit and Traffic (BRG48-43-10-13). The Bureau of Highways let Contract 2611, 'Bituminous Concrete Resurfacing of Waverly Parking Lot', with bids due May 7, 1980 in a $100,000 to $250,000 range: 760 tons of asphalt, 1,940 feet of curb, 5,500 square feet of sidewalk, lighting, benches and plantings. R. Marcantoni & Sons of Broening Highway won it, received notice to proceed June 19, 1980 and finished November 22, 1980, with 84 days of authorized shutdown for the planting season. The city accepted the lot at a final inspection on March 3, 1981, with a two-year guarantee on the wood benches. In July 1981 it granted a 13-day extension for delays from a cable relocation and revised grades, and in October 1981 Hunter asked Recreation and Parks to check which trees and shrubs needed replacing. City Archives BRG48-43-10-12.

An undated DHCD delivery survey of the stores backing on Merryman's Lane, made for the parking lot design (about 1979) records the Princess Shops at 3210 Greenmount taking three or four deliveries a week by 20-foot truck through the Greenmount front door. City Archives BRG48-43-10-12, pages 52-54.

An undated DHCD delivery survey of the stores backing on Merryman's Lane, made for the parking lot design (about 1979) records Jason Shoes at 3216-18 Greenmount taking daily deliveries by tractor-trailers, trucks and vans through the Greenmount front door. City Archives BRG48-43-10-12, pages 52-54.

An undated DHCD delivery survey of the stores backing on Merryman's Lane, made for the parking lot design (about 1979) records Boulevard Hardware at 3224 Greenmount as a 'new location', taking all deliveries through Merryman's Lane, while its store at 432 E 32nd Street was still listed. An undated DHCD delivery survey of the stores backing on Merryman's Lane, made for the parking lot design (about 1979) records Little Tavern at 433 Merryman's Lane taking daily deliveries by 20-foot truck on Merryman's Lane. The copy of Sanborn map sheet 654 (Baltimore vol. 6, copyright 1953) in the city's Waverly Parking Lot file marks a filling station at the corner of 33rd Street and Merryman Lane, the station later described as 'the old Gulf station' that Seven-Eleven bought in 1978. Three years after the lot opened, the city adjusted it. On April 30, 1984 Margaret E. Williams, Director of the Commercial Revitalization Division, by then part of the Neighborhood Progress Administration, asked the Bureau of Highways to widen the curb at the Barclay Street entrance to a 20-foot radius, giving up the first parking space and its meter, under Interdepartmental Work Order 140938 for about $800, with the new island to be landscaped. On June 8, 1984 David Hunter asked Highways to add a new four-foot concrete sidewalk and a curb ramp at the Barclay and 32nd Street corner, drawn by Bob Quilter, on the same work order. City Archives BRG48-43-10-13, pages 2-6.

The lot's landscape plan, drawn by Hurst-Rosche Engineers for DHCD, set a planting schedule: ten Kwanzan flowering cherries in staggered rows along 32nd Street; seventeen littleleaf lindens along Merryman's Lane and the island; three Japanese black pines in a planter at the north end; and about 785 winged euonymus as hedging around the perimeter and island. A brick wall, a vinyl-coated 'Woodland Green' chain-link fence and a triangular planted 'triangle park' at the Merryman's Lane corner completed it. The landscaping estimate based on the drawings of August 9, 1979 came to $36,347, and included 145 feet of brick wall, 525 feet of fence, two benches and one 'I.D. Pylon' at $3,000, the WAVERLY PARKING identification pylon. Transit and Traffic approved the layout on August 3, 1979 on condition that the second row of meter posts west of Brentwood Avenue be protected from backing cars. The landscape plan went to Recreation and Parks on March 25, 1980, ahead of the April 18 advertisement of Contract 2611. City Archives BRG48-43-10-14.
Feature on Pete's Grille, the cash-only Waverly breakfast counter at 3130 Greenmount Ave, still drawing lines after decades (Tue-Sun, single long counter, Michael Phelps connection)

A city survey photo from about 1977, looking north along Greenmount from Vinson's Animal Hospital, shows a round 'RCA Victor Records - Radio Center' sign hanging over the west side of the 3100 block, beyond Becker's Shop and Sunny's Surplus, and 'Radio Center' also appears on the sponsor board of the merchants' free-parking lot. The 1958 Waverly Park and Shop directory placed the Radio Center at 3118 Greenmount, so the business was still trading about twenty years later; the photo does not show the house number. City Archives BRG48-43-10-1, page 23.

The sponsor board on the attendant booth of the merchants' free-parking lot, photographed by the city about 1977, lists 'Roeth's Jewelry' among the stores that 'make your free parking possible'. The 1958 Waverly Park and Shop directory placed Roeth's Jewelers at 3120 Greenmount, so the placement here is by that earlier address. City Archives BRG48-43-10-1, page 18.

A city survey photo from about 1977 shows the arrow-shaped 'BECKERS SHOP' sign over the west side of the 3100 block, just north of the Northside Bar, with the Bruce Insurance sign ('Auto - Liability - Fire - Theft - Collision - Budget Payments') and a Manhattan Shirts sign beside it. Becker's also appears on the merchants' parking sponsor board. The 1958 Park and Shop directory placed Becker's at 3106 Greenmount, part of this parcel. City Archives BRG48-43-10-1, page 23.

A city survey photo from about 1977, looking north along the west side of the 3100 block, shows a 'Purple Bone' sign among the storefront signs beyond the Radio Center. Allan Keyser of the Purple Bone, 3122 Greenmount, sat on the 1976 merchants' steering committee. City Archives BRG48-43-10-1, page 23.

City survey photos from about 1977 show the old Waverly Town Hall with a 'NORTHSIDE BAR - Package Goods - Food' sign on its corner and 'Northside Bar, Music Fri. & Sat. Nites' painted on the first story, and next to it the 'Bruce Insurance' sign advertising auto, liability, fire, theft and collision coverage on budget payments. Bruce Insurance was at 3104 Greenmount, now part of this parcel. City Archives BRG48-43-10-1, page 23.

A city survey photo from about 1977, looking west along Gorsuch Avenue toward Greenmount, shows 'PARK TAILOR' signs on the corner building at the near end of the south side of the block, east of Robinson's Gorsuch House restaurant and the Mr. Nifty cleaners at the Greenmount corner. A 'Park Custom Tailoring - Alteration' billboard stood nearby at the Hack's corner in the 3400 block. The placement at 525 Gorsuch, the end parcel of that row, is inferred from the photo. City Archives BRG48-43-10-1, page 20.

The photograph on the 1977 Maryland Historical Trust survey form for the Waverly Theatre shows, south of the theatre's 'WAVERLY' front, a large dark-faced store with a 'Kings Court' sign, and beyond it a 'Prin... Ch...' sign for the Princess Shops; north of the theatre is Rabai's Bakery. Kings Court's trade and exact address are not recorded; it is filed on this parcel by its position in the photo. City Archives BRG48-43-10-6, page 17.

Peter George Engelman, who as a young man worked in his father's toy and hobby store at 3117 Greenmount Ave (Engelman's Kiddie-Land) before becoming a CPA, author and publisher, died July 2, 2025 at his Pikesville home, age 85.

Jin Pyo Hong and Auk J. Hong executed an $86,250 purchase-money Deed of Trust to Banking Services Corp. (trustees J. Rodney Baker and John F. Novak), secured by 3117-3119 Greenmount Ave, recorded alongside their purchase from Eyring Realty Enterprises.

Maryland National Bank, successor to Equitable Financial Corporation, certified Jin Pyo Hong and Auk J. Hong's Aug 29, 1988 Deed of Trust fully paid and discharged, releasing the lien shortly after their sale of the property to the Koos.

Bank of America, N.A., successor to NationsBank of Maryland, appointed PRLAP, Inc. as substitute trustee and certified Nam Seo Koo and Seon Gyu Koo's Dec 24, 1992 Deed of Trust (Liber 3518, folio 465) fully paid and discharged, releasing the lien more than a decade before their 2017 sale to 3117 Greenmount Avenue, LLC.

A gardener seeking a situation gives 'CHARLES HAMILTON, Florist, Waverley, York road' as his contact, the earliest dated evidence in hand of Hamilton trading as a Waverly florist, two years before he opened the Waverly Hotel.

A German gardener experienced in greenhouses, graperies and orchards takes replies 'for three days' at Charles Hamilton's, Waverley, York road: Hamilton's place served as the local hiring point for nursery labor.

'The new Waverly Hotel at Waverly, York road, will be opened on Wednesday evening next, 17th instant. Mr. Charles Hamilton, the proprietor, invites his friends.' Primary source for the white paper's 1873 hotel claim: the opening was December 17, 1873.

Fifteen Waverly men, among them A. S. Abell (publisher of the Sun), Jos. Merryman and J. T. Dillehunt, gave Charles Hamilton, 'proprietor of the new Waverly hotel,' a pair of engraved Dahlgren breech-loading pistols 'for endurance and pluck, 2 a.m., April 14th, 1874' after he captured the chicken thief Harker; 'choice wines flowed freely' at the hotel. Shows the hotel as the village's social center within months of opening.
Chas. Hamilton, 'Waverly Hotel, Waverly, Baltimore county,' advertises a roan milch cow taken up astray: Hamilton still keeping the hotel, with enough ground to pen livestock, in 1876.

The first reform mass meeting of the 1876 campaign was called for September 28 'in front of Waverly Hotel, Waverly,' with Hon. J. Morrison Harris speaking: the hotel frontage served as Waverly's public assembly ground.

Hamilton's standing ad (first run April 6, 1878, 'tf'; clipped September 14 and again November 2) sells hot-house, green-house and hardy plants; bouquets, pyramids, wreaths, crosses and crowns to order; and 'Cemetery Lots and Gardens laid out.' Alongside the hotel he ran a working nursery with greenhouses and a funeral and cemetery-landscaping trade, so the pre-livery ground was glasshouses and gardens as much as hostelry.
The young men of Culpeper, Va., gave a ball at the Waverly Hotel for visiting young ladies from Baltimore, Washington and other cities: the hotel drew summer boarders and out-of-town society.
The County Commissioners awarded Charles Hamilton, 'the Waverly florist,' the contract to supply the Towson Court House park with flowers, a service he had performed for several years.

Miss Ella Hamilton, daughter of Charles Hamilton the florist, applied for Waverly postmistress against the incumbent, Mrs. Sarah A. Bonsal. Per Anna Cole (1933), the post office had moved from the tollgate into rooms in the Hamilton Hotel under Mrs. Bonsal, so the contest was over an office housed in the Hamiltons' own building.

Wm. Joesting offers the stock and fixtures of his grocery store at 1023 York road, Waverly, 'splendid stand for Grocery and Provision.' Joesting was the tenant grocer at the Bateman stand eight months before Bateman advertised it vacant.

James S. Bateman, of 1021 York road, offers a 'first-class business stand, suitable for Grocery and Meat Business; best situated Store in North Baltimore; two fronts, 1023 York road and 101 Old York road' (ran Nov 11-13, 1899). Five years later the Provident Savings Bank built its one-story brick Waverly branch at 1023 York road, and the 1915 Sanborn marks 'Bank' at 1023 on this lot.

A streetcar hit a wagon owned by Emory W. Childs, 100 Old York road, driven by Fred Behm of 102 Old York road. Childs lived across from the rear front of Bateman's stand (101 Old York road) thirteen years before Polk lists W. C. Childs & Son's livery at 3117 (1915-1917): an early trace of the family that later ran the stable on this lot.
Moses Zalis advertises new and unclaimed freight furniture at 819 Greenmount Ave: 'We are moving, all prices reduced.'
The same classified that ran on May 22 from '819 Greenmount Ave.' runs on May 23 from '3117 Greenmount Ave.' Moses Zalis's furniture store opened here the weekend of May 22-23, 1971.

County fire notes: the No. 4 engine house at Waverly is receiving a 50-by-25-foot addition giving it a depth of 100 feet; a Holloway double-tank engine will replace the small engine; four cells are going into the ground floor of the station-house, with bunk and sitting rooms above.

A large unoccupied frame dwelling on Charles Street avenue north of the toll-gate (formerly Joseph Merryman's, bought by Jere. D. Mallory) burned; 'the chemical engine from Waverly reached the scene too late ... but assisted in saving adjoining property.'

A parade of the Baltimore County fire department came up the York road to Waverly for the formal acceptance of No. 4 Company's new engine, truck and station-house. The house was brick, 100 feet deep by 25 feet front, with tracks, box stalls, a feed room and a sliding pole; a 12-by-50-foot section held a magistrate's office and four cells, with bunk rooms overhead. The new Holloway chemical engine had two 85-gallon tanks. Capt. John P. Dillehunt commanded. The building was a combined fire station, lock-up and magistrate's court.
'A four-hundred-pound bell was placed in the tower of the Waverly fire-engine house Monday. Its alarm can be heard in Hampden.' The daughter of City Councilman John B. Hart was to christen it.

The fire chief's report urges an engine company 'in the vicinity of York road and Gorsuch avenue,' abolishing chemical engine No. 4 and moving its men to No. 7 hook-and-ladder, to share one building: the reorganization that produced the 1902-03 rebuild.

Chief Horton's annual report for 1903 again recommends an engine company for 'York road, Waverly (quarters No. 7 Hook and Ladder Company),' a second-size truck at No. 7's quarters, and moving the combination truck to Homestead: pressure that led to Engine 31 joining Truck 7 here.

James S. Bateman, 'a well-known resident of Waverly,' died at home in his 82nd year. 'For many years he kept a grocery on the York road, at Waverly. He retired about eight years ago' (about 1892): his 1899 ad was a landlord re-letting the stand, not a working grocer.
Orphans' Court: administration accounts passed for the estates of Mary A. Bateman ($3,295.31) and James S. Bateman ($505.24).

Miss Clara V. Bateman, 'for many years a teacher in the primary department of the Waverly public school,' died at her residence, 3109 York road, of pneumonia. The 1915 Sanborn prints '1021 / 3109' on this house: her father advertised from 1021 York road in 1899, so the family home carried both numbers.

Transfer: Walter I. Dawkins to Clara V. Bateman, west side Old York road, 2 lots, $3,050. This conflicts with Clara V. Bateman's reported death in February 1902: either the deed was recorded late, or a second Clara Bateman is meant (the village history names a 'Miss Clara S. Bateman').
Building permit: 'Provident Savings Bank, one-story brick bank building, 1023 York road; estimated cost $1,000.' Provident's first purpose-built Waverly branch, on Bateman's former grocery stand.
Permit list: 'Provident Savings Bank, dig well, 1023 York road.' Waverly still relied on wells in 1904.

Sanborn Baltimore Vol. 7 (1915) sheet 718 prints the old York Road number 1023 beside a small one-story brick building labeled 'Bank' at the Greenmount frontage, with two-story brick stores behind it on the Old York Road side. The dual numbers on the plate (1021 = 3109 to the south, 1027 = the livery to the north) fix 1023 York Road as this lot.

Sanborn Vol. 7 (1915) sheet 718 draws a two-story frame 'LIVERY' filling this lot from the Greenmount frontage back to Old York Road, numbered 1027 (the old York Road number of Zoll's stable), directly south of the Engine 31 / Truck 7 firehouse. The map confirms the white paper's identification of 1027 York Road with this parcel and shows the frame stable standing until the 1928 rebuild.

Crain & Hershey's trustee's sale notice (auction March 14, 1904) for the 35-foot lot on the east side of the York Turnpike Road, 204 feet 6 inches north of the start of the Taggert-to-Coffield grant (1865), running back to the west side of Old York road; subject to $175 ground rent and 'improved by a 2-story FRAME STABLE.' Primary source for the white paper's 1904 entry.

'For sale: Runabout team, complete, very cheap. WAVERLY STABLES, 1027 York road' (ran March 25-27, 1908). The earliest dated use in hand of the 'Waverly Stables' name for Zoll's livery, five months before the August 1908 ad.

Automobile registration no. 8315: 'Hamilton Stanpaugh, 3119 Greenmount avenue, Maxwell' (the white paper spells it Stampaugh). A car owner living at the livery's north half in 1914, as motor vehicles began to replace the horses the stable let out.

The 1907 appropriation bill funds an 'Engine Company—York road, Waverly (quarters of No. 7 Hook and Ladder Company). Salaries and equipment, $26,125': the money that put Engine 31 into Truck 7's house.

Sanborn Vol. 7 (1915) sheet 718: 'Fire Dept. Eng. Co. No. 31, 20 men, 9 horses; Truck Co. No. 7: La France 3rd size steamer, 1 comb. chem. & hose wagon, 1 comb. Holloway truck, 3700 ft 2½-inch hose, 50 ft chem. hose,' with a 30-foot hose tower on the roof. The white paper's 1915 entry counts thirteen horses; the insurance survey counts nine.

Sanborn Vol. 7 (1915) sheet 717, block 10, west side of Greenmount between Vineyard Lane and E. 30th St. At the Vineyard Lane corner the plate prints '3020' over '922' on a 2-story frame dwelling with a porch, with a detached 2-story outbuilding and a hatched stable block behind it toward the lane. Mid-frontage it prints '3014' over '920' on a large 2-story frame house with 2-story and 1-story ells, standing about 100 ft back from the street behind an open yard; no dairy sheds are drawn, although the O'Neill dairy was listed there. At the south end it prints '918' on a 1-story store (modern 3008). The long range of one-story 'Green Houses, Glass Roofs' stands behind that 918 store, on the florist lot south of this parcel (modern 3000-3008, where Wm. H. Wolfe, florist, is listed from 1914), not on 3010-3020. Vineyard Lane was Gilmor Lane, the old tollgate road, so the glass houses are probably the nursery ground 'a little below the tollgate' that the 1933 Waverly history gives to Charles Hamilton's hothouses; Hamilton was listed at 908 York Road in 1893, and a florist still traded at 3000 Greenmount in 1922.

Rental classified: 'Greenmount Ave., 3117, over York Rd. Building & Loan Assn.; 4 rooms, bath; $30.' Three months after the March 1928 lease and building contract, and four months before Miller Bros.' first dated ad (September 1928), the new building housed the York Road Building & Loan Association on the ground floor and a four-room apartment upstairs. The 1932 trustees' sale describes the building as 'a 2-story brick dwelling with store front.'

Miller Bros. Furniture Co., Inc., 3117 Greenmount Ave., phone Homewood 9188, advertises the new Sparton Equasonne Model 930 radio at $189.50 complete with tubes, sold and serviced by 'factory trained men.' The store's own display ad, alongside the dealer list of February 7, 1929.

In the Czech-language weekly Telegraf, Klecka, Levy & Russy, Inc. (2232-34 East Monument Street, near Patterson Park Ave.) advertise the remaining bankrupt stock of Miller Bros. Furniture Co., Inc., 3117 Greenmount Ave., at '50c na dolaru' (50 cents on the dollar), sold both at their Monument Street store and at 3117. The buyers of the failed Waverly store (per the Evening Sun of Oct 26, 1932) marketed the liquidation to Baltimore's Czech neighborhood.

'Title to the sub-ground rent and reversion of $1,200 under the building at 3117 Greenmount avenue was conveyed by Dorothy Dietrich and others to the Eyring Realty Corporation for merging and extinguishment, stamps on the deed indicating a consideration of $19,000,' through the Maryland Title Guarantee Company, 'subject to the original ground rent of $150.' Primary source for the white paper's 1936 Dietrich entry. Update Oct. 14, 2026: the deed is read (742:mdlr-scl5686-215-dietrich-eyring-subrent-merger-1936): Dorothy and Wilhelmina Dietrich and Helen Dietrich Butler, Dec. 30, 1936, $19 in stamps.

A 'national corporation' recruits 'dismissed CWA workers or unemployed married men (white)' for salaried sales work, interviews at six offices including 3117 Greenmount Ave. The Civil Works Administration had just laid off its relief workers (spring 1934). The ad restricted hiring by race, and it ran while Century Furniture occupied 3117 and was advertising for door-to-door appliance salesmen.

Hecht's Furniture House ('Originators of Complete Outfits,' '1935 our 51st year,' so founded about 1884) advertises three rooms for $248, $2.50 weekly, from its main store at 930-38 S. Charles St. and its uptown store at 3117-3119 Greenmount Ave. ('Take No. 8 or No. 17 cars'). The Greenmount branch was reached by the York Road streetcar lines.

Full-page Red Tag Sale ad for Joe the Motorists' Friend (auto accessories, tires, radios, fishing tackle, bicycles, paint), listing the chain's stores including 3117-19 Greenmount Ave., Baltimore. Exact source for the white paper's undated 1940 entry.

Classified under Marine Engines: 'July sale on outboards. Easy terms. Special prices. Joe, the Motorist's Friend, 417 S. Conkling st.; 3117 Greenmount ave.' In 1940 the chain had two Baltimore stores, Highlandtown and Waverly.
'Salesmen in auto accessory store, exp. Chance for advancement. Apply 3117 Greenmount ave.' (ran Aug 18 and 23, 1941).
'Salesgirls for accessory store. Apply 3117 Greenmount Ave.' In 1941 the store hired salesmen; by May 1944 it was recruiting women, the wartime labor shift at the counter of an auto-parts shop.

'Wanted, two future store managers ... apply to our Merchandise Manager Mr. A. P. Livingston who will be at our store, 3117 Greenmount avenue.' Joe the Motorist's Friend, Inc., 3117-19 Greenmount ave. Exact date and named officer for the white paper's 1949 entry.

Joe the Motorists' Friend, Inc., 3117-19 Greenmount Avenue, Baltimore 18, seeks four men for two years of chain-store management training; 'Apply Monday, August 14 ... Mr. Marlin Shuey.' The white paper gives the name as 'Marvin Shney'; the ad reads Marlin Shuey.

Joe the Motorists' Friend Christmas ad (clock radios, waffle irons, Sunbeam Mixmaster, $1.25 a week) lists '3 great stores in Baltimore: Waverly, 3117-19 Greenmount Ave.; Highlandtown, 415-19 Conkling St.; Dundalk, 35 Shipping Place.' Dundalk had opened since June 1950.

The chain's store block lists 21 stores across Maryland, Pennsylvania, Virginia and West Virginia, with 3117-19 Greenmount Ave. first, between the '20 Great Stores' of April 1954 and the '22' of late 1955.
A model-contest ad names 'Engelman's Kiddieland, 3117 Greenmount Ave.' among the area's hobby shops, alongside Citywide TV & Hobby, Feild's of Catonsville and the three Gamerman's stores.

'Dolls: Talking Casper $5.55; Chatty Cathy $10.95; Barbie clothes $1 up. Engelman's, 3117 Greenmount Ave.' The toy business was still running at Christmas 1961, eight months after the April 1961 coin-dealer ad that the white paper reads as the end of Kiddie Land.
'Baseball gloves—Selling out. Engelman's, 3117 Greenmount.' The closing-out sale was under way by mid-March 1962, three weeks before the white paper's April 3 'terminal liquidation.'

The Maryland Bridge Association awards a 'Paul Engelman Memorial Trophy' to the master player with the most points in a year (won by Ellie Zepp of the Reisterstown YWCA club). Probably the Paul Engelman of Kiddie Land, who died in 1976; the identification is not yet confirmed.

'Office furniture: 7-drawer desk $45; typewriter chair $15; file cabinet $25; heavy safe $50. Moses Zalis Furn., 3117 Greenmount Ave, 467-9100.' Zalis was still at 3117 in March 1991, apparently selling off his own office fixtures, fifteen months after the December 1989 ad the white paper treats as his last.

The Baltimore City tax-sale advertisement lists 3117 Greenmount Ave (Block 4076A, Lot 14; 34-11 x 138-9), assessed at $297,233, to 3117 Greenmount Avenue, LLC, with $8,351.05 due. 3107 Greenmount (4076A-10) appears directly above it.
The Baltimore City tax-sale advertisement lists 3107 Greenmount Ave (Block 4076A, Lot 10; 47-3 x 114-11), assessed at $302,367, to 3107 Greenmount Avenue, LLC, with $8,495.07 due.

The 1940 'Your Town' feature finds Miss Louisa Frederika Aull, 96, at 3116 Greenmount: 'Her father started Waverly'; her brothers Jacob and Louis built many of the mansard roofs and cut much of the scroll work that survives. Her house 'is not the rambling white clapboard house her father built, but one that her brother, Jacob, constructed on the site of the old homestead about thirty-five years ago' (about 1905), and 'the entire block, except this house, has been engulfed by the new Waverly shopping district.' Old Land Marks captions the sisters' residence '1895'; the two dates for the rebuild disagree.

The Baltimore Sun of March 15, 2023 (p. S20) lists 3117 Greenmount Ave (4076A-14), assessed at $362,400, to 3117 Greenmount Avenue, LLC, with about $11,643 due. This is the second consecutive year on the list (2022: $8,351.05 on a $297,233 assessment); the assessment rose 22 percent in a year.

SDAT filing history for Eyring Realty Enterprises, Inc.: articles of incorporation April 30, 1948 (two days before the May 3, 1948 internal deed that moved 3117 into it); stock issued February 3, 1949; change of resident agent 1980; forfeited by proclamation October 10, 1990, two years after it bought the Crittenton block and resold 3117 to the Hongs (1988). The Eyring family's tie to 3117 ran from building the showroom in 1928, through ownership of the building from 1933 and the ground from 1936, to 1988.

A Washington-area flyer ("Who Will Be Next?") lists a week of Black Panther support events, Dec. 14-17, 1969, after the Chicago police raid that killed Fred Hampton and Mark Clark: a teach-in with Baltimore Panther speakers at the University of Maryland student union on Dec. 16, and a Dec. 17 Justice Department picket memorializing Hampton. This is the raid Jim Keck remembered as the moment the Panthers pulled out of the joint clinic.

Cover of the journal's first issue, "Inherent Nature or Cultural Conditioning?", $1.25, with the fist-in-Venus logo. The socialist-feminist collective edited, laid out and mailed the journal from the building; it ran about 25,000 copies an issue and lasted into the early 1980s (Parry says 1985; Clark says it folded about 1983). Full runs are at the Enoch Pratt Library and the Sophia Smith Collection, Smith College.

A subscriber's copy of the winter 1970 issue. Her handwritten notes on the cover record a $4 check sent Nov. 1 (1969) for four issues, $5 for the next year sent April 19, 1970, and another $5 on Aug. 2, 1971 for back issues: a reader's-eye trace of a mail-order journal run from Greenmount Avenue.
Cover of the fall 1970 issue, $1.00, a linocut of a model in an art class. Published while the journal's office was on the second floor at 3028 Greenmount, over the five-month-old free clinic.

A late issue (ISSN 0043-7433, $2.00), around 1980, from the journal's last years. Clark notes the collective kept printing lesbian and straight writers side by side (the 1977 "Women Loving Women" issue) rather than splitting.

Photograph of 3026 (the porch-front end house) and 3028 with its three Queen Anne dormers, under a continuous awning reading "3028" and "People's Community Health Center" with a phone number, and a ramped entrance. It dates to after the ca. 1990 unified storefront and before the 2014 foreclosure; 3026 had joined the clinic assemblage by 2010.

The Sun of July 2, 1913, p. 12: 'FOR SALE-3026 and 3028 GREENMOUNT AVE., in Waverly; 6-room, porch-front; up-to-date, with every convenience, on most accommodating terms. Location unsurpassed. AULL, 210 East Lexington st.' The run code j2-6t means six insertions from July 2; the ad also ran in the Sun of July 3 (p. 14) and July 4 (p. 10) and in the Evening Sun of July 2, 3 and 4 (p. 11). It offers the pair as 'up-to-date' houses; it does not say they are new. The west side of the block had been renumbered before it appeared: Polk 1913, canvassed in the autumn of 1912, already prints Zepp Photo Supply Co. at 3044, the building that had been 3030. So '3026 and 3028' are two of the four brick dwellings Jacob H. Aull put up on the old toll-house lot, for which the permit was issued in April 1912. In December 1912 Aull had leased the four houses for 99 years to Alice M. Chapman and sold only the four ground rents to F. X. Hooper (S.C.L. 2787/374 and /376), so what was for sale here was the houses, held under the lease and subject to the rents; whether Chapman had by then assigned them back to Aull is not shown in the deeds read.

A help-wanted ad seeks a young woman to demonstrate Kerr's Pure Food Products during the Made-in-Baltimore Exposition, at good salary. Applicants were to see Mr. Sanner at 3028 Greenmount Ave. between 3 and 5 o'clock Thursday.
Mr. Clark, going out of the Saratoga chips (potato chip) business, offers two work horses cheap with a 10-day guarantee. Apply in the rear of 3026 Greenmount Ave.

Clark's, rear of 3026 Greenmount Ave., advertises a 3-ton truck for $550, a 1915 Ford delivery for $185, a 1915 Ford touring car for $185 and a Kline for $175. The ad appears under an 'Open Sunday' heading.

Clarke, rear of 3026 Greenmount Ave., offers a 3-ton truck, Kline touring, Buick roadster, Ford touring, 7-passenger Paige, Oakland touring, Buick touring, two Overland tourings, a truck body, and a 'fine Saddle Horse.'
A marriage license was issued to George P. Plitt, 22, and Ella H. Shields, 20. The applicant was C. D. Shields, 3032 Greenmount Avenue.

A roundup of five accidents the day before. In one, the automobile of Charles D. Shields, 3032 Greenmount Avenue, struck 14-year-old Ernest ('Renest') Fortney of 3325 Payne Street in Wyman Park. Fortney was cut and bruised and taken to Mercy Hospital. The other accidents (Warwick near Savage, Baughn/Shavetz, Twyne, Papagno) are unrelated.

Charles Shields of 3032 Greenmount Ave. was driving his friends Mr. and Mrs. George M. Cosgriff (3017 Barclay St.) home from their usual morning drive through the parks. His car collided at Guilford Avenue and Twenty-seventh Street with a car driven by Kenneth Harford of 420 Tuxedo St. Cosgriff, 65, died at Homewood Hospital of a brain concussion, and his wife had a skull fracture and was not expected to live. Harford was arrested. His passengers Tony Staylor and Charles G. McCleary (2718 Barnard St.) fled, and Coroner John J. Morrissey ordered them arrested.

At 11 a.m. at Guilford Avenue and 27th Street, a large car driven by Kenneth Harford, 21, of 420 Tuxedo Street, reportedly owned by Flora F. Dashew of the Park Circle Apartments, hit a small car. The small car was thrown against a lamp post. Mr. and Mrs. George W. Crosgriss of 3017 Barclay Street were thrown out and taken in serious condition to Homewood Hospital. Charles Shields of 3032 Greenmount Avenue, the owner and driver of the small car, was cut and bruised. Harford was arrested by Sergeant Rudel and Patrolman Pazourek and held at the Northern Police Station.

Edith R. Shipley (nee Mills), wife of Charles Shipley, died August 10, 1929. The funeral was held from the residence of her sister, 3026 Greenmount Avenue, on Tuesday at 3:30 p.m., with burial in Baltimore Cemetery.

A fragment of a list (likely zoning appeals or permits) includes 'Barber shop at 3032 Greenmount avenue,' after an entry for extending a store and dwelling at 4616-4618 Eastern Ave. Dr. Court Robinson later remembered the early clinic sitting "behind an actual barber shop," and in 1974 the clinic owned a small storefront next door.
Help-wanted ad seeking a barber for Fridays and Saturdays at 3032 Greenmount Avenue. This implies a barbershop operated at 3032 in 1940.

Early that morning, fire wrecked a one-story brick garage at 3018 Vineyard Lane behind Oriole Park, destroying eleven cars and a tractor. Patrolman John T. Mooney discovered it about 5 a.m. and ran to No. 31 Engine Company on Greenmount near 32nd Street; two alarms were sounded. The M. M. McCormack family was roused from a frame house at 3016 Vineyard Lane. Smoke filled the 3000 block of Greenmount and made four houses untenable. The residents who fled: the John Spellmans and two children (3026), Mr. and Mrs. William Wantland (3028), Mr. and Mrs. Davis McCoy and son (3030), and Mrs. Alva Shields and two sons (3032). The garage was owned by the Bay State Oil Company, and the cause was unknown. The four households: Spellman (3026), Wantland (3028), McCoy (3030), Shields (3032).
