Photo caption: Mrs. Alva Shields and her son Charles were among the Greenmount Avenue residents forced from their homes when a fire wrecked a garage at 3018 Vineyard Lane, destroyed eleven cars and sent smoke into the houses. They live at 3032 Greenmount Avenue. The caption also says John and Helen, children of Mr. and Mrs. John Spellman, were driven with their parents from their home at 3026 Greenmount. A separate item in the same caption covers the rescue of a Mrs. Brandenburg from a burning building at 5 West Franklin Street by Fireman Edward G. Sullivan.

On Monday, a group of Black boys walking on York Road at Old York Road and Thirty-Sixth Street met white boys, who shouted racial slurs, and a fight followed. William Richardson, 14, of 926 Springfield Avenue was treated at Union Memorial Hospital for cuts to the face and head. Charles Shields, 16, of 3032 Greenmount Avenue struck Richardson as he walked away, and other white boys kicked him. Police arrested Shields, who faced a juvenile court hearing on assault charges.
The Waverly Juniors have an open date for Sunday and want to hear from 14-year-old indoor baseball teams. Contact D. F. Shields, 3032 Greenmount Avenue, or phone University 5856 between 6 and 9 p.m.

John M. Amend, widower of Sarah Amend, died suddenly May 7, 1937, at his residence, 3030 Greenmount Avenue. The funeral was held at the William Cook Mansion, St. Paul and Preston Sts., on Monday at 10 a.m., with burial in St. Peter's Cemetery.
Marriage-license listing: Frank Elder, 33, of 3030 Greenmount Avenue, and Catherine Kinsella, 34.
Ad for a refinished 28-foot Chris Craft runabout with a new motor, 50 mph, priced at $3,000. Phone CH. 9696. It is at Joe's Garage, rear of 3026 Greenmount Avenue.

Mr. and Mrs. John T. Spellman Jr. of 3026 Greenmount Ave. announced the Aug. 7, 1942 marriage of their daughter Helen Mae Spellman to George W. Hyde, USA, son of Mrs. Dudley F. Hyde and the late Mr. Hyde of 2411 Talbot Road. The other notices on the clip (Cohen-Nordin, Caughy-Brown, Kelley-Chance, Austin-Bures) are unrelated. The Kelley-Chance item mentions 3026 Baker Street, not Greenmount.

Martha V. Berterman of 3030 Greenmount Avenue died May 8, 1942, aged 71. She was the widow of Herman I. Berterman. Funeral services were at the William Cook Mansion, St. Paul and Preston streets, the following Monday at 1:30 p.m., with interment in Parkwood Cemetery.

Mrs. Ida H. Caples of the Blackstone Apartments married Dr. Nicholas Interrante of 3030 Greenmount Avenue on June 26, 1943, at Towson Baptist Church, with the Rev. H. J. Evans officiating. The couple planned to live at 506 McCabe Ave., Govans.

J. Holliday Riepe, Inc. reports the sale of an apartment dwelling at 3028 Greenmount Avenue to William Freitag. It also reports sales of 1926 Parksley Ave. to Louis Schlining and 1904 Harlem Ave. to Mrs. Frances Forrest, and a three-year lease of 5,000 sq ft at 7-11 East Balderston St. to Pioneer Plastics Corporation for Liberty Wholesale Drug Company. The start of the Freitag ownership that ended with Charles C. Freitag's 1975 deed to the clinic.
Help-wanted ad for an A-1 auto mechanic, good pay and conditions, apply Saturday or Monday at Joe's Garage, 3020 Vineyard Lane, rear of 3026 Greenmount Avenue.

A marriage license was issued to Delmond Shields, 31, of 3032 Greenmount Ave., and Virgina [Virginia] Whalen, 34. The other license entries (Schloss-Adelberg, Trentler-Dodge, Volandt-Lankford, Klein-Rogers, Tucker-Hardesty, Dunaway-Taylor) are unrelated. The Shields family's tenure at 3032 runs at least 1919-1946.

For-sale ad for a Bush Pressman 2 1/4 x 3 1/4 camera with a Carl Zeiss lens, Abbey gun, and Argus C-3 with rangefinder and flash unit, in excellent condition. Call at 3028 Greenmount Avenue before 6 p.m.
Business-directory ad: Lake Home Improvements, 3028 Greenmount Avenue, telephone BEl. 8999.

A one-line classified ad offers an electric Coca-Cola machine, 'reasonable', at 3028 Greenmount Ave, phone CHesapeake 9601. It shows 3028 in private or commercial hands selling off equipment in early 1949, four years after the Freitag School of Music is said to have been founded (1945).

The Associated Builders and Contractors of Maryland will hold a meeting at 8 o'clock Monday night at 3028 Greenmount avenue on 'Tips on Your Income Tax' and 'Income Tax Frauds in Contracting'. Speakers are Louis Judges of Stegman & Co. and Eli Baer, attorney and tax specialist. Charles H. Feihe, C.P.A. and board chairman of the association, will moderate a panel.

William F. Freitag Sr., 70, a former Baltimore Symphony Orchestra trombonist, died Thursday at Union Memorial Hospital. In recent years he had directed a music school at 3028 Greenmount avenue. He founded the Freitag School of Music in 1945 and ran it until shortly before his death. Before that he taught trombone at the Peabody Conservatory for 25 years and was a soloist with the symphony and the municipal park band. Survivors: wife Belle Hackett Freitag (married 50 years on Feb 20, 1959); daughters Dorothea Freitag and Mrs. Eudrice H. Timmons; sons William F. Freitag Jr., Charles C. Freitag and Orville H. Freitag. Services at the Leonard J. Ruck funeral establishment, 5305 Harford road; burial in Moreland Memorial Park. The obituary gives the middle initial F. and a 1945 founding for the Freitag School of Music, which settles the white paper's William E. / public-web William H. discrepancy in favour of William F.

Classified list of commercial rentals includes 'Retail Store - 3028-30 Greenmount Ave. Low Rent.' Others listed: 3,738 sq ft W. Balto.; 5,500 sq ft at Jones Falls Expressway; 309 E. Saratoga St.; 122 S. Howard St.; 782 W. Pratt St. The 3028-30 space was on the market about eleven months before the free clinic opened there in May 1970. Eleven months before the clinic opened, and around when Women: A Journal of Liberation was being planned.

Rev. Philip Berrigan, 43, a Josephite curate at St. Peter Claver Church for 18 months, led a four-man picket through downtown Baltimore (Howard street) with signs counting the 'bombing days until Christmas'; the squad had picketed daily since December 16. The picket was organized by the Baltimore Inter-Faith Peace Mission, formed in mid-October 1966, which had grown from 10 to 25 members, held vigils at War Memorial Plaza and the Civic Center, and met Senators Tydings and Brewster. Berrigan, a WWII infantry officer, had been moved to Baltimore in 1965 after peace activity at Epiphany College, Newburgh, N.Y. Lineage: Peace Mission (1966) -> Baltimore Defense Committee (1968) -> free clinic (1970).

Profile of Thomas Lewis, 26, Baltimore artist and painting teacher, who had produced 120 silk-screen 'No More War - Peace' signs and 100 'God Is Love' signs for anti-war marchers at War Memorial Plaza, the Civic Center and Washington. He says he would go to jail rather than to Vietnam and had served eight years in a National Guard missile program. He has an exhibition at One Charles Center, a studio at 51 South Gay street, earlier had a studio in the 1500 block of (Bar)clay street, and is on the steering committee of the Inter-Faith Peace Mission. Born in Uniontown (Pa.), came to Baltimore 1958, graduated Mount St. Joseph High School, teaches at a Baltimore county adult program and Mercy Hospital.

Weldon Wallace's feature on Rev. Philip Berrigan's two campaigns: against the Vietnam war, and for housing in his St. Peter Claver parish on Fremont street off Pennsylvania avenue (Census Tract 15-1), where seminarians from Woodstock College and St. Mary's Seminary did a house survey, organized block clubs and picketed landlords. It covers his WWII service, civil rights work in New Orleans, freedom rides, his 1965 transfer from Epiphany College, Newburgh, to Baltimore, and his role instigating the Baltimore Inter-faith Peace Mission. Photo shows him with residents of a rehabilitated street.

July 4, 1967 roundup. About 25 protesters held a 'beach-in' at Sandy Point State Park, played football, handed out about 500 leaflets asking 'Is this the spirit of '76?' and talked about Vietnam with about 20 beachgoers. Thomas Lewis, an artist who made the silk-screen signs and a leader in the Inter-Faith Peace Mission, organized it. The rest covers holiday closures, a beer strike, a hippie gathering at Mount Vernon, and a civil-rights carnival at Brookfield and Newington avenues.

AP wire story datelined Baltimore. Four peace offices are counseling young men on conscientious objection as an alternative to military service. David Eberhardt, one of the organizers, says most of the work is in the inner city's Black community. His group calls itself the Inter Faith Peace Mission. One office is at the Vietnam Summer headquarters, a project begun at Martin Luther King's suggestion. Two to three men a week file exemption claims at one of the four offices.

AP wire photo and story: the Inter Faith Peace Mission has set up four draft-counseling 'peace offices' in Baltimore as a counter to military draft boards. Organizer David Eberhardt says counselors emphasize conscientious objection and that most of their work so far is in the inner city's Black community. One office operates at the Vietnam Summer headquarters, a project started at Dr. Martin Luther King's suggestion. Pictured: Rob Engorn, 19, with counselors Dave Eberhardt, Eric Feinblatt and Robert Wade.

AP wire photo. Rob Engorn, 19, seeks information on the military draft at one of four offices set up in Baltimore by the Inter Faith Peace Mission. Dave Eberhardt (left rear) said on Wednesday [Aug 9, 1967] that counselors stressed conscientious objection as an alternative to fighting in Vietnam. The other counsellor is Eric Feinblatt.

AP story. Four peace offices were operating in Baltimore as a counter to draft boards. Organizer David Eberhardt said counselors emphasized conscientious objection and that most work so far was 'in the inner city in the Negro community.' His group, the Inter Faith Peace Mission, ran one office at the headquarters of Vietnam Summer, a project begun at Dr. Martin Luther King's suggestion. Eberhardt said two or three men a week filed conscientious-objector claims at one office, and that 'All we do is within the law.'

Carl Schoettler reports that the Inter Faith Peace Mission has opened a network of four 'inner city anti-draft boards' to counsel draft-age youths on their Selective Service rights, and hopes to open more. Organizer David Eberhardt says they discuss all alternatives to military service, emphasizing conscientious objection and Form 150 (the C.O. form). He estimates two or three people a week are filing the form through the centers. The photo shows Rob Engorn, 19, with workers Dave Eberhardt, Eric Feinblatt and Robert Wade.

The Inter Faith Peace Mission has opened a network of four 'inner city anti-draft boards' to counsel draft-age youths on their Selective Service rights. Organizer David Eberhardt says they discuss all alternatives to military service, emphasizing conscientious objection.

At a 'happening' Sunday in a coffee house on West Twenty-second street, war protesters ripped up a huge paper American flag. Thomas P. Lewis, 27, artist and art teacher, organized it, wearing an 'Uncle Sam' top hat and red-white-and-blue bathrobe, then an Asian peasant's hat. The folk-rock band 'The Sons of Eden' played; Mr. Eberhardt read Rimbaud, and John Dash, 23, of the Inter-Faith Peace Mission, read a poem by George Hitchcock. Participants were mostly late teens and early twenties.

Anti-war leaders reported three acts of vandalism: rocks through the glass front door (Saturday about 4 P.M.) and a ground-floor front window (Sunday evening) of the Peace Action Center, headquarters for Baltimore's peace organizations in the 2500 block of Maryland avenue, and a rear window at the 2700 block St. Paul street home of William O'Connor of the Inter-Faith Peace Mission steering committee. David Eberhardt, the mission's secretary, tied it to Friday's demonstration in which blood was poured on Selective Service records at the Custom House. Rev. Philip F. Berrigan and Thomas P. Lewis were fasting in the City Jail infirmary; Eberhardt and Rev. James L. Mengel (United Church of Christ) were released on recognizance. Eberhardt cited static and beeps on the peace center's phone as evidence of FBI wiretapping. The Peace Action Center became the Baltimore Defense Committee's base, the People's Action Center, where the clinic was planned.

Roger J. Nissly reports on a poverty 'trial' sponsored by the Rescuers from Poverty on a Tuesday night at the First Apostolic Faith Church. The panel included Sen. Joseph Tydings, a representative of the governor, a City Councilman, a peace spokesman and two militant civil rights activists. Legal Aid attorney Arthur Cohen, U-JOIN organizer Walter Lively, Dr. Gilbert Ware and Robert Douglass spoke. When a representative of Father Berrigan arrived, Tydings called the pouring of blood on government records 'most unfortunate.' Dave Eberhart, secretary of the Inter-Faith Peace Mission, warned that Black soldiers may come back 'in a pine box' or 'with real violence.' Danny Gant of CORE Target City and Mrs. Peggy McCarty, head of Rescuers from Poverty, also took part.

Stephen J. Lynton reports that Robert Libershal, who said he was the son of Lt. Col. Theodore M. Libershal (stationed in Iran), burned what he said was his Army induction notice on the Custom House steps. He had refused to report for induction that morning, objecting to Selective Service and the Vietnam war. Demonstrators organized by the Inter-Faith Peace Mission handed him about $60. The story continues on page C7, which is not clipped.

AP: the defense was to begin that day as the federal jury trial of four antiwar demonstrators reopened in U.S. District Court, Baltimore. Judge Edward S. Northrop had postponed it day-to-day because of the April 1968 civil disorders; the last session was Friday, April 5. The defendants were accused of pouring blood on Selective Service records in Baltimore the previous October. All pleaded innocent and all belong to the Baltimore Interfaith Peace Mission. They are Rev. Philip F. Berrigan, 44, a Catholic priest; Rev. James Mengel, 38, a United Church of Christ minister; Thomas Lewis, 27, an artist; and David Eberhardt, 26.

The Baltimore chapter of SANE (National Committee for a Sane Nuclear Policy) and Maryland Veterans for Peace in Vietnam withdrew from the Peace Action Center. The center had been supported mainly by four groups: the Inter-Faith Peace Mission, the Fellowship of Reconciliation, and the two that left. They left chiefly over the center's journal, the Peace and Freedom News, which called itself 'Baltimore's first underground newspaper.'

A disagreement among Baltimore peace groups has halved the membership of the Peace Center in the 100 block of West 22nd Street. The Baltimore chapter of SANE and the Maryland Veterans for Peace withdrew over publication of the 'underground' Peace and Freedom News. The Inter-Faith Peace Mission and the Fellowship of Reconciliation remain.

The Baltimore Defense Committee called on anti-draft supporters to demonstrate against the Federal Court trial of the Catonsville Nine, charged with burning about 800 draft files with napalm at the Catonsville Selective Service office on May 17 (1968); trial set for October 7. The committee planned a mass march to 'free the Catonsville nine' and criticize Governor Agnew, and applied for a permit to march south on Charles street from 29th street to Lexington avenue, 10 A.M. to noon Oct 7. Expected: David Dellinger, Bishop James A. Pike, Tom Hayden, Dick Gregory, Joan Baez. Mary Moylan, who proposed the clinic in 1969, was one of the Nine.

City Solicitor George L. Russell Jr. said the Baltimore Defense Committee would get permits for two marches on the opening days of the federal trial of the Catonsville Nine. The Monday march would go from Wyman Park to War Memorial Plaza, with the city requiring Howard Street rather than Charles Street, then picketing to the Post Office where the trial would be held. An October 8 march would go from Mount Vernon Place to the Customs House (Gay and Water streets), where city draft boards were. Gren Whitman, a BDC official, applied for the permits. Expected marchers included Bishop James A. Pike, David Dellinger, Thomas Hayden, Dick Gregory and Joan Baez. The Nine were charged with damaging about 800 draft files taken from the Catonsville Selective Service office and burned on May 17.

AP. The Catonsville Nine were going on trial that day in U.S. District Court, Baltimore (Chief Judge Roszel C. Thomsen). They were accused of seizing about 600 draft records at the Catonsville draft board on May 17 [1968] and burning them with homemade napalm. The Baltimore Defense Committee, an outgrowth of the Baltimore Interfaith Peace Mission, organized a demonstration: a march of about 1,000 from Wyman Park to War Memorial Plaza, then picketing the Post Office Building. Gren Whitman was BDC's full-time organizer. Expected speakers included Episcopal Bishop James A. Pike and David Dellinger. The defendants: Rev. Philip F. Berrigan, 44, and Thomas P. Lewis, 27, both already serving six years for the October 1967 blood-pouring; Rev. Daniel Berrigan, 47; Brother David Darst, 26; John Hogan, 33; Thomas Melville, 37, and his wife Marjorie, 38; George Mische, 33; and Mary Moylan, 'a registered nurse from Washington.'

A columnist mocks the Baltimore Defense Committee's use of 'leaflet' as a verb in its schedule of events. This included 'leafleting' Fort Meade the previous Sunday to protest bloodshed in Vietnam, and a picket line that day at Hubert Humphrey's $100-a-plate dinner at the Pikesville armory. A further unrelated item concerns a public takeover of the Baltimore Transit Company.

Paul D. Samuel reports that the Baltimore Defense Committee planned demonstrations for November 7-8 around the sentencing of the Catonsville Nine, who were convicted October 10 on three charges. It was writing to out-of-towners who had come during the October 7 trial week, when about 1,500 people gathered. Plans: a reading by Father Daniel Berrigan at Goucher College gym at 8 p.m. Nov 7, a march to the Battle Monument (renamed the 'island of life'), and an all-night vigil. On Nov 8 there would be a 9 a.m. War Memorial Plaza rally and march to the federal courthouse for sentencing by Chief Judge Roszel C. Thomsen, then a 7 p.m. 'political prisoners' rally at St. Ignatius Hall, 700 block N. Calvert Street, which had served as the October headquarters. Spokesman Grenville Whitman expected a smaller turnout and said the committee spent about $1,500 on the trial-week campaign and would be 'surprised if we spend $200 now.'

Continued from page E8: at a federal hearing before Judge Frank A. Kaufman on remanding H. Rap Brown's case, William Kunstler argued that moving Brown's trial from Dorchester County (40 per cent Black) to a county under 10 per cent Black violated the Civil Rights Act, while Mr. Sweeney argued for state jurisdiction. The Baltimore Defense Committee issued a release demanding an end to the harassment of Brown ('Free Rap Brown') and quoted the Kerner Commission. It warned that whites as well as Blacks would 'take to the street.' The story identifies the BDC as the successor to the Baltimore Inter-Faith Peace Mission.

H. Rap Brown, through attorney William M. Kunstler, asked federal Judge Frank A. Kaufman to have his arson and riot charges from the July 1967 Cambridge riot tried in Dorchester county rather than Harford, which he said was chosen for its small Black population. Deputy attorney general Robert F. Sweeney defended the transfer. About 75 supporters attended, and several people from the Baltimore Defense Committee, 'a group which opposes the Viet-nam war', appeared with signs outside. A short item below reports Henry C. Tate, 50, of the 1200 block North Gilmor street, died in a Western district cell.

By Stephen J. Lynton. Elijah C. Boyd, Jr., 24, a lieutenant and self-described No. 3 man in the local Black Panther Party, was arrested at 12:40 P.M. Tuesday [Dec 24, 1968] at the Trailways bus terminal by Allie Morton, a Walso Bureau private guard. The charges were disorderly conduct and resisting arrest, and he was released on $1,250 bail. Boyd said he was distributing the party newspaper and was Maced and kneed. Morton denied using Mace. Boyd described himself as liaison officer in charge of ties with the Baltimore Defense Committee, 'a predominantly white anti-war group.' He lived in the 200 block of Chestnut St, Turners Station (Dundalk), and gave the local Panther headquarters as the 1200 block of North Eden Street. The party did not admit white members but welcomed ties with sympathetic white groups. Earliest documented Panther-BDC tie, a year before the joint clinic plan.

In its newsletter, the Baltimore Defense Committee sent mock congratulations to two newly promoted detectives from a city police intelligence unit that infiltrates 'underground' groups: Sgt. Edward V. Woods, 31, and Sgt. Clarence M. McGee Jr., 43. The newsletter called them 'loyal comrades' who 'get involved in everything we do.' Maj. Maurice M. du Bois, director of inspectional services and their superior, said they were very gentlemanly and probably had some friends in the committee.

AP, Washington. Nine people entered Dow Chemical's Washington offices 'yesterday' (Sat March 22, 1969). They poured what they said was human blood on furniture and threw records out a fourth-floor window in protest of Dow's napalm, defoliants and nerve gas. Those arrested included four men who said they were Roman Catholic priests and a woman who said she was a nun teaching at a nearby Catholic seminary. A reporter had been tipped two weeks earlier by a representative of the Interfaith Peace Mission in Baltimore that a 'happening' would occur. All nine were charged with second-degree burglary and destroying property. Also on the clip: an unrelated item on Harlem Hospital closing and an advertisement.

Whitney Gould reports on the Milwaukee 14, who on Sept. 24, 1968 (including five Catholic priests) doused and burned thousands of draft records at a Milwaukee Selective Service office. They face state arson, theft and burglary charges plus federal conspiracy charges, and bail cost $95,000; their state trial is set for May 5 before Judge Charles L. Larson. Co-counsel Percy L. Julian Jr. and William Kunstler want a federal 'political trial'. The article quotes Fr. Daniel Berrigan, who burned draft records 'with eight others last May in Catonsville, Md.' A 'Who Are the 14?' sidebar says Fr. James Harney spent a year working in Baltimore poverty areas and co-founded the Baltimore Inter-faith Peace Mission. Other stories on the page (Iowa student survey, conservation column) are unrelated.

Continuation. Protesters kept a 'death watch' at the Custom House from 9 A.M. to 11.40 (A.M.) beside seven placards of Dr. King and a banner 'How Many Deaths Till We Know Too Many People Have Died', then walking teach-ins, then a 90-minute vigil from 1.55 P.M. The Baltimore Defense Committee planned a gathering in Wyman Park and soap-box speeches, and an 'Easter Peace Parade' from City Hall Plaza to Wyman Park the next day. No violence or arrests.

Easter Sunday parade, part of the 'April Action' in 45 cities coordinated by the Philadelphia-based National Action Group and marking the anniversary of King's assassination. About 630 left City Hall plaza at 2.40 P.M., swelling to about 800 near the 30th block (police said 750); they gathered at the Civil War monument in Wyman Park. Six teenagers wearing National States' Rights party armbands heckled. The BDC announced William Hinton, author on Communist China, would speak at 8 P.M. Wednesday at the Enoch Pratt Free Library, 400 Cathedral street.

Jump from page 1. Friday's (June 20, 1969) anti-war demonstration at Fort Meade was planned by the Baltimore Defense Committee. It protested the arrest eight days earlier of three high-school students handing out antiwar leaflets in the base housing areas; trespassing charges against them were later dropped. Protest leader Dean Pappas said the group also wanted soldiers to know 'we were here and that we care'. Marchers were told to move on by military police. An unrelated 'Smith wins in Rhodesia' headline is also clipped.

Local anti-war groups plan to step up organizing among soldiers at Fort Meade after Military Police arrested three high school students, Christopher E. Darling, 17, Edward Johnson, 16, and Lillian Taylor, 16, all of Baltimore, for handing out anti-war leaflets in the Meade Heights housing area at about 2.30 P.M. Thursday. The Baltimore Defense Committee, organizing the campaign, issued a leaflet announcing the arrests. Arraignment set for July 9 on trespass charges. Adjacent: City Council passes the anti-loitering bill.

Three Baltimore women who say SDS and other left groups deny women equal footing will publish 'Women: A Journal of Liberation', first issue due in August (1969). Spokeswoman Dee Anne Pappas, a former English instructor at Goucher College and Park School, plans to work on it full time; co-editors are Mrs. Donna Keck and Mrs. Vicki Pollard. Her husband Dean Pappas is a leader of the anti-war Baltimore Defense Committee. She says the Baltimore women's movement is a year old. Dee Anne's husband Dean led the BDC; Donna's husband Jim founded the clinic.

Tonight's events listing includes a lecture, 'The New Left: Who? What? Why?', given by speakers from the Baltimore Defense Committee at the Randallstown branch of the Baltimore County Public Library at 8 p.m. The other listings (Eric F. Goldman on the LBJ years, dinner theaters, a Leary 'Graffiti' cartoon) are unrelated.

Continuation of a Moratorium-weekend teach-in at four downtown stops. Two speakers asked for community control of hospitals and an end to profit in medicine; Willa Walsh of the Women's Liberation Movement said the health system exploits women by denying abortion and natural childbirth and underpaying women hospital workers. At the Blaustein Building, Dean Pappas of the BDC called for support of the Brazilian revolutionary movement. Speakers also stopped at the Custom House; the largest crowd was at Johnson Square near the Maryland Penitentiary, where Black Panther party speakers joined. A van cruised Gay street chiding marchers; some carried a Viet Cong flag. Six months before the clinic, its two sponsors were already making health care a political demand. Speaker Willa Walsh is Willa Bickham of Viva House.

The two-day 'Operation Native Son' recruiting program for college seniors drew 800 seniors and about 20 anti-war demonstrators in its first four hours. Four members of the Baltimore Defense Committee got into the Civic Center and handed out leaflets before police escorted them out. They joined other protesters on Lombard Street with signs such as 'Work For People-Not Profit' and 'Join The People's Movement.'

About 20 BDC demonstrators were refused a literature table inside the Civic Center at 'Operation Native Son', a Chamber of Commerce career drive by 105 companies aimed at June college graduates, attended by over 1,000 seniors. Eric C. Hallengren, 25, an Eastern High School teacher, asked chamber official William K. Weaver for space and was refused; police (Sgt. Richard M. Catania, Maj. George C. Schnabel) moved them to the sidewalk, where they leafleted 13 employers as tied to the military-industrial complex until 2 P.M.

The Black Panther Party and the Baltimore Defense Committee need $4,000 to establish 'The People's Free Medical Clinic in the Franklin Square area of west Baltimore.' A newsletter says the clinic will serve both Black and white patients, because existing institutions 'never served the needs of the poor.' Some doctors and equipment are available, but no building has been acquired. They hope to buy a building where renting out the parking lot, basement and apartments would pay the mortgage. A Community Information Center staffed by BDC, the Panthers, Women's Liberation and hopefully a Welfare Rights group would offer legal, housing, birth-control, abortion-counseling and pre-natal help. Donations were to go to The People's Clinic Support Fund, 5907 Ridgedale Rd., Baltimore 21209. Three months before the clinic opened at 3028 it was still planned for West Baltimore, with a Community Information Center; in 1974 the clinic's storefront next door carried a "Community Information Center" sign.

By Sandra Grant. A free clinic, believed to be the only one in Baltimore not tied to a hospital or public agency, was due to open at 6 P.M. that day (Mon May 4, 1970) at 3028 Greenmount Avenue. It was sponsored by the Baltimore Defense Committee and the Women's Liberation Movement and would charge no one, whatever their ability to pay. Volunteer staff were to include doctors, medical students, nurses, psychiatrists, social workers, technicians, and counselors for abortion, birth control, drug abuse and alcoholism. James Keck, a high school teacher and Baltimore Defense Committee member, is quoted. The clipping stops at the jump (Continued, Page D2, Col. 2).

Continued from page D20: Mr. Keck describes the planned free clinic. No one will be charged even if they can pay; there will be only a donation box. Operating money has come from individuals and from high school students who collected donations, the largest single gift being $50, and drug companies have donated medicine. At first it will be open 6-10 p.m. Mondays and Thursdays, since the volunteer doctors and staff work elsewhere by day. It will treat minor illnesses and chronic conditions such as diabetes, high blood pressure and some heart disease, refer and follow up on other cases, and run a women's counseling service offering early pregnancy testing, birth control and abortion counseling, prenatal classes and natural-childbirth classes. Keck says medical problems can't be divorced from social and economic ones (for example, heat and landlord problems), and the clinic will be a place for people to organize for adequate care. Only the jump page was clipped; the front half (page D20) is still to find.

By Sue Dinges. Johns Hopkins president Dr. Lincoln Gordon was among 34 college presidents who signed a letter to President Nixon (sent May 4, 1970) urging him to end the war quickly and warning of youth alienation. The Johns Hopkins Strike Committee, student leaders from three other colleges, the Baltimore Defense Committee and the Central Committee of Baltimore High Schools (a black student group) were planning a march and rally at the War Memorial and Federal plazas Friday afternoon [May 8, 1970]. Continued on C3.

A free clinic, believed to be the only one in Baltimore not connected with a hospital or public agency, opened Monday at 3028 Greenmount avenue. It is sponsored by the Baltimore Defense Committee and the Women's Liberation Movement and is free to anyone regardless of ability to pay.

By Sandra Grant. The People's Free Medical Clinic at 3028 Greenmount had been 'swamped with patients' since it opened May 4. It had almost 700 visits by more than 400 patients and about 50 patients on each of its two nights a week (Monday and Thursday). Coordinator of clinic services Howard Evans said the clinic took in about $300 a month through a pledge system, was not in debt, and had ten volunteer doctors rotating, four per night. It began as a project of the Baltimore Defense Committee and the Women's Liberation Movement. About 50 women had sought early pregnancy detection or abortion and birth-control counseling, and about 50 people had sought VD diagnosis. Photo by Carl D. Harris shows a crowded waiting room. Coordinator Howard Evans is the "Howie Evans" Jim Pickett said left to run the Baltimore Experimental High School.

Garrett Bang's feature ahead of the August 26 nationwide Women's Strike. The main force in Baltimore is Women's Liberation, formed in August 1968 by about 10 women active in the Baltimore Defense Committee, since joined by mostly white, middle-class, college-educated women with jobs and families. As an organized group it works out of a double row house at 3028 Greenmount avenue, across the street from a church, a cemetery and a shopping center. The building is shared with the Free Medical Clinic, and the women pay about half of the $375 rent from pledges. Photo (Richard Childress): women reading to children under posters including 'War is not healthy for children and other living things'. The "church, cemetery" across the street is St. John's, 3009 Greenmount, whose parish hall Dr. Robinson recalled the clinic using for meetings.

Continuation of Garrett Bang's feature (starts p.18). Karen Whitman, 27, a founder, lists what the group points to: the free clinic 'which we sponsored and continue to support', the birth and abortion counseling program, the magazine 'Women: a Journal for Liberation' 'which we put out here', and a summer child-care program run with fathers; a Women's Liberation seminar at Catonsville Community College is planned. It describes a consciousness-raising meeting on Wed Aug 19 at Julie Wilkenson's 2d-floor apartment, 2900 Silver Hill road. The Birth and Abortion Counseling Clinic 'is part of the Free Medical Clinic which takes up half the building at 3028 Greenmount avenue', open Monday and Thursday nights 6-10, run by coordinator Leah Schofield (the only full-time Women's Clinic worker, on subsistence pay) and 12 women counselors. In its first 20 evenings it counseled 77 women; abortions for women with money cost $400-$700 through private doctors. Husbands profiled: Robert Pollard (Vicki's husband, Hopkins sociology grad student), Wolfgang Fuchs, 28 (Towson State philosophy teacher, runs a play group at Stoney Run Friends Meeting House), Brian Schofield (Hopkins Medical School research assistant, Leah's husband).

By George Hanst. Eric Hallengren, 26, a former city-schools English teacher who lived in the 2900 block of North Calvert Street, denied in Criminal Court (Judge Paul A. Dorf) that he caused the May 13 [1970] riot at the Flower Mart near the Washington Monument. He also denied hitting a policeman with a cherry snowball. He testified that he was an active member of the Baltimore Defense Committee, an anti-war group, and well known to police. Richard Hurley, 26, testified that a police lieutenant singled out Hallengren's arrest record and said 'Hey, we've got a real radical here.' Kiser D. Barnes of the state Human Relations Commission and witnesses Mavis J. Duff and Alan DeJardin described police overreaction, clubbing and Mace. Prosecutor Stephen L. Miles said Hallengren cursed police and urged the crowd on.

Feature by Barbara Gold on Women: A Journal of Liberation, a Baltimore quarterly. Dee Ann Pappas, Donna Keck and Vicki Pollard conceived it at the beach in summer 1968. They first worked out of Keck's Mount Washington house. The staff now 'work at an office on the second floor of the Women's Liberation Center at 3028 Greenmount avenue.' The first printing was 3,000 copies, with 10,000 more reprinted, and the current first printing is 20,000. SUNY Buffalo and the University of Washington ordered it for courses, and it is cited in 'Sisterhood is Powerful' and a New York Times editorial. It is a leaderless collective with no editor. Donna Keck (husband Jim, an infant son) and Karen Whitman (husband Gren, a 5-year-old) co-own a Guilford Avenue row house and share child care. The fourth issue has an article on lesbianism. The Kecks and the Whitmans (Gren of the BDC) shared a Guilford Avenue row house.

Glenn Ehasz, 28, known for two years in Baltimore as a modest photographer, was asked in October 1969 to become an unpaid staff photographer for Harry, Baltimore's underground paper. He photographed demonstrations and went with Baltimore radicals to two out-of-town leftist conferences. His friends learned he was a police agent when he testified for the Baltimore Police Department at a trial the previous week.

Continuation of Antero Pietila's story. Glenn Ehasz testified that since graduating from the Police Academy in September 1969 he had been a $10,500-a-year special agent for the Baltimore Police Department doing surveillance of the radical left, in the roughly 20-member Inspectional Services Division ('Red Squad') that answers directly to Commissioner Donald D. Pomerleau. One of his first assignments was to infiltrate the Maryland Peace Action Center in the 2500 block of Maryland avenue, headquarters for many radical groups including the Baltimore Defense Committee. He went with BDC members to a Weatherman SDS meeting in Chicago (fall 1969) and with Thomas V. D'Antoni to a Milwaukee conference, and worked as a photographer for the underground paper Harry under pseudonyms (Leiky Leica, Kosmic Konica, Papa Topcon, Gordon Leach). It also notes Jimmie L. Foxworth, a patrolman who infiltrated the Black Panthers until his arrest in summer 1970. Ehasz was arrested at the February (1971) Charles Center Laos rally, shot film of Rev. Joseph Wenderoth, and testified against Frederick Freeman ('Hank Smack'). His undercover years span the clinic's planning and opening.

AP story: Glenn Ehasz, 28, a photographer for Baltimore's underground paper Harry, revealed himself as a police undercover agent. He had spent two years spying on the radical left for the BPD 'Red Squad.' He joined the force as a $10,500 special agent and became Harry's unpaid staff photographer in October 1969, with department approval. He infiltrated the Baltimore Defense Committee and went with its members to a Chicago Weatherman SDS meeting. A year later he went to the Strategic Action Conference in Milwaukee with Harry staffer Thomas D'Antoni. He testified about film he shot at a February 1971 anti-Laos rally, used against a leftist charged with inciting to riot and attempted murder of a policeman. Commissioner Donald D. Pomerleau had denied him a press pass, and Harry sued. He left last week for a Florida criminology school.

AP: Glenn Ehasz, 28, son of a wealthy Long Island City, N.Y. consulting engineer, spent two years as a Baltimore police undercover agent. He was hired as a $10,500 special agent for the department's 'Red Squad' surveilling the radical left. From October 1969 he was an unpaid staff photographer for Harry, Baltimore's underground paper. His film of a February (1971) rally against U.S. involvement in Laos was used in a case against a leftist charged with inciting to riot and attempting to murder a policeman. He infiltrated the Baltimore Defense Committee, went with its members to a Chicago meeting of the Weatherman faction of SDS, and a year later attended the Strategic Action Conference in Milwaukee with Harry staffer Thomas D'Antoni. When Commissioner Donald D. Pomerleau denied him a press pass, Harry sued. He left the previous week for a criminology master's at Florida State University.

Sun Magazine feature by Cei Richardson (photos Ellis Malashuk) on the People's Free Medical Clinic. Its logo swaps the caduceus wings for a clenched fist and its letterhead reads 'Medical Care Is a Right, Not a Privilege'; it runs on 130-150 volunteers and donations only. The idea was born at a meeting of the now-defunct Baltimore Defense Committee, which spent nearly a year planning; BDC members included Mary Moylan of the Catonsville Nine. The clinic occupies a green stucco-front former music school in the 3000 block of Greenmount in Waverly; on its opening night in May 1970 only 17 patients came (6-10 PM). Sixteen months later it is open four nights a week (Tuesdays reserved for women), has treated about 3,400 patients in 6,750 visits; only three GPs serve a 115-square-block area of 25,000 residents east of Greenmount and south of 33rd. The magazine counts 17 patients on opening night; Keck remembered 12.

Continuation. A Union Memorial Hospital spokesman, four blocks away, says its ER handles about 50,000 visits a year near capacity and 35% of ER patients are not true emergencies; the new Union Memorial will take three years to build. The free clinic can handle at most 50 patients a night and must screen; coordinator Arthur Roach says they would rather see 30 well than 60 sloppily. Diane Wilson, 35, a coordinator at the nurse's station, came to the clinic when no doctor would see her feverish child; she volunteers one night a week and her 12-year-old daughter helps in the child care room upstairs. A Maryland League of Nursing pilot survey (April) found ERs impersonal; the PFMC assigns every patient a trained 'advocate'. Photo: Arthur Roach, 21, checking a patient file.

Male volunteers (brothers, husbands, friends of members) were to run a bake sale from noon to 4 P.M. Saturday [Nov 6, 1971] in front of Vermont Federal Savings and Loan in the Northwood Shopping Center to raise money for the local Women's Liberation counseling center. The Women's center at 3028 Greenmount had opened 1-1/2 years earlier. It advised and referred women with legal, physical or emotional problems, published a newsletter, and hoped to start a day care center.
The Baltimore Women's Liberation Movement will hold a 'Men's Bake Sale' on Saturday, Nov. 6, 1971, at Northwood Shopping Center. Proceeds go toward funding the Women's Center at 3028 Greenmount Ave.

Tail end of a notice about an all-day Saturday meeting to form a Maryland Women's Caucus, with workshops on influencing the legislative process and running for office, plus four more, including one on the caucus's structure. It is sponsored by 44 Maryland women active in politics, business and education, with a $2 fee, open to all Maryland women. The contact given is the Baltimore Women's Political Caucus, Women's Center, 3028 Greenmount avenue, 366-6475.

A 'Women's Weekend' of speakers, workshops, seminars and films on women's issues is set for Saturday and Sunday, Jan. 15-16, 1972, at the Belvedere Hotel, Charles and Chase Sts. The featured speakers are Mickey Zakuto of New York Radical Feminists and Delegate Hildegardeis [Hildegarde] Boswell. The sessions run from 10 a.m. Saturday and 11:30 a.m. Sunday to about 5:30 p.m. Arrangements are coordinated at the Women's Center, 3028 Greenmount Ave., 366-6475.

A pre-Roe service box listing five places women can call for pregnancy testing or abortion advice, all free, with contributions welcome. No. 3 is the People's Free Medical Clinic, 3028 Greenmount avenue, 467-6040, reachable noon-5 PM Monday-Friday and 5-11 PM Thursday. The others are Planned Parenthood of Maryland (809 Cathedral St.), Florence Crittenton Homes (West 32d St. and Crittenton Place), the Baltimore City Health Department maternity center (211 West Lombard St.) and the Personal Rights Organization (169 Duke of Gloucester St., Annapolis).

By Sharon Dickman. Baltimore Women's Liberation (BWL) kept a low profile at 3028 Greenmount. Its Women's Center shared 'the crowded household' with the People's Free Medical Clinic and Women: A Journal of Liberation, and had a large second-floor meeting room. Donna Keck, one of about 12 women at the first 1968 meeting, said she and others started Women: A Journal of Liberation in 1969. Office manager Karen Dickinson earned $35 a week and was behind on rent. Kee Hall assigned women to consciousness-raising groups (about 25 in the area, 2 lesbian, 1 co-ed), and more than 500 women got the newsletter. The center planned to move to a rented house, and Waverly Presbyterian Church at Old York Road and 34th Street offered space for a non-sexist day care center expected to open July 1 if $2,000 could be raised. Sidebar: Francine Brown, who ran the office when the center opened two years earlier, recalled the original meetings at the Peace Action Center and painting the Women's Center walls. Waverly Presbyterian at Old York Road and 34th Street (3401 Old York Road) offered space for the movement's day care, likely the Red Wagon Day Care Center later watched by police.

Death notice for Marion Ramsay of Arlington, Va., formerly of Baltimore, who died Monday May 22, 1972. He was husband of Alma Gaines Ramsay, father of Andrew Ramsay (Annapolis), Jeanne Ramsay Bunyon (Honolulu) and Walter G. Ramsay (Tabriz, Iran), and brother of Theodore Ramsay (Baltimore). Viewing was at W. W. Chambers Funeral Home, 3072 M St NW, Washington, with services May 30 and burial at Culpeper National Cemetery. In lieu of flowers the family asked for contributions to the Peoples Free Medical Clinic, 3028 Greenmount avenue.

One entry in a list of community groups, apparently those taking booths at a fair. Neither the clinic nor the Waverly People's Free News had officers. The two were independent but had similar aims. The News (1,200 circulation, nickel donation) was produced monthly by 5 to 10 people meeting in homes. The clinic had about 150 volunteers, with a community meeting the fourth Sunday of each month at 3028 Greenmount. The day staff met Tuesday afternoons and night staff on their own night. The clinic's service area ran from Charles St (west) to Loch Raven/Ellerslie (east), 39th-York-33rd-Charles (north) and 25th St (south). The News covered BGE rate increases, the median strip controversy and recreation, and helped force PSC rate hearings. Adjacent entries: Waverly Youth Group (Bob Rosenteel, 618 E. 30th St) and Western Community Improvement Association.

By Jon Franklin. The People's Free Medical Clinic still flew its upraised black fist sign. In January 1974 the national Junior Chamber of Commerce named it one of the country's most outstanding self-help programs. Volunteer Dr. John Ruckdeschel, 28, of Hopkins and the Baltimore Cancer Research Center, said a $1,500 furnace replacement left $300 in the bank against about $2,000 a month in costs. The clinic had about 6,000 patient visits a year, pledges bringing a steady $250 a month, and Medicaid paying about $6 a visit. It already owned a small storefront next to the main clinic at 3028 Greenmount, but paid $375 a month rent on the main building. The lease was about to run out, and buying the main building needed about $10,000 down (about $200 a month in payments). Photos by Carl D. Harris show the storefront sign and Ruckdeschel with patient Kathy Farrell and staffer Leon Bankard. The storefront is 3032: the Rubenstein estate assigned it to the clinic in Oct. 1972, and its sign read "People's Free Medical Clinic / Community Information Center," the name of the drop-in center planned for the aborted 1970 Franklin Square clinic.

AP Washington story: a senior Ford adviser says CIA Director William E. Colby's 50-page report to the President substantially supports allegations that the CIA engaged in illegal domestic spying on U.S. citizens. Senate Watergate transcripts show John W. Dean 3d testified 18 months earlier that the Nixon White House got regular intelligence reports on demonstrators and radical groups from the FBI and sometimes the CIA. Dean described an Interagency Intelligence Evaluation Committee that operated from late 1970 to July 1973. Continues on A6 (not clipped).

Jump page of the ISD exposé. Mr. Smeak, a Northern District patrolman (later a sergeant), says he began feeding the BPD Inspectional Services Division in February 1970. He hand-carried reports on the Peace Action Center at 2525 Maryland Ave. (later the People's Action Center) to Sgt. Burritt and Sgt. William H. Bowen, who ran car tags through the MVA onto index cards. His beat ran 25th St. to University Pkwy.; he watched the Friends Meeting House (3107 N. Charles) and 2700 St. Paul, where William Kunstler and Daniel and Philip Berrigan stayed, plus 600 Cator Ave. (M.A.N.). Maj. Norton admits ISD infiltrated or watched groups including the Baltimore Defense Committee, Black Panthers and Catonsville Nine, says two boxfuls of files were burned, and claims political surveillance stopped in late 1973. Gov. Mandel has demanded a full report.

Letter from Dean Pappas of Baltimore. He learned that Self-Help Housing, the city agency he worked for in early 1969, was on the ISD's watch list. The News American reported that a county police informant infiltrated Baltimoreans Against Retaliatory Evictions (BARE), which Pappas helped organize as Self-Help's housing adviser to lobby against evictions of complaining tenants. The Sun reported that two anti-war groups he belonged to, Teachers Concerned About Vietnam and the Baltimore Defense Committee, were also watched by ISD. He rejects Commissioner Pomerleau's 'disorder, revolution, and strife' justification. An unrelated letter ('Cry for Help') on Baltimore County federal funds shares the clip.

The People's Free Medical Clinic at 3028 Greenmount celebrated its fifth anniversary the week of April 29, 1975. It had about 100 volunteers offering general, gynecological, pediatric and dental care, early pregnancy detection, and abortion counseling and referral, free to about 7,500 patients a year from Waverly and Charles Village. Events included blood pressure screenings at 25th and St. Paul, Eddie's Market (3100 block St. Paul), The Rotunda and 34th and Greenmount, and films on abortion and adolescent problems at the clinic counseling center, 3032 Greenmount. Also planned: a square dance at Levering Hall (JHU), an auction at St. Johns Church (27th and St. Paul), a street festival at Vinyard and 30th, and a community supper at Montpelier Mini-Park on May 4. Contact: Jim Keck.

Letter from (Ms.) Carol V. Calhoun of Baltimore attacking Harry Kaufman's proposals (in an earlier Sun letter) to remove illegitimate children after the second from their mothers, and to force 'voluntary' abortion or sterilization on unmarried women. She argues the answer is free contraception, abortion and sterilization for any woman who wants them. She notes she works for the People's Free Medical Clinic at 3028 Greenmount avenue, which gives contraceptive and abortion-referral services free to the community. An unrelated 'Sundance' letter by Joseph I. Paper (on Mayor Schaefer) shares the clip.

Thomas Pepper (Sun Washington Bureau) reports the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence (Church Committee) found the FBI tried to discredit Martin Luther King Jr., including an anonymous letter read as urging suicide. The committee also said that in the 1960s FBI agents looked into a Baltimore women's liberation group, concluded its aim was to free women from being 'only a wife and mother', and kept watching it anyway; chief counsel F.A.O. Schwarz 3d asked what it was all worth. Same page: former Black Panther leader Eldridge Cleaver was taken into FBI custody on arrival at Kennedy Airport from Paris. Other front-page stories (Rumsfeld defense bill, parking tickets, Spanish Sahara) are unrelated.

Jump of the Church Committee story. It covers ex-FBI agent Arthur Murtagh's testimony that he was asked to help block Andrew Young's 1972 election, William C. Sullivan's 1963 memo on taking King 'off his pedestal', the 16 bugs and 8 wiretaps, and the text of the anonymous 1964 letter. It states that the surveillance of the Baltimore women's group involved an organization identified in an FBI document as the 'Women's Liberation Movement', headquartered in 1968 at an office of the Baltimore Defense Committee, an anti-war organization, in the 2500 block of Maryland avenue. It also describes FBI anonymous letters meant to disrupt activists (a 1970 St. Louis example).

James H. Bready profiles Mary Jane Lupton (Baltimore), Janice Delaney (Washington) and Emily Toth (Grand Forks, N.D.), co-authors of 'The Curse: A Cultural History of Menstruation', due from Dutton in late August 1976. Lupton came to Charles Village in 1968 married to a Morgan State English teacher, and joined Morgan's English faculty in 1969 under Nick Aaron Ford. After consciousness-raising meetings she helped with the new 'Women: A Journal of Liberation', 'published in those years from movement headquarters' at 3028 Greenmount. The article calls it the oldest serious publication in its field, with two or more issues a year circulating nationally and still going strong. She also wrote an Elizabeth Barrett Browning biography for the Feminist Press and worked on a textbook-sexism report; at 37 she became Morgan's first white female full professor.

The Baltimore School (TBS), an anarchist-tilted alternative 'learning network', ran a left-perspective 'A Newcomer's Guide to Baltimore' bus tour led by coordinators Glenda Morris, Howard Ehrlich and Vicki Dello Joio. First stop: the site of the 'Baltimore Peace Defense Committee' in the 2300 block of Maryland Ave. The bus passed the People's Free Medical Clinic on Greenmount and parked on 31st St., in what Ehrlich called Waverly's cluster of alternative institutions. Per Ehrlich, whites and Black Panthers planned the clinic in 1969, but the Panthers pulled out at the last minute to start their own clinic, which never happened, and police confrontations destroyed the local Panthers. On 31st St. were the Bread and Roses coffeehouse (a meeting place for the New American Movement, Baltimore Gay Alliance and TBS) and, across the street, Sam's Belly (a year-old food co-op) and the 31st Street Bookstore. The page also carries an unrelated German-wine column.

The People's Free Medical Clinic, 3028 Greenmount, was to sponsor concerts by the Hadley Square Singers at 8 p.m. July 7 and 2 p.m. July 8 [1978] at St. Bernard's Church hall, 928 Gorsuch Avenue. Tickets were $2.50 for adults and $1.75 for children. Contact: Joan Biegeleisen, 396-7250.

The People's Community Health Clinic, formerly the People's Free Medical Clinic, planned a 'gauze cutting' reopening celebration from 5 to 8 p.m. Wednesday, Sept. 30 [1981] at its facility, 3028-3032 Greenmount Ave. The renovation was aided by a Baltimore City Department of Housing and Community Development grant. Phone 467-6040. The renovation had a city DHCD grant.

Barbara Pash feature (photos Ellis J. Malashuk) on the People's Community Health Clinic, a private nonprofit, at 3028 Greenmount avenue (photo caption). Director Patricia Cassatt stresses informed patients. The clinic reopened in September 1981 after a year of renovation, in three adjacent rowhouses in the 3000 block of Greenmount, with volunteer professionals (physicians, PAs, nurse-practitioners, a nurse-midwife) and lay patient advocates. It was founded in 1970 by anti-Vietnam war and feminist groups and a few doctors. Volunteer coordinator Lenore Meyers; Dr. Randy Barker, internist, has volunteered about 10 years and follows about 30 patients.

Services include general and geriatric medicine, pediatrics, podiatry, Tuesday-night gynecology and family planning, TB tests, pregnancy tests, blood pressure checks and WIC screening. In 1980 the clinic changed its name from the People's Free Medical Clinic. Dr. Bob Cotter, board secretary since the beginning, says 'free' never meant no cost. A new fee schedule ($20 initial medical visit, $15 pediatric) applies, but no one is refused. Health services coordinator Diane Wilson says about 80% of patients have no coverage; about 3,500 patients a year, nearly 70% women. Nurse-midwife Jasmine Lampadarios runs the Tuesday women's night with all-female advocates. There are 14 professionals (two dentists joining) and 30 advocates (20 women, 10 men); board president Barbara Dent says it is the only clinic in the city with patient advocates.

Photo: Cecil Arthur gets a blood-pressure check from physician's assistant Esther Thrasher. Dr. Cotter says for the first four or five years the clinic ran on the energy of anti-war organizers; as they left, a board of trustees was formed and grants paid for a staff of five and renovations. Original founder Dr. Lee Randol, a pediatrician, still volunteers. The U.S. Public Health Service Hospital provides back-up lab work and a loaned PA. The service area is Waverly, Charles Village and Harwood. During the year-long closure the buildings were boarded up and 'some people thought we'd died', with services at neighborhood sites. The Baltimore Center for Counseling Services rents space in the newly opened buildings. Board president Dent cites rising costs and the threatened closing of the PHS Hospital. Hours: noon-5 weekdays and 7-10 PM Tue/Wed/Thu; 3028 Greenmount; 467-6040.

By Wanda L. Dobson. The Baltimore Center for Counseling Services had closed nine months earlier when $82,000 in block grant funds from the Urban Services Commission ended. It reopened about three weeks before (mid-October 1981) with $4,000 in private money under a 10-member board. After 10 years at North and Eutaw streets, it now had free office space donated by the 'People's Committee [sic] Health Clinic' at 3028 Greenmount in Waverly. Twelve counselors, eight of them original staff, volunteered crisis and family counseling. The center had served about 1,200 people a year and more than 20,000 in all. Board member Patricia Cassatt said it needed about $15,000 a year. Urban Services' Lloyd Michener said the center had ranked low in evaluation. The crisis line was 243-1112.

By Carl Schoettler. The front-page (D1) half of a feature on the People's Community Health Center, 'one of the very few survivals of the 1960s activism still extant in Baltimore.' About 3,500 people would make 5,000 visits that year. Executive director Pat Cassatt said it was 'the first independent clinic on the East Coast,' started by 'progressive' doctors at about the same time as the Berkeley Free Clinic. The logo raises a clenched fist out of the caduceus. The William Hotz photo shows Cassatt in front of the 'People's Community Health Center' storefront.

Continuation (full page D2 clipped). Pat Cassatt had been director about 3-1/2 years. The center opened in Waverly in 1970 in the first of the three rowhouses it now occupied in the 3000 block of Greenmount. It would mark its 14th year with a 1960s dance, 'Dancin' in the Streets,' at St. John's United Methodist Church, 27th and St. Paul. Bob Cotter, 41, an early patient advocate and later board member, said the founders came mostly from the Baltimore Defense Committee, formed during the Catonsville Nine trial, plus the Baltimore Women's Liberation Movement. He said the Black Panthers were involved but 'bowed out early' to pursue a school lunch program in a black neighborhood, and 'the parting was amicable.' Services by then included outreach in six schools, geriatric care, $4.20 tooth fillings and a volunteer podiatrist. Photo: Jessica Brain and her month-old daughter Jennifer with Cassatt. The rest of the page is unrelated (Bratt murder trial, Wise narcotics case, bank-records bill by Gwen Ifill, trooper case). Three versions of the Panther exit: Keck (a national order after the Chicago raid), Cotter here (amicable, for a lunch program), and 1990 (safety problems).

After a January 25, 1985 fire, which the fire department calls suspicious, heavily damaged its storefront headquarters at 1817 East Baltimore St., the Baltimore Welfare Rights Organization is seeking money for new offices. The building's use had been donated by the United Methodist Missionary and Church Extension Society. Director Bobby Cheeks said the group has since been using space at the Black United Fund headquarters at 3028 Greenmount avenue. Families can call the Black United Fund at 467-7460 to reach caseworkers, who are working from home. The group also needs used clothing.
The People's Community Health Center will hold a 15th anniversary party from 6 to 8:30 PM on Sept. 11, 1985 at the Health Center Facility at 3028-3032 Greenmount Ave.; call 467-6040.

Display ad for Peoples' Community Health Center, Inc., 3028 Greenmount Ave., 467-6040. It lists family planning, gynecology, primary medical general care, podiatry, dentistry, pediatrics, WIC screening, geriatrics, TB tests, blood pressure screening, pregnancy tests and prenatal care.

By Ellen Hawks. Many patients of the People's Community Health Center at 3028 Greenmount Ave. had no insurance. Health outreach worker Erin N. Grace, a Lutheran Volunteer Corps volunteer from Ohio (Valparaiso University), said the center took the $19 per visit Medicaid paid. The non-profit had a 13-member board and about 20 employees, with Patricia Cassatt as director and Dr. Murray West as medical director. It was partly state-funded for family planning. History as told here: in 1969 the Baltimore Defense Committee and the Black Panthers, who had opened other clinics, joined forces. The Panthers pulled out over safety problems at other clinics, the Coalition of Women's Liberation joined, and the center opened in 1970. When Cassatt took over in 1980 costs rose, some staff were hired, and patients began paying on a sliding scale. Federal designation failed under a funding freeze. Sidebar: nurse Susan Sharp, a Union Memorial nurse who volunteers as patient advocate, and dentist Dr. Harvey (Hank) Landay (UMD Dental 1970), a volunteer of more than 15 years. Here the Panthers left over safety problems at other clinics.

By Sue Miller. Doctors and nurses from the University of Maryland and Johns Hopkins, with independent social workers and others, held a news conference 'today' at the People's Community Health Center at 3028 Greenmount Ave. They opposed the federal Title X 'gag rule' barring abortion counseling at federally funded family planning clinics, which Congress had voted to overturn and President Bush had threatened to veto. Dr. David A. Nagey, director of maternal-fetal medicine at UMD School of Medicine, said the rule threatened care for 100,000 poor Maryland women at 95 clinics statewide. Several practitioners said they would defy it.

Jonathan Bor reports that about a dozen people from Baltimore health-care centers met at a private clinic on Greenmount Avenue, the People's Community Health Center, 3028 Greenmount Ave., on Nov. 14, 1991. They protested President Bush's threatened veto of a bill lifting the ban on abortion counseling at federally funded family planning centers, and several said they would defy the 'gag' rule. Dr. David A. Nagey, chief of high-risk pregnancy at University of Maryland Medical Center, would rather violate the rules; Johns Hopkins physicians and a city health clinic also vowed defiance, while Planned Parenthood of Maryland said it would give up federal funding. Continued on 3D (not clipped).

Four gifts totaling $45,500 will let the People's Community Health Center expand services. They are a $20,000 Harry and Jeannette Weinberg Foundation challenge grant matched by the Abell Foundation, $5,000 from the William G. Baker Jr. Fund and $500 from the Morton and Sophia Macht Foundation. The money will buy property near the center, which 'has been providing free medical care for 25 years at 3028 Greenmount Ave.' Administrative offices and certain services will shift to 3011-3013 Greenmount, per executive director Patricia S. Cassatt.

Legal/bid notice: the People's Community Health Center seeks bids for a new elevator, masonry enclosure and interior alterations at its facility at 3028 Greenmount Avenue. Drawings are available at CMC Reproduction and Associates, 8847 Orchard Tree Lane, Towson, and can be viewed at Dodge Reports, 1301 York Road, Lutherville. A pre-bid site meeting is set for 10 AM Nov. 2, 1995; sealed bids are due at the center by 3 PM Nov. 17, 1995 and will be opened publicly.

Ad/appeal for People's Community Health Centers Inc. (PCHC), a Federally Qualified Health Center serving uninsured and underinsured residents of Baltimore City and Anne Arundel County. It seeks donations for capital improvements to expand to Brooklyn Park and Pioneer City (Anne Arundel) and to West Baltimore on Franklintown Road. Board chair Robert O'Hatnick; executive director Patricia Cassatt; contact Terry McDaniels, 3028 Greenmount Avenue, Baltimore 21218, [phone redacted] x239, www.peoplesCHC.org. Slogan: 'Health Care is a Right, Not a Privilege.'

Foreclosure auction ad by K&L Gates LLP (1601 K Street NW, Washington), acting as substitute trustees, for a medical office building at 3028-3032 Greenmount Ave., Baltimore 21218. The auction is Thursday, Dec. 4, 2014 at 12:00 PM at the Calvert Street door of the Clarence M. Mitchell Court House, 100 N. Calvert St. Alex Cooper Auctioneers (Paul Cooper, [phone redacted]) is handling it, with a $15,000 deposit.

Deed dated March 6, 1912, read on the page image (a poor bilevel scan of the handwritten record copy; words in brackets are doubtful): The President, Managers and Company of the Baltimore and Yorktown Turnpike Road, a body corporate, to Jacob H. Aull, 'in consideration of the sum of two dollars ($2) and other valuable consideration', in fee simple, 'so much of the following described lot or parcel of ground ... as is outside of both the charter line and the present actual boundary line of the Baltimore and Yorktown Turnpike Road': from the intersection of the west side of the York Turnpike with the north side of Gilmor Lane (38 ft wide), 57 ft north on the turnpike, 100 ft west at a right angle, 51 ft 7 1/2 in south to the lane and 100 ft 1 3/4 in east on the lane. The intersection is tied to a stone [eight] ft to the north marking the beginning of land conveyed to David Mumma in 18[44] (Baltimore County T.K. 354), and the company held the lot by a deed of July 5, 187[-] from David [S.] Wilson [et al.] (Baltimore County E.H.A. liber, number illegible). The deed is recited in later instruments, among them the 1981 mortgage, and later deeds use its north line as the north line of 3032. Its 57 ft of frontage is exactly the four lots Aull leased on Dec. 6, 1912 (15 + 14 + 14 + 14 ft; S.C.L. 2787/374), so the lot took in all of 3026-3032. Thompson's 1889 plat letters the corner lot 'York Rd Turnpike Co.', 41 ft 5 in on the road and 117 ft 6 in deep, with a one-story stone dwelling, brick and frame outbuildings and a stable; the difference from the 1912 figures is not explained. Bromley's plates of 1896 and 1906 show no row there, and the old toll house was to be torn down at the end of July 1907 (Sun, July 28, 1907). A month after the purchase Aull announced four two-story brick porch-front dwellings (Evening Sun, Apr. 6, 1912; architect Jacob F. Gerwig) and took the permit as owner and builder (Sun, Apr. 21, 1912: 'northwest corner York road and Gilmore lane', 15 by 47 ft each). Polk 1913 (canvassed in autumn 1912) has no household at 3026-3032. The houses stood by Dec. 6, 1912, when Aull leased them for 99 years to Alice M. Chapman at $72 and $66 a year, and on Dec. 16 he sold the four ground rents to Frank X. Hooper for $4,500 (S.C.L. 2787/376; Sun, Dec. 17, 1912). Polk 1914 has households at 3028, 3030 and 3032, and Polk 1915 adds 3026. In July 1913 'Aull, 210 East Lexington st.' advertised 3026 and 3028 for sale. Aull (1848-1921, Register of Wills estate 176148) was a Waverly real-estate man from the founding shoemaker family and held at least four lots on Gilmor Lane and Waverly Avenue in 1889. Update Oct. 14, 2026: a fresh copy reads the company's title as E.H.A. 70 folio 92, a deed of July 5, 187[ ] from David S. Wilson et al. (725:research-scl2727-29-second-look-eha70-92). Update Oct. 14, 2026: E.H.A. 70/92 is negative (725:negative-eha70-92-96-not-the-wilson-trustees-deed); the recital's worn liber is probably 76 or 78. Update Oct. 14, 2026 (late): the turnpike company's own deed is read (726:mdlr-eha80-97-wilson-trustees-turnpike-first-toll-gate-house-lot-4-1871): Lot 4 of the Wilson estate's Huntingdon plat, 57 by 100 ft at Gilmor's Lane with 'the First Toll gate House', July 5, 1871, $3,000.

By a deed of assignment dated October 12, 1972, Hyman B. Rubenstein, personal representative of an estate, assigned the leasehold of 3032 Greenmount to People's Free Medical Clinic, Inc. (Liber RHB 3152 folio 289, which falls in 1974 in the city's recording sequence, so the existing Aug. 2, 1974 row is probably the recording date). This was the clinic's first property, bought more than two years before it owned 3028. It fits Ken Albright's story of buying the vacant house next door, whose elderly occupant had died, after his summer-1972 bike trip, and the March 1974 Evening Sun report that the clinic "already owns a small storefront next to the main clinic." 3032 had housed a barber shop in 1930-40 (Robinson: the clinic was once "behind an actual barber shop"); by April 1975 it was the clinic's counseling center. Update Oct. 14, 2026: the deed is read (726:mdlr-rhb3152-289-delmond-shields-estate-clinic-3032-1972): the estate is Delmond F. Shields's, who died May 2, 1971 (Register of Wills file A 1328); Alva M. Shields had deeded him 3032 on May 25, 1960 (J.F.C. 873/14). Leasehold at $66; recorded Aug. 2, 1974.

Deed dated Feb. 14, 1975, recorded Feb. 19, 1975, read on the page image: David Siegel to People's Free Medical Clinic Inc., in fee simple, the lot 43 ft north of Vineyard Lane, 14 x 82 ft, running to 'the northernmost outline of the whole lot of ground described in a Deed from President, Manager and Company of the Baltimore and Yorktown Turnpike Road to Jacob H. Aull dated March 6, 1912 ... Liber SCL No. 2727, folio 29': No. 3032. Recitals: the lot is 'fourthly described in a Lease dated December 6, 1912' from Jacob H. Aull and Mary A. J. Aull to Alice M. Chapman (S.C.L. 2787/374), with a $66 rent payable June 1 and Dec. 1; 'THE REVERSION IN FEE together with the annual ground rent was granted and conveyed by a Deed dated November 13, 1964 ... Liber JFC No. 1800, folio 528 from Mercantile-Safe Deposit and Trust Company, Trustee, to David Siegel'; and the leasehold came to the clinic by a deed of assignment of Oct. 12, 1972 from Hyman B. Rubenstein, personal representative (R.H.B. 3152/289). Frank X. Hooper had bought the four rents of the row in 1912 and Mercantile Trust Co. was his trustee in 1945, so the 1964 seller was very probably his trust. Transfer tax not required. The deed merged the 1912 rent with the leasehold the clinic had held since 1972: the 1981 mortgage calls it a deed of merger, and the 2009 and 2014 papers call it a redemption deed. Same day and book as Charles C. Freitag's deed of 3028 and 3030 (folio 657). 3030 kept its separate $90 rent, created in 1951, which later instruments still recite. Update Oct. 14, 2026: Siegel's 1964 deed is read (726:mdlr-jfc1800-528-mercantile-hooper-trust-siegel-3032-1964): $825 from Mercantile-Safe Deposit and Trust Co., surviving trustee under Francis X. Hooper's will, recorded Nov. 30, 1964.

Deed dated Feb. 14, 1975, recorded Feb. 19, 1975 at 11:03 A.M. (Robert H. Bouse, clerk; Title Guarantee Co. application H-85818), read on the page image: Charles C. Freitag to People's Free Medical Clinic Inc., 'those two lots of ground', for 'the sum of Five Dollars, and other valuable considerations'; transfer tax not required. First lot: on the west side of Greenmount Avenue (formerly York Turnpike Road) 15 ft north of Vineyard Lane (formerly Gilmor Lane), 14 ft front through the partition walls and 82 ft deep to a 4-ft alley, No. 3028, in fee simple. Second lot: 29 ft north of the lane, the same size, No. 3030, 'for all the residue of the term of years yet to come and unexpired therein, with the benefit of renewal forever, subject to the payment of the annual ground rent of $90, payable in equal semi-annual installments on the fifteenth days of March and September'. Recital: the April 1, 1969 deed to Freitag from Deborah C. Zimmerman (R.H.B. 2497/414). The $90 rent, created in 1951, belonged to Belle H. Freitag, who subordinated it at the same closing (R.H.B. 3207/653); the closing also carried a $22,850 first mortgage from The Equitable Trust Company (R.H.B. 3207/659), Freitag's $3,250 purchase-money second mortgage (R.H.B. 3207/664) and David Siegel's deed of the 3032 reversion (R.H.B. 3207/655). The 1981, 2005, 2009 and 2014 instruments all recite this deed. The clinic had rented 3028 from Freitag since 1970 at $375 a month; in March 1974 it needed about $10,000 down to buy. Charles was a son of the music-school founder William F. Freitag Sr. (d. 1959).

F. N. Iglehart & Co. reported a six-year lease of the two-story store-front building at 3200 Greenmount avenue, from Mrs. Elizabeth R. Samstag to Benjamin A. Kriger, druggist. The building was to be remodeled for the lessee, who ran a chain of drug stores in the city. This is the Kriger lease: 1929 to 1935, not a lease beginning in 1936. Frederick H. Samstag had died that January, so the building was in his widow's hands.

Kriger's Drug Store wants a young man experienced with the soda fountain and patent medicines. The address is printed as 3100 Greenmount avenue (Evening Sun, July 30, 1929), and it is not a misprint: Kriger's Waverly store was at Greenmount and 31st street from at least October 1928, his full-page advertisement of July 21, 1929 lists '3100 Greenmount Ave.', and his advertisements first give 'Greenmount & 32nd St.' on September 29, 1929, after the corner building he had leased in June was remodeled. The advertisement belongs to the store he was about to leave.

The existing row saying Kriger leased 3200 for five years from Jan. 1, 1936 conflicts with the White Coffee Pot lease of the same building from Jan. 15, 1936, and most likely describes his new store at 3236.

By Theodore W. Hendricks. George J. Bluso, 43, of the 5600 block of Purdue avenue, was described by tax agents as the area's top gambling banker and lay-off man. He was sentenced in Federal Court to one year and fined $5,000 after pleading guilty to three lesser counts (no Federal gambling stamp). He was arrested in 1960, and the probe began in 1957 when his wife was found calling gamblers in a dozen cities. His lawyer, William Greenfeld, said Bluso had since built a prosperous dry-cleaning business in the 3200 block of Greenmount avenue. Bookkeeper David B. Miller, 36, was fined $4,050. Chief Judge Roszel C. Thomsen gave Bluso until Oct 1 to begin his sentence.

The Vinson family held 3015 from 1934 and 3017 from 1943; with 600 E 31st (bought in 1970) the three lots stayed with the family and the Vinson-named corporations (Vinson's Animal Hospital, Inc. from 1982, Vinson's Kennels, Inc. from 1986) until the foreclosure sale of 2004 (FMC 6085/1351).
