Deed dated January 8, 1873 and recorded January 15, 1873 (Baltimore County Liber E.H.A. No. 79, folios 35-37; this was county ground until the 1888 annexation). David S. Wilms, Thomas J. Wilms and Henry R. Wilms, Trustees under the last will and testament of James Wilms, late of Baltimore City, deceased (will dated January 22, 1848, proven and recorded in the Baltimore City Register of Wills), conveyed a lot to Gustar Ruppersberger of Baltimore County. The deed recites that the will gave the trustees full power to sell any of the estate's property; that a chancery bill, William C. Wilms and others v. said trustees and others, was filed in the Circuit Court for Baltimore City over division of the estate; that under a sales plat the trustees filed in that case, they sold "Lot No. 3" at private sale on January 27, 1871 to Ruppersberger for $1,700; and that the court duly ratified and confirmed the sale (with others made at the same time) before the purchase money was paid in full. The lot: situate in Baltimore County in "the Village of Huntingdon or Waverly," beginning at a post on the west side of the York Turnpike Road at a point North 4 degrees East 57 feet from the corner of the turnpike and Gilmor Lane (later Vineyard Lane); thence binding on the turnpike North 4 degrees East 56 feet 6 inches; thence North 85 degrees West, binding on Lot No. 4 of the same plat, 155 feet 3 inches; thence South 5 1/2 degrees West 57 feet to a point 50 feet 9 inches north of Gilmor Lane; thence South 85 degrees East 157 feet 6 inches back to the beginning. Five days later Ruppersberger split the lot and sold the southern half (28 feet 3 inches of the 56 feet 6 inch frontage) to John Schuman for $2,700 -- more than he had just paid for the whole lot, on half the land (729:mdlr-eha79-35-schuman-1873). Signed D. S. Wilms, Thos. J. Wilms and Henry R. Wilms, Trustees, each under seal; acknowledged January 8, 1873 before John I. Maddox, J.P., City of Baltimore; certified by George Robinson, Clerk of the Superior Court of Baltimore City; recorded per Edw. H. Ady, Clerk. Research lead: the trustees' 1871 sales plat evidently numbered at least four lots (No. 3 sold to Ruppersberger, No. 4 adjoining it to the north) along this stretch of the York Turnpike -- worth locating the full chancery case file or plat to see whether Lots 1, 2, 4 and beyond line up with other Corridor parcels on this block. Update Oct. 12, 2026: 'Wilms' here is the clerk's spelling of Wilson. The trustees' deed to John Bolgiano of Jan. 14, 1871 (Baltimore County E.H.A. 70/115-118, scan on file with 3326 Greenmount, mdlandrec-eha70-115) names the same three trustees, David S., Thomas J. and Henry R. Wilson, under the same will of James Wilson dated Jan. 22, 1848 (Register of Wills D.M.P. 24/154), and recites the same Circuit Court for Baltimore City case, William C. Wilson and others against the trustees (decree of Oct. 7, 1869, reports ratified Jan. 7, 1870). Both deeds sell numbered lots on a plat (Lots 16 and 17 there, Lot No. 3 here); neither says whether it is the same plat.

Two same-day instruments, Baltimore County Liber E.H.A. No. 65, folios 405-408 (recorded March 11, 1870): (1) a deed, David S. Wilson, Thomas J. Wilson and Henry R. Wilson, Trustees, to the President, Managers and Company of the Baltimore and Yorktown Turnpike Road, of a lot on the west side of the York Turnpike Road "a short distance north of the present first toll gate"; (2) a $3,000 bond from the Turnpike Company to the Huntingdon Land Company of Waverly, reciting that the Turnpike Company has sold this same lot to Huntingdon Land Co. for $1,500 (due October 1, 1870) and binding itself to convey the fee once paid. The bond describes the lot by the same metes and bounds as the trustees' deed, and adds: "on which piece of ground moreover is now building a public hall erected by the aforesaid Huntingdon Land Company of Waverly." That pushes the start of construction to early 1870 at the latest, earlier than "1872-73," the date this chain had carried until now. David S., Thomas J. and Henry R. -- the same three first names and initials, trustees for an estate settling multiple lots along the York Turnpike in Waverly at almost the same moment -- also sold "Lot No. 3" a few blocks south to Gustar Ruppersberger in 1871-73 (EHA 79/35, property 729), acknowledged and recorded by the same clerk, Edward H. Ady. That deed spells the surname "Wilms"; this one spells it "Wilson." The surname is spelled 'Wilson' in this deed and 'Wilms' in the 1873 deed, and it is now confirmed to be one set of men: the trustees' deed to John Bolgiano of Jan. 14, 1871 (Baltimore County E.H.A. 70/115-118, scan on file with 3326 Greenmount, mdlandrec-eha70-115) names David S., Thomas J. and Henry R. Wilson as trustees under the will of James Wilson dated Jan. 22, 1848, and the 1873 deed (729) recites the same will and the same Circuit Court case. This deed does not itself recite the will, so that these 1870 grantors are those trustees rests on the names, the county and the year, not on a recital.

Assignment dated March 1, 1870, recorded March 11, 1870 (Baltimore County Liber E.H.A. No. 65, folios 408-409). Jacob Aull of Baltimore County assigned to the Huntingdon Land Company of Waverly, for $5, a small lot on the west side of the York Turnpike Road (beginning at a stone marked "D.B. No. 1"; roughly 25 feet on the turnpike by 34 feet deep) -- the unexpired residue of a ground-rent leasehold, renewable forever, rent one cent a year. The lot came to Aull by two earlier ground leases, neither yet pulled: from John Wakeman, dated September 10, 1839 (Baltimore County Liber P.K. No. 92, folio 84), at $32/year rent; and from William R. Jones and Richard H. Townsend, executors, dated May 25, 1842 (Liber P.K. No. 320, folio 150), at one cent/year rent. Signed Jacob Aull, witnessed Thomas H. Robinson, acknowledged March 1, 1870 before a Baltimore County justice of the peace; recorded per Edward H. Ady, Clerk.

99-year ground lease dated March 8, 1870, recorded March 11, 1870 (Baltimore County Liber E.H.A. No. 65, folios 409-411). Jacob Aull and his wife Christina, of Baltimore County, leased to the Huntingdon Land Company of Waverly a lot "being a part of a tract of land called 'Huntingdon,'" beginning at the northeast corner of a lot belonging to the Baltimore and Yorktown Turnpike Road Company (99 feet along that lot, 107.5 feet, 66 feet, back to the beginning). Rent: $24/year from October 1, 1869, paid $12 semiannually each April and October, with the usual re-entry-on-default clauses and a covenant to renew forever. Aull also covenanted that at any time, on payment of $400 plus accrued rent, he would convey the fee simple, freed and discharged of the rent. The lot came to Aull from James Wilson and wife, by deed dated May 28, 1846, recorded among the Land Records of Baltimore County in Liber A.W.B. No. 367, folio 140 (not yet pulled) -- a different Wilson deed than the trustees' 1870/1873 sales (see 735:mdlr-eha65-406-turnpike-bond-1870 and 729:mdlr-eha79-35-wilms-1873), and not yet shown to be the same family. Signed Jacob Aull and Christina Aull, and Henry Taylor, President of the Huntingdon Land Company (as its attorney, under corporate seal); witnessed Jas. H. Strow and Thomas H. Robinson; acknowledged March 8, 1870 before a Baltimore City justice; recorded per Edward H. Ady, Clerk.

The OCR text of an Evening Sun classified page on Newspapers.com includes 'HIGHEST prices paid for furniture ... Call Moses Zalis', with a Vernon (VE.) exchange phone. So Moses Zalis started as a buyer of used furniture, which fits the store's later 'new and unclaimed freight' trade. I saw only the search-result text, not the page, so the date and exact wording are not confirmed. The Vernon exchange points to the 1930s-1950s. Source: The Evening Sun (Baltimore), classified page, Newspapers.com page 373435906.

Moses Zalis died Sept. 25, 1953, of a heart attack at his home, 2326 Anoka Ave., having worked at his store at 819 Greenmount Ave. until the month before. A native of Russia who came to the U.S. alone at 17, he opened a small furniture shop on South Charles St., dealt in used and new furniture, and shortly after 1900 moved to the Greenmount Ave. site that became a furniture center. He sat on the board of Shaarei Zion Congregation; married first Mary Kleiman (d. 1930), then Anna Kolodner; survived by son Dr. Daniel L. Zalis, daughter Mrs. Philip V. Hendelberg, brothers Jacob and Samuel Zalis, and sister Lena Kamerow of Chicago. Source: The Baltimore Sun, Sept. 26, 1953, p.14.

Retirement-sale ads in the Sun and Evening Sun (April-May 1989) announce that Roeth's Jewelers, 3120 Greenmount Ave. (phone 235-9561, the number on the 1979 sign-in sheet), is closing May 20, 1989 after 59 years in Waverly, which puts its opening about 1930. The ads offered 25% then 50% off diamonds, jewelry, watches and clocks and asked customers to collect repairs by May 15; an April 11, 1989 version is headed 'Going Out of Business Sale'. Source: The Evening Sun, May 9, 1989, p.46 (same ad Sun May 6, 1989 p.50, image 378087573; Sun Apr 19, 1989 p.18, image 378112742).

An Evening Sun advertisement's list of participating jewelry stores names 'William H. Roeth, 3120 Greenmount Ave.' in October 1937, the earliest dated Newspapers.com placement of the Roeth store at 3120 found in this pass. The same list names Kibler's Jewelry Store at 3222 Greenmount Ave. Source: The Evening Sun, Oct. 25, 1937, p.21.

Board of Supervisors of Elections lists of registration and polling places in the Sun (Sept.-Oct. 1912, Aug.-Oct. 1913, Sept. 1914) give the Twelfth Ward's First Precinct as 3120 Greenmount Avenue, years before Roeth's Jewelers opened there about 1930. Source: The Baltimore Sun, Oct. 25, 1912, p.5 (also Sun Aug. 23, 1913 p.9, image 365373121; Sun Sept. 12, 1914 p.13, image 214621231).

Judge Joseph L. Carter convicted George J. Bluso, 34, of the 5600 block Purdue Avenue, and Samuel Heilpern, 31, of the 5500 block Nome Avenue, of gambling and conspiracy on March 24, 1953, after Lt. Joseph Byrne's raid on a third-floor room in the 600 block of North Calvert Street on Dec. 2, 1952. The age puts Bluso's birth about 1918-19. This is 25 years before he signed the Waverly merchants' newsletter as association president. Source: The Baltimore Sun, March 25, 1953, p.24 ('Two Found Guilty In Gambling Case').

Four IRS tax agents and a U.S. marshal raided a building at the northwest corner of Madison and Calvert streets and took away a truckload of evidence. George J. Bluso, 40, of the 5600 block Purdue Avenue, and David Miller, 34, of the 3900 block Park Heights Avenue, were arraigned before U.S. Commissioner Allen H. Mezger and released on bail; Bluso posted ,500. A 1961 Sun story says the charge was bookmaking without a federal gambling stamp. Source: The Baltimore Sun, Sept. 29, 1960, p.48.

After gunmen fired on restaurateur and bail bondsman Edward Corbi outside his Southwest Baltimore home, police called in Henry Block (a private club in the 400 block E. Baltimore St.), Julius Salisbury (owner of the Oasis Club, 500 block E. Baltimore St.) and George J. Bluso of the 5600 block Purdue Avenue, then free on bail on the bookmaking charge, to view a suspect because they had had trouble with thugs. The suspect, a 27-year-old salesman, and a second man, Fifer, were released. The Sun adds that Bluso, 42, had been convicted of gambling in 1953. Source: The Evening Sun, May 17, 1961, p.64 (also Sun same day p.25, image 377681047, 'Suspect Freed In Corbi Case').

A twenty-page federal indictment details the alleged wagering business of George J. Bluso and David Miller between Feb. 1 and Nov. 1, 1960; a new automobile, office machines and other equipment were seized in the Baltimore raid, part of Operation Cedar, in which IRS agents made 75 arrests in 30 cities on one day. U.S. Attorney J. Hardin Marion 3d called organized crime a continuing investigation. The two men had been free on bail since their Sept. 28, 1961 arraignment. Source: The Evening Sun, May 31, 1962, p.47.

A Sun wedding announcement records the marriage of Lucille F. Bluso, daughter of Mr. and Mrs. George J. Bluso, to J. Graham Beck, son of Mr. and Mrs. Archie Beck; Rev. Philip J. Stark, S.J., officiated. Lucille appears in her mother's 2004 death notice as Lucille Beck Papaloizos. Source: The Baltimore Sun, Sept. 23, 1973, p.98 (read from Newspapers.com's extracted marriage details, image not rendered).

Help-wanted ads ask for a dry-cleaning superintendent at 50 a week for 44 hours, to supervise the plant, set prices, control productivity and manage employees, two years' experience, 'Call Mr. Bluso, 467-5710', the phone number George J. Bluso wrote on the Oct. 24, 1979 sign-in sheet. The ad ran again in January 1980 at .16 an hour plus overtime. It shows Mr. Nifty ran its own cleaning plant with a staff under a supervisor. Source: The Baltimore Sun, May 1, 1979, p.37 (Jan. 28, 1980 p.33, image 377434186).

Angelina M. Bluso died April 27, 2004. She was the wife of George J. Bluso, mother of Lucille Beck Papaloizos (husband Gus) and Kathy Thanner (husband Larry), and sister of Marie Whitehurst. Visitation was at Ruck Towson Funeral Home, 1050 York Road, with a Funeral Mass at the Carmelite Monastery on Dulaney Valley Road and entombment at Dulaney Valley Memorial Gardens; memorial gifts went to the Calvert Hall College High School capital campaign. The 1958 death notice of Frand Gottuso of 1811 Eutaw Place lists daughters Angelina Bluso and Marie C. Whitehurst, so her maiden name was Gottuso. Source: The Baltimore Sun, April 28, 2004, p.B5 (Gottuso notice: Sun Jan. 4, 1958 p.17, image 375087971).

Albert Morris Plaine, 84, of 3908 West Strathmore Avenue for more than 30 years, died at the Levindale Hebrew Geriatric Center. A Baltimore native, he began his own retail shoe business in Walbrook in the mid-1940s, which his son purchased in 1950; he then worked for Hess Shoes, as a shoe buyer for Irvin's department stores, and later for Factory Shoe Outlet in Brooklyn. He was a Baltimore Shoe Club and 210 Club member and a 50-year member of Chizuk Amuno Congregation; survivors were his wife, the former Edith Schlossberg, and son Stanley G. Plaine. The 1991 profile of Stanley calls the family business Jason Shoes, so Jason Shoes began in Walbrook about 1945 and had been Stanley's for five years when it opened at 3224 Greenmount in 1955. Source: The Baltimore Sun, June 26, 1978, p.10 ('Plaine, 84, once owned shoe store'; also Evening Sun same day p.6, image 371800742).

A Sun retirement-section profile says Stanley Plaine, after Navy service, gave up plans for a PhD to take over his family's business, Jason Shoes, made it a success, yet 'thoroughly despised the business.' In 1981 he nearly died of heart problems and Legionnaires' disease caught on a trip to Canada; he then volunteered with Baltimore County's Office of Aging, created its Senior Box Office (free arts tickets for seniors, about 50 volunteers), helped start the Senior Prom, and got WJZ-13 to create a senior beat. Baltimore County declared 'Mr. Stanley Plaine Day' on April 26, 1985 and he was in the Maryland Senior Citizen Hall of Fame; his daughter is the organizing author Sunny Schlenger. The illness dates his step back from the stores to 1981, two years after Jeffrey Plaine signed for Jason Shoes at the 1979 meeting. Source: The Baltimore Sun, April 14, 1991, p.189 ('Plaine created Senior Box Office').

The Sun's marriage record gives Stanley Gordon Plaine's full name: his daughter Sonia Eileen Plaine married Donald Lee Schlenger, son of Jacob Robert Schlenger. She is the Sunny Schlenger named in the 1991 profile. Source: The Baltimore Sun, March 7, 1971, p.114 (read from Newspapers.com's extracted marriage details).

A commercial-leasing column reports that Jason Shoes Inc. leased 2,000 square feet in the Reisterstown Plaza for use as a family shoe store (broker KLNB). The chain was still opening stores in 1990. Source: The Evening Sun, June 27, 1990, p.81.

Help-wanted ads for a part-time salesman of 'better family shoes' at Jason Shoes, 3224 Greenmount Ave. (1960, and again in Nov. 1965 at top salary for three nights and Saturday) show the Waverly store still operating a decade after it opened. Source: The Baltimore Sun, March 6, 1960, p.109 (also Sun Nov. 9, 1965 p.44, image 376756258).

Harry Orman died Aug. 18, 1993 at the North Oaks Retirement Community after a series of strokes, aged 83. He owned Harry's Liquors on Greenmount Avenue in Waverly for 50 years, retired in 1984, and was known as a wine and liquor expert who offered charge accounts and home delivery. Before the store he had been a partner with his father in a wholesale candy business. Born in Baltimore, he graduated from City College, earned an accounting degree at night at Johns Hopkins, and belonged to Woodholme Country Club and Har Sinai Congregation. His first wife, Rosalie Cohen, died in 1980 and his second, Margaret Palmbaum, in June 1993; he was survived by son Alan Orman of Pikesville (the 1979 sign-in's 'Harry's Jr.') and daughter Betsy Kahn of Greer, S.C. Fifty years before 1984 puts the opening about 1934, just after Repeal. Source: The Baltimore Sun, Aug. 19, 1993, p.144 (also pp.88, 31, 25 same day).

A notice reads: 'We will be closed Monday, Nov. 10 due to the death of our beloved wife and mother, Rosalie Orman. Harry's Liquor Store, 3113 Greenmount Ave.' Source: The Evening Sun, Nov. 10, 1980, p.3.

An Evening Sun survey of wine shops scored Harry's highest and called Harry Orman, his son Alan, and assistant Milton Feldman 'the most formidable triumvirate of wine expertise in the Baltimore area', noting its Bordeaux, Burgundy, German, Spanish and Italian stock and discounts of up to 16.66 percent. A 1982 Sun wine guide again lists 'Harry's Liquor Store, 3113 Greenmount avenue, 235-4883. Ask for Harry Orman, Alan Orman or Milton Feldman.' Source: The Evening Sun, June 26, 1978, p.28 (1982 guide: Sun Feb. 10, 1982 p.32, image 377558260).

Rosen's Liquors ran display ads headed 'Attention Harry's Customers: Now that Harry Orman (of Harry's Liquors on Greenmount Avenue) has retired...', offering credit and free delivery, in April-May 1985. The obituary gives 1984 as his retirement year. Source: The Evening Sun, April 11, 1985, p.64 (also Sun April 12, 1985 p.38, image 378085918).

In an August 1973 Sun story about shortages, 'Harry Orman of Harry's Liquors, Greenmount avenue' is quoted after a grocer who couldn't get mayonnaise or 10-cent potato chips. Source: The Baltimore Sun, Aug. 16, 1973, p.44 (only the attribution line was read).

A dealer list in a 1956 hardware advertisement gives 'Boulevard Hardware, 432 East 32nd St.', putting the store at the address on the 1979 sign-in sheet at least 23 years earlier. Source: The Evening Sun, May 3, 1956, p.62.

Help-wanted ads for a hardware clerk give 'Boulevard Hardware, 3314 Greenmount Ave' (July 1987; Nov. 1988 with phone 235-0749), and Servistar dealer lists in 1989-90 name 'Boulevard Hardware, Inc., 3314 Greenmount Avenue'. A Sept. 1988 ad for an assistant manager says 'Call 235-0749, Mr. Rudow'. So the store's later home was 3314, not (or not only) the 3224 'new location' named in the c.1979 survey. Corridor should check which parcel covers 3314. Source: The Evening Sun, July 2, 1987, p.31 (also Sun Nov. 8, 1988 p.37, image 378246282; Sun Sept. 8, 1988 p.61, image 377964552; Servistar list Sun Jan. 31, 1990 p.150, image 376747604).

The death notice for Elaine Rudow (nee Chesler), who died Nov. 15, 1999, names her husband Maurice G. Rudow and children Scott Rudow, Howe Rudow, Ann Moffett and Lee Rudow; Scott's wife is Gay Rudow (Gay L. Ossman, whose engagement to Scott P. Rudow of Cockeysville ran in the Sun March 9, 1980, image 377647766). A 1984 Evening Sun feature says Elaine owned the Sweet Tooth Candy Shop in the Parkville Shopping Center; whether Maurice started Boulevard Hardware is not established. Source: The Baltimore Sun, Nov. 16, 1999, p.28 (1984 feature: Evening Sun July 25, 1984 p.14, image 372682085).

The Sun obituary of Jennie Alexander, the woodworker known for 'Make a Chair from a Tree', says that as a child she was a regular customer of the old Boulevard Hardware store in Waverly, whose owner gave her Stanley Tools handouts on tool use. It is a small cultural footnote tying the store to one of American green woodworking's best-known figures. Source: The Baltimore Sun, Aug. 4, 2018, p.A10.

A full display ad for the 'Sample Store, 3031 Greenmount Ave.' offers a pre-Christmas sale on corduroy coats at the 'Sample Store Price' of $17.88 and wool flannel pants, with Charge-It, International Charge and N.A.C. credit. It is the earliest dated Sample Store ad at 3031 found in this pass; Sun ads run through the 1960s, and the Afro-American carried one in March 1970 (image 1135262075), so the store also courted Black shoppers. Source: The Evening Sun, Nov. 30, 1960, p.77.

At a September 1968 court hearing, Harry C. Bowie, a clerk at the Red Shed in the 3100 block of Greenmount Avenue, testified that the defendant came into the store on a Monday afternoon, pulled a pistol and forced him and another clerk to hand over the money. So the Red Shed was operating by 1968. Source: The Baltimore Sun, Sept. 18, 1968, p.12.

A 1970 Evening Sun ad for the 'Sample Store-Red Shed' sensational storewide Memorial Day sale runs under a banner for the Waverly Merchants' Customer Parking Lot, with two entrances at 32nd and 33rd Streets on Barclay and tickets validated by participating merchants. The two names ran as one business. Source: The Evening Sun, May 28, 1970, p.25.

A 1974 help-wanted ad seeks salespeople and cashiers 'for brand new Waverly Men's and Ladies Wear Store', full and part time, 'Apply in person, Mon. 10 A.M. to 5 P.M., RED SHED, 3031 Greenmount Ave.' By 1980 the Red Shed was advertising designer jeans (Jordache, Calvin Klein; Sun Nov. 13, 1980, image 377524906). Source: The Baltimore Sun, Sept. 8, 1974, p.160.

James H. Bready's Sun books column profiles the 31st Street Bookstore, started in May 1974 by Betsy Millemann and Francine Brown at 425 East 31st Street and still there, larger and better stocked. In four years it had tripled its floor space and sales; neither partner had ever drawn a salary. The partners joked that the store had been put on a Congressional Record blacklist for selling 'terrorist literature'; it served as a carpool point for the July 9, 1978 ERA March on Washington; and the poet Adrienne Rich visited after reading at Waverly Presbyterian Church. Brown was a Chicagoan with a degree from Evanston's National College of Education; Millemann came from New Hampshire by way of George Washington University and work in psychology. Corridor files the store at 3048 Greenmount; the press address is 425 E. 31st St., the 31st Street side of the same corner (the Belly was at 427). Source: The Baltimore Sun, July 23, 1978, p.62 (James H. Bready, 'Books and authors').

After 13 years in which the store 'rarely made money', its most recent owner, Amy Gaver, decided to sell in 1987. About 450 customers and supporters raised nearly $27,000 and converted it into a consumer cooperative; attorney Barbara Samuels said the store would not have survived without Baltimore's lesbian community, which provided the bulk of the financing. New manager Shirley Hartwell had left an IBM operations-analyst job: 'I couldn't just sit idly by and watch the store close.' It was then one of almost 100 women's bookstores in the country. Source: The Baltimore Sun, Aug. 20, 1987, p.17 (continued p.20, image 377847066).

A Sun books column notes the 31st Street Bookstore Cooperative's 21st-birthday party and 21-percent-off sale at 425 E. 31st St., with readings by Mariah Burton Nelson, Anndee Hochman and Penny Mickelbury. A '21st birthday' in 1994 implies a 1973 start, a year earlier than the May 1974 date the founders gave in 1978. Source: The Baltimore Sun, July 31, 1994, p.66.

A 2021 Sun list of Baltimore LGBTQ landmarks gives the 31st Street Bookstore, 425 E. 31st St., as a literary and social gathering place for lesbians and feminists, alongside the Lesbian Community Center around the corner on Greenmount Avenue. Citing Louise Parker Kelley's book 'LGBT Baltimore', it dates the store 1973 to 1995, says nearby Abell Avenue was nicknamed 'Lesbian Lane', and says Normal's Bookstore succeeded it in the space. Source: The Baltimore Sun, Oct. 3, 2021, p.A6.

A Sun feature by Melody Simmons describes The Belly food cooperative on 31st Street near Greenmount Avenue as a holdover from the '60s back-to-nature movement, 17 years old (so founded about 1975). Its membership file, once 400, held only 75; a $15 membership bought a 5 percent discount. Ms. Tweedy, a former hospital aide who had worked there since 1985, explained the name: 'It was a political thing to have a cooperative and control your own food... You can take anybody to their knees on their belly.' A 2005 Sun article (Apr. 20, 2005, image 248504603) says the Belly, 'a Waverly mainstay', closed more than ten years earlier. Source: The Baltimore Sun, Aug. 20, 1992, p.21.

A 1978 Sun Magazine profile of Howard Ehrlich and his anarchist network (the Baltimore School free university, TBS Radio Forum, and the research branch RG-1) says he surveyed customers' needs and complaints for 'Sam's Belly, the neighborhood food co-op', and ran a readership survey for the Plain Talker, the Waverly-Charles Village community paper. It gives the co-op's fuller name in the 1970s and ties it to the same 31st Street alternative scene as the bookstore. Source: The Baltimore Sun, Sept. 10, 1978, p.321.

An Evening Sun item says Timmons Roberts, an ecologist and Johns Hopkins graduate student, wanted to set up a cooperative exchange between the Belly Co-op in Waverly and the Santa Maria Co-op in Limay, Nicaragua (in one of Baltimore's sister-city areas), trading products and people with Nicaraguans who needed tools and materials. Source: The Evening Sun, Sept. 26, 1986, p.13.

A 1971 Sun classified reads 'FURNITURE & APPLIANCE SALE - EVERYTHING REDUCED. Peddlers Village, 418 E. 31st St. (Waverly), 235-7224'. 235-7224 is the number Nancy C. Smith wrote on the 1979 sign-in sheet. The store kept running furniture classifieds ('Big savings - 1/3 off & more, Peddlers Village 418 E. 31st St.', July 1973, image 377145852; a household and appliance clearance in Nov. 1978, image 373296267), so it was a secondhand-goods store before Corridor's 'antiques' label. Source: The Baltimore Sun, March 22, 1971, p.35.

The same 1978 Sun column on the 31st Street Bookstore lists the neighboring enterprises Brown and Millemann passed on their walk: Sam's Belly, a food co-op; Bread & Roses, a cafe with bookshelves then featuring Ebenezer and the Bludgeons; the Charles Village Shop; Peddler's Village; and the If and When Shop, a cluster that located itself as 'Waverly/Charles Village'. Source: The Baltimore Sun, July 23, 1978, p.62.

The Baltimore-based women's apparel chain Princess Shops, founded by Eli Miller in 1932, had 35 stores in Philadelphia, Baltimore and Maryland at its 1987 peak but shrank to seven, and by May 1989 only three (Reisterstown Road Plaza, Mondawmin Mall, Belvedere Plaza) would remain. The closings followed a disagreement between the two owning families over expansion; president Alvin Miller called the breakup amicable. Daily operations had been run by son Alvin, daughter Beverly Max, her son Robert (vice president) and other Max family members. McCrory, the variety chain, was to open in five locations Princess was leaving in early 1989: Monument Street, Greenmount Avenue, Light Street, Eastern Avenue and Pennsylvania Avenue. The Millers and Maxes said they would keep managing the real estate, which fits Corridor's Miller Realty to Max Properties (1989) transition. Source: The Baltimore Sun, Dec. 30, 1988, p.15 ('Most Princess Shops stores closing', David Rosenthal).

A Board of Liquor License Commissioners notice for Class BD-7 beer, wine and liquor licenses lists 'Northside Bar-Lounge, Inc. (Close Corp.), Jaffe, Sidney, Jaffe, Jeanne: Forming Close Corporation; 3100 Greenmount Ave.' The business on Jeanne Jaffe's line of the 1979 sheet, read as 'North Star Bar & Lounge', is almost certainly the Northside Bar-Lounge, and its address, unknown until now, was 3100 Greenmount. Source: The Baltimore Sun, Oct. 7, 1974, p.41.

Death notice: Sidney Jaffe, beloved husband of Jeanne Jaffe (nee Glassman), brother-in-law of Mrs. Geri Harris, died Aug. 31, 1979; services at Sol Levinson & Bros., interment Beth Tfiloh Cemetery; the family mourned at 6659 Sanzo Road, Apt. D. So Jeanne signed the Oct. 24, 1979 sheet as a new widow running the bar alone. Her own death notice (Sun Oct. 21, 2000, image 173158473) gives her death as Oct. 20, 2000: 'loving wife of the late Sidney Jaffe', sister of Fred and Doris Glassman. Source: The Baltimore Sun, Sept. 1, 1979, p.25 (also Evening Sun same day p.12, image 371244439).

Classified ads list 'Moses Zalis, 3117 Greenmount Ave., 467-9100' from October 1971 (sofabeds and studio couches), again in 1973 and 1976, and a 1987 bunk-bed ad still gives 467-9100. The number had belonged to the American Friends Service Committee, 319 E. 25th St., in 1969 (image 377481406). So 467-9100 on Jeanne Jaffe's line means either that she signed with the furniture store's number or that the sheet's lines are shifted. It matters because the Zalis line ('Walter Neilsen for Moses Zalis') has no phone at all. Read the original sheet again before relying on either attribution. Source: The Baltimore Sun, Oct. 10, 1971, p.181 (also Sun Oct. 7, 1973 p.187, image 377358901; Sun May 2, 1976 p.180, image 377664648; Sun Oct. 11, 1987 p.95, image 378090421).

Help-wanted ads for barmaids name the 'Northside Bar, 3100 Greenmount Ave.' in May 1967, again in 1973 and 1974 (phone 243-9441), and in January 1977 ('Northside Bar, 3100 Greenmount Ave., 243-9441, ask for Sid'), tying the bar to Sidney Jaffe before and after the 1974 incorporation. It was a working-class corner bar at the south end of the Waverly strip for at least 12 years. Source: The Baltimore Sun, Jan. 1, 1977, p.26 (1967: Sun May 20, 1967 p.28, image 377323824; 1974: Sun June 16, 1974 p.129, image 376966855).

A Sun business feature on the North Greenmount Community Development Federal Credit Union, preparing for its fourth annual meeting, quotes executive director Ward Smith ('It'll last for hours, and we'll have the finest potluck supper in Maryland'). He had been a community organizer in Hampden before moving to Waverly and advised members not to borrow; assets grew 70 percent in 1982 while loan volume fell about 5 percent. The photo caption places Smith and resource developer Mary Jo Kirschman in front of the office at 416 East 31st Street, 'bought by the credit union in 1981'. The average family income in the area served was $11,000. This confirms the brief's guess that Ward Smith's 'Community Credit Union' is this one. Source: The Baltimore Sun, Feb. 21, 1983, p.31.

The North Greenmount credit union in the 400 block of E. 31st St. was found insolvent and closed in July 1987. The National Credit Union Administration expected to pay its 800 depositors in full by Aug. 10 (about $1.364 million in deposits). NCUA liquidation director Anthony LaCreta said it had been started eight years earlier (1979) on a federal loan of $100,000 or $200,000 that was never fully repaid, was awash in bad loans with delinquencies approaching 60 percent, and suffered from weak collections and the neighborhood's depressed economy; it was one of several government-created inner-city credit unions, many of which had failed. A 1982 Sun story compared it with the Matanuska Valley credit union in Alaska (Sun June 27, 1982 p.24, image 225707804). Source: The Evening Sun, July 16, 1987, p.58 (also EvSun July 17, 1987 p.51, image 372521086; Carroll County Times July 17, 1987, image 869145845).

Part of the resource described under 3021 Greenmount Avenue in the historic district listed December 31, 2013.

Contributing building in the historic district listed December 31, 2013. Originally 2-story town hall built in 1873, ca. 1910 divided into multiple commercial spaces with entrances on E. 31 st St. and Greenmount Avenue, 1-story rear addition built ca. 1920, 1-story addition on north side built ca. 1950, windows infilled and storefront altered ca. 1970. This white Georgian-style brick building with some green trim celebrated its centennial in 1973 by commemoration of the Maryland State Senate. It is known historically as the Waverly Town Hall. This building was historically used as the Waverly Post Office ( 1928) and later Mildred Mae Wonneman' s beauty shop ( 193 7). A portion of this building was historically addressed as 3102 Greenmount Avenue and was apartments and Seward's Drug Store in 1928 and later a plumber's shop, a hat cleaner, and a dentist's office in 1937. In 1936, an addition was made onto the back (west side) of the building that is addressed 422-428 East 31 st Street.

The 1915 Sanborn Fire Insurance map (LoC item sanborn03573_014, sheet 718 -- NOT sheet 717 as the existing prod row for this parcel cites; the 1915 volume's own printed street index gives Greenmount Ave '3009-3229' as sheet *718, the odd/east side; sheet 717 covers the even/west side of a different stretch, 3129-3223) shows one continuous 2-story brick building spanning both 3019 and 3021, split into two units each explicitly labeled 'Office.' This physically corroborates the Polk directory's real-estate/Building-and-Loan-Association office at 3019 in the same years.

Companion finding to the 3019 entry: the same 1915 Sanborn sheet 718 (corrected from the existing prod row's sheet 717 citation) shows 3021 as the other half of the shared 2-story brick building, also labeled 'Office' -- consistent with Dr. George S. Marwood's dental office there, 1912-1918 (Polk).

The 1928 Sanborn (LoC item sanborn03573_018, sheet 735 -- this citation on the existing prod row is correct) shows the same building footprint, still spanning 3021 and 3019 together, now labeled 'S' for store rather than 'Office.' The conversion from professional office (1915) to retail store (1928) happened sometime between the last office-era Polk hit (1918, Marwood) and 1928, and lines up with the shoe-repair/baker's-shop uses NPS records for this period. The adjacent 'office' label visible on the same crop belongs to the separate building at 3017, not to 3019/3021 -- a mis-attribution risk this unit caught and corrected before writing up the finding.

Better Business Bureau records the registration date of Main Street Hats, a family-owned, minority-owned hat shop, as 2009-03-05, at '3019 Greenmount Ave # 3021, Baltimore, MD 21218-3939' -- explicitly spanning both storefronts. Owner Clyde M. Davis-El, with his wife and business partner Elaine, sold Stetson, Biltmore, Dobbs and Scala hats and offered hat cleaning/blocking services; customers travelled from as far as upstate New York and Atlanta for fedoras and Panamas (Baltimore Fishbowl, 2013-05-07). Davis-El had bought 3019 from Michael S. Nelson in 2006 ($40,000) and 3021 from Jihye Han in 2007 ($17,000) -- the same 'abstract deed-chain name IS the family's own storefront' pattern the corridor memory documents for Kirkley Flowers at 3413 Greenmount.

Companion finding to the 3019 entry: Main Street Hats' registered business address, '3019 Greenmount Ave # 3021,' explicitly includes this parcel. See the 3019 finding for full detail (owner, founding date, products, customer draw).

A Maryland Department of Housing and Community Development press release (2016-08-10) announced a grand-reopening ribbon-cutting for Main Street Hats on 2016-08-13 following more than $40,000 in interior and exterior renovations: Baltimore Development Corporation ($20,000), MD DHCD's Baltimore Regional Neighborhood Initiative ($6,000+), Johns Hopkins University ($5,000) and Wells Fargo ($10,000), designed by Gensler and Associates and constructed by Rebuilding Together Baltimore and Second Century Homes. This is a directly-dated, multi-funder commercial-corridor investment in the same storefront the Waverly Main Street program's 2013 master-planning effort (Baltimore Fishbowl, naming Davis-El's shop as a corridor draw) had targeted.
Companion finding to the 3019 entry -- the rehabilitated storefront spans both addresses. See the 3019 finding for full funder/date detail.

Survived by wife Ada Becker (married 61 years), daughters Joanie Becker Cohen and Barbara Becker, son Dr. Larry Becker, 10 grandchildren and 9 great-grandchildren. Brandau of Stoneleigh, raising an open question (not resolved here) of whether the 1937-1953 'John Brandau' is Arthur's father, as assumed, or his brother John E. -- the obituary's own wording ('the brothers had opened a store...') is at least as consistent with the latter reading.

City directories show George H. Condon (b.1851, per prod's existing FindAGrave record) listed as running 'shoes' at 3210 Greenmount from at least 1917, with son Ernest J. Condon (b.1897) listed alongside him as 'clerk,' and wife Henrietta B. Condon also named 'shoes' by 1918 -- a genuine three-person family operation, not a business a 20-year-old Ernest started alone. This reframes units.json's own seed question about a '20-year-old inheriting/starting' the business: it was already his father's.

By decree of the Circuit Court of Baltimore City (case 108A-112), A. J. Billig & Co. auctioned the retail stock of the Trust Estate of Ira Adler, trading as "the Hole in the Wall and Discount Book Store," at two premises on March 21, 1968. At 3219½ Greenmount Ave (this parcel's absorbed 3219 lot) the sale covered greeting cards, ribbons, wrapping paper, cosmetics, jewelry, stuffed animals, novelties, stationery, purses, soaps and 12 maple card racks; a separate lot of books, magazines and journals was sold the same morning at 3222 Greenmount Ave (a different, even-side parcel outside this campaign unit, noted only as a cross-reference). Trustee: Sanford A. Harris (Sagner, Stevan & Harris, 440 Tower Building) — not related to the Harris Garage family at pid 745/3122. This closes a ~36-year gap in the parcel's record between the 1942 Wagner's grocery ad and the modern 2005+ deed chain. Ira Adler's own identity/dates were not found on the open web this session.

Baltimore City Register of Wills records show Nettie Garonzik died 1929-09-27 and her estate was filed 1929-09-30 under two entries (estate #9951, type RE, and #UN-0033G, type UN) — consistent with Aaron Garonzik, the partner named in the 1922 Polk directory line "Garonzik Aaron (Nettie; Garonzik & Goldberg)," becoming a widower that year. A full-surname Register of Wills pull for "Garonzik" produces no independent estate filing for an "Aaron Garonzik" in either Baltimore City (12 estate rows, 1929-2020) or Baltimore County — a confirmed null in both jurisdictions, re-verified live in both counties this review pass, not merely an unqueried gap. "Garonzik & Goldberg" as a firm name produced zero hits anywhere on the open web (WebSearch). These vital-record facts are solid. What is NOT established is any family relationship: Aaron was tentatively read as the father or brother of Robert Garonzik (grocer at 3221, this parcel, 1922) on the sole basis of the two names' adjacency on the same 1922 Polk directory page — but Polk directories are alphabetized by surname, so any two "Garonzik" entries would sit adjacent regardless of whether they were related. Same rare surname, same block, same era — a plausible but unconfirmed relationship, not a demonstrated one.

A Baltimore Sun real-estate item reports Peoples Service Drug Stores closing a ten-year lease on 3223 Greenmount Ave (SE corner of Gorsuch Ave) -- through broker B. Howard Richards -- 'from Robert Garonzik and wife,' displacing the longtime tenant M. Malin & Son. This documents Robert Garonzik (grocer at neighboring 3221 in 1922, with 'Garonzik Bros' cigars next door at 3223 in 1918) holding a leasehold or ground-rent interest in 3223 by 1929. It does NOT establish fee ownership that early: prod's own MDLandRec fee-title chain for this corner (767:mdlr-3223-root) documents the Garonzik family's FEE ownership as beginning only in 1950, purchased from a non-Garonzik grantor (Marion Elliott) -- there is no room in that chain for continuous Garonzik fee ownership back to 1929. The 1929 lease is consistent with, but does not prove, the family holding a longer-running non-fee interest (ground rent or trust) that predates their 1950 fee purchase; prod's existing 1977 row (765:owner-roster-1977) lists 3223's owner of record that year as 'Roland Garonrik, Equitable Trust Co., Trustee' (almost certainly a transcription of Garonzik), which is consistent with but does not confirm a decades-long family trust interest.

A pencil design on tracing paper for the sign that stood at the merchants' parking lot while Contract 2611 was built. It reads 'Improving the Waverly Parking Lot', with two cartoon cars, a row of round trees under the word WAVERLY, the HCD and DPW marks, the city seal, 'Mayor William Donald Schaefer and the Citizens of Baltimore', and 'Contract #2611, For Information Phone 396-0215'. The sign is undated; the lot contract ran from 1979 to 1981. City Archives BRG48-43-10-27, page 0002.

A handwritten DHCD tally of the lot's full cost. Acquisition came to $149,353.18: $148,178.68 paid to the owner plus $674.50 in title costs, a $100 appraisal and a $400 appraisal commission. That is about $18,000 over the $130,000 the city had offered, which Lifetime Communities turned down in July 1979. Relocating the last residents and parking tenants cost $40,000. Construction was Marcantoni's $126,180.92 bid plus $11,356.28 of inspection ($137,537.20), with about $11,500 of utility work (C&P Telephone $1,000, BG&E $6,000, street lighting and conduit $3,000, waste water $1,500), $11,000 of engineering and $4,000 of demolition. With $20,071.85 for Transit and Traffic's parking meters, the total was $373,462.23. City Archives BRG48-43-10-24, page 0002.

A handwritten list of the city's internal work orders for the Waverly Off-Street Parking Lot: IWO 127324 for $137,537.20 of construction on May 20, 1980; IWO 128080 for $3,000 of lighting and IWO 128081 for $1,500 of water on June 10, 1980; and IWO 128098 for $20,071.85 of Transit and Traffic meters on Oct. 16, 1980, $162,109.05 in all. Notes beside it assign acquisition to 'Aaron' and demolition to 'Rudy J.' City Archives BRG48-43-10-24, page 0003.

The Bureau of Highways advertised Contract 2611, 'Bituminous Concrete Resurfacing of Waverly Parking Lot', in The Daily Record on April 18 and 19, 1980, with bids due at the Comptroller's office in City Hall at 11 a.m. on Wednesday, May 7. The notice gave a $100,000 to $250,000 cost range, required contractors to be prequalified, promised minority businesses full opportunity to bid, and was approved by George G. Perdikakis (acting head, Bureau of Highways), Richard H. Trainor (deputy director of Public Works) and Hyman Aaron Pressman (secretary, Board of Estimates). The paper billed $188.99 (invoice 36901), paid by Direct Payment Order 801810 on April 29, 1980. City Archives BRG48-43-10-24, pages 0004-0006.

A plan of 32nd Street from Brentwood Avenue to Greenmount shows the widened north-side walk paved in brick with four tree squares, running along Merryman's Lane beside the parking lot, and 'Mac Lot' across Brentwood. Red notes mark 'Move 2' west' and 'Space for sign' at each end. City Archives BRG48-43-10-30, page 0007.

A meeting notice for the Waverly Development Committee: Thursday, February 9, 7:30 p.m., at the Gorsuch House Restaurant, 511 Gorsuch Avenue, with Pat Massey of HCD (396-5817) as contact. The agenda was a marketing brochure for Waverly (theme, demographics), efforts to recruit new businesses, a realtor-developer workshop and a joint committee-HCD work program. No year is printed; February 9 fell on a Thursday in 1978, when the program's logo and brochure work was under way. City Archives BRG48-43-10-26 (the 'Waverly Logo' file), page 23.

Bids for Contract 2611 opened May 7, 1980: R. Marcantoni & Sons about $125,326, B.A.P.C. $133,639, Salco $147,609, a Robbins and Schweizer (?) firm $148,648, Mahoney Brothers (the streetscape contractor) $150,298, then Flanigan, Benhoff (?), Flintkote, and Potts and Callahan at $194,145. An HCD staffer wrote in red 'Hot damn! poor George - his should have been lowest', meaning George Mahoney. An $855 arithmetic correction brought Marcantoni's bid to the $126,180.92 on file. The line-item bid sheet prices wood benches at $750, Kwanzan cherries and lindens at $230 each and 825 euonymus at $13.80. The city dates the award May 28 and the notice to proceed June 19, 1980; Hurst-Rosche's July progress narrative gives May 21 and June 16. City Archives BRG48-43-10-29, pages 03, 07, 36, 38.

The preconstruction notes for Contract 2611 record 'Farmer's market requirements, 1/2 open on Sat.': the new 32nd Street Farmers Market, opened May 30, 1980, kept half the lot on Saturdays while Marcantoni rebuilt it. The lot's interim attendant, Carroll F. Marble, a temporary Housing Authority employee, was let go at the notice to proceed. Progress meetings were held at the library at 33rd and Barclay; a C&P phone booth on 32nd Street was removed; the electrical subcontractor, Enterprise Electric (Gilbert Reynolds), queried the 27-foot-6 versus 32-foot-6 light poles and a missing main breaker; and BG&E charged $241 to wire the lot at 3201 Barclay. The work was conditionally accepted Sept. 4, 1980, before the benches were built. On Oct. 29, 1981 Calvin Buikema of Recreation and Parks reported 'all plants alive', and a June 8, 1984 sketch by Bob Quilter added a diagonal sidewalk and curb ramp. City Archives BRG48-43-10-29, pages 02, 05-06, 13-21, 32, 37, 39-40.

The Passano-O'Neill card for 3014 Greenmount (citing Aull's Old Land Marks, pages 46-47) describes the site as a rambling frame 'country seat' built around the end of the Civil War by the seedsman Abram G. Mott as a retreat from his business near Belair Market. At his death the property was taken over by the Waverly dairyman Michael F. O'Neill, who gradually covered the grounds with stables that became garages as he moved into auto repair. The house survived into at least the early 1950s and was replaced by the present one-story commercial row. Mott died on October 3, 1895, at his home, 918 York road, aged about 85 (Baltimore Sun, October 4, 1895, p. 10), so he was born about 1810; the card's dates for him (c1820-1897) are wrong at both ends. The O'Neill house was 920 York road from 1899, and which lot Mott's 918 was is contested. The commercial row went up bay by bay, about 1954 to 1958.

The Passano-O'Neill card for 3020 Greenmount (citing Aull's Old Land Marks, pages 60-61) says that about 1845 Lawrence Leicht (1809-1892), a German immigrant who had arrived in Baltimore around 1837, built a two-story frame house on the south-west corner of Greenmount Avenue and Vineyard Lane and moved in, and that he was a stallholder at Richmond Market on Howard Street, selling the produce he raised in Waverly, until his death. His widow, Wilhelmina, kept the house until her death on May 24, 1902, at Jersey City; her funeral left from 922 York road, the house's old number (Baltimore Sun, May 27, 1902, p. 4). The card gives her death as 1903.

There were several sites for the first, or Waverly, tollgate of the Baltimore & York Turnpike Company. The earliest was apparently the northwest corner of Greenmount Avenue and Merryman's Lane; sold derelict to the Huntingdon Company in 1869, it became the site of Waverly Hall. In 1870 the turnpike company apparently bought the building on the northwest corner of Greenmount and Gilmor's Lane (now Vineyard Lane) as its replacement. Hollifield describes that house as built in the 1770s, long and low with a porch across the front and many small rooms, earlier a country store, a recruiting station in the Mexican and Civil Wars, and a hospital for Union soldiers with fevers; it served as the gatekeeper's house until the tollgate was removed in 1894, stood vacant a long time, then was a private residence. Because it extended into the road, residents asked for its removal in 1900 and sent a delegation to the United Railways & Electric Company, which controlled the turnpike; nothing was done until the road was paved northward in 1907 and the house was torn down. The card notes the surviving photograph is hard to square with the description.

The card records two illustrations in Mitchell's Baltimore transition (1998), pages 194-195: a view of about 1890 looking northwest from the confluence of Greenmount Avenue and Old York Road, and the same view in 1997.

Suburban communities of the nineteenth century considered a meeting place central to their identity. In 1869 the Huntingdon Company, early developers of the neighborhood now called Waverly, bought this land for such a hall, which opened in 1872. The two-story brick building held shops on the ground floor, whose rent paid the taxes, and a lofty public hall on the second story for lectures and public meetings; Hampden had a similar hall at 3551-3553 Roland Avenue, since converted to apartments. 'Waverly Hall' last appeared as such in the 1923 city directory, after which the auditorium was apparently divided into apartments. In 2012 the building became a registered Baltimore City historic landmark as 'Waverly Town Hall'.

A semi-detached, story-and-a-half frame house on this site was long the home of Jacob Aull (1805-1876), pioneer promoter and developer of the Greenmount Avenue communities of Waverly, Oxford and Friendship. It was probably pulled down after his death by his son and partner Jacob H. Aull (1848-1921), who replaced it with a row of more modern Victorian cottages, installing his two unmarried sisters in one of them, No. 3114.

A rambling complex of outbuildings around a two-and-a-half-story house was for many years Waverly's principal grocery store, run first by Andrew J. Huff (1815-1864), then by his widow Elizabeth D. Huff (1816-1882), and finally by their son Henry C. Huff (1845-1916). After the son's death the building was sold out of the family, demolished and replaced by a one-story brick automobile garage covering the whole lot. Built in the 1920s and home to a vast assortment of tenants since, the garage still stood in 2012, divided into two premises.

A wide but shallow two-story frame house stood on this site just north of the Greenmount Avenue edition of the Waverly M.E. Church (3101-3103), which is visible at the right of the only surviving photograph of 3105-3109. The house outlasted most of those around it because an addition between it and Greenmount Avenue let it be converted into retail premises.

Jacob Aull (1805-1876), a major developer of Waverly, had two unmarried daughters, Margaret E. (born 1840) and Louisa F. (born 1844). Under his will they inherited the two-story frame house at 3116 Greenmount and lived there until their deaths; Louisa's, when she was nearly a hundred, may have complicated the settlement of her estate, and the house still stood in 1951, long after 3112 next door had become Charles Mall's hardware store. By 1956, 3116 and the vacant lot at 3114 had been replaced by a one-story brick commercial building that for many years housed a branch of Sunny's Surplus. That closed in 1995, and by 2012 the store was The Red Shed.

Waverly, like every Baltimore County community, was on its own for firefighting and protected only by volunteers long after the city organized a paid force in 1859. In time the county helped: a firehouse was built on this site and a 'chemical engine' (the county's fourth) stationed in it; the Sun of May 18, 1882 covered the county fire department's parade celebrating the opening. When the city annexed Waverly in 1888 it inherited the two-story firehouse, the chemical engine and its men, and the Waverly Volunteers, who became the city's Hook & Ladder Company No. 7. In 1901 the chemical engine company was merged into the hook and ladder company and a larger firehouse built for it on the old site. When the city's hook and ladder companies were restyled truck companies in 1908, H&L No. 7 became Truck No. 7, and it kept watch over Waverly until the station was closed for economy.

The lot was still vacant when the Waverly Amusement Company bought it in late 1909 and put up a classic early movie theater: a shallow brick structure entered through a rounded archway with the theater's name in the brickwork over the door. In 1920 it was sold to the Crystal Amusement Company of Benjamin Cluster, who ran several east Baltimore theaters; he turned the original building into the lobby of a much larger 750-seat auditorium built to its east. The Durkee chain acquired the Waverly in 1929, replaced Cluster's square marquee with a triangular one, removed the old vertical sign, and showed movies until 1969. It was then a Goodwill store for about a decade, and since the early 1980s, shorn of its marquee but otherwise in excellent shape, a Shoe City shoe store.

Probably a small grocery serving Waverly at first, the building was absorbed about 1919 into the Knobloch Bros. grocery chain, an east Baltimore operation that seems to have sold out entirely to A&P about 1929; A&P kept a store here until 1937. In 1938 Louis Rabai (died 1957) bought the building, gave it a fresh Art Deco facade and made it Rabai's Bakery. Its spot beside the Waverly Theater must have helped, because Rabai sold it to another baker shortly before his death: from 1956 the directories list Burri's French Bakery, through 1978. The Waverly closed in 1969, but the shop became the Butter Crisp Bakery in 1979 and stayed one through the 1988 directory. Then its luck as a bakery ran out and it became Blackstone Menswear, still there in 2007. Corridor's own rows place Rabai's founding in the 1920s and at 3205 in 1936, before this Art Deco store.

By 1877 Baltimore County had one of its rare public schools on this site for the village of Waverly. When 'The Belt' passed to the city in 1888 the brick schoolhouse became 'Annex School #2', and the Board of Commissioners of Public Schools complained from the outset: four teachers and their classes were housed in the basement of a church two squares away (the 60th annual report, 1889; the card identifies it as Waverly Hall), two teachers shared one room (61st), several classes sat in rented rooms in the neighborhood (62nd). Revived in the mid-1890s, the 67th report chose overcrowding over 'small, badly-lighted, heated and ventilated rooms' for rent, the 68th repeated the 62nd word for word, and the 69th and 70th (the last to consider buildings individually) asked for an enlarged main building at 'Gilmore Lane, near York Road'. Nothing much was done beyond renaming it Public School No. 51 in the 1900 reorganization, until it was demolished about 1911 for the eastward extension of 33rd Street from Charles Street. The school then got a new building at 800 East 34th Street, and the Greenmount site was developed with the stores standing there in 2010.

Row of five single-story brick stores built in 1926, with five similar ones to their west at 419-427 East 33rd Street, by the architects Smith & May for the developers C.B. Baker & Co. Christened the 'Baker Block', an inscription that survives in the stucco of the facade, the buildings were in the then-fashionable Spanish style and took advantage of a strategic corner where the relatively new 33rd Street crossed venerable Greenmount Avenue. The Sun of July 29, 1926 noted construction of the block, in stucco, with space for a dozen stores. Aull's Old Landmarks pictures the two-story stone house that occupied the site before the 1920s.

A clipping on the Passano-O'Neill card, from the Sunday Sun Magazine's 'This was Baltimore 50 years ago' column of Aug. 4, 1957, reprinting the Sun of Sunday, July 28, 1907 ('Passing of Toll Gate', p. 20): 'Built 130 years ago, when building lines and gradings were matters that did not cause the folks much concern, the old toll gate house at York road and Gilmor lane is to be torn down in a few days to give way to the onward march of the paving which has gradually extended up the York road from North avenue. The family of Mr. Charles Clarke, who have been occupying the house, moved yesterday.' The family therefore left on Saturday, July 27, 1907, and the demolition was to begin on Monday, July 29.

A black-and-white photograph, circulated by the Flickering Treasures project, of the Waverly Theatre's front: the original round-arched brick facade with WAVERLY worked into the brick over the entrance, a rectangular marquee lettered WAVERLY, and a tall vertical sign on a steel frame above the roof. Cobbled Greenmount Avenue with streetcar rails runs in the foreground; a shop awning is at left and a parked car at right. The Passano-O'Neill card says Benjamin Cluster's Crystal Amusement Company bought the house in 1920 and made the 1909 theatre the lobby of a 750-seat auditorium behind it, and that the Durkee chain, which took over in 1929, replaced Cluster's square marquee with a triangular one and removed the old vertical sign. Both the square marquee and the vertical sign are here, so the photograph dates between the February 1921 reopening and the Durkee changes of about 1929.

A two-panel composite. Left, a Google Street View of the block about 2017: Shoe City in the old theatre front, with its stepped parapet clad in vertical metal siding, next to the 'Grocery & Dollar Mart' at 3209 and a nail spa beyond. Right, a black-and-white photograph of the same front in the 1970s: the marquee still reads WAVERLY but the attraction board says GOODWILL and 'Goodwill Industries', the sign of a bakery (the frame reads 'Buddi's Bakery', the Burri's French Bakery listed at 3215 from 1956 to 1978) is next door, a 'Kings' sign hangs at right, and a late-1960s sedan is parked out front. The Passano-O'Neill card has the theatre closing in 1969, Goodwill occupying it for about a decade, and Shoe City there since the early 1980s, so the photograph falls in the 1970s. The two panels show the marquee and stepped parapet survived into the Goodwill years and were stripped before the shoe store.

A color photograph, posted by Marvin Welch to Baltimore Past and Present Photos on December 7, 2021 as 'The Old Waverly PS#51 School on 35th street near Memorial Stadium circa unknown'. It shows a three-story buff-brick school with a Spanish-baroque center gable, two copper-domed cupolas, an arched entrance porch and a corner lamp, with Memorial Stadium's light towers at left, a boarded one-story shop with a Diet-Rite Cola sign at right, and cars of about 1980 parked in front. The Passano-O'Neill card for 3226-3232 Greenmount says Public School No. 51 left the Greenmount site when it was demolished about 1911 for the extension of 33rd Street and got this new building at 800 East 34th Street, so the caption's '35th street' is off by a block; the building faced the 801-827 East 34th rowhouses across the street. Filed on the Greenmount school lot as the continuation of that story, since no parcel carries the 34th Street address.

A sharp, large photograph of the theatre's front: the stepped brick gable, a heavy cornice, the half-round window with radiating muntins under a WAVERLY arch, a bulb-lined canopy with WAVERLY lettered on it, poster cases either side of the doors, a chimney at right, and at lower left the edge of the A&P with a window sign about a weekly special. No vertical blade sign shows in this crop. The poster dated it 1931 and gave no photographer or source; it looks like an archival print, and the post drew no comments. It is the clearest view Corridor has of the 1909-10 facade as the Waverly Amusement Company and then Benjamin Cluster's Crystal Amusement Company left it. The A&P at the left is the store at 3213-15 that the Passano-O'Neill card says A&P ran until 1937.

A colorized photograph (SITE of OLD Baltimore, over a print with a faint 'Baltimore Memories' mark) looking north from the northwest corner of 32nd and Greenmount: the White Coffee Pot's oval sign and coffee-pot logo in the foreground, a Roberts sign and a row of 1950s cars, and across the street the Waverly whose marquee lists Macdonald Carey, Rhonda Fleming and 'Odongo', a 1956 film. One commenter argues it could be 1957 because the Waverly ran second-run pictures. Corridor's rows put the White Coffee Pot at this corner from a five-year lease beginning January 15, 1936, which answers a dispute in the thread: Larry Curcio thought it had moved to 32nd and Greenmount by the 1970s, but Phil Smeak says it was always there, and the lease supports him. People remember hamburger steak with onions and gravy and rice pudding, a table-top jukebox with 'Yakety Sax' five times running for a quarter, a father who met his cronies there every morning, and a grandmother who took a child for 'fine dining'. The corner is now Greene's deli, per one commenter. Two more places came up: Robinson's Gorsuch House restaurant, the Robinson family's crab-cake restaurant with a bowling alley (Corridor has it at 511 Gorsuch), and Waverly Crab, where a commenter worked in the mid-1980s. The post's opening 'Saturday Night at the Waverly, 1956' story is fiction and was not used.

A color slide of the theatre's front as a shoe store. Above a metal-clad ground floor with a SHOE CITY, 'The Family Shoe Store' sign and two roll-down gates, the old stepped parapet survives behind dark glass panels with white bands, and a small 'W' still shows at its peak. A tall chimney rises behind, and the neighbor at right, under vertical metal siding, carries a red 'PRINCE...' sign (presumably the Princess Shops, which Corridor has on the 1976 steering committee at 3203, beside the old Crown 5&10 site at 3207-09) with 'Winter Clearance' and 'Sale' signs in its window. At left, a cream-brick shop with a 'Grand Opening' banner and the tail of a '...ERY' sign; the Passano-O'Neill card has Butter Crisp Bakery in that building through the 1988 directory, then Blackstone Menswear, so the banner may mark that change. The poster (Kevin Anthony Mueller, February 2021) gives 1988 for the photograph and paired it with the 1930s marquee view; the winter sale signs suggest early 1988. It shows the theatre after Goodwill (Corridor's 1977 survey has the Goodwill; Shoe City opened in the early 1980s per the card) and after the marquee and vertical sign were gone, but with the top of the original facade still in place, as the 1931 photograph shows it when new.

Jacques Kelly's columns of January 9, 2021, May 22, 2021 and January 1, 2022, and a March 9, 2024 follow-up, read through a summary rather than the full text. The 1870 Waverly Hall at Greenmount and 31st, a long-neglected building last the Northside Bar, once held a public school, a private library, a post office, a drugstore and a cigar factory making a 'Waverly' brand; named tenants include Forney's restaurant, the Northside tavern, Dr. Joseph Jameson's dental practice, and the Kelly brothers' grocery in the 1920s annex. The Central Baltimore Future Fund bought three contiguous vacant properties in 2018 for $414,000 (Corridor's deed shows $414,000 from WABKF LLC in November 2018) and, with State of Maryland support, planned a $1.5 million restoration into seven apartments and five retail spaces, with street-facing shops on Greenmount and 31st. Sarah Keogh, the Fund's executive director, and developers Ted Rouse and Jacob Wittenberg are named; Better Waverly, Abell and Waverly Main Street are credited with the push. When the boarding came off a painted 'Prescriptions' sign from the original drugstore appeared, and inside workers found a second-floor chamber with old-growth timber trusses and an unusually broad staircase. By January 2022 the interior had been gutted and rebuilt as loft apartments with a food operation at street level and tenants due to move in February 1. In March 2024 Kelly wrote that the Thai restaurant, after more than 23 years, was moving to the hall's rear annex on East 31st, the former Guilford Grocery Co. space, with Wittenberg as co-owner. Corridor's deed rows for the hall run from 1943 to 2023 and stop short of this story.

A photograph taken from Greenmount Avenue of the Greek Revival hall with its front storefronts removed: a pedimented, stuccoed upper story with a bracketed cornice, windows open to the sky, a painted tag, a surviving brick-arched doorway, temporary steel posts holding the upper floor, blue construction fencing, and workers at a dumpster full of old brick. Macra Nay, who posted it as 'I snapped this just now', links two Baltimore Sun pieces on the renovation and says she had not seen the 31st Street side; the Sun's 'Peeking inside' column ran May 22, 2021 and the trees are in full leaf, so the photograph is from about June 2021, the months Corridor's deeds put the hall in Waverly Arts LLC's hands (May 3, 2021) with a Reinvestment Fund loan (March 2, 2021). It is a rare record of the hall's two-story front with the later storefronts removed. Another post in the same group, of a still from a video, shows the building before work started, blue-awninged and tagged, with a Quik Tax Service beside it.

A vertical strip of an aerial photograph, gray-toned and scratched, north up: Greenmount Avenue runs the full height from North Avenue at the bottom to 33rd Street at the top, with the streets numbered in white along the left (22nd up to 33rd), the diamond and stands of Terrapin Park, also called Oriole Park (V), wedged in a corner at 29th and 30th west of Greenmount, and the railroad cutting across the lower third near 26th and 27th, labeled with the Baltimore and Ohio's name. The poster gives 1927 and identifies the park; a commenter says the ground later held Peabody Heights Brewery, Guilford Elementary and the extended Barclay Street. East of Greenmount the fabric is looser and greener, with rowhouse blocks and patches of open ground. A commenter adds that RC Cola was made on the ballpark ground after the park closed and moved at 13 to 30th Street, two doors down across from the cola company 'when it was going strong'; another's family lived at 514 East 26th Street, just east of where Greenmount dead-ends at the railroad, from 1920 to 1960, with open fields and a tunnel mouth beyond the house. No source or photographer is given for the aerial.

A press-style photograph of the clearance for the garden-style Waverly Apartments: a crawler crane with a long boom working behind a cinder-block garage and a two-story building still standing, piles of earth, a photographer with a camera at his chest, a woman and a uniformed officer watching, a car with a police shield on its door and a light-colored 1950-era sedan, and in the foreground a white sign reading WAVERLY APARTMENTS. The caption says properties designated by the city's redevelopment commission were razed to make way for the apartments, circa 1953. Jacques Kelly comments that many of the original Baltimore Colts players lived there with their wives in the days of low salaries, and a former resident says he lived there on a union machinist's pay. It ties the Sun's June 1950 report of the mayor's four slum-clearance bills, one for 17 acres east of Greenmount at 28th Street, to what was built: Corridor's 'Yard' rows describe the 17-acre Waverly clearance between 27th and 30th, and a commenter on the Waverly Theatre photographs remembers residents of the Waverly Apartments sleeping on the lawn on hot mid-1950s nights. The photograph's exact spot and the photographer are not given.

Comments under a modern photograph of the McDonald's corner at Greenmount and 29th, in a thread about the 1944 fire. Jacques Kelly writes that the park sat west of the picture and 'the bleachers were just above the white building which was once Gus Rau's tavern'; a woman whose family lived nearby remembers watching Rau's customers leave at all hours from her back bedroom. Several recall the WWIN radio station and its tower in the middle of the parking lot (Corridor's 1957 Waverly Tower opening row is on the parcel beside this corner), and one who lived on Ilchester Avenue says the street ran perpendicular to the WWIN tower. Jeffrey A. Howard puts home plate on what is now the east side of Barclay Street about 145 feet north of the north curb of 29th Street, which can be checked against the 2015 Martenet survey Corridor holds. Another commenter lists the Peabody Heights Brewery, the Salvation Army building and the Barclay school as the site's later occupants and adds that Barclay Street did not exist between 29th Street and a point her comment leaves unfinished. The Sun's July 1, 1994 story on the fire is linked in the thread. Corridor already covers the July 4, 1944 fire in detail; these are the neighborhood details around it.

A Baltimore City Archives photograph: a two-story stuccoed corner building with 'Drugs, Run Right to Read's, Soda' on fascia boards along both faces, display windows lettered 'Perfumes' and 'Prescriptions', a recessed corner entry, an awning, pedestrians in 1940s coats, a barrier reading 'Street Closed' with a pile of dug-up earth and lumber at the curb, and at the right a square brick tower, which the Archives' own 'Then and Now' post of July 22, 2022 identifies as the tower of Engine Station No. 31. The Archives' caption says circa 1948, that William H. Read founded the Read Drug and Chemical Company in the 1890s, that the Nattans family bought the business in 1899 and grew the chain to about forty stores by 1934, that the Waverly store opened sometime in the 1920s, and that the building held a Rite Aid when the caption was written (Corridor's 2021 deed rows show a Walgreens parcel after a sale-leaseback, so the drugstore use has run for about a century). The barrier and rubble show street or utility work in front of the store. Commenters recall Read's as the after-school stop for snacks and ice cream (an Eastern High graduate of 1963), the prescription pads from Read's that got a doctor's patients a free ice-cream cone, a section of 'Miss Nancy' toys advertised on Romper Room, cherry sundaes, and the slogan 'Run Right to Read's'. This gives an address to the Read's that two other threads place 'with the Waverly' and 'on Greenmount and 32nd': 3133, at the corner of 32nd Street, with one storefront between it and the Engine 31 firehouse at 3121-3123, a short walk south of the Waverly Theatre. The Archives' 2022 post adds that Read's hosted Hendler's ice cream stands, that streetcar tracks show in the Belgian block street and the sidewalk on the north side of the store was under construction in the photograph, that a storefront then stood between Read's and the fire station but the two properties have since merged into one larger store, and that the corner held a Rite Aid until recently and is now a Dollar General (Corridor's 2021 deed rows show the sale-leaseback to DG Greenmount LLC).

Comments under a Baltimore Past and Present post by Kevin Wendell about the Radio Center, the record store in the middle of the Waverly business district. His text describes the sign projecting over the sidewalk, an oversized metal likeness of an RCA Victor record edged by a neon Nipper, the terrier listening to 'His Master's Voice', and notes that Baltimore had another Nipper on Russell Street, atop an RCA wholesale appliance store, the one now displayed elsewhere. The photograph attached to the post is the Russell Street building, not the Greenmount store, which set off a long argument in the comments; one commenter points out the post never said it was on Greenmount, and John Spurrier confirms the Radio Center itself was on Greenmount. Norm James posted 'the Radio Center sign today', so the sign survives. Ricky Herman writes that Greenmount Loan and Jewelry is now at the Radio Center location and that Herman's Discount is in the old Becker's building in the 3100 block (the Sun's March 2024 piece names both businesses); another commenter calls the old record store 'a pawn shop now'. Corridor has the store at 3118 Greenmount with a 1948 trade-directory ad and a June 1958 ad for RCA long-playing records at $1.98.

Facebook posts in the Baltimore Past and Present groups give the chain's history (text apparently from its public encyclopedia entry): Sunny's Surplus began in 1948 selling World War II surplus, taking the name of the first store's manager (another post credits the founder as Sidney Weinman); at its peak it had 29 stores in Maryland, Virginia and Delaware, added camping gear, and in 1990 renamed itself Sunny's The Affordable Outdoor Store. It filed Chapter 11 in 2000 and emerged 13 months later, filed a second time, began liquidation sales in January 2007 and closed its remaining stores on March 16, 2007; three stores briefly reopened that fall and closed again by March 2008. It appeared in Barry Levinson's 'Liberty Heights' and in 'Homicide'. The pictured store is, per a commenter, the Washington location in the former Joy Theatre building, not Waverly. Waverly's branch, which the Passano-O'Neill card puts in the one-story building at 3114-3116 that stood by 1956 and closed in 1995 (later The Red Shed), is remembered in other threads as where 'everybody got their army jackets'; Frank Mikulski, who managed a Sunny's store from 1990 to 1999, says the chain was hurt by expanding too quickly.

Joe Stewart's 2009 photograph of the former home and office of Louis J. Aull, built in 1888 at 414 Waverly Avenue, at 3101 Talbot Street, now East 31st Street and Brentwood: a Queen Anne house in yellow clapboard with red scalloped shingles on the second-floor bay, teal trim, a pointed gable with a Gothic-arched attic window, a storefront-style ground floor of paned windows, a red door with a large red bow, deep snow on the roofs, and in front a big painted fish sculpture lettered 'We all swim...'. He notes that in the 1990s the space became a tea room celebrating old Waverly village and that merchants in this century added the 'Fish out of Water' sculpture. His notes on the family: Henry Jacob Aull, a Bavarian shoemaker, bought a gravel pit on the west side of the York Turnpike in the 1830s, built a house and opened a cobbler shop, 'considered to be the first non-agricultural enterprise' there, where there were said to be a corn-husk depot, a blacksmith and three small stone houses. Jacob Aull (1804-1876) and his wife Christiana Gusema (1812-1880) had five children: a daughter who married and whose name he has not found; two daughters who lived at 3116 Greenmount, Louisa Frederika and Margaret Eva; and two sons, Louis J. at 414 Waverly Avenue and Henry Jacob at Eagle Nest on York Road near 25th Street, both in building and real estate. That matches the Passano-O'Neill cards (the two Aull sisters at 3112-3116, and the 2520-2528 card, where the son is Jacob H. Aull, 1848-1921, and whose house Corridor's Old Land Marks rows call Eagle Nest) and Corridor's own rows on the 1836 cottage, Christiana's death in 1880 and Louis Aull's death at 414 in March 1912. Stewart's text uses 'Henry Jacob' for both the immigrant and the younger son; the cards give the father as Jacob (1805-1876) and the son as Jacob H. (born 1848).

A sepia group portrait in front of the firehouse's rusticated brick ground floor with its wide arched door and carved keystone, three tall second-floor windows with stone sills above, and a clapboard neighbor at right: an early motor fire engine with 'Fire Department' lettered on its hood, a brass bell and a spherical headlamp, two officers on the seat, two men on the rear bench, and six firemen in double-breasted uniforms and brimmed caps standing in front. McCully posted it as 'Waverly firehouse, undated (Courtesy of Joe Stewart)'; a reader says he sees his grandfather third from the right and another in the back row at the left. The building is the one opened March 2, 1903, and the motor apparatus puts the picture after the horse era Corridor's 1915 row remembers for Engine 31, probably the 1910s or 1920s. It is the first crew portrait of the house Corridor has.

A blurred black-and-white snapshot of a three-horse hitch pulling a ladder wagon at speed on a bare, dusty road, a fireman on the tail step, two more on the high seat, a board fence and a large house at left and a store front at right. The poster (Sandra Lee Harper, in a post about firemen and policemen traveling by horse, with a police wagon photograph above) captions the top picture as from Greenmount Avenue in Waverly. It is undated. The road is plainly unpaved: the Passano-O'Neill card on 3026-3030 and a 1907 Sun item have the turnpike being paved northward from North Avenue only about 1907, and the city inherited the Waverly volunteers in 1888 (they were Hook & Ladder No. 7 by 1890 in Corridor's rows), so the picture falls between those years if it is the Waverly company at all, which the post asserts but does not prove.

The Baltimore City Fire Department's Engine 31 page (Waverly's firehouse) posted: 'On this date in 2000, Truck 7 was disbanded.' Truck 7 had been housed with Engine 31 except for a short time before its disbandment, when it was moved to Engine 42. When Truck 7 left Waverly, Medic 3 was relocated in from the station it had shared with Engine 33 on Gorsuch Avenue. Medic 3 was itself disbanded in 2016 when the department went to a two-tier EMS system, and Ambulance 3 was placed in service at Engine 31's station. Code 3 Collectibles made a model of Truck 7's 1994 Seagrave tractor-drawn aerial (the post's picture is that model). Comments from firefighters and neighbors add that the house had been the No. 7 truckhouse and a chemical company before Engine 31 was organized there, and before that a Baltimore County volunteer and then career station (which fits the Passano-O'Neill card), that Engine 33's house closed and Engine 33 moved to a 25th Street station, with a firehouse later used for Ladder 49 (the comment does not say which), that Truck 7 later became Truck 5, and one who remembers visiting as a child in the white-and-orange paint days, the sirens 'like background music'. The Passano-O'Neill card leaves the year blank for when the station's truck company ended ('19__'); this post supplies 2000 for Truck 7. Corridor had no row for Engine 33's Gorsuch Avenue station, which is a lead for a parcel near Gorsuch.

An old halftone-style photograph, undated, of a brick church with a square bell tower with an arched louvered opening, a round stair turret capped with a curved spire, a gabled front with a tall Gothic window with tracery, smaller pointed windows, and overhead wires across the view. Joe Stewart, on September 2, 2022, describes it as 'the original church built on Greenmount Avenue before there even was an East 33rd Street', which puts it at the Waverly M.E. church Corridor records at 3101-3103 Greenmount (Old Land Marks has it built in 1871 at the two-mile marker, opposite 31st; the congregation's own history page has the predecessor church founded in 1872 and moving to 33rd and Frisby on September 24, 1922). The Passano-O'Neill card for 3105-3109 uses the church as the landmark beside the two-story house it describes. Nothing in the post dates the picture, and the building is gone; this is the first image of it Corridor holds.
