Joe Stewart's photograph of a banner on the lawn of New Waverly United Methodist Church, in front of its stone church with a red door and a 'Welcome to New Waverly' sign: 'New Waverly United Methodist Church, Celebrating 140 years and continuing to do God's work in the midst of the community', with the pastor, Rev. Irance' Reddix McCray, MD, the address 644 E. 33rd Street, Baltimore 21218, a website and a red-rose graphic with 'I am the Rose of Sharon, a lily of the valley'. His post says he finally read the banner, shows the original Greenmount church, and adds the new Waverly Y and Stadium Place early-learning center and hospice buildings on the old stadium ground, with a picture of the property after Venable Stadium came to the newly opened 33rd Street. The banner's 140 years counts back to 1882, while the church's own history page, which Corridor holds, dates its predecessor Waverly M.E. Church to 1872 (150 years in 2022) and Old Land Marks to the building of 1871; the discrepancy is the banner's or a different reckoning, such as a charter or a rebuilt church, and is worth asking the church.

The handwritten caption on the print reads 'Aug 9 22, S. side 29th St. W. of York Road.' A long row of two-story rowhouses, the near ones brick below and siding above with boxy bay projections, turns down an unpaved gravel and dirt lane behind wire fences; a tall pole with heavy cross-arms carries drooping wires over the middle; laundry and awnings hang along the backs, two small children stand far down the lane, and a large brick block closes the view. York Road is Greenmount Avenue's old name, and 29th Street's south side ran along the ballpark block, Oriole Park (Terrapin Park), which was then the International League Orioles' home, so this is the neighborhood that lived beside the park. One of ten Waverly-area prints in a run of Department of Public Works street views taken August 9 to 12, 1922 for City projects; the Archives' Facebook post about item 60 says the series' 68 photographs were digitized by a volunteer and put on Flickr. Nothing in the record says why the Waverly views were made.

The caption reads 'Aug 11 22, Looking W. on 29 St. E of Huntington Ave.' Two tall poles with heavy cross-arms and a bracketed street lamp dominate a sky of crossing wires; a dark brick building with a shop awning stands at the right, another dark building at the left, and the street drops through trees toward a low, open horizon. One of ten Waverly-area prints in a run of Department of Public Works street views taken August 9 to 12, 1922 for City projects; the Archives' Facebook post about item 60 says the series' 68 photographs were digitized by a volunteer and put on Flickr. Nothing in the record says why the Waverly views were made.

Walking south on the west side of Greenmount at 32nd Street, the tour points to Pete's Grill, notes its '1925' date marker, and says nothing on the building refers to its former use as the Baltimore Trust Company, which failed in 1933. It adds that during the Depression a city van delivered free potatoes to hungry Waverly residents and children went down to the tracks along 27th Street looking for coal. Corridor's rows on 3130 begin with a hardware store in 1914 and a Hooper's restaurant in 1948 and carry the 1925 date only through the historic-district nomination, which does not name the tenant, so the bank is new here. The Baltimore Trust Company's failure in 1933 is a matter of wide record; that this branch stood at 3130 is the tour's word and worth confirming in the 1925 to 1933 city directories or a Sun bank-closing story. The tour is a neighborhood-produced guide with no footnotes, so each claim rests on its authors; Corridor treats it as a lead to confirm in records.

Walking north from the firehouse to 32nd Street, the tour says the Rite Aid at the corner was formerly Read's Drug Store, 'above which was Esther Adams Beauty Shoppe specializing in lash and brow dying'. Corridor's row on Read's, from the City Archives' post, places the drugstore beside Engine 31 with one storefront between; this adds a second-floor tenant. The tour gives no dates for the beauty shop. The tour is a neighborhood-produced guide with no footnotes, so each claim rests on its authors; Corridor treats it as a lead to confirm in records.

At the northwest corner of Greenmount and 31st the tour says villagers met upstairs from Livingston's Drug Store and an adjoining cigar store and factory where 'Waverly' was a brand name for hand-rolled stogies, and that a clipping headed 'Merchants Thrive' (date unknown) says a dozen drugstores had succeeded Livingston's. It says the Maryland Senate marked the Town Hall's centennial with a 1973 resolution that called Waverly a source of the city's firsts (organized baseball, electric streetcars, modern elementary-school construction), cited a US Commerce Department rating of Waverly as the most progressive shopping center in the country, and quoted former mayor Thomas D'Alesandro on the greatness of the country beginning in its separate communities. A 1973 centennial fits Corridor's Town Hall dating to 1872-73 (Waverly Hall, built by the Huntingdon Company); the resolution itself and the Commerce Department rating are the tour's report and are worth pulling from the Senate journal. Corridor already holds E. C. Livingston, druggists, at 3100 Greenmount in 1912; the cigar factory and its brand are new. The tour is a neighborhood-produced guide with no footnotes, so each claim rests on its authors; Corridor treats it as a lead to confirm in records.

The tour says Brentwood (formerly Talbot) was an African American enclave, as was Barclay, that relatives of Thurgood Marshall lived here and ran a concrete contracting business, and that there is still a Marshall imprint in the sidewalk on the south side of 32nd Street near Abell. It says children from these blocks attended a segregated school, No. 115 in the 'Colored District', on the site of the farmers market until after the 1954 Supreme Court decision, and that its students called it 'the chicken coop, because that is exactly what it looked like'. It also says a marker at Schoolhouse Garden on Merryman at Brentwood dedicates the space to the teachers and students of the old colored school. Corridor's rows already place School No. 115 on this parking-lot parcel (Belco 1977, the 1903 map) and its teacher George W. Biddle; the nickname, the 1954 end date and the Marshall-family detail are new, and the link to Justice Marshall is a family-lore claim to check before it is repeated. The tour is a neighborhood-produced guide with no footnotes, so each claim rests on its authors; Corridor treats it as a lead to confirm in records.

Going north up the west side of Greenmount, the tour passes Main Street Hats and Next Level, 'where once was Arundel Ice Cream below Waverly Billiards', then Goodwill, which it says was the site of the first Waverly Methodist Church and whose building 'later featured a miniature golf course on its second floor', with Crown 5 and 10 Cent Store further up. It lists the entertainments of the strip as a bowling alley, pool hall, nightclubs, ice-cream parlors, juke boxes and taverns, and names Green Door, Northside, Judge's, Sweeney's, Schuman's, Donohue's and Dutchman's, and says it lacks the space to tell what went on behind them or how drinkers got around Prohibition. It notes the engraving above the former Waverly Grill, which in 1936 was 'Provident Savings Bank'. Corridor holds the Methodist church at this corner (Old Land Marks, 1871), Sweeney's at 3128 and Schuman's saloon at 3034, the Crown store and the 1936 Provident building permit; the miniature golf floor, Arundel Ice Cream and Waverly Billiards are new, undated in the tour. The tour is a neighborhood-produced guide with no footnotes, so each claim rests on its authors; Corridor treats it as a lead to confirm in records.

The Waverly Village self-guided walking tour (2010; updated edition posted in 2019), at its first stop, the Waverly toll-gate site on Vineyard Lane, says an ad book from the 1940s shows the west side of Greenmount Avenue between 30th and 31st Streets, the block of 3000-3048, 'featuring Coney Island Lunch, Zeppe's Photo Supplies, Dunk N' Donuts, John Spellman Plumber and a wallpaper business'. The tour gives no house numbers and does not identify the ad book. Directories and deeds place two of the five: John T. Spellman, plumber, at 3026, and the Zepp photo firm at 3040-3044; the other three are not placed, and none is shown at 3028-3032. The tour is a neighborhood guide without footnotes, so each name rests on its authors until a 1940s directory or the ad book itself is found.

The tour says that from 1901 until the 1950s a trolley ran on a single track along Gorsuch Avenue between Greenmount and Harford Road, with wicker seats that swung back and forth for east-west rides, and that along Gorsuch stood a Boulevard Restaurant, later a gay nightclub called The Porthole, and at Gorsuch and Old York a Stadium Shoe Shine Parlor. The historic-district form already names The Porthole and the Stadium shoe parlor on the Gorsuch parcels; the trolley and its dates are new here. It sits in the record beside the 1922 Gorsuch Avenue street view from the City Archives, which shows the wires over the street. The tour is a neighborhood-produced guide with no footnotes, so each claim rests on its authors; Corridor treats it as a lead to confirm in records.

Read on the page image: 'Assignment, Leasehold, Individual Grantor, Long Form', made April 27, 2005, recorded May 18, 2005, 'PREPARED WITHOUT TITLE EXAMINATION OR JUDGMENT SEARCH': Jody M. Kropp, the lessee under the 99-year lease of the same day from WKJN #4, LLC (F.M.C. 6518/286), to WKJN #4, LLC, for $5, 'the leasehold interest' in 3010 Greenmount Avenue, subject to the $1,440 rent payable April 15 and Oct. 15; 'the total payment amount received for transfer of title to the above property is $-0-'. The assignment is dated 2005; the 2006 deed's recital of it as 'April 27, 2006' (F.M.C. 7709/233) is a typing slip. The lease, the deed of the rent (F.M.C. 6518/291) and this assignment were one closing for no consideration, so the lessee was an intermediary: the recorded chain before 2005 runs through WKJN #4's deed of July 5, 2000 (F.M.C. 513/38) and the 1985 trustee's deed (S.E.B. 503/357), not through the lessee.

Read on the page images (all recorded May 18, 2005, each 'PREPARED WITHOUT TITLE EXAMINATION OR JUDGMENT SEARCH'). (1) 'Lease for Ninety-Nine Years' made April 27, 2005 (F.M.C. 6518/286-290): WKJN #4, LLC, by its managing member, to Jody M. Kropp, 'No. 3010 Greenmount Avenue, being Ward 12, Section 20, Block 3856, Lot 002', as described in the deed recorded July 5, 2000 (F.M.C. 513/38); 99 years from the date, renewable forever on a $10 fine; rent 'One Thousand Four Hundred Forty dollars ($1,440.00)' a year in half-yearly instalments from April 15, 2005; the rent 'may be redeemed at any time after 3 years from date hereof at a 6% capitalization' (that is, $24,000); 'the total payment amount received for transfer of title to the above property is $-0-'. (2) 'Deed of Ground Rent' made the same day (F.M.C. 6518/291-294): WKJN #4, LLC to Lynne Komins and Anne Needle, as tenants in common, 'Five Dollars ($5.00), the actual consideration being none', the rent and the reversion, subject to the lessee's term. (3) The same day the lessee assigned the leasehold back to WKJN #4 (F.M.C. 6518/295). The net effect is what the 2006 recitals describe: Komins and Needle held the $1,440 rent and WKJN #4 kept the building. But the mechanism was a lease from WKJN #4 to an intermediary lessee, not a lease from Komins and Needle to WKJN #4; the lease and the rent deed are separate instruments at folios 286 and 291 (the 2006 recitals cite both at 291); and the lease's term is 99 years (left blank in the 2006 recital). The rent was extinguished when the lot was sold in March 2006 (F.M.C. 7709/225).

Same closing as the $710,000 deed of March 30, 2006. Lynne Komins and Anne Needle, for no stated consideration, 'grant and assign' to 3010-20 Greenmount Avenue, LLC 'the aforesaid rent payable out of said lot and the reversion thereto ... forever in FEE SIMPLE; to the end and intent that said annual ground rent and the reversion thereto may be forever merged and extinguished, the Grantee herein being the owner of the leasehold interest.' The day of March is blank in the recorded copy. From then on the company held the fee and the leasehold together; it is the fee simple that the 2017 deed sells. Tax ID on the cover: 12-20-3856-002.

Purchase Money Deed of Trust dated March 30, 2006 from 3010-20 Greenmount Ave, LLC to Susquehanna Bank (Timonium), with two trustees, maximum lien $700,000. The collateral is called '3010-16 Greenmount Avenue' in both the deed of trust and the companion Assignment of Leases and Rents (FMC 7709/248), which is why the 2017 release papers also say 3010-16. The loan was 98.6 percent of the $710,000 price. It was released in June 2017 after the sale.

Certificate of Satisfaction (MB 19268, p. 497) of the March 30, 2006 deed of trust at FMC 7709/239, and Termination of Security Instrument Assignment of Leases and Rents (p. 495) of the instrument at FMC 7709/248, both signed June 12, 2017 by a vice president of Susquehanna Bank 'nka Branch Banking and Trust Company'. The 11-year loan was paid off at the May 2017 sale. Both papers still caption the collateral '3010-16 Greenmount Ave.'

Baltimore City Department of Public Works, Property Location Division, Ward 12 Section 20 Block 3856. The title block reads 'Date June 1985'; the revision block, read at 300 dpi, lists: BLOCK REDRAWN; LOT 2/3 PER SUB-DIV & DEEDS C.SH. 85-549; LOT 2A & 3A FROM ST. BED PER B.S. C.SH 89-636; LOTS 2, 2A, 3 & 3A PER DEED, C.SH. 91-053; LOTS 31 & 32 CONS'D PER O.O.; CH. SH. 15-130. The chart sheet number was earlier misread as 'C.S.M. 91-065' (the plat reads C.SH. 91-053) and the final line, CH. SH. 15-130, was missed, so the sheet shows the block revised through 1991 and once more in 2015 (lots 31 and 32 consolidated); lot 3 carries an area note dated 8-28-90 (earlier readings of the date as 1965 are wrong). Chart sheet 91-053 charts a 1991 deed covering lots 2, 2A, 3 and 3A that has not been identified (probably the City's conveyance of Vineyard Lane street-bed slivers to the owners; the DPW Property Location Division can give its liber and folio from chart sheets 85-549, 89-636 and 91-053). Lot 2, labelled '3010/20', has 105 ft 2 7/8 in on Greenmount and 0.335 acre (about 14,593 sq ft); lot 3, 3001 Vineyard Lane, 0.235 acre. The plat shows the frame-lot row on the north-west side of Vineyard Lane numbered 3000-3016 (23-ft lots, then an 18-ft and a 12 ft 7 in lot at 3014 and 3016), the 30-ft Vineyard Lane meeting Greenmount at the corner of lot 2, Cat Bird Lane (the alley), and 3026-3028 across the lane.

Sanborn Fire Insurance Map, Baltimore Vol. 6 (1928), sheet 654, the west side of Greenmount at Vineyard Lane. The same two frame dwellings as in 1915, on the same footprints. The hatched stable is gone; the 2-story rear outbuilding is labelled 'A' (auto garage); a new 1-story building with a grey border, also 'A', stands north of the old yard; and the 3014 house has an open first story ('OP. 1ST'). 3008/918 is still the 1-story store, and the glass houses behind it read 'GREEN HOS.', with 'WOLFE FLORIST' at the sheet edge. It is the physical trace of the change from dairy to garage in the directories (garage 1917-18; an auto repairer at 3014 in 1920).

The 1951 printing of Vol. 6 (Library of Congress sanborn03573_029, 'Vol. 6, 1928 - May 1950', sheet 654) is the 1928 sheet with pasted correction slips. On this block the slips redraw the 3014 house (2-story frame with porches, set far back) and the 3008 store, but 3020 (a 2-story dwelling with a 1-story porch) and 3014 are both still frame houses, the garages are where they were in 1928, and there is no building on the 3010, 3012, 3016 or 3018 frontage. So the row was built after May 1950, and SDAT's year built of 1950 is not supported by the map. A correction date shows the state of the sheet in May 1950, not how long the houses stood afterwards.

On the best available scan of plate Q, north to south, the tracts are '...Light' (probably Leight, for Lawrence Leight, who had lived at the lane corner since about 1845), 'A. M. ...' (possibly A. G. Mott, whom the directories place in Waverley in 1882-85), 'Chas Hamilton' (with a two-bar glass-house shape drawn behind the house, consistent with Hamilton's listing as a florist in 1880) and 'Jno. T. Cross(e)'. The first two names are blurred, so this is a possible, not a probable, pin of Leight and Mott to the 3020 and 3014 tracts; the 2006 deed's metes (a sublease to Lorenz Leight) and Polk's 922 York rd place Leight at the corner independently.

Jacob H. Aull's captioned photograph booklet carries two Leight pictures. Item 30 is 'Lawrence Leight, 1845. Corner York Road and Gilmor Lane', the frame house at the south-west corner of Vineyard Lane (3020 Greenmount, old 922 York road); the Passano-O'Neill card for 3020 cites the booklet's pages 60-61 for the same view. Item 24 reads 'Residence Lawrence Leight, 1842. Birthplace Louis Leight, 1844. J. H. Hartman's House. West side York Road, near Gorsuch Avenue': the family lived first in an 1842 house on the west side of the road near Gorsuch Avenue (J. H. Hartman's by about 1906) and moved north to the lane corner in 1845. Louis W. Leight (1844-1924) is the child born in the first house. The captions are read from a transcript; the photographs themselves have not been seen.

Jacob H. Aull's booklet caption for the big frame house at 3014 (old 920 York road); the Passano-O'Neill card for 3014 cites the booklet's pages 46-47 for a view of the Mott/O'Neill house from the Greenmount side. It fixes the sequence, Mott then O'Neill, in print by about 1906, when Michael F. O'Neill, dairyman, had been at 920 York road since at least February 1899. Mott's own address in 1890-95 was 918 York road; which lot his house stood on is contested.

Woods prints no house numbers for Waverly, so the tie to the lane corner is by name (and by the 922 York rd lines from 1887). Lawrence Leight, cabinetmaker, 'Waverley' in 1872, 1874-75 and every year 1880-86; Henry, cigarmaker, 1873-86; Geo. E., cigar packer then cigarmaker, 1875-86; Chas. (1880-81) then Chas. G. (1882-86), cigarmaker; Lewis W., helper, huckster, laborer, and a partner in Kramer & Le[ight], produce, 1873-86 (Friendship and Waverley). The four sons are the Louis W. (b. 1844), Henry (b. 1853), George E. (b. 1856) and Charles G. (b. 1858) of the St. John's churchyard. Woods spells the surname Leicht or Leight interchangeably; the spelling settles as Leight in the 1870s.

The first numbered directory with Waverly (Polk 1887, p. 678) lists 'Leight Lawrence, 922 York rd'; the 1888 (p. 678), 1889 (p. 710), 1890 (p. 744, cabinetmaker), 1891 (p. 780) and 1892 (p. 746, cabinetmaker; the text layer prints 923, the page image reads 922) volumes repeat it. Chas G Leight, cigarmaker, is at 922 in 1890 and 1892. The 1915 Sanborn plate prints 922 beside 3020 on the lane-corner house. Lawrence Leight died on March 6, 1892, aged 82.

Polk 1889 lists 'Leight Chas G & Bros (Chas G, Geo E and Henry Leight), cigar mnfrs, 1020 York rd', and the 1893-94 business directory still gives 1020 York rd (that old York road number is not placed on a modern lot). Charles G. Leight died in 1893 and the firm kept his name. Polk 1901, 1903 and 1904 and the 1905-06 business directory list it as '(Henry and Geo E Leight), cigar mnfrs, 3104 York rd'; after Henry's death in June 1904 it is 'Chas G & Bro (Geo E Leight)' in 1914, 1915 ('3104 Greenmt av') and 1918, and 'Chas G & Bros (Geo E Leight), 426 e 31st' in 1920 and 1921. 3104 Greenmount and 426 E. 31st are both part of the Waverly Hall block at the north-west corner of Greenmount and 31st. George E. Leight died in 1929. Charles T. Leight's 1949 Sun memoir places his father's and uncles' cigar store and factory in the same building, and these directory lines give the firm's years there.

Polk's business directories list 'Kramer & Leight, 44 Richmond Mkt' in 1890 and 1893 and 'Kramer & Leight, city mkts' in 1905. Woods shows Lewis W. Leight as a partner in 'Kramer & L.' from 1880. The Passano-O'Neill card for 3020 says Lawrence Leight 'was a stallholder at Richmond Market on Howard Street, selling the produce he raised in Waverly, until his death'; the Kramer & Leight stall is his son Louis W.'s partnership, and whether it is the same stall is not shown. Louis W. Leight (1844-1924) is the man; the Kramer partner is not identified.

922 York rd in 1901 (p. 899) and 1903 (p. 1067): Mrs. Wilhelmina Leight, Chas T Leight (clerk) and Henry Leight (of the cigar firm); 1904: Chas T and Henry; from 1905 (pp. 1036-37) Mrs. Susan Leight replaces Wilhelmina and Henry is gone (he died in June 1904). 1906-1912: Chas T (clerk) and Susan. Renumbered 3020 Greenmt av in 1914 (p. 1226) and in 1918, 1920, 1921, 1922 and 1923 (the 1915 volume prints 3022); 1921: 'Susan (wid Henry), 3020'; 1922: 'Chas T (Ella B), auditor, h 3020'. The 1923 volume is the last directory online. Charles T. Leight (1880-1953) lived in the house from at least 1901 to 1950. The ground was leased (a sublease to Lorenz Leight; the Clemens fee), so these lines record a household, not an owner.

1950 census, Baltimore City, ED 4-560 ('bounded by 30th, Vineyard Lane, Greenmount Ave., 29th, Calvert'), sheet 1, lines 1-4, dwelling 1, 3020 Greenmount: Leight, Charles T., head, white, male, 69, widowed, born Maryland; Flahart [Flayhart], Catherine B., daughter, 44, widowed; and her two sons, aged 13 and 11. The household is repeated as Individual Census Report lines on sheet 74 of ED 4-559. His wife, Ella B. Harris Leight, had died on March 10, 1950. This is the last census count of the frame house. By his death on August 12, 1953 he was 'formerly of 3020 Greenmount avenue', and the 3020 end of the lot was being offered 'will build to suit' in January 1956.

ED 4-560 sheet 1 line 5: '3016 [Greenmount], dwelling 2: no one at home, see sheet 71 lines 1-2'; sheet 71, lines 1-2: Davenport, Anna L., head, white, female, 67, widowed, born Maryland, keeping house, and one other household member. No directory or Sanborn plate shows a separate house numbered 3016 before the 1950s row. Whether the enumerator's 3016 is the big Mott/O'Neill house (advertised as 3014 in November 1939) or another building on the lot is an open question.

Woods lists John O'Neill as a partner in O'Neill & Bro (milk) and Michl. F. O'Neill as a milk dealer, both 'York rd nr Sixth' (the old Waverly-district cross-street numbering, about 25th-26th Street). It is the first appearance of the milk business whose Michael F. O'Neill is at 920 York road from 1899. That 'near Sixth' is the lane corner is not shown, so the earlier dairy is a possible antecedent only.

Every volume from 1903 to 1909, and 1912, lists 'O'Neill Michl F, dairy, 920 York rd' (1903 p. 1303; 1904 p. 1281; 1905 p. 1297; 1906 p. 1562; 1907 p. 1477; 1908 p. 1493; 1909 p. 1513; 1912 p. 2416), with the sons Walter I. (engraver 1903, student 1906-08, draftsman 1907-09) and Clarence L. (student 1907-08, clerk from 1909) at 920, and Mrs. Elizabeth J. Stinchcomb at 920 in 1903-06, a lodger or relative.

The 1914 and 1915 directories print Michl F O'Neill, dairy, 3014 Greenmt av, 'h do' (home at the same address), with Walter I. (draftsman), Clarence L. (clerk) and Harry F. (clerk) at 3014 (1914 pp. 1503-04; 1915 pp. 1548-49). 920 York road is 3014 Greenmount: the household is the same across the renumbering, and the 1915 Sanborn plate prints 3014 over 920 on the house. Catherine C. O'Neill's death notice of December 1913 is the first print of the new number.

The 1917 volume (p. 1503) lists Michl F O'Neill with the occupation 'garage' ('b do', boarding at the address), Walter I. as photographer, and Clarence L. and Harry F. as clerks; the 1918 volume (p. 1606) drops the occupation. The big house takes its first listed lodger, Ernest J. Southerington, draftsman (1917 p. 1849; 1918 p. 1948). It is the directory side of the 1928 Sanborn's garages and of the Passano card's line that O'Neill's stables became garages as he moved into auto repair.

1920 volume: Walter I. O'Neill, photographer, and Harry F. O'Neill, artist, at 3014; Jas. H. Bennett, clerk; Earle Harrington, auto repairer, and Kath. A. Harrington, clerk. 1921: the same. 1922: 'O'Neill Harry F (Edith), cartoonist, h 3014'. 1923: Wm. H. Borring, painter, 3014. Michael F. O'Neill is not listed after 1918; his death has not been found. The 1923 volume is the last directory online; the Pratt Library holds the later volumes.

Alex Jay's Stripper's Guide profile (August 2016) builds Harry F. O'Neill's life from the records: born in Baltimore on September 1, 1891; the 1900 census lists him as 'the youngest of four children born to Michael and Kate', living at 920 York Road, the O'Neill dairy house (now 3014 Greenmount). The other children in 1900 are presumably Walter I., Clarence L. and a daughter (a Miss Marie O'Neill of 920 is in the Sun in 1911); a son, William L., had died in February 1899. A secondary source citing census pages not seen here.

Per the Jay profile: on his June 5, 1917 draft card Harry F. O'Neill gives 3014 Greenmount and the occupation newspaper artist for the Baltimore American; the 1920 census finds him married to Edith, with a son of 21 months, at 3014 Greenmount. (Jay also quotes a 1913 directory line for him at '3304 Greenmount Avenue'; the 1912-13 directories print 920 York rd for the family.) Polk 1922 prints 'O'Neill Harry F (Edith), cartoonist' at 3014, so his early strips, Old Pals (from 1920) and Us Kids (from November 1921), were presumably drawn at the old Mott house. A secondary source.

Strips: Old Pals (1920 to Nov 5, 1923), Us Kids (Nov 21, 1921 to Aug 4, 1923) and Broncho Bill, first Young Buffalo Bill and Buckaroo Bill (June 7, 1927 to July 8, 1950; syndicated to as many as 130 papers by United Features), with the companion Sunday feature Bumps. A former Baltimore Sun sports cartoonist and advertising layout artist; taught cartooning at the Baltimore Institute; toured as a circus and vaudeville acrobat as a teenager (New York Times). Death: Jay gives March 31, 1958 at Yonkers General Hospital, as does Lambiek; Wikipedia and the AP obituary in the Evening Sun (April 2, 1958, p. 4) say April 1, 1958. The conflict is unresolved. The Sun page does not name 3014, so the identification with the dairy family rests on the Jay profile's census and draft-card addresses and on Polk.

From a mirror of the SDAT business-entity records (not yet re-read on Business Express): Quality Film Lab, Inc., Department ID D00290908, incorporated June 25, 1969 (film F740, folio 617), resident agent Robert C. Prem, 929 N. Howard St.; principal address 3010 Greenmount Ave. The lab that traded as 'Quality Film Labs' in 1966 incorporated four months before the BG&E photograph of October 1969. Its successor, Quality Film and Video, says it has been in the film business 'for well over 50 years'.

From a mirror of the SDAT business-entity records: Datah, Inc., Department ID D04670592, articles of incorporation April 24, 1997, articles of amendment November 14, 2005; address 3014 Greenmount Ave, mailing 'Pizza Bravo Plus, 3014 Greenmount Avenue'. A March 2024 Street View capture shows the 'Pizza Plus' awning and yellow roll-down shutters on the 3014 bay.
From a mirror of the SDAT business-entity records: Invest, Inc., Department ID D06254379, chartered April 2, 2001, address 3012 Greenmount Ave (resident agent at 3010), forfeited October 7, 2003.

From a mirror of the SDAT business-entity records: The World Is Yours, Incorporated, Department ID D10374064, chartered December 29, 2004, resident agent at 3010 Greenmount Ave, forfeited October 6, 2006.

From a mirror of the SDAT business-entity records and OpenCorporates: Hook 'Em Up, LLC, Department ID W12237665, formed October 5, 2007, and Hook'Em Up Inc., D12400172, chartered March 4, 2008, for the 3010 Greenmount bay; both forfeited in 2009-2010.

From a mirror of the SDAT business-entity records: High-Quality Transportation, LLC, Department ID W15386949, formed August 2, 2013, address 3016 Greenmount Ave, with resolutions filed in 2014 and 2016.

Sun death notice of February 22, 1899: William L., son of Michael F. and Katie C. O'Neill, died February 21, 1899, and the funeral left 'his late residence, No. 920 York [road]' on Thursday at nine. It is the earliest print of the O'Neills at 920 York road (Polk first lists 'O'Neill Michl F, dairy, 920 York rd' in 1903). Katie C. is the Catherine C. O'Neill whose 1913 death notice names 3014 Greenmount. The clipping cut the surname heading and the word 'son'; both are supplied in brackets.

Sun, September 6, 1900, a three-insertion classified (from September 5): a quantity of 'GALLONS JERSEY MILK daily at C[...] [...]rt Station. Address M. F. O'NEILL, 92[0] [York r]oad.' The edges of the clipping cut the first words, and the last digit of the house number is supplied from M. F. O'Neill's address at 920 elsewhere. It puts Michael F. O'Neill in the milk trade at 920 York road three years before Polk first prints 'dairy' (1903).

Sun death notice of Friday, June 14, 1901: Catherine R. Hanson, widow of the late William H. Hanson, died June 13, 1901 'at her late resi[dence], No. 920 York road'. No relationship to the O'Neills is printed; Polk 1903-06 also lists a Mrs. Elizabeth J. Stinchcomb at 920. A household member of the 920 York road house (later 3014 Greenmount).

Sun, December 1, 1913, p. 6 (also Evening Sun, same day, p. 10, and Sun, December 2, p. 6): Catherine C. O'Neill, wife of Michael F. O'Neill (the Polk dairyman of 920 York rd), died November 30, 1913; the funeral left 'her late residence, No. 3014 Greenmount avenue' on Tuesday, December 2, at 8.30, with a Requiem Mass at Sts. Philip and James' Church and burial in Bonnie Brae. It is the first newspaper print of the modern number 3014 and shows that the O'Neill house at 920 York road is 3014 Greenmount (Polk 1913 still printed 920).

Evening Sun 'Deaths' column, April 2, 1958 (AP, Yonkers, N.Y.): Harry F. O'Neill, 66, 'who formerly drew the comic strip Broncho Bill', died the day before (April 1, 1958); a former sports cartoonist for the Baltimore Sun; the strip was syndicated from 1928 to 1950 to as many as 130 newspapers; born in Baltimore. Polk has a Harry F. O'Neill at 3014 Greenmount as a clerk (1914-17), artist (1920-21) and cartoonist (1922), son of the dairyman Michael F. The column names neither 3014 nor his parents, so the link rests on name, craft and Baltimore birth, with the Jay profile's census and draft-card addresses: probable. A different Harry F. O'Neill, of Whittier, California (died January 1927), is not the cartoonist.

Sun death notice of May 27, 1902: Wilhelmina Leight, aged 83, 'beloved [wife of t]he late Lawrence Leight', died May 24, 1902 at Jersey City, N.J.; 'Her funeral will take place from her late resi[dence, N]o. 922 York road, on Wednesday afternoon' (May 28). It puts Lawrence Leight's widow at the lane-corner house, 922 York road (3020 Greenmount), and dates her death to 1902; Polk lists 'Leight Wilhelmina Mrs' at 922 in 1901 and 1903.

Sun, Thursday, June 9, 1904, p. 6: 'Mr. Henry Leight, senior member of the firm of Leight Bros., cigar manufacturers, of Waverly, died suddenly yesterday morning at his home, 922 York road.' He was 50, 'a resident of Waverly for many years', and left a widow and one child. The Sun calls the firm (Chas G Leight & Bros in Polk) Leight Bros. His widow was Susan Leight; the one child was probably Charles T. Leight.

Sun death notice of June 10, 1904: Henry Leight, 'in the 51st year of his age, beloved husband of Susan Leight', died suddenly June 8, 1904; the funeral left 'his late residence, No. 922 York road' that afternoon, with burial in St. John's Cemetery, Waverly, the family's burial ground. Polk lists Mrs. Susan Leight at 922 from 1905.

Sun, Sunday, June 14, 1914, p. 3, 'Embroidery Classes End': the children's embroidery classes run by Joel Gutman & Co. on North Eutaw Street closed with an exhibition; about 100 pupils. 'First--Catherine Leight, 8 years old, 3020 Greenmount avenue.' The earliest print of 3020 Greenmount. Catherine Leight (born about 1905-06) is Charles T. Leight's daughter, later Mrs. Catherine B. Flayhart.

Evening Sun, September 2, 1932, p. 39 (repeated September 3 and 4 in both papers): Susan Leight, widow of Henry Leight, died September 1, 1932; the funeral left 'her late residence, 3020 Greenmount avenue' on Sunday, September 4, with burial in St. John's Cemetery, Waverly. Polk has her at 3020 as 'wid Henry' in 1921; the old 922 York road house was a Leight home from at least 1887 to 1932.

Evening Sun, December 25, 1941, p. 29: William H. Flayhart Jr., husband of Catherine B. Flayhart (nee Leight), died suddenly December 24, 1941; the funeral service was held at the home, 3020 Greenmount avenue, with burial in St. John's Cemetery, Waverly. Charles T. Leight's daughter Catherine (the eight-year-old of 1914) and her husband lived in the 3020 house in 1941.

Evening Sun, March 11, 1950, p. 12: Ella B. Leight (nee Harris), wife of Charles T. Leight and mother of Mrs. Catherine B. Flayhart, died March 10, 1950; the funeral was at William J. Tickner & Sons, with burial in St. John's Cemetery, Waverly. No residence is given; the April 1950 census still has Charles T. Leight at 3020. Her maiden name resolves Polk's 'Chas T (Ella B)'.

Sun, August 13, 1953, p. 23 (also Evening Sun, August 12 and 13, and Sun, August 14): Charles T. Leight died August 12, 1953, 'formerly of 3020 Greenmount avenue', husband of the late Ella B. Leight and father of Mrs. Catherine B. Flayhart; funeral at William J. Tickner & Sons, burial at St. John's Cemetery, Waverly. He is the Polk clerk and auditor of 1901-1922 and the author of the Sun Magazine memoir of November 27, 1949. 'Formerly of' means the family had left the 3020 house before August 1953.

Sun, February 2, 1929, p. 16 (repeated in the Evening Sun and on February 3): George E. Leight, husband of the late M. Emma Leight (nee Holmes), died February 1, 1929; the funeral left his residence, 629 Homestead Street, with burial in St. John's Cemetery, Waverly. George E. Leight is the cigar packer and maker of the Woods directories and a member of the Chas G Leight & Bros firm; the tie to the family rests on the surname, the trade and the burial ground, not an address: probable.

Sun Magazine, November 27, 1949, p. 154, 'I Remember... The Old Squire of Waverly', by Charles T. Leight, who was 'a boy in the 1880's'. He describes Waverly as a country town along the York road from Thirtieth Street to Merryman's lane, the magistrate Squire William D. Wright, and the renaming from Huntingdon in 1870, and says: 'Most of [the old Waverly buildings], like my house, have had new fronts built on.' The writer is the last Leight of the 3020 house. The memoir's passages on the York road toll house and on his family's cigar factory are filed as their own rows.

From Charles T. Leight's Sun Magazine memoir of November 27, 1949 (p. 154): 'An example is the York road toll house, which stood just north of our home, on the northwest corner of Gilmore lane. It was operated, for the purpose of collecting money to improve York road, by Mrs. T. S. Bonsal, who took over after her husband died. The toll-gate building also contained the post office; Mrs. Bonsal was postmistress, too. Tillman Schofield succeeded Mrs. Bonsal as toll keeper.' So the Leight house (922 York road, 3020 Greenmount) stood on the south-west corner of the lane, across from the toll-house lot on the north-west corner. The memoir does not say 'Vineyard'; Gilmore (Gilmor) lane is the lane now called Vineyard Lane, per the National Register nomination and the 1915 Sanborn plate.

From Charles T. Leight's Sun Magazine memoir of November 27, 1949 (p. 154): 'One that means a great deal to me stands on the northwest corner of Greenmount and Thirty-first street, which was Waverly avenue. It means a lot because it housed my father's and my uncles's cigar store and factory. The factory, with its rich tobacco odors that I can smell today, employed ten men, who rolled cigars by hand. The cigars went under brand names such as Waverly, and were sold in wholesale lots to restaurants and retail stores.' He sold cigars over the counter after school and after he went to work for a railroad. 'Upstairs was the town hall, a large meeting room used principally by the Waverly Masonic Lodge, and later by the Baltimore Temple of the Knights and Ladies of the Golden Eagle. Occupying downstairs quarters next to the cigar factory was a drug store operated by Edwin C. Livingston, who later became a City Councilman.' The firm is Chas G Leight & Bros, listed by Polk at 3104 York road in 1901-05 and at 3104 Greenmount in 1915. The writer's father was Henry Leight (died 1904); the family lived at 922 York road, now 3020 Greenmount. This is the primary source for the cigar factory at Waverly Hall.

Sun, February 28, 1915, p. 9, and a run of about 19 insertions to March 15 (Evening Sun, March 15, p. 13): 'GOING out of the odorless excavating business will sell 12 HEAD OF HORSES AND MULES; ALSO WAGONS AND HARNESS. Call at RESIDENCE, Greenmount ave. and Vineyard lane, Waverly. York road car to door.' No name, and no side of the lane. An odorless excavator cleaned privy vaults. Polk's directories point to the seller: Charles H. Clark is listed under Odorless Excavators at 1000 York rd in 1907 and 1908, at 10 Gilmor la (the lane's old name) in 1909 and at 8 Vineyard la in 1914 and 1915, with his home at number 10 ('Clark Chas H o e a 8 Vineyard la h 10 do', 1914, p. 494), and the 1915 Sanborn draws a 2-story frame house numbered 10 on the lane behind 3026. A year later the Evening Sun (March 8, 1916, p. 15) carries 'GOING OUT OF BUSINESS--Must sell four good Young Work Horses ... Apply at MR. CLARK'S, rear of 3026 Greenmount ave.', and by 1922 Chas. H. Clark kept a garage at 418-20 Vineyard Lane. Probable, not proven: the ad prints no name. The residence stood on the lot that is now 3020 Vineyard Lane, not on 3026's own lot.

Evening Sun, March 31, 1916, p. 19 (six insertions): 'FOR LEASE--50-foot Waterfront Lots; Cypress Park, six miles view over Magothy river; near Annapolis Boulevard and Short Line Railroad station. Apply to S. J. ZEPP, 3014 Greenmount avenue, Baltimore, Md.' Polk 1915 still has the O'Neills at 3014, so Zepp, a waterfront-lot dealer, was an office tenant in the house or shared the address. A Zepp family ran Zepp Photo Supply farther up the block (3042-3044) from 1911.

Sun, April 20, 1920, p. 24, part of a three-day run (April 20-22): 'FORD BODIES--1 Touring [...] 3014 Greenmount ave.' in the auto-parts classifieds; the edges of the column hid the rest of the line. It fits Polk 1917 ('Michl F garage 3014 Greenmt') and Polk 1920-21 ('Earle auto repr 3014'): the dairy stable turned garage.

Evening Sun, September 2, 1924, p. 25, first of a five-day run (September 2-6): 'HOUSE WIRING. D. & H. ELECTRIC [CO.], 3014 Greenmount avenue. Homewood 7223.' An electrical contractor at 3014 in 1924, between the auto repairer of 1920 and the house for rent of 1928.

Sun, November 4, 1928, p. 44, first of six insertions (November 4-25), house-rent classifieds under S. Realty Co.: '3014 GREENMOUNT AVE.--$50; 6 [rooms], bath and attic; newly papered and [...] large lot.' The old dairy house was a six-room rental with a large lot in 1928; the 1928 Sanborn shows it on the same footprint.

Evening Sun, June 24, 1935, p. 25 (run of June 24-26): 'PFIEFER.--On June 22, 1935, MARGARET D. (nee Ervin), beloved wife of George H. Pfiefer. Funeral from her late residence 3014 Greenmount avenue, on Wednesday at 2 P. M. Interment in Parkwood Cemetery.' A family lived in the former O'Neill house in 1935.

Sun, March 29, 1957, p. 36, first of a four-day run: 'SALESMAN--We have a good debit for the right man. Apply in person, Home Beneficial Life Ins. Co., 3014 Greenmount ave.' A year later the Evening Sun of March 25, 1958 (p. 31) prints the company's annual-statement display ad listing 'District Office No. 1, W. R. McCarty, Manager, 3014 Greenmount Avenue'. The recruiting ad of March 1957 comes before the Sun's report of June 9, 1957 that Home Beneficial had leased 'a new office building being erected by Edward Costanza, builder, at 3014'; whether the company used the address before the building was finished is not settled.

Sun, October 22, 1972, p. 184, first of a run to April 1973: 'WAVERLY -- 3014 GREENMOUNT AVE. MODERN AIR CONDITIONED ONE-STORY STORE OR OFFICE TYPE BLDG. 25'x80' WITH OFF-STREET PARKING. CHAS. GREENBLATT, Realtor.' It gives the 3014 unit's size (25 by 80 ft) and the agent, the same Chas. Greenblatt who reported the Time Finance lease at 3016 in 1958 and advertised 3010 in 1973.

Sun, November 15, 1988, p. 82: 'BLOOD DONORS NEEDED / MD BIOLOGICAL SERVICES / 3014 Greenmount Ave / Mon-Fri 8AM-4:30PM / Cash Paid! $8 + $7 Bonus w/Ad-Nov 14-30.' The same ad, without the bonus line, opens the run on September 11, 1988 (Sun, p. 124, image 378103426); the run of about 196 pages ends on January 13, 1989 (Evening Sun, p. 40). A whole-blood collection company called Maryland Biological Services is listed today on Belair Road; that it is the same firm is possible but unproven (no charter record seen).

Sun, December 2, 1956, p. 169 (weekly Sunday run to January 20, 1957): Chas. Greenblatt's build-to-suit ad, 'WE WILL BUILD AND LEASE TO YOU -- SITES AVAILABLE AS FOLLOWS FOR STORES OR OFFICES: PARK HEIGHTS & HAYWARD (Adjoining new S. & H Redemption Center); 3016 GREENMOUNT AVENUE (Adjoining Gen'l Elect. & Ins. Co.); HILTON NR. FREDERICK ...'. So in December 1956 the 3016 site was still unbuilt. Which neighbours 'Gen'l Elect. & Ins. Co.' means is open: General Electric's X-ray branch was at 3012, and 3014 lies between 3012 and 3016; the phrase may mean General Electric and an insurance company (Home Beneficial Life was at 3014 by March 1957).

Sun, March 23, 1958, p. 93, 'Leases Reported' column: 'Mr. Greenblatt also reports the leasing of the commercial properties listed below: New office building to be erected at 3016 Greenmount avenue for a term of years for E. Costanza to Time Finance' (the column is cut by an advertisement). It names the lessor, E. Costanza (probably Edward F. Costanza, builder, who died in December 1960), and the tenant, and dates the 3016 building to 1958.

Evening Sun, June 17, 1958, p. 34, the first Time Finance help-wanted ad: 'ADJUSTORS--For Finance Co. Salary $300 mo. plus car allowance ... Time Finance Co., 3016 Greenmount Ave.' Three months after the lease was reported, the office is open. The same office's help-wanted and display ads run through the 1960s: a secretary, 'Assistant to manager of credit dept.' (Sun, October 3, 1962, p. 34), and display ads of January 8, 1964 (Evening Sun, p. 5), March 1, 1966 (p. 39) and June 3, 1969 (p. 33) listing Time Finance Co., 3016 Greenmount Ave., with branches at Liberty and Old Court Roads, 2 Patapsco Avenue, and Bladensburg.

Sun, February 26, 1971, p. 38: 'CLERK TYPIST -- H.S. grad ... Apply MR. POSNER, 3016 GREENMOUNT AVE. CITY FINANCE.' The office that advertised as Time Finance Co. in June 1969 is 'City Finance' by February 1971, a rename or takeover between those dates. The 3016 help-wanted ads end in 1972.

Sun, August 18, 1920, p. 20, 'Bolt Hits Florist's Shop': 'The store of William H. Wolf, flo[rist], 3012 Greenmount avenue, was dam[aged] by lightning. The roof caved in, but [the] hothouse in the rear of the building [es]caped with slight damage.' The only pre-1950s print that really reads 3012. Polk 1914-23 and the National Register inventory (1928 directory) place Wm. H. Wolfe, florist, at 3008, the next lot south, with its glass houses behind. Either the Sun used 3012 for 3008 or the shop straddled the line: contested.

Evening Sun, May 2, 1955, p. 2, repeated May 3-5: 'CARPENTERS--Exp. Commercial work. Apply 3012 Greenmount ave.' in Help Wanted--Male. The ad is unsigned. Someone was hiring carpenters for commercial work at 3012 while the row was going up; possibly a contractor's job office for the new building, not proven.

The Capital (Annapolis), March 23, 1970, p. 14, a coupon ad: 'MAIL TO THE ORIGINAL PRIME-O-SASH CORP. 3012 GREENMOUNT AVE. BALTIMORE, MARYLAND. I am interested in [ ] Window [ ] Siding ...' The same coupon runs in the Evening Sun of March 30, 1970 (p. 11). Replacement windows and siding, sold statewide by coupon from 3012 until October 1973.

Sun, October 25, 1973, p. 12, the last Prime-O-Sash print: a display ad 'MD. PRIME-O-[SASH] / WAREHOUSE & [...] / 3012 GREENMOUNT AVE. / BALTIMORE, MD. 21218'. The firm now calls the address a warehouse.

Sun, February 1, 1987, and the Evening Sun and Sun of June 24, 1987 (p. 48), the ends of a 63-page run: PharmaKinetics, which paid volunteers for drug studies ('you can earn up to $1800'), announces a 'NEW LOCATION' at 3012 Greenmount Ave., moving its clinic from 2126 Maryland Avenue in early 1987.

Sun, June 18, 1926, p. 3, in a list of zoning applications: '... Building and loan association office at 17 South Highland avenue. Sign at 3010-3014 Greenmount avenue.' The first real print of 3010. A sign for a non-residential use on the house and garage lots at 3010-3014 in 1926; the applicant is not named.

Evening Sun, April 11, 1973, p. 76, first of 13 weekly ads (to July 4, 1973), Chas. Greenblatt, Realtor: 'STORES--OFFICES / ... / 3010 Greenmount Ave.--21x75'.' The 3010 unit was vacant in spring 1973 and measures 21 by 75 ft; with 3014 (25 by 80 ft) the row's storefronts are bays of 21 to 25 ft.

Evening Sun, April 4, 1981, p. 11, first of a 30-page run to May 1982: 'WE NEED DONATIONS of clothing, furniture, household, etc. for the House of Heros, 3010 Greenmount Ave. in order to raise money for a Recreation Fund for Disabled War Veterans.' The last page read, Sun, May 29, 1982, p. 22, advertises a 'FLEA MARKET FESTIVAL ... 3010 Greenmount Ave.' A veterans' charity thrift and flea market in the 3010 bay.

Sun, February 13, 1983, p. 45, a feature on local independent filmmakers: 'One who has been helping, working with and even employing them for years is Pete Garey of the Quality Film Lab. "Filmmaking used to be a kind of secret, but that's long since over. I've been in the field since 1958," he says.' No address; by then the lab was at 5800 York Road. Filed with 3010 because the lab was at 3010 Greenmount in 1966-1973: possible.

Sun, December 18, 1960, p. 27, 'Costanza Dies at 67': Edward F. Costanza, board chairman of a large Baltimore construction company, died at Union Memorial Hospital; he lived at 105 Witherspoon Road, Homeland; born and educated in Augusta, Sicily, he came to the United States at 14, worked in Nazareth, Pa., New York and Camden, N.J., 'came to Baltimore in 1934 and founded the Costanza Construction Company, 3001 Vineyard lane. His son, Michael, is president of the firm.' Projects named: the Baltimore City Fire School, Catonsville High School, the new Franklin High School in Reisterstown and Security Senior High School. He is the 'Edward Costanza, builder' of the 3014 building (1957) and very probably the 'E. Costanza' of the 3016 lease (1958).

Read on the Sun (p101): 'COSTANZA.--On December 17, 1960, EDWARD F., of 105 Witherspoon road, beloved husband of Rose Costanza (nee Spinnato), devoted father of Mrs. Edna C. Bianco and Mr. Michael L. Costanza. Services from the Leonard J. Ruck Funeral Home, 5305 Harford road at Echodale avenue, on Tuesday at 9 A.M. Requiem High Mass at the Cathedral of Mary Our Queen, Charles street near Belvedere, at 10 A.M. Interment in Holy Redeemer Cemetery. Friends may call between 2 and 9 P.M.' Gives the heirs who inherited the Greenmount holdings: Rose, Edna C. Bianco, Michael L. Costanza.

Sun, Monday, March 7, 1892, p. 6: 'Mr. Lawrence Leight, the oldest resident of Waverly, died yesterday afternoon of catarrh of the stomach, at his home, corner Gilmor lane and York road. Mr. Leight was born in Helburg, Saxe-Coburg, March 15, 1809. He came to Baltimore in 1837 and removed to Waverly in 1842. On March 22, 1841, he married Miss Wilhelmina Strohmer. In March of 1891 Mr. and Mrs. Leight celebrated their golden wedding. He was a cabinetmaker, but retired from work several years ago. His widow, four sons and two daughters survive him.' The primary document for the parcel's earliest named occupant: the house at the corner of Gilmor lane (Vineyard Lane) and York road is the south-west corner house, 922 York road, 3020 Greenmount. It fixes 1842 as the year the Leights settled in Waverly and dates his death to March 6, 1892. His Find a Grave memorial gives his birthplace as Bavaria, against the Sun's Helburg, Saxe-Coburg.

Sun, Thursday, March 12, 1868, p. 2 (first printed March 11): 'RAHE.--In Baltimore county, on the 9th instant, JOHANNAH C., beloved wife of Charles Rahe, aged 26 years and 2 months ... from the residence of her father, Waverley, York road.' The notice names neither Leight nor her father. Find a Grave (memorial 207551815) identifies her as Johannah C. Leicht, born December 29, 1841, married to Charles M. Rahe on June 16, 1862, died March 9, 1868; her age fits, and so does Lawrence Leight's 1892 obituary (married March 1841; 'four sons and two daughters' surviving, with Johannah dead). If so, this is the earliest newspaper print of the Leight house and the tie between the Leights and the Rahe shoemakers of Waverly: probable, not verified.

Sun, September 13, 1904, p. 7, 'Death Of Mr. Charles M. Rahe': he died 'yesterday at his home, corner Fair Oak avenue and Old York road, Waverly'; one of the oldest residents of Waverly, having lived there 45 years; born in Osnabruck, Germany, came to this country in 1856; 'one of the oldest shoe merchants in the city'; lately retired and succeeded by his oldest son, L. William Rahe; twice married, survived by a widow, four sons and four daughters; the funeral from St. John's Protestant Episcopal Church, Waverly. The Rahe shoe store was at 1007 York road, the 3015 building, in 1903-1912. His first wife, Johannah C. (died 1868), is identified by Find a Grave as a daughter of Lawrence Leight of the lane-corner house across the road, which would make L. William Rahe (1865-1932) a Leight grandson: probable, since no page names Leight beside Rahe.

Sun, June 27, 1907, p. 8, Judge-at-Large docket: '... Charles G. Leight & Bro. vs. Howard E[...] $182.01.' The docket gives no address. The firm, run after Charles G. Leight's death in 1893 by his brothers Henry (died 1904) and George E. Leight under his name, is listed at 3104 York road in 1901-05 and at 3104 Greenmount in 1915, the Waverly Hall block; Charles T. Leight's memoir puts the factory there.

Find a Grave memorial 31044714: Henry Leight, born November 10, 1853, Maryland; died June 8, 1904 (aged 50); Saint Johns Episcopal Cemetery. Son of Lawrence and Wilhelmina Leicht; husband of Susan Leight (1848-1932); father of Charles T. Leight (1880-1953). The death date matches the Sun notice of June 10, 1904. A user-created memorial.

Find a Grave memorial 31044625: Charles T. Leight, born August 15, 1880, Maryland; died August 12, 1953 (aged 72); Saint Johns Episcopal Cemetery; son of Henry and Susan Leight; husband of Ella B. Harris Leight (1882-1950); father of Catherine B. Leight Flayhart (1905-2002). His age agrees with the 1950 census (69 in April 1950), and he is the memoirist of 1949 and the Polk 'Chas T (Ella B)' of 3020. A user-created memorial.

Find a Grave memorial 207551815: Johannah C. Leicht Rahe, born December 29, 1841, Baltimore County; died March 9, 1868; 'married Charles Rahe on 16 June 1862. Her death notice ran in the Baltimore Sun on 12 March, the same day as her funeral from her father's home on the York Road, Waverly.' Spouse Charles M. Rahe (1836-1904); children Sophie Wilhelmine Rahe (1863-1937) and Louis William Rahe (1865-1932). A user-submitted memorial; the Sun notice itself does not name her father.

Sun, February 24, 1957, p. 55, first of a five-page run: a display ad 'GENERAL ELECTRIC CO. / X-RAY DEPARTMENT / 3012 Greenmount Ave. / Baltimore 12, Md.' The Sun of August 3, 1958 (p. 47) repeats the address ('GENERAL ELECTRIC CO. X-RAY DEPT. 3012 Greenmount Ave., Balto. 18'). The branch is in the medical journals' branch lists at 3012 from November 1955 to November 1961.

Sun, July 21, 1978, p. 21, in a nightlife column: 'Betty's Coffee Cup, 3010 Greenmount avenue, is open 11 P.M. to dawn. Cover charge $1, coffee $1. Betty's will be moving in a week or two to Barre street.' An after-hours coffeehouse in the 3010 bay in 1978.

Sun, November 21, 1979, p. 30, actions of the Board of Municipal and Zoning Appeals: '3010-20 Greenmount avenue. A request by Seeber Bodine to use portion of building at 3012 for making of engraved signs and nameplates--disapproved.' A small sign-engraving use was refused in the 3012 bay; the city addressed the building as 3010-20 Greenmount.

Evening Sun, April 3, 1984, p. 38 (and Sun, April 5, p. 68): display ad 'This Month Only 25%-40% OFF list price ... MORTON'S UPHOLSTERY 3010 Greenmount Ave.' The 3010 bay after the House of Heros (1981-82).

Sun, November 23, 1987, p. 71 (and the Evening Sun; repeated April 19 and 26, 1988): an electrical contractor's display ad, '100, 150, or 200 Amps / 110/220 Volts / ... / 3010 Greenmount Ave. / Baltimore, Md. / CALVIN H. BROOKS / Master-Electrician'.

Sun, May 9, 1954, p. 72, business-opportunities classifieds: 'SELF-SERVICE Laundry & Dry Cleaning--All new machines. Wonderful opportunity for right person. Good going business. Apply 3010 Greenmount Ave bet. 8.30-1 P.M. except Sats.' A self-service laundry was trading at 3010 by spring 1954, so the south end of the row was built by then (the May 1950 Sanborn still showed the frame houses). The 3010 hits of 1950-54 before it are telephone numbers.

Sun, March 6, 1955, p. 49, a display list of the Wee-Wash-It self-service laundries: '... Harford Wee-Wash-It 1531 Harford Ave.; Greenmount Wee-W[ash-It] 3010 Greenmount [Ave.]; ...' The 3010 bay was the chain's Greenmount branch in 1955.

Sun, Sunday, June 9, 1957, p. 111, 'Business Transfers' column (the top is cut): '[...] Green Stamps, and leasing to Home Beneficial Life Insurance Company for ten years of a new office building being erected by Edward Costanza, builder, at 3014 Greenmount avenue.' It names the builder of the 3014 building, Edward Costanza (founder of the Costanza Construction Co.), and dates it to 1957, with a ten-year lease. It is the first page to name Costanza as builder on the row.

Sun, May 5, 1934, p. 16, incorporations column: 'Costanza Construction Company. Incor[porators] [...] Harry K. Lott, Harry Silver and C[...] Cohen. Authorized capital stock, 100[...] shares, no par value.' The incorporators named are not Costanza; Edward F. Costanza's obituary says he came to Baltimore in 1934 and founded the company, so the identity rests on the name and the year. The firm later bid public work (a City fire training school, 1955; Catonsville Senior High School, 1952).

Sun, Sunday, March 21, 1954, p. 54, real-estate classifieds: 'VALUABLE LOT & property in the heart of Waverly. 3010 to 3020 Greenmount Ave. Lot 105x286. Call CH. 3-9265 or MA. 3-7314.' No seller or agent is named; it is a lot offering. A 105 by 286 ft lot is about the present lot 2 (about 139 ft deep) together with lot 3 on Vineyard Lane. Seven weeks later a laundry with 'all new machines' is trading at 3010 (May 9, 1954), so the 3010 store, or its plans, may predate this ad.

Sun, January 8, 1956, p. 64, store and office rentals: '3020 GREENMOUNT AVE.--Approx. 5,500 square ft. on ground floor. Will build to suit. With 14 parking spaces for cars.' No agent or owner named. The 3020 end of the lot was being offered as build-to-suit in January 1956.

Sun, December 28, 1956, p. 24, first of a four-day run: 'WAITRESS--Over 21, hours 5 P.M.-2 A.M. Connolly Seafood, 3020 Greenmount Ave.' A seafood restaurant open until 2 A.M. in the new store at the north end of the row by December 1956.

Sun, November 10, 1939, p. 27, rooms for rent: 'TRUE BALTO. charm & atmosphere rm., lovely old house, 2-acre [...], twin beds, fireplace. 3 exposures [...] 3014 Greenmount ave.' (the right edge of the column is cut). After the six-room house for rent of 1928 and the Pfiefer household of 1935, the old O'Neill house on its large yard was let as rooms in 1939. The two-acre figure is the ad's own.

Sun, October 27, 1904, p. 3 (two insertions), lost and found: 'LOST--MILK ROUTE BOOK, in alley rear of Calvert st., near 25th st. Reward if returned to M. F. O'NEILL, 920 York road.' A retail milk route in the streets a mile south of the dairy.

Sun, July 10, 1906, p. 6, a runaway story cut at the right edge: a mule team ran down North avenue toward Greenmount; 'A milk wagon belonging to [M. F.] O'Neill, 920 York road, was at [North and] Greenmount avenues, and the car[t crashed] into it, breaking the shafts and [injuring] the horse's shoulder.' The dairy's wagons worked the city end of Greenmount Avenue, a mile and a half from the stable yard.

Sun, September 9, 1911, p. 10, a fair prize list: 'Miss Marie O'Neill, 920 Old York road, Waverly--Second, landscape or marine in water colors; second, landscape or marine in oil.' The print says Old York road, a different street from York road (Greenmount); the number 920 and the Waverly address make her probably the dairyman's daughter at 920 York road (the 1900 census has four O'Neill children), but no page names her parents.

Evening Sun, October 9, 1912, p. 14: 'Other appointments made by the Sewerage Commission yesterday were: Walter I. O'Neill, 920 York road, draftsman, $75 a month.' Walter I. is Michael F. O'Neill's son (Polk: engraver 1903, draftsman 1907-15, photographer 1917-21).

Sun, October 17, 1907, p. 7, a list of out-of-town visitors: 'Mrs. Lousia Kotta, Jersey City, N. J.--922 York road. Seymour Cerf, Jersey City, N. J.,--922 York road.' Louisa Kotta, born Leight, is named as a daughter of Lawrence and Wilhelmina Leight in a family tree (probable); Wilhelmina Leight died at Jersey City in 1902. The Leight house at 922 kept its ties to a Jersey City branch of the family. Update Oct. 14, 2026: 'Louisa Katto' of Hudson County, New Jersey is one of Lawrence Leight's heirs in the 1903 deed of the corner (719:mdlr-ro1999-329-leicht-heirs-henry-susan-leight-1903): 'Mrs. Louisa Kotta' of Jersey City visiting 922 York Road in 1907 is very probably the same woman, a Leight relative.

Sun, October 4, 1895, p. 10, news obituary: 'Mr. Abram G. Mott, whose age was about eighty-five years, died yesterday at his home, 918 York road, from pneumonia.' He had ridden the electric cars from Waverly to Towson and walked to the Timonium fair, caught a cold in the rain on the way home, and it became pneumonia. A Baltimorean by birth, until two years before he had been in the agricultural implement and seed business on Ensor Street near Belair Market; a Mason and Odd Fellow; his wife, formerly Miss Thompson, survived him; they had no children. So Mott was born about 1810 and died on October 3, 1895. He is the man the Passano-O'Neill card and Old Land Marks name as the first occupant of the frame house later numbered 3014; his own address is 918 York road, and which lot that was is contested.

Sun, March 3, 1968, p. 109, a film-festival preview: 'Offering $750 in awards, the festival has been made possible through the contributions of the Equitable Trust Company and Miss Alice Falvey, sponsors; J. F. Theaters, Inc., Quality Film Labs, Atlantic Photo Supply Company, Inc. and Walter Gettinger, patrons.' The Evening Sun of March 3, 1969 (p. 5) repeats the lab as a patron, with Jonas Mekas and P. Adams Sitney as judges. No address; the lab was listed at 3010 Greenmount in 1966 and photographed there in 1969: possible.

On Hopkins' 1876 atlas (Vol. 1, Plate Q, 'Parts of 9th and 12th Districts', MSA frame 0810) the label TOLL GATE sits on the west side of York Road where Gilmor's Lane (Vineyard Lane today) reaches the road. Across the lane to the south is the lot lettered 'Light' (the Leicht house, today's 3020), with A. G. Mott's and Charles Hamilton's lots below it. North of the label is a lot lettered '...AVERLY' (probably the Waverly post office) and above it the North Baltimore Railroad depot. The scan is too coarse to draw a footprint, and the label shows neither the house nor which side of the lane it stood on. The placement agrees with the Passano-O'Neill card (northwest corner of Greenmount and Gilmor's Lane) and with Thompson's 1889 plat, which names the turnpike company as owner of the lot directly north of the lane. The plate prints no house numbers.

Thompson's Plats of the Twenty-First and Twenty-Second Wards (1889), 6th Precinct, Section 2, printed p. 132 (MSA frame 0546; the sheet is turned so that north is to the right and York Road runs along the bottom). Fronting York Road on the north side of the mouth of 'Gilmor Lane' is a lot lettered 'York Rd Turnpike Co.': 41 ft 5 in on the road (50 ft at the lane end), 117 ft 6 in deep, improved with '1 S Stone D., 1 S B B., 1 S F B., 1 1/2 S F Stable' (a one-story stone dwelling, a one-story brick building, a one-story frame building and a stable). South across the lane is 'I. Leicht' (36 ft 4 in, the 3020 corner). North of the company lot the plat reads J. Schumann (27 ft 6 in, a two-story frame saloon and dwelling, later 1002 York Rd and today 3034), Geo. Ruppersberger, U. A. & I. Spring (54 ft 9 in) and the N. Balto. Pass. R. Ry. Co. (65 ft). J. H. Aull is lettered on at least four lots along the north side of Gilmor Lane and on Waverly Avenue (now E. 31st St.); Jacob H. Aull bought the company's lot in 1912. The one-story stone dwelling on the company's lot is probably the 'long, low structure' of one story that the Sun described when the toll house came down in 1907. The company's lot is the lot that became 3026-3032, though its printed frontage (41 ft 5 in to 50 ft) is shorter than the 57 ft of the four houses of 1915.

Bromley's atlases of 1896 (Part of Ward 22, Plate 18, MSA frame 0215) and 1906 (Plate 18, frames 0429-0431) show the same lot on the north side of the lane: a three-cell attached block on the York Road frontage, an L-shaped building and two boxed sheds behind it, with no street number on any of them. South across the lane the Leicht house is lettered 922; north of the lot the frame saloon is lettered 1002 (today's 3034), then 1004 and 1006. The four brick dwellings of the 1915 Sanborn are on neither plate. Which building was the toll house is not labelled: the three-cell block on the road, or the L-shaped building behind it, which fits the 1907 description of a house that 'rambles in its one story and far back into a field' at least as well. The block measures roughly 20 to 30 ft across, too narrow for three 14-ft brick bays, so it is not an earlier form of the later row, and the two plates do not support the National Register inventory's 'built ca. 1900' for 3028.

Woods' Baltimore City Directory lists Townsend S. Bonsall as 'keeper 1st tollgate, York' in every volume from 1871 to 1875 (printed pp. 64, 74, 71, 69 and 73). No house number is printed, because Waverly was Baltimore County ground until 1888, and Woods gives no place beyond 'York'; the Hopkins atlas of 1876 puts the first gate at the mouth of Gilmor's Lane. His listing in the 1876 and 1877 volumes has not been confirmed on the page. The Woods volumes of 1860-1870 name no keeper for this gate. Bonsall (1836-1877 on the St. John's Church interment roll) died in 1877, and his widow, Sarah A. Bonsall, succeeded him as Waverly's postmaster. Old Land Marks (about 1906) names the gate's keepers as David Mumma, William Eaton, T. S. Bonsal and T. Schofield.

Woods lists 'Schofield Tilghman, tollgate keeper, Waverley' in 1878 (p. 605), 1879 (669), 1880 (697), 1881 (755), 1882 (786), 1883 (879), 1884 (968), 1885 (1161) and 1886 (1186), with 'Schofield Tilghman jr., clerk, Waverley' in 1883, 1884 and 1886. His first listing follows Townsend S. Bonsall's death in 1877. A Sun classified of Oct. 21, 1884 is addressed to 'Mr. Schofield, Keeper of Toll Gate, Waverly, York Road'. Tradition says he painted 'Waverly' on the toll-house signboard when the post office forced the change of name from Huntingdon. No house number was ever printed for the toll house.

After annexation Polk prints Schofield at the toll gate without a house number: 'Schofield Tilghman, tollgate kpr, Waverly' (1888, p. 980), 'toll gate kpr, York rd' (1890 p. 1078, 1891 p. 1124, 1892 p. 1087), with Tilghman jr. as clerk at the toll gate each year. The Rev. F. H. Stubbs lived 'York rd opp toll gate' (1889-1890), on St. John's side of the road. Polk 1892 is the last volume read that lists a keeper; the volumes for 1893 to 1900 and 1902 are not online, so the years between the last keeper on record and the 1903 tenants of '1000 York rd' are blank. The elder Schofield died at 405 Montebello Avenue on May 24, 1901, and the Sun's report of his funeral says he kept the gate for 17 years.

Baltimore County Union, Feb. 10, 1900, p. 3, local column: the people of Waverly want the general manager of the United Railways and Electric Company to remove the old toll-gate house at the corner of the York road and Gilmore lane, which 'has stood for perhaps 150 years'. It is the source, dated here to the week, of the Passano-O'Neill card's line that residents asked for the house's removal in 1900. The request went to the railway's general manager, though the turnpike company still held the lot, which it sold in 1912. The house was still standing in July 1907, when the city ordered it down because it extended 'several feet over the street line'.

Polk prints '1000 York rd' for: David W. Frazier, bricklayer, Ellen V. Krauss and Chas. Williams, carpenter (1903); Wm F. Dorsey, driver (1904); Jennie Winneberger, grocer, with George E., driver, and Winfield E. (1905); Chas H. Clark, excavator (1906, 1907, 1908); Henry S. Wheeler (1907); Percy W. Jones, clerk (1909). On the west side Polk runs 918 (today 3008), 920 (3014), 922 (3020, Leicht), [1000], 1002 (3034), 1004 (3036), 1006 (3038); no plate prints 1000, and the 1915 Sanborn gives the brick row no York Road number, so 1000 belongs to the turnpike company's lot by position only. The Sun of 1907 says the toll house had lately been 'inhabited by private families'. Polk 1908 and 1909, canvassed after the house came down in July 1907, still list people at 1000: either other buildings on the lot (Thompson's 1889 plat shows brick and frame outbuildings and a stable) stayed in use, or the number is not the toll house itself.

The Department of Public Works plat of Ward 12 Section 20 Block 3856 (dated June 1985, with revisions to 1991; an earlier reading of the title block as June 1965 was wrong) prints lot 4 (3026, 15 ft on Greenmount, 82 ft 1 in deep along Vineyard Lane), lot '5/7' (3028, 42 ft front, 82 ft deep), lot 8 (3034, 28 ft 3 in), then 9 (3036), 10 (3038), 11 (3040-3044), 12 (3046) and 13/14 (3048), with a 4-ft alley behind lots 4 and 5/7, the 3020 Vineyard Lane lot (39/41) and a 15-ft alley beyond it, and Vineyard Lane at the south. The slash in '5/7' reads as the consolidation of original lots 5, 6 and 7, three 14-ft bays, which in street order would be 3028, 3030 and 3032; that reading is an inference. SDAT lot 12-20-3856-005 is 42 by 82 ft (3,444 sq ft) and carries only the 3028 address; the SDAT real property search has no account for 3030 or 3032 (September 2026), and the city's parcel layer has no record for either. So 3030 is the address of the middle bay, not a tax parcel. The evidence of an original separate lot is the lease of Dec. 6, 1912, which describes 3030 as the third of four separately leased lots (S.C.L. 2787/374); the $90 ground rent recited in the 1975 deed dates only from 1951 (M.L.P. 8386/75).

Polk 1914 lists 'Hill Hazel, dressmkr, 3030 Greenmt av' in the run under Hill (printed p. 972) and again in the name index; Polk 1915 repeats 'Hill Hazel, 3030 Greenmt av' (p. 2386). It is the earliest numbered record of the bay, and the 1914 volume (canvassed in autumn 1913) is the first in which any household appears on the row. No estate or other record of Hazel Hill has been found.

Polk 1915, p. 814, in the run under Gardner: 'Harry A solr h 3030 Greenmt av' (the text layer reads 'Marry A', and the first name has not been compared with the page image). 'Solr' is Polk's abbreviation for solicitor, a canvassing trade. The 1917 and 1918 volumes show Wm A. Gardner, solicitor, in the same house, so the 1915 first name may be a misreading of Wm A. or a relative.
Polk 1917 (p. 792) and 1918 (p. 874) list 'Gardner Wm A, solr, h 3030 Greenmt av'; the 1918 column head GARDNER was read on the page image. He follows Hazel Hill in the bay and precedes John Mathews.

Polk 1922 prints 'Gardner Wm A (Klein & Gardner) h 3030 York rd' (the 1922 volume uses the York rd form for the 3000 block of Greenmount); the firm is 'Klein & Gardner, 113 n Eutaw', soft drinks, whose partners are Peter E. Klein (Lenora) and Wm A. Gardner (Frances). Polk 1923 has Wm A. (Frances; Klein & Gardner) at 427 Eversham, so he left 3030 in 1922-23. Whether he is the William A. Gardner whose Baltimore City estate (179825) records a death on Sept. 20, 1923 is untested; no death notice for him was found in the Sun for that month.
Polk 1920 and 1921 list 'Mathews John, clk, h 3030 Greenmt av' (1921 under the column head MATHEWS, p. 1433). Mathews is a common name, and nothing more is known of him.

Polk 1923, printed p. 1187 (read on the page image): 'McCoy David S (Mary E) lieut Salvage Corps h 3030 Greenmt'. Polk 1923 lists the Salvage Corps' No. 1 company at 27 N. Liberty St. and No. 5 at Waverly and does not say which he served in. The Evening Sun's report of the garage fire of Aug. 5, 1931 lists 'Mr. and Mrs. Davis McCoy and son' among the households driven from 3026-3032. The same surname at the same address makes it probably the same household, but the paper prints Davis, not David, names neither the wife nor the son, and nothing is known for 1924-1930, so the two dates are points, not a proven tenure. An Evening Sun report of Nov. 27, 1931 (p. 50, Newspapers.com image 369505921) of a Salvage Corps truck collision names 'Regularmen David S. Mc[Coy] and William Camel' among the men on the truck; the surname is cut at a line end, and a regularman ranks below a lieutenant, so this is he or a namesake (possible). The Register of Wills has no David S. or Davis McCoy estate for the period.

Polk 1923 (p. 563) lists 'Cullen Martin, fire dept, 3030 Greenmt av' (column head CULLEN read on the page image), in the same volume that has the McCoys at 3030. No Martin Cullen estate is in the Baltimore City index.

Polk 1914 (leaf 1568): 'Sanner John B, rectifier, 3028 Greenmt av' and 'Sanner Laurence W, com trav, h 3028 Greenmt'; 1915 'Sanner John F, distiller, 3028' and Laurence W., salesman. A Mr. Sanner hires a demonstrator from 3028 in the Sun of Sept. 2, 1915. Polk 1917 and 1918 (leaf 773): 'Godwin John G, slsmn, h 3028 Greenmt av'. Polk 1920 and 1921 list a Lawrence W., ironworker, then salesman, at 3028 (column head unresolved; Sanner by the name), with Jas G., carpenter (1921), and Nellie, clerk, and Omar, conductor (1922), under heads not yet resolved. Polk 1922 and 1923 (leaf 1384): 'Morris Chas E (Lillian), mtrmn, h 3028 Greenmt av'. The Wantlands follow by 1931. The middle bay, 3030, sits between this house and the Shields house at 3032.

Polk 1915 (leaf 408): 'Connors John K, solr, h 3032 Greenmt av'; 1917 'John K, h 3032' (the trade garbled in the text layer); 1918 and 1920 'John K, slsmn, h 3032'; 1918 'Geo F, foreman, h 3032' in the run under Foust; 1914 'John E, lab, h 3032' (column head unresolved). The Shields family follows by Sept. 1919 (C. D. Shields of 3032 applies for a marriage licence, Sun, Sept. 19, 1919). The '3032 Greenmt' of Polk 1912 is the Waverly Building Association office under the older numbering, now 3046.

A search of the Baltimore City Register of Wills estate index in September 2026 found no estate for John M. Amend (who died at his residence, 3030 Greenmount, on May 7, 1937) or his late wife Sarah, none for a Frank Elder (of 3030 when licensed to marry in July 1939), and none for Martha V. Berterman (of 3030, died May 8, 1942) or her late husband Herman I. Berterman. These are gaps in the index, not evidence against the newspaper notices.

The substitute trustees' auction of 3028-3032 was set for noon on Thursday, Dec. 4, 2014 (Sun, Dec. 3, 2014). The same day the health center's corporation (Maryland charter D00311068, the former People's Free Medical Clinic, Inc.) filed a voluntary Chapter 11 petition in the U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the District of Maryland, No. 14-28461. The petition in its second case, No. 15-10228, filed Jan. 7, 2015, lists the earlier case and its Dec. 4, 2014 filing date under prior filings (Doc. 1, p. 2). The CourtListener docket for No. 14-28461 (54599172) shows the case assigned to Judge Robert A. Gordon and terminated Dec. 24, 2014; those two facts rest on the docket summary alone. On Dec. 29, 2014 the corporation filed articles of amendment changing its name (SDAT).

Petition and schedules, In re The People's Community Health Centers, Inc., No. 15-10228, U.S. Bankruptcy Court, D. Md., filed Jan. 7, 2015 (Doc. 1, 52 pp.). Schedule A (p. 9) lists '3028-3032 Greenmount Ave.', fee simple, $425,000, secured claim $383,339; '3011-13 Greenmount Ave.', $75,000; and '3026 Greenmount Ave.', $65,000. Schedule D (pp. 14-15) and the list of the twenty largest creditors (p. 4): Partners for the Common Good, Inc., of Washington, D.C., first lien on 3028-3032 and 3011 Greenmount, claim $383,339; BB&T, first lien on 3026 and on 3011-3013 and a second lien 'up to $143,000' on '3028&3030 Greenmount', claim $478,409. Page 39 lists the two chief executives and the chief financial officer who left during 2014. The deed of 3028-3032 to 3028 Greenmount Avenue LLC followed on Aug. 17, 2016 for $275,000 (LGA 18376/272), about 35 percent below the scheduled value.

Maryland SDAT record W17112798 (OpenCorporates mirror): articles of organization Mar. 11, 2016 (the same day as Real Estate Specialists, LLC, W17111162, and five months before the Aug. 17, 2016 deed of 3028-3032), a resolution Aug. 1, 2022, and forfeiture by department action Oct. 1, 2024; registered and principal address 1401 Madison Avenue, Suite B (Barrus Realty). The LLC holds lot 3856/005 (3028-3032) and lot 004 (3026, bought in Oct. 2017 from the clinic's liquidating trustee for $80,000), and deeds of trust on 3028-3032 were recorded in 2020 and 2022. Real Estate Specialists, LLC, whose registered office is 3030 Greenmount Ave, Suite 200, is the registered agent for the 3010, 3015, 3313 and 3326 Greenmount LLCs.

Maryland SDAT record D01622141 (marylanddb.com mirror): Baltimore Unemployed Workers' Health Clinic, Inc., articles filed Oct. 14, 1983 (film F2613/3588, 9 pages), resident agent at 201 N. Charles St., principal office 3028 Greenmount Avenue; change of principal office Feb. 6, 1984; forfeited Oct. 15, 1986. It falls between the clinic's 1981 reopening and the 1985 Black United Fund and Welfare Rights use of 3028, and it is not mentioned in the clinic histories read. Nothing about its patients or funding has been found.

A USPTO trademark search by owner address (September 2026) returns OFFICEFLEX (serial 90210313, registration 7164612, filed Sept. 25, 2020; Officeflex, LLC, 3028 Greenmount Ave., Suite 200) and four more marks at 3028 (Suite 200, #1043 and #2007), and 32 marks filed 2024-2026 whose owners give '3030 Greenmount Ave, Ste 300, PMB' with a private mailbox number. The filings do not show whether any of those owners operates at the address. The same building holds Real Estate Specialists, LLC's registered office (Suite 200), BNBD's principal office since July 2026 (Suite 200) and Still Waters Health Systems (Suites 150, 155 and 185). The number 3030 survives as a suite and mailbox designation inside the combined 3028-3032 building.

The Sunday Sun, July 28, 1907, p. 20. Headline block: 'PASSING OF TOLL GATE / House On York Road Is Soon To Be Demolished. / HAS SERVED MANY PURPOSES / Was Successively Country Store, Postoffice, Recruiting Station, Hospital And Private Residence.' The house at York road and Gilmor lane was to come down 'in a few days' for the paving that 'has gradually extended up the York road from North avenue'; it 'extends several feet over the street line', and the city had 'imperatively ordered' it demolished. The family of Mr. Charles Clarke moved out on Saturday, July 27, and the tearing down was to begin on Monday, July 29. The article says the house was built '130 years ago', according to the late David Mumma, 'who for nearly a decade collected tolls at the old gate'; that it served as the crossroads country store, the post office, a recruiting station for men to serve in the Mexican and Civil wars, and a hospital for fever-stricken soldiers 'sent to Gilmor lane'; and that the keepers held the gate 'until ten years ago, when the United Railways bought the road, ruts and all', after which 'the old place was idle for a long time. Lately it has been inhabited by private families.' It describes 'a long, low structure, lifted from parts of the low ground by piles of stones. It rambles in its one story and far back into a field', with rooms added by an early storekeeper 'of rapidly growing family'. The Baltimore County Union reprinted the article on Aug. 3, 1907, p. 3 ('The Old Waverly Toll-Gate House to Go'), and the Sunday Sun Magazine's 'This was Baltimore 50 years ago' column reprinted its opening in 1957. The article gives no house number and does not say which of the later lots 3026-3032 the house stood on; its '130 years' and 'ten years ago' differ from the Union's 'perhaps 150' years of 1900 and from the 1894 removal of the gate on the Passano-O'Neill card.

The Evening Sun's building notes of Saturday, Apr. 6, 1912, p. 5, a month after Aull bought the turnpike company's lot (SCL 2727/29, Mar. 6, 1912): four semi-detached, two-story, porch-front dwellings with pressed-brick fronts trimmed in white marble, $9,000 in all, each 15 by 48 ft, plans by the architect Jacob F. Gerwig. No house numbers existed yet; the place is 'York road near Gilmor lane'. The Sunday Sun of Apr. 7, 1912, p. 5 (image 372412215) printed a fuller version: 'Four two-story brick dwellings will be built by Jacob Aull on the York road, near Gilmor lane, at a cost of $9,000. They will have semi-detached porches. The fronts will be of pressed brick, with marble trimmings, and the houses will be lighted by electricity. Each building will measure 15 by 48 feet. Jacob F. Gerwig is the architect.' Both say the houses 'will be built', so the row did not yet stand in April 1912. The permit list of Apr. 21 names Aull as 'owner, builder'.

The Evening Sun of Wednesday, Apr. 10, 1912, p. 5, dates the permit application itself ('Application was made today at the Building Inspector's office'), four days after the first announcement.
