Leight, widower, of Baltimore City, to Jacob Rashbaum and Rheba Rashbaum, his wife, as tenants by the entireties, for $5 and other considerations, 'those three lots': (1) the corner of the west side of Greenmount Avenue (formerly York Turnpike Road) and the south side of Vineyard Lane, 36 ft by 76 ft 4 in, No. 3020; (2) from 36 ft south of the corner, 67 ft 11 2/5 in on the avenue to the southern outline of the land formerly of Mary Clemens, 215 ft deep, wrapping around the lot of 'the Sub-Lease from John D. Nicholl to Lorenz Leight' (A.W.B. 394/156), No. 3010; (3) a lot on the southeast side of Vineyard Lane beside the lot Mary Clemens leased to Allen K. Wood in 1901 (R.O. 1928/77). Federal documentary stamps $20 + $10 + $5 + $2 + $1 + 50 cents = $38.50, seventy units of $500 at 55 cents: a price of about $35,000. Recitals: 3020 from William H. Flayhart, Jr. and wife to Charles T. and Ella B. Leight, Oct. 5, 1932 (S.C.L. 5328/111); 3010 by assignment from Lula Smith to Charles T. and Ella B. Leight, Oct. 31, 1931 (S.C.L. 5263/428), 'The said Ella B. Leight having since died thereby vesting full interest' in Charles T. Leight, with further deeds from William H. Wolfe and wife of June 21, 1948 (M.L.P. 7491/449) and Oct. 24, 1950 (M.L.P. 8259/53); the lane lot from William H. Wolfe and wife, Feb. 4, 1953. The 1932 grantor was the husband of Leight's daughter Catherine, so the corner stayed in the family. Leight, 'formerly of 3020 Greenmount avenue' in his death notice, died five months after the sale, on Aug. 12, 1953. The sale ended more than a century of the Leight family at the corner (the sub-lease of 1848, A.W.B. 394/156). Update Oct. 12, 2026: the Leights' title to these lots is now read: 3020 was bought as a leasehold in 1919 and its reversion in 1924 (S.C.L. 5328/110 recites both); 3010's $180 leasehold was bought in 1927, put in the Wolfe and Leight entireties in 1931 (S.C.L. 5263/428), and merged into the fee by the Wolfes' deed to Charles T. Deed made Sept. 22, 1954, acknowledged that day, read on the page image (The Title Guarantee Company, application H-9852): Jacob Rashbaum and Rheba Rashbaum, his wife, of Baltimore City, to Costanza Construction Company, Inc., a Maryland corporation, for $5 and other valuable considerations, in fee simple, the same three lots (3020 at the corner; 3010 around the Nicholl-to-Leight sub-lease lot of A.W.B. 394/156; the Vineyard Lane lot). Stamps: federal $30 + $30 + about 50 cents, about $60.50, or 110 units of $500 at 55 cents; Maryland $22 + $22 + $11 and a partly legible fourth: a price of about $55,000. Recital: the March 2, 1953 deed from Charles T. Leight, widower (M.L.P. 9085/400). The Rashbaums held the ground about 18 months and sold for about $20,000 more than the stamps show they paid. The 3010 bay was already trading as a self-service laundry by May 1954, four months before this deed, so it went up while the Rashbaums held the ground (who built it is not recorded), and the Sun's March 21, 1954 offer of the '105x286' lot at 3010-3020, which names no seller, was probably theirs. Under Costanza ownership the rest of the row followed, 3012 by late 1955, 3020 in 1956, 3014 in 1957 and 3016 in 1958; Edward Costanza is named as builder at 3014 and 3016.

The Sun's real-estate transfers of Sunday, Feb. 18, 1917, p. 15, print two lines about the row that Jacob H. Aull built on the old toll-house lot in 1912: 'Jacob H. Aull to John T. Spellman, Jr., and wife, n.w.c. Greenmount ave. and Vineyard lane, g.r. $72.' and 'Alice M. Chapman to Jacob H. Aull, 4 lots.' The northwest corner of Greenmount Avenue and Vineyard Lane is 3026, and $72 is the yearly rent that the lease of Dec. 6, 1912 put on the corner lot (the other three lots paid $66 each; S.C.L. 2787/374). Read together, the lines show the four leaseholds that Aull had put in Alice M. Chapman's name in 1912 most probably coming back to him, and the Spellmans buying the 3026 house subject to the ground rent, which Frank X. Hooper had owned since Dec. 16, 1912 (S.C.L. 2787/376). The column gives no price and no liber. It is the earliest record of the Spellman family as owners of 3026; Polk's 1917 directory lists John T. Spellman Jr., plumber, living in the house ('h 3026 Greenmt av'), so he may have been there as a tenant before the purchase. The family held the house until Dec. 8, 2006 (FMC 8778/605, recited in FMC 9256/107). The two lines are given as transcribed from the page image; the deeds themselves (Chapman to Aull and Aull to Spellman, early 1917) have not been read.

Other Spellman plumbers share that address: George A. (1908 to 1923) and William P. (1917, 1920). The son, John T. Jr., first appears as a plumber at 2649 in 1905; opens his own shop at 2909-2911 York rd in 1909, still living at 2649; is listed at 2649 again in 1912 and 1914; and is at 3026 from 1917. His age in the 1950 census, 63, puts his birth about 1886 or 1887, which fits a father at work as a plumber from 1878. An article clipped from the Evening Sun of Nov. 25, 1930 (p. 44, continued on page 3, which is not in the file), headed 'Officers, Niece Carry Out Aged Invalid In Fire ... Flames Damage Former Church ... Start In Miniature Golf Course And Spread To Stores'. At 2 A. M. 'today' Patrolman Leonard Atkinson saw a red glow on the second floor of the Oriole Miniature Golf Course, which the paper places at 3105 Greenmount avenue, ran to No. 7 Truck Company and sounded an alarm. Neighbors told Patrolmen Atkinson and Royce Battee about an invalid, and they 'entered the home of Miss Anna Sage', 80, who had not left it in two years; the officers, 'assisted by Miss Mary Van Dorn' (the niece of the headline), carried her through the smoke to a neighbor's. The fire spread from the golf course to the first-floor stores of the J. W. Crook Company and the Gold Bros. Notions and Dry Goods Store, then to the wooden part of the old church tower; part of the tower 'crashed through the skylight of the Western Auto Supply store at 3107'. Fireman Fred Krause of No. 7 Truck was treated for shock by the department surgeon, Dr. Olver S. Lloyd. The addresses do not agree with the maps. The paper calls the church building 3105-3107 and puts the golf course and Miss Sage's home at 3105 and Western Auto at 3107. Woods' Baltimore directories print no house numbers for Waverly but carry the family by name: Chas. D. Bateman, clerk, Waverley (1874); James J. Bateman, bookkeeper, Gorsuch av, Waverley (1876); James S. Bateman, store, Waverley (1878 to 1881) and grocery (1882 to 1886); Clara V. Bateman, teacher, Waverley (1881). Polk prints the same James S. and Clara V. Bateman at 1023 York road in 1887 and 1888 and the sons at 1021 York road from 1889. The Woods lines are name-level entries tied to this lot only by those later listings.

Thompson's 1889 plats of the 21st and 22nd wards letter the lot north of the Waverly M.E. Church (55 ft, '2 S. B. B.') 'J. S. Bateman': 69 ft on the York Road, 74 ft 6 in on Old York Road, with the improvements '2 S. F. D., 1 S. F. K., 2 S. F. B. B., 2 S. F. Store & D.' (a two-story frame dwelling, a one-story frame kitchen, a two-story frame back building, and a two-story frame store and dwelling). North of it is Charles Hamilton's 79 ft (two-story and mansard brick saloon, stables, office), then an alley and sewer strip and Engine House No. 4. The 69 ft matches today's 3107 lot (47 ft 3 in) plus the 3111 bank lot (24 ft). Read on the plate.

Polk prints the family at 1021 York road (1889, 1891, 1892, 1903, 1905, 1909), at '3109 York rd' (1901, 1904, 1907, 1908) and at 3109 Greenmt av (1914, 1915): Clinton A. Bateman (clerk, later bookkeeper), W. Ernest (clerk), Leonard (clerk; real estate in 1904), Charles E. (cafe, 1892), Clara V. (teacher, 1901) and M. Estelle, also printed 'M. Estella' and 'Mary E.', evidently one woman, who is the only Bateman left from 1905. M. Emma (Mary E.) Kumpf is listed at the same address from 1903 to 1915. James S. Bateman himself, the grocer, and in 1887-88 Clara V. and W. Ernest, are printed at 1023 York road, the store next door (3111). The 1915 Sanborn plate prints '1021' and '3109' together on the frame house. The lines were checked against the page images of the archive.org volumes by a second machine reading of each line, the 1901 M. Estelle line by eye.

Not read: known from recitals. The survey description in the 1992 deed of 3107 Greenmount (S.E.B. 3136/493, Exhibit A, read on the scan) begins 'at the end of the first line of the lot of ground described in a deed from M. Estelle Bateman to Provident Savings Bank of Baltimore dated March 18, 1904 and recorded among the Land Record of Baltimore City in Liber R.O. No. 2062 folio 398'; the 1993 and 2007 deeds of 3107 repeat it. The Provident lot therefore adjoined 3107 on the north, which is this parcel, and M. Estelle Bateman, who owned the house next door, was its grantor. The description in this parcel's own 2002 deed, which recites the 1934 Sinclair assignment, begins from the fourth line of an earlier assignment from Estelle Bateman to the Provident Savings Bank, evidently the same instrument; whether it conveyed the fee or a leasehold will not be known until it is read. Two months later, in May 1904, the bank took permits for a one-story brick bank building and a well at 1023 York road. The city's 33rd Street plat of about 1913 shows the Provident bank at the street end of No. 3111 (21.6 ft) with James M. Sinclair's lot behind it, so the 1904 instrument probably covered only the street front of the old Bateman grocery stand, the rest coming to the bank from the Sinclairs in 1934. Update Oct. 14, 2026: the deed is read (738:mdlr-ro2062-398-bateman-provident-bank-lot-1904-read): $2,000, a 24-ft one-cent leasehold of the Coffield tract, part of M. Estelle Bateman's 1902 purchase from Clara V. Bateman's estate.

The Baltimore City Archives plat numbered M 3678-F7 (BRG12-1-209, image 0159), the survey of owners made for the opening of 33rd Street on the line of Merryman's Lane, is undated; it is of about 1913. On the east side of the York Road frontage it names, from north to south: Fire Dept. Engine House (46.0 ft); J. H. Deitrich, No. 3117 (38.2 ft), No. 3115 (19.3 ft) and No. 3113 (24.7 ft); No. 3111 (21.6 ft), divided between the 'Providence Savings Bank' in a small box at the street and James M. Sinclair behind it; 'M. Estelle Bateman' (44.8 ft); the Waverly M.E. Church (54.0 ft); and Robert Rainey (47.8 ft). The Bateman lot is today's 3107 lot (47 ft 3 in by the city's dimensions). J. S. Bateman's 69 ft of 1889 had by then lost its north 22 to 24 ft to the bank and Sinclair lots. Read on the plat image. Update Oct. 14, 2026: by Oct. 11, 1921 Edna L. Rainey, widow, held the Bateman lot (3105 to 3109) and sold it to M. Lillian Slade (S.C.L. 3787/503, recited in 737:mdlr-scl5580-582-slade-chertkof-3105-3109-1935); the Raineys were the neighbours south of the church on this plat.

Bauman, a grocer at 1600 Patapsco, rooming at 3109. Polk 1923: Moshkevich, men's furnishings, 3107; 'La Dore Hat Shop (Mary Van Doren) 3105 Greenmt av'; and 'Eversfield Chas P (Phyllis) elec contr 3109 Greenmt av', also listed under Electrical Contractors. The Elgert, Kelly, Moshkevich, Van Doren and Bauman lines were checked against the page images by a second machine reading; the La Dore, Dimling and Eversfield lines are from the archive.org text of the volumes only. The 1915 Sanborn plate shows only the house on the lot and the 1928 plate three one-story brick stores numbered 3105, 3107 and 3109, so the stores were built between 1915 and the 1921 canvass for the 1922 directory.

The east side of this frontage is on sheet 718 of the 1915 volume, not sheet 717. The sheet prints the old and new numbers together, '1021' over '3109', beside a two-story frame dwelling ('D') with a one-story frame porch across its front and one-story frame rear ells. The house stands well back from the street (about 30 ft by the sheet's scale), with open ground between it and the sidewalk and a strip of open ground between it and the Waverly M.E. Church to the south (two-story brick with a stone front, steam heat, electric light, 28 ft to the eaves). To the north the sheet prints '1023' on a small one-story brick 'Bank' at the street line, with a two-story frame store standing behind it, then 3115 and the livery. No 3105 or 3107 is printed: the three stores came later. Read on the sheet; distances are scaled, not printed.

Sheet 735 of Vol. 7 in the corrected volume the Library of Congress dates '1928 - May 1950' (a 1928 printing with later changes pasted over it) shows the lot as in 1928: three one-story brick stores (12 ft high) numbered 3105, 3107 and 3109 at the street line, and behind them the two-story frame dwelling ('D') with its one-story rear ells. Correction slips are pasted on three sides of the house: a cinder-block 'Tire Mounting' building (15 ft) between it and Ready Avenue (Old York Road), the 'Bank' at 3111 (one and two stories, 20 ft) to the north, and the two-story store building numbered 3103 and 3101 on the church site to the south. The stores and the house themselves carry no slip. Since the correctors revised every neighbour and left the house, it very probably still stood at the last correction; that is an inference from an unrevised part of a corrected sheet, not a statement on the sheet. The state assessment roll gives the present building a year built of 1954. Read on the sheet.

Deed dated November 12, 1976, acknowledged that day and recorded November 17, 1976 (Liber R.H.B. 3415, folios 175-176), read on the scan of the record copy. Grantor: Arthur H. Katz, Successor Trustee. Grantee: The Hotspot Family Restaurant, Inc., a Maryland corporation. Consideration: 'Five Dollars, and other valuable considerations'. Estate: fee simple. Notice in the Sun of July 4, 1871: 'Ninth District Baltimore County. The Democratic Association of the First Precinct of the above District will meet at Sinclair's Hall, Waverley, on Wednesday evening, July 5th, at 8 o'clock', signed John Erdman, Jr., Chairman. The notice gives no street. Notices of 1888 and 1901 put Sinclair's Hall at York road and Merryman's lane, and a 1977 history has Waverly's Methodists meeting about 1870 over J. E. Sinclair's store at that corner. James E. Sinclair had ground on both sides of the lane: the apex lot north of it (this parcel, lettered 'J. E. Sinclair' on Thompson's 1889 plat) and a corner lot south of it. The hall is filed here as probable, by inference: Polk's 1887 and 1888 directories list the Waverly Cornet Band at 1102 York road, the apex building. Which building held the hall in 1871 is not stated in any source read.

The Sun of April 13, 1888, under 'For Annexation. Enthusiastic Belt Meetings. Mayor Latrobe Takes the Stump': 'A rousing annexation meeting was what the Waverly Annexation Club held last night at Sinclair's Hall, corner of York road and Merryman's lane. Not only was the seating capacity of the hall occupied, but an interested and enthusiastic crowd stood in the aisles and at the rear of the hall. Mr. Geo. W. Hyde presided, and F. N. Hoen was secretary.' Mayor Latrobe then spoke for extending the city over the Belt. The club's notice of April 10 had called it the 'first mass-meeting under the auspices of the Waverly Annexation Club, Sinclair's Hall, Thursday, April 12, 8 P.M.', with Winfield J. Taylor, John V. L. Findlay and C. Bohn Slingluff to speak and Gen. F. C. Latrobe to attend. That spring the hall served both sides: annexationists 'crowded Sinclair's Hall, at Waverly, almost to suffocation' on May 4 (Sun, May 5), and 'the anti-annexationists held a meeting in Sinclair Hall, Waverly' (Sun, May 15). On July 18 a meeting 'of those in favor of opening Jefferson street' was held there (Sun, July 19). Placement on this parcel is an inference. The notices say only the corner; James E. Sinclair had lots on both sides of the lane; and Polk's 1888 directory lists the tinner Wallace W. Sinclair and the Waverly Cornet Band at 1102 York road, the apex building, which makes its upper floor the probable hall. The corner south of the lane, where the Sinclair tinshop stood by 1900, is not excluded.

The Sun of November 24, 1888, 'Protest Against Election Arrests': 'About a hundred citizens of the twenty-second ward met at Sinclair's Hall, York road and Merryman's lane, last night and protested against the arrest of three colored men of the ward, John Payne, Horace Holmes and Louis Cheeseman, on the night of November 5. They were charged with registering illegally, and, after being held for five days, were dismissed by the grand jury.' Louis P. Hennighausen said that 'part of the evidence against these citizens was part of a scheme and conspiracy to defraud the people of Baltimore in the election'. Charles C. Cox said: 'When we came into the city I did not expect that the twenty-second ward would be so suddenly plunged into the contamination to which the other wards in the city had been schooled.' Addresses were also made by E. A. McAllister, Henry Lingenfelder (the print is worn), James E. Hooker, F. Albert Kurtz, A. Pillsbury, A. A. Reinhardt 'and James Robson, colored'. The meeting resolved that 'the arrests were instigated and made with the intention of depriving the men of their votes at the presidential election' and 'that the instigators and perpetrators be brought to justice'. The call, printed the day before, was for an 'indignation meeting' at 'Sinclair's Hall, York road and Merryman's lane, to take action about the unlawful arrest of citizens of the ward on the evening of November 5', signed E. J. Guyton, Secretary. November 5, 1888 was the eve of the presidential election. The hall is placed on this parcel by inference, not by any notice: see the entry for the annexation meeting of April 1888.

Notice in the Sun of Monday, September 29, 1890, headed '22d Ward Republicans': 'At a meeting of Republicans held Friday night at Sinclair's Hall, the undersigned committee were appointed to request the Republicans of the 22d Ward to assemble at Sinclair's Hall, Waverly, Monday, Sept. 29, at 8 P.M., to name for First Branch City Council a candidate suitable to all factions in this ward.' Signed A. A. Reinhart, Chairman, and J. C. Watts, F. L. Sibley, J. E. Sinclair, Charles Hamilton, Oden Hawkins and Nathan Lemond, Committee. The J. E. Sinclair on the committee is presumably James E. Sinclair, the hall's owner. The notice gives no street. The hall is placed on this parcel by inference, not by any notice: see the entry for the annexation meeting of April 1888.

The Sun of April 16, 1901, under 'Tried And Found Wanting': 'Mr. Thomas R. Clendinen was the principal speaker last night at a meeting held at Sinclair's Hall, York road and Merryman's lane, in the First precinct of the Twelfth ward, to indorse the candidacy of Mr. George C. Morrison for the Democratic nomination for the First Branch of the City Council.' The 'Grand Rally' notice for the same evening gives only 'York road and Merryman's lane'. This is the latest use of the name Sinclair's Hall found. In 1900-01 the ground floor of 1102 York road was William H. Reilley's saloon, and James Sinclair's tinshop stood 'at York road and Merryman's lane' on the other corner (Sun, April 19, 1900), so by 1901 the hall could have been over either. It is filed here as probable, not settled.

The Sun of June 13, 1883 lists patents dated June 11, 1883 issued 'to persons in this city and neighborhood', among them, under Maryland, 'James E. Sinclair, valve, direct-acting steam pump, super-heating steam engine, three patents'. The list gives no town. Identification with the Waverly man is an inference from the name and the trade: Woods' directories of 1885 and 1886 list James E. Sinclair, machinist, at McKim and Neighbor streets, and Polk's volumes of 1888 and 1889 list 'Sinclair Jas E, mach, 1048 York rd', with his house a few doors north of this corner (1112 York road in 1888, about today's 3220 Greenmount). Thompson's 1889 plat letters the apex lot at Merryman's Lane 'J. E. Sinclair', 28.8 feet on York Road, with improvements read as a two-story brick store and dwelling. The patents themselves have not been pulled.

A liquor-license list printed in the Sun on March 7, 1900 carries 'Reilley, W. H., 1102 York road' with the figure 12, the ward. Polk's 1901 directory lists William H. Reilley, saloon, 1102 York road; police had raided 'saloon 1102 York road' in December 1899; and in April 1900 a man 'fell in front of Riley's saloon on the York road, near Merryman's lane'. 1102 York road is today's 3200 Greenmount: the 1915 Sanborn plate prints both numbers on the corner building.

The Sun's 'Local Briefs' of March 5, 1902: 'The Liquor Board yesterday rejected the application of Charles Barber for a saloon license at 1100 and 1102 York road.' The board rejected a second application, for 1100 York road, in May. Polk's 1903 directory has a house-furnishing store at 1102 and its 1904 volume a pool room and a barber shop; the next saloon keeper it lists there is Joseph Black in 1905.

A rental list of Chas. Francis Smith, 213 St. Paul street, in the Sun of April 17, 1902, has under 'Stores': '1100 York rd., Waverly. $16.00'. The same list offers a dwelling at '1114 York rd., Waverly' for $12. 1100 and 1102 York road were the two fronts of the corner building. A month later the Liquor Board rejected the application of a Charles F. Smith for a saloon license at 1100 York road; whether he was the agent is not established.

The Sun of May 20, 1902, under 'Protest Against Liquor License': 'The applications of Charles F. Smith and Fred L. Richardson for saloon licenses at 1100 York road and 700 East Monument street, respectively, were rejected by the board without a hearing.' The item's main subject is a protest by property owners against a saloon at 1801 Friendsbury Place. Charles Barber's application for 1100 and 1102 York road had been rejected in March; the directories next list a saloon at 1102 in 1905.

Classified in the Sun of November 15, 1902: 'Corner grocery in Waverly; $125 if sold at once. Apply at N. W. corner York road and Merryman's lane.' The northwest corner is this parcel: the Sun's real-estate column of November 10, 1910 puts 1100 and 1102 York road 'at the northwest corner of Merryman lane and York road'. The grocer is not named. The advertisement falls between the saloon-license rejections of 1902 and the house-furnishing store of 1903.

Classified in the Sun of June 29, 1903: '$100 will buy house furnishing store; good stock; rent $10. Corner York road and Merryman's lane.' The advertisement does not say which corner. Polk's 1903 directory lists Tedford Browne, house furnishings, 1102 York road, which identifies the store. Polk's 1904 volume has a pool room and a barber shop at the address instead.

Polk's 1904 Baltimore directory lists '*Fisher Wm L, pool, 1102 York rd' (printed p. 567) and '*Wright Clinton, barber, 1102 York rd' (printed p. 1864). The asterisk before a name is the directory's mark for colored persons. 1102 York road is today's 3200 Greenmount. The two listings fall between the house-furnishing store of 1903 and Joseph Black's saloon of 1905; no other volume read lists either man at this address, and neither has been traced further. A notice in the Afro-American of September 27, 1918 names 'the Barber shop, York Road near Merrymans Lane' as a place to leave Waverly news for the paper; whether that shop had any connection with Wright's is not known.

Polk's directories list 'Black Jos, saloon, 1102 York rd', with his house at 629 Jefferson, in 1905, and 'Muller Geo, saloon, 1102 York rd' in each volume from 1906 to 1909 (the 1910 and 1911 volumes are not available online). The Sun's permit list of August 2, 1905 has 'George Muller, 1102 York road, sign; no charge', and its liquor-license list of February 13, 1911 still carries 'Muller, George, 1102 York road'. Frederick H. Samstag is on the license list for 1100-2 York road in February 1912.

The Sun's real-estate column of November 10, 1910: 'The Cityco Realty Company has sold to the Auxiliary Realty Company, of Baltimore city, 1100 and 1102 York road. The lot is triangular, with a long front on York road. The property is at the northwest corner of Merryman lane and York road. The sale was made by A. Robinson White.' Six weeks earlier Auxiliary had transferred five houses, 1100, 1102, 1104, 1112 and 1114 York road, to Cityco. The Evening Sun of November 11 described the property as 'the three-story store and dwelling at 1102 York road'. In June 1911 the corner passed to Frederick H. Samstag and wife. The same clipping is also filed on 3224 Greenmount.

The Sun's annual liquor-license lists carry 'Samstag, Fred. H., 1100-2 York road' (February 2, 1912), 'Samstag, Frederick H., 1100-02 York road' (February 13 and 15, 1913) and 'Samstag, Fred H., 3200 Greenmount ave' (April 11, 1918), each with the ward figure 12. Der Deutsche Correspondent printed 'Samstag, Frederick H., 3200 Greenmount-Avenue' on February 8, 1916. The change of address between the 1913 and 1916 lists is the renumbering of this stretch of York road as Greenmount avenue; Polk's directory already prints 3200 Greenmount for him in its 1913 volume.

The Sun of October 7, 1907: 'The funeral of Mr. Moses Samstag, formerly proprietor of the Hotel Samstag, who died Saturday at his home, 1717 Madison avenue, will take place today from the home of his sister, Mrs. Samuel Strouse, 1724 Eutaw Place. Mr. Samstag kept the hotel, which was on Lombard street, near Sharp, for many years. He was 72 years old and was born in Germany.' He left three daughters, and 'the sons, Messrs. Frederick H. Samstag and Isaac Samstag, also survive him'. The Sun's notice of Frederick H. Samstag's marriage in 1909 gives him the same address, 1717 Madison avenue, so the Frederick H. Samstag who took this corner in 1911 and kept its saloon was the hotel keeper's son. That settles the kinship left open on the 1891 Hotel Samstag advertisement filed here.

The Sun of August 9, 1909, headed 'Samstag-George': 'Mrs. Elizabeth George, daughter of Mr. and Mrs. William C. Hewitt, Maryland avenue and Twenty-fourth street, was married yesterday to Mr. Frederick H. Samstag, a well-known Elk, who lives at 1717 Madison avenue. The ceremony was performed at the home of the bride by Rev. Dr. William H. Rosenau.' The notice adds that Mrs. Samstag, 'who was a widow, is an Episcopalian and attended Old St. Paul's', and that the couple would live at the bride's home. Two years later the transfer list has the corner conveyed to 'Frederick H. Samstag and wife'. The corner's later papers name his wife three ways: 'Mrs. Elizabeth R. Samstag' leased it in 1929 and 1935, his 1929 death notice says 'beloved husband of Ruth Samstag', and a 1924 block-book entry has 'Ruth E.'. They are probably one woman, but no single document read ties the names together.

The Sun of June 27, 1918, under 'Cuts His Wife's Throat. Ellwood Appleby Escapes After Crime In Grocery': 'Mrs. Emma Appleby, 51 years old, 509 Gutman avenue, Waverly, was murdered by her husband, Ellwood R. Appleby, shortly before 5 o'clock yesterday afternoon as she stood in the grocery of Chimack Cohen, 2462 Buchanon street, not far from her home.' She was dead on reaching St. Joseph's Hospital. 'Following the crime Appleby calmly walked from the store, went to the saloon of Fred H. Samstag, 3200 Greenmount avenue, and after telling several men in the place that he had killed his wife and was going to make away with himself he ran out and was last seen climbing the fence that guards the Baltimore and Ohio Railroad tracks.' The paper says that Mrs. Appleby, the mother of nine children, had been separated from her husband for two years; that the previous August she had sworn out a warrant for his arrest for disturbing the peace, which was never served; and that police searched a freight train at Bayview Junction without finding him. The article does not report his capture, and what followed has not been traced. The corner's part in the event is the saloon, named with its keeper and its address.

The Sun of December 29, 1926, at the end of a report on dry-law enforcement that quotes the United States District Attorney, Amos W. W. Woodcock, about another place: 'Other raids and arrests made were as follows', and among five entries, 'Saloon, 3200 Greenmount avenue; J. R. Chenoweth charged with sale and possession.' The paper calls the place a saloon and names only Chenoweth. It does not name the owner or keeper of the premises or say what was found there. Chenoweth has not been identified further, and the outcome of the charge has not been traced.

Death notice in the Sun of December 8, 1946: Ruth Samstag died suddenly on December 7, 1946 at her residence, 2906 Reisterstown road, 'beloved wife of the late Fred H. Samstag and devoted mother of Benno Samstag', of Washington, D. C.; funeral from the Sondheim Home, 1902 Eutaw Place. Fred H. Samstag, owner of the corner from 1911, had died in January 1929, and 'Mrs. Frederick Samstag' sold 3200 Greenmount in December 1936.

Benjamin A. Kriger's advertisements trace the move. October 5, 1928: 'B. A. Kriger, Greenmount Ave. & 31st St.' (Sun). March 16, 1929: 'Kriger's Drug Store, Greenmount ave. and 31st st.' wants a boy (Sun). June 29, 1929: the lease of the two-story store-front building at 3200 Greenmount from Mrs. Elizabeth R. Samstag is reported, the building to be remodeled for him. July 21, 1929: a full-page advertisement announcing 'our third drug store in Baltimore' lists three stores, 'Howard & Centre Sts., Poplar Grove St. & Lafayette Ave., 3100 Greenmount Ave.' July 30: help wanted at 'Kriger's Drug Store, 3100 Greenmount avenue' (Evening Sun). September 29, 1929: '3 Drug Stores, Howard and Centre, Poplar Grove & Lafayette, Greenmount & 32nd St.' So the Waverly store was at 3100 Greenmount before it was at 3200, and it moved between the end of July and the end of September 1929; the day is not given. The '3100' of the July help-wanted advertisement was not a misprint.

The liquor-license list printed in the Sun on January 5, 1934, a month after Repeal, has under 'Class A, Beer, Wine and Liquor, Off Sale': 'Kriger, Benjamin A., 3200 Greenmount Ave.', with Read Drug and Chemical Co. and six other names. Whether the list is of applicants or of licenses granted is not shown in the clipping. In the list of December 28, 1935 his Class A entry is at 3236 Greenmount, the store he moved to when the White Coffee Pot took the corner. The same newspaper page is filed on 2745 Greenmount for a different licensee.

Display advertisement in the Sun of Sunday, July 3, 1938: a 50-cent Sunday chicken dinner, with the menu, under the name 'The White Coffee Pot' and six addresses: Edmondson Avenue and Monroe Street, Greenmount Avenue and 32nd Street, 3515 Eastern Avenue near Conkling and 1423 N. Charles Street, each marked 'Air-Conditioned', and 2503 Pennsylvania Avenue near North and 304 W. Franklin Street. The trade mark at the top is a coffee pot crossed by an arrow. The restaurant had leased the corner from January 15, 1936.

Display advertisement in the Sun of May 14, 1943 for waitresses, 'Girls and Women for Restaurant Work', day or night work, at the White Coffee Pot: apply at 5124 Park Heights Ave., 1423 North Charles St. or 3200 Greenmount Ave., or at the employment office at Monroe St. and Edmondson Ave. The chain's menu advertisements of January and February 1945 list 3200 Greenmount among seven restaurants; a signed advertisement of July 11, 1946 ('Myles Katz, President') lists Greenmount Avenue and 32nd Street; and waitress advertisements name 3200 Greenmount in October 1954, December 1956 and June 1957.

These reports are about the chain whose restaurant stood on this corner, not about this restaurant by name. Afro-American, December 22, 1956: an interracial group of 45 staged a sit-in at the White Coffee Pot in a northwest Baltimore shopping center, and Jerome and Myles Katz, owners of the chain, are reported as saying that 'fear of loss in revenue was their reason for keeping the restaurants for white only'. March 30, 1957: a citizens' committee had been trying for six months to make the chain change its practice; the centre of the dispute was the Mondawmin restaurant, with pickets also at the Monroe and Edmondson, Howard and Baltimore, and Park Heights and Belvedere restaurants. September 20, 1958: Myles Katz reported to police that a Black customer had sat down at a counter where, in the paper's words, 'colored persons are only allowed to obtain "carry-out" orders'. October 8, 1960: the actress Diana Sands told the paper that she and Lonnie Elder went to the White Coffee Pot near the theatre and were told 'Only carry out'. Against these, the Sun's obituary of Alan R. Katz (January 24, 2020) quotes a family member: 'The restaurants were integrated in the 1950s before it became federal law.' The two accounts disagree. The contemporary reports show the carry-out-only rule in force at named restaurants as late as October 1960. None of the four names the restaurant at 32nd and Greenmount, and when it first seated Black customers is not documented here.

A waitress advertisement in the Sun of August 24, 1966 for White Coffee Pot Family Restaurants, which calls itself Maryland's fastest and largest growing chain, tells applicants to apply in person at twelve places, the first of them '32nd & Greenmount Ave.' An Evening Sun advertisement of January 4, 1965 also begins with 32nd and Greenmount. These are the latest dated notices of the restaurant at the corner found so far. The trustee under the Katz deeds of trust sold the building in November 1976, and a city contact list names the Hot Spot Restaurant there in April 1977.

An undated black-and-white photograph (two copies in this parcel's gallery, images 1440 and 248) looks north up Greenmount Avenue from the 32nd Street crossing. At the left edge is the corner building with a sign reading 'COFFEE POT'; behind it the three-story mansard building of 3204-3206, then signs for Family Finance and Brandau's Marlboro clothes. On the right are a fruit and flower stand under a Heinz oven-baked beans billboard and hanging signs for the W. L. Douglas 'Cinderella Shoe Shop' and Weatherbird Shoes; a lamp post carries an 'E 32nd St' sign. The automobiles date it to the late 1930s, after the White Coffee Pot's lease of January 1936. The photographer, the date and the original source are not recorded. The same view is described on 3201 Greenmount, the opposite corner.
The Evening Sun's list of restaurant closings, March 8, 1979: 'Hot Spot Family Restaurant, 3200 Greenmount avenue, closed Feb. 6, 68 points and roaches, re-opened Feb. 8.'

Tax-sale list in the Sun, April 24, 1981: 3200-3202 Greenmount Ave., Lot 1, Block 3882, 36 feet by 53 feet 3 inches, 'Improved by 2 one story bldgs. Assessed for $20,580 to The Hotspot Family Restaurant Inc.', amount $1,261.55. Evening Sun, April 16, 1982: the same lot, assessed for $19,230 to The Hotspot Family Restaurant Inc., amount $1,449.41. The parcel had been on the 1979 list as well, there described as improved by a two-story building; the 1981 list's 'one story' is not explained. In March 1983 the holder of the 1976 mortgage declared it in default.

John Dorsey's dining column in the Sun of April 5, 1981 surveys places to eat near Memorial Stadium and calls Shalimar (3200) an intriguing Indian restaurant: 'In the daytime it's what it looks like, a lunchroom', where a ham-and-egg plate can be had, and from 5 p.m. it serves curries and biriyanis at low prices; he warns off anyone squeamish about how places look. His column of December 28, 1980 had said that Shalimar, at Greenmount and 32d street, 'looks dreadful' but that its Indian food, served only at dinner, was very good. Shalimar had opened at the corner by September 1980, in the building the Hotspot corporation owned.

Known from recitals, not from the deed itself. The 1974 assignment of 3011 (R.H.B. 3116/426) and the 2007 description (F.M.C. 9050, p. 275), both read on the scans, begin the 3011 lot 'at the end of the first line of the firstly described lot of ground in the deed from J. Holliday Reipe (single) to James M. Sinclair and Edna M. Sinclair, his wife, dated March 1, 1927', recorded in Liber S.C.L. No. 4707, folio 12, and run back along that lot's lines. The recitals give no price and do not say what estate Reipe held; by 1954 the lot was a leasehold under a $66 ground rent. 'Firstly described' shows that the 1927 deed conveyed more than one lot; the other is not identified. Sinclair had kept his tin shop at 1001 York road, the old number of this corner, since 1907 and at 3011 Greenmount since 1915, so the deed made the tenant the owner. His wife is 'Edna M.' in these recitals, '(Ena)' in Polk's 1922 directory, and 'Ena M.' in the recital of the couple's 1934 assignment of the 3111 Greenmount ground to the Provident Savings Bank. J. Holliday Reipe has not been identified. A Mrs. V. Dallas Reipe, widow of Joseph, lived on Walker Avenue near York Road in 1918 and at 2130 Madison Avenue in 1922 (Polk) and died Feb. 22, 1938 (Baltimore City estate 26873); she may be of the same family. The deed itself has not been read. Correction/pointer, Oct. 13, 2026: S.C.L. 4707/12 is read (720:mdlr-scl4707-12-riepe-sinclair-entireties-1927): it is the return half of a Sinclair to Riepe to Sinclair pass-through of three lots recorded March 7, 1927 at 2:00 and 2:01 P.M. (the first deed is 4707/11, 720:mdlr-scl4707-11-sinclair-riepe-1927); 3011 and 3013 were fee simple in 1927, so the $66 rent on 3011 dates from the Weber and Plack lease of 1954, not from before 1927.

Known from a recital, not from the instrument. The 1974 assignment out of Max Silen's estate (R.H.B. 3116/427, read on the scan) says the 3011 lot is 'the same lot of ground which by deed of assignment dated August 2, 1954 and recorded among the Land Records of Baltimore City in Liber M.L.P. No. 9546, Folio 143, was granted and conveyed by Elizabeth McC. West to Max Silen'. The Silen ownership of 3011 therefore begins in August 1954. How Elizabeth McC. West came to hold the lot that James M. and Edna M. Sinclair bought in 1927 is not known (James M. Sinclair died Jan. 6, 1948; Baltimore City estate OLD48532). Whether she was an heir, a buyer or a straw party would show in the instrument, which has not been read. The price is not recited. Update Oct. 12, 2026: M.L.P. 9546/143 is now read (720:mdlr-mlp9546-143-west-max-silen-3011-1954), with the Weber and Plack deed's last page (9546/142) and the Belair Road release (9546/146): the leasehold is 99 years renewable at $66 a year, the same-day deed created it, and the Webers and Placks, who had mortgaged 3011 on June 19, 1954 (M.L.P. 9513/64), took the loan off the same day. Correction/pointer, Oct. 13, 2026: the lot West assigned is the one the Sinclairs held in fee in 1927 (S.C.L. 4707/11 to 14, read); the $66 rent was created in 1954, not carried forward from a lease older than 1927.

Known from a recital, not from the instrument. The 1974 assignment (R.H.B. 3116/428, read on the scan) says the 14-ft 3013 lot is 'the same lot of ground which by deed of assignment dated August 25, 1954 and recorded among the Land Records of Baltimore City in Liber M.L.P., No. 9566, Folio 459, was granted and conveyed by John E. Minor to Max Silen'. With the assignment of 3011 on Aug. 2, this put the two lots of today's tax lot 4076A/001 in one owner's hands. Who held the 3013 lot between William L. Fink (1898) and John E. Minor is not known; no Baltimore City estate for a John E. Minor was found in the Register of Wills index. The instrument has not been read and the price is not recited. Update Oct. 12, 2026: M.L.P. 9566/459 is now read (720:mdlr-mlp9566-459-minor-max-silen-3013-1954), with the Obrecht deed of the day before (9566/461, Charles F. and Alice F. Obrecht to Samuel G. Silen, the reversion and one-cent rent): the Silens held both estates of 3013 from Aug. 25, 1954. John E. Minor's leasehold came from a Dec. 20, 1943 sale-leaseback to the Obrechts (M.L.P. 6544/521, not pulled).

Thompson's 1889 plats of the 21st and 22nd Wards (6th Precinct, Sec. 2, p. 132) draw the wedge between the York Road and Old York Road. The southernmost lot is marked '88.' along the York Road and '8.' across its cut-off point. The name 'Miss Tredway / Jno. T. Ensor Guardian' is lettered across it and the two lots north of it, which are 62 ft and 63 ft on the York Road (the '60.' and '34' printed on Old York Road belong to those two lots, not to the tip). The improvements printed on the tip lot are '2 S. B. B., 2 S. B. B. B., 1 1/2 S. F. B. B., 1 S. F. Shop'. Read against the plat's other entries ('2 S. F. D.' for a two-story frame dwelling, '2 S. F. B. B.' for a frame back building), that is a two-story brick building, a two-story brick back building, a story-and-a-half frame back building and a one-story frame shop. The plat does not show where on the 88 ft they stood. The later deeds give 3011 and 3013 together 72 ft 4 in from an 8 ft 6 in point, and 87 ft 4 in with the 15-ft lot of 3015. So the 1889 tip lot either took in the 3015 ground as well, or was measured from a point further south before the east line of Greenmount Avenue was fixed in 1898; the plat alone does not settle which. Either way it covers the ground of 3011 and 3013. The directories of 1888 and 1889 put a shoe store at 1001 York road and the justice of the peace at 1003, the two old numbers the 1915 Sanborn plate prints on the two-story brick shop at the tip, and Bromley's 1896 atlas draws a brick building at the tip with open ground north of it. The brick building of the plat was therefore probably at the tip, on the site of 3011, and the frame shop may be the 1005 York road store (3013) where Joseph J. Willis, carpenter, was listed from 1887 to 1889. Neither placement is printed on the plat.

Sanborn's 1915 atlas, Vol. 7, sheet 718 (the east side; sheet 717 is the west side), draws the tip of the wedge between Greenmount Avenue and Old York Road. South of the buildings the point is open ground. Then comes one establishment lettered 'Plumbing & Tin Shop' in two two-story brick blocks with 8-inch walls: the south block, cut off at an angle on the Old York Road side, with the height figure 20 ft, and the north block, with the figure 30 ft. One-story frame strips run along the front and the north side, and a one-story frame building fills the triangle behind. The frontage line prints '1001' and '1003' on these two blocks with no Greenmount number. North of them '1005 / 3013' is a one-story frame store, and '1007 / 3015' follows. This is James M. Sinclair's shop, listed by Polk at 1001 York road from 1907 and at 3011 Greenmount from 1915.

Polk's bank pages of 1889 and 1890, read on the page images, list the North Baltimore Savings Bank with a main office on West North Avenue (No. 2 in 1889, No. 4 in 1890) and 'Branches, 1003 York rd, open Saturday, from 5 to 8 P M, 15 North, open from 10 A M to 2 P M'. The officers are J. M. Littig, president, and F. D. Morrison, treasurer, in 1889; F. D. Morrison, president, and Townsend Scott, treasurer, in 1890. The alphabetical entries repeat the branch: 'branches, 15 w North av, 1003 York rd' (1890) and 'branches 15 w North av and 1003 York rd' (1891). No entry for the bank was found in the text of the 1892 volume. The bank was two years old. The Baltimore County Union of May 21, 1887 (p. 3, 'A Belt Savings Bank') reports that 'the citizens of the Belt and North Baltimore held a meeting on Monday night, for the purpose of organizing a savings bank to be located in the Belt', F. D. Morrison presiding, with directors Robertson Taylor, Calvin T. Davidson, John H. Wight, John M. Littig, John S. Ditch, Fred. D. Morrison, John W. Mittendorf, John H. Grimes, Ernest Hoen, Wm. H. Moffit Jr., James H. Smith and Ogden A. Kirkland; 'The bank will be known as the North Baltimore Savings Bank of Baltimore County.' The issue of June 11, 1887 notes its articles of incorporation filed with the County Clerk. The Belt was the county strip annexed to the city in 1888. (The 1887 items were read in the Library of Congress text of the pages, not on the images.) 1003 York road is the north block of today's 3011 Greenmount, the same address as the justice of the peace's office in these years.

Polk lists 'Wright Wm D, justice of the peace, 1003 York rd' from 1888 to 1892; from 1901 to 1908 he is 'real estate, 1003 York rd', living at 650 York road (1901-04) and 2642 York road (1905-08). The business directories of 1890 and 1893 also list him at 1003; the residential volumes of 1893 to 1900 and 1902 are not available. Constables shared the address: 'Mahool Thos, constable, 1003 York rd' in 1888, and George Wise in the business lists of 1890 ('Wise Geo W', a misprinted initial) and 1893 ('Wise Geo Y'); the residential volumes have 'Wise Geo Y, constable' at Gutman Avenue (1890) and at 55 Mount Street, Waverly (1891-92). Wright was the village magistrate before the annexation of 1888: Woods prints 'Wright Wm. D. clerk, Waverley' in 1882 and 'Wright Wm. D. magistrate, Waverley' in 1884, 1885 and 1886, and a William D. Wright at Peabody Heights near Waverly from 1872. The 2013 National Register inventory says of 3011 that 'it was the office of local magistrate W.D. Wright'. A Thomas Mahool appears in Woods as a partner in Sears & Mahool (1879-80) and Mahool & Probest (1881-82), commission merchants, 'Waverley'. Whether the constable was that man, and whether either was related to Mayor J. Barry Mahool (1907-11), is not established. In 1909 the number is Winfield S. Brannock's, carpenter. 1003 York road is the north block of today's 3011: the 1928 Sanborn plate prints '3011 / 1003' on the building. The lines of 1889 to 1908 were checked on the page images; the 1888 line and the Woods entries are from the directory text.

Polk's directories of 1887 and 1888 print '*Garnett Adelaide, laund, 1003 York rd'. The asterisk is Polk's mark for a colored person; it and the number were read on the 1887 page image. 1003 York road is the north block of today's 3011, the address that in 1888 was also the justice's office. The line does not say whether she lived or worked there, and she is not listed at the address in 1889 or in the later volumes available. Woods' 1885 directory lists an Adelaide Garnett, widow of Jeremiah, at 74 Bolton Street without the mark Woods used for colored residents, so that is probably a different woman. No estate for her was found in the Baltimore City Register of Wills index.

Two Polk publications of 1905, both read on the page images, disagree by one digit. Polk's Baltimore business directory for 1905-06 lists under Undertakers 'Brooks Robt & Son, 1204 w Balto, 17 s Calhoun and 1001 York rd'. The Baltimore city directory for 1905 prints the firm's own entry as 'BROOKS ROBERT & SON (Robert and Robert L Brooks), Undertakers, 1204-1206 w Balto, 3101 York rd and 17 s Calhoun', and its classified list as '17 s Calhoun and 3101 York rd'. 1001 York road is the tip block of today's 3011, between the Rahe shoe store (there to 1901) and James M. Sinclair's tin shop (from 1907). 3101 York road was also a real address in these years, in the block above 31st Street: the 1904 directory has a confectioner there and the 1905 a laborer, and other 3100-block numbers were already in use beside the old 1000 numbers. Which printing is the misprint has not been settled, so the branch cannot be placed at 3011 with confidence. Neither the 1904 nor the 1906 and 1907 directories list a York road branch for the firm.

Polk prints 'Willis Jos J, carp, 1005 York rd' in 1887 and 1888 and, in 1889, 'Willis Jos J, carp, 1005 York rd, h 1339 do'; the business lists of 1889 and 1890 repeat 1005. The one-story frame shop that Thompson's 1889 plat prints on the tip lot may be his, though the plat does not place it. The directory text follows him before and after: Woods has him a carpenter at 'Oxford, York rd' (the Harwood hamlet) in 1872-75, at Waverley in 1876-78 and at Friendship in 1883-85; Polk has him at 1329 York road in 1890 and, as a builder, in 1892; in 1901 he is of the firm Willis & Mason and sergeant-at-arms of the City Council, and from 1904 to 1907 Willis & Mason are at 1193 York road. 1005 York road is the number the 1915 Sanborn plate prints with 3013.

Polk lists 'Fink Bertha, dry gds, 1005 York rd, h 845 do' in 1901, 1903 and 1904. 1005 York road is the 14-ft lot conveyed to William L. Fink in April 1898, and 845 York road was his home when he kept a dry goods store at 1047 York road in 1890-92, so Bertha Fink was of his household and the family ran its store on its own lot. From 1905 the store is Rosa Vicary's: 'Vicary Rosa, dry gds, 1005 York rd, h 1429 Patterson av' (1905), then 'h 1837 Pa av' (1906-08), and 'Vicary Rosa, milliner, 1005 York rd, h 1837 Pa av' in 1909. She had been a dressmaker at 805 South Sharp Street (1888-90) and a partner in Ankrim & Vicary, 4 South Broadway (1892). By 1913 the store is Harry Peiser's tailor shop, under the new number 3013. The lines were checked on the page images; the homes and earlier careers are from the directory text. Update Oct. 17, 2026 (Fink deeds S.C.L. 2559/393 and 3126/290 read): Bertha Fink of 1005 York road is one of William L. Fink's four children (she married Samuel F. A. Kiel by 1910: S.C.L. 2559/393), and 3013 York Road 'formerly 1005' is the 1898 lot (S.C.L. 3126/290, May 1, 1917).

Polk 1901, read on the page image: 'Sinclair Jas E, clk, 1112 York rd' and 'Sinclair Jas M, tinner, 1112 York rd'. 1112 York road is the number the 1915 Sanborn plate prints with 3220 Greenmount. James E. Sinclair is listed at 1112 York road in 1891 and on the 1899 Twelfth Ward list, and in 1888 as a machinist at 1048 York road with his home at about that number. By 1903 James M. is at 410 East 31st Street (410 Waverly Avenue), where James E. is also listed in 1905 and 1909, and in 1907 James M. opens at 1001 York road, today's 3011 Greenmount. The shared addresses make the two men one household; the directories do not state the relationship.

Polk lists Harry Peiser at '3013 York rd' in 1913 and at '3013 Greenmt av' from 1914 to 1918, as tailor (dyer in 1915), living at 3403 Piedmont Avenue. The 1913 line uses the new number with the old street name. The directory text follows him from East Baltimore: tailor at 1024 Watson Street (1889) and 1111 Granby Street (1890), Peiser & Goldstein with Meyer Goldstein (1891), Ashland Avenue (1892-1903), 825 North Caroline Street (1905) and 1741 East Preston Street (1907-12). From 1920 to 1922 his shop is around the corner at 424 East 31st Street, and the 1922 volume names his wife Rosa. No estate for him was found in the Baltimore City or County Register of Wills index.

Polk 1923 lists 'Hull Irving T & Co (Irving T Hull, David Gough) sea food 3013 Greenmt av', and repeats the firm at 3013 in its business list. Irving T. Hull had been a clerk at 268 Old York Road in 1905-09 (Polk). The Northwestern Miller reports him resigning from the Baltimore grain inspection department in January 1920 and names him, with S. H. Ruth & Co., millers' agents, in 1921 and March 1923 (read in the archive's text of the issues). The sea-food firm appears in the one directory year; the 1922 volume has James M. Sinclair's sheet-metal works at 3013.

A two-line classified in the Evening Sun's help-wanted column reads 'BOY (COLORED) TO DRIVE TRUCK. 3011 GREENMOUNT AVE.' No name is given. In 1928 3011 was James M. Sinclair's sheet-metal shop: he had bought the lot the year before, the 1928 Sanborn plate letters the building 'TIN SHOP', and the National Register inventory cites the 1928 directory for his workshop. The advertisement specifies the race of the worker wanted, as help-wanted columns of the period commonly did; it is the one sign found so far of who else worked at the shop. The date and page are those of the clipping's file name.

A large display advertisement, read on the clipping: 'Scotty says: Follow the WCAO Spotlight, Thursday Night, October 6th to 3011 Greenmount Ave... home of Maryland Thrift Savings & Loan Association Inc.' Twenty people 'will win $100.00 in cash prizes' by unscrambling a phrase on an entry blank left at the office before the drawing there on Thursday, Oct. 6, at 8 P.M.; the first twenty correct answers each win a $5 savings account. A kilted cartoon Scot holds a '4 1/2% current dividend' disc and a shield reading 'Accounts INSURED, Security Financial Insurance Corp., Baltimore, Md.' The foot of the advertisement gives two offices: '3011 Greenmount Ave. "In the Heart of Waverly" Baltimore, Md. Call BElmont 5-9753' and 'Silver Spring, Md. 8417 Georgia Ave. JUniper 7-8206'. The insurer named on the shield was not a government agency but the private company at the centre of a later federal mail-fraud case, and the association was in receivership proceedings by August 1962. The date and page are those of the clipping's file name; Oct. 6, 1960 was a Thursday.

OpenCorporates' copy of the Maryland record: Upstairs Social Club, Inc. (D03563947), articles of incorporation filed Dec. 31, 1992, registered address 3011 Greenmount Avenue, Baltimore 21218, forfeited by proclamation Oct. 3, 1994. It falls between Service Photo Supply's last printed 3011 listing (1990) and the health center's purchase in April 1995. What the club was is not known.

Banner investigation of vacancy in the Waverly Main Street Historic District (Greenmount Ave, 29th to 35th St): more than 1 in 4 buildings appear empty. Community leaders blame landlord Matt Herman, whose LLCs own 11 Greenmount Ave properties, most with empty storefronts and about $123,000 in unpaid water bills; his spokesperson says he is in talks to sell most of the portfolio. Herman-owned buildings named: 3028 (Barrus Real Estate Group office), 3030 (yoga contest space, vacant notice), 3026 (proposed cafe, collapsing porch, vacant notice), 3326 (former Mayflower Chinese, empty 5+ years), 3313 (former Zehbras Fitness). Also profiles Red Emma's at 3128 (bought and renovated buildings Herman had acquired for under $400,000 in 2016, $1.6M total) and Jinji's Chocolate at 3100 (opened Oct 2023). Quotes Kate Khatib (Red Emma's) and Jeff Jetton (Toki Underground).

Profile of Farm Alliance of Baltimore (15th year, 41 member farms, executive director Denzel Mitchell Jr.), reported from its stand at the Waverly Farmers Market on 32nd Street, alongside vendors Atwater's, Taco Loco and The Big Bean Theory.

Cornell historian Tejasvi Nagaraja presented his book 'Troop Movements: Labor, Race, and Global Freedom Struggles in America's World War II' at Red Emma's on Thursday Oct 1, in conversation with Hopkins historian Stuart Schrader; discussion included the 1942 killing of Black serviceman Thomas Broadus by a Baltimore police officer.

Existing conditions assessment of 3224 Greenmount Ave by PI.KL Studio (Ryan Couto) for the Maryland Historical Trust Waverly Main Street study, draft dated 5 October 2026 from field surveys in June and July 2026. Overall building condition as drafted: Poor. A narrow, vacant two-story storefront whose first floor is sitting on makeshift posts over a damp crawl space, with tired roofs and rear brickwork but a surviving storefront, mantel and transoms. First life-safety item in the report: No loads on the first floor until an engineer checks the temporary posts.

Existing conditions assessment of 3200-3202 Greenmount Ave by PI.KL Studio (Ryan Couto) for the Maryland Historical Trust Waverly Main Street study, draft dated 5 October 2026 from field surveys in June and July 2026. Overall building condition as drafted: Poor. A vacant corner restaurant building that keeps its triangular form but has worn-out roofs, failing siding and parging, corroded drain pipes, and partly demolished upper-floor walls. First life-safety item in the report: Find out whether the electric, gas and water services are live.

Existing conditions assessment of 2958 Greenmount Ave by PI.KL Studio (Ryan Couto) for the Maryland Historical Trust Waverly Main Street study, draft dated 5 October 2026 from field surveys in June and July 2026. Overall building condition as drafted: Poor. A vacant, stripped two-story corner shell with open holes through the roof and no upper floor deck, so rain falls straight through to the first floor and basement. First life-safety item in the report: Open floors with no guarding; holes in the roof let rain fall through to the basement.

Existing conditions assessment of 3010-3020 Greenmount Ave by PI.KL Studio (Ryan Couto) for the Maryland Historical Trust Waverly Main Street study, draft dated 5 October 2026 from field surveys in June and July 2026. Overall building condition as drafted: Poor. A one-story four-storefront range, two units open and trading, where water standing on a failing roof has brought down the ceiling of the former pizza restaurant. First life-safety item in the report: Keep the old pizza shop closed until the hanging ceiling is taken down.

Existing conditions assessment of 3011-3013 Greenmount Ave by PI.KL Studio (Ryan Couto) for the Maryland Historical Trust Waverly Main Street study, draft dated 5 October 2026 from field surveys in June and July 2026. Overall building condition as drafted: Poor. A vacant corner building stopped partway through a gut renovation: the floor framing looks sound where it can be seen, but the roof is worn out, the wiring is in an unknown and unsafe state, and there is an open hole in the second floor. First life-safety item in the report: Guard the open hole in the second floor.

Existing conditions assessment of 3015-3017 Greenmount Ave by PI.KL Studio (Ryan Couto) for the Maryland Historical Trust Waverly Main Street study, draft dated 5 October 2026 from field surveys in June and July 2026. Overall building condition as drafted: Poor. A vacant, gutted building with weakened second-floor joists in its south half, an open hatch to the crawl space, water getting in at the third floor, and almost no working services. First life-safety item in the report: Keep weight off the weakened second-floor joists.

Existing conditions assessment of 3026 Greenmount Ave by PI.KL Studio (Ryan Couto) for the Maryland Historical Trust Waverly Main Street study, draft dated 5 October 2026 from field surveys in June and July 2026. Overall building condition as drafted: Poor. A vacant, partly stripped 1912 porch-front rowhouse that has been entered and slept in, with roof leaks and loose glass and boards over the sidewalk, but with sound walls, framing and much of its historic trim. First life-safety item in the report: Specialist clean-out of syringes before anyone goes in; secure the loose boards over the sidewalk.

Existing conditions assessment of 3028-3032 Greenmount Ave by PI.KL Studio (Ryan Couto) for the Maryland Historical Trust Waverly Main Street study, draft dated 5 October 2026 from field surveys in June and July 2026. Overall building condition as drafted: Good. Three 1912 rowhouses combined into one occupied, well-kept office and shipping-center building, with a roof that holds water, one leak into the shop ceiling, crumbling brick at the top of the side wall, and an elevator out of service. First life-safety item in the report: Water in a ceiling void with wiring, over an occupied room.

Existing conditions assessment of 3107 Greenmount Ave by PI.KL Studio (Ryan Couto) for the Maryland Historical Trust Waverly Main Street study, draft dated 5 October 2026 from field surveys in June and July 2026. Overall building condition as drafted: Poor. A vacant, water-damaged store building whose failed upper roof, crumbling chimney and building-wide mold need attention first, with its three-arch storefront probably intact behind the roll-down doors. First life-safety item in the report: Keep clear below the chimney, which is dropping brick.

Existing conditions assessment of 3117 Greenmount Ave by PI.KL Studio (Ryan Couto) for the Maryland Historical Trust Waverly Main Street study, draft dated 5 October 2026 from field surveys in June and July 2026. Overall building condition as drafted: Poor. A vacant 1920s brick furniture showroom with a handsome terracotta front and pressed-metal ceilings, whose basement holds standing water around the electrical panels and whose roof, parapet and plaster are failing. First life-safety item in the report: Power off, and an electrician before anyone enters the flooded basement.

The Colored Teachers' Association of Baltimore County met at Howard Normal School and discussed methods of teaching arithmetic and history, with Miss Victoria Johnson, Miss Nannie B. Groomes, P. C. Roberts, George W. Biddle, Charles R. Uncles and Miss Josie M. Jones taking part. Officers elected: president Richard Riggs; vice-president Charles R. Uncles; treasurer Miss Sadie Burkett; secretary P. C. Roberts; assistant Miss Fannie Barbour; sergeant-at-arms L. N. Harris; executive committee Wm. H. Butler, Richard Frey, George W. Biddle, J. M. Jones and Miss Roberta Sheridan.

In the Sun's baseball roundup, 'The Quicksteps, of Towsontown, and the Spread Eagles, of Waverly, both colored clubs, played at Towsontown yesterday, the score standing 9 to 17 in favor of the Quicksteps.' The paper added that several players were knocked down by the pitchers and many small injuries inflicted by the ball.

In the Baltimore County School Board's list of appointments for 1883-84, under 'Colored Teachers,' the Ninth District entries are 'No. 1, Cornelius Smith, Towson. 2, Daniel Williams, Govanstown. 3, George W. Biddle, Waverly.' The same list names Roberta B. Sheridan, 132 Chesnut street, to First District colored school No. 2, Nannie B. Groomes to No. 1 at Catonsville, and a Grant Riddle (as printed), 255 Dover street, to Eighth District colored school No. 4.

Roberta Sheridan, colored, was appointed a teacher at the Waverly colored public school. The Sun called it the first appointment of a colored teacher in Baltimore, made under an ordinance passed before annexation that colored teachers be appointed to all colored schools coming into the city's possession. She was born in Baltimore and graduated from the colored high and grammar school and the colored normal school. The item adds that another colored teacher would be appointed to the Waverly school the following week, and notes the growth of the Belt schools since annexation.

In the city School Board's proceedings, the list of teachers elected as assistants includes 'Miss Roberta Sheridan, colored, annex 1,' alongside white teachers assigned to other annexes (the Belt schools taken over at annexation).

In the Sun's report of Baltimore's first Arbor Day in the schools: 'At annex colored school, No. 1, Waverly, the principal, Geo. W. Biddle, Misses Roberta Sheridan and Nannie B. Grooms each gave a reading before the scholars, and each teacher then planted a tree in the yard. The trees were given the names of Phoebe Carey, Alice Carey and Harriet Beecher Stowe.'

Reporting the reopening of the city schools, the Sun said the new colored school at the corner of Carrollton and Riggs avenues opened for the first time, the first school in the city proper employing colored teachers; 'there are two schools in the annex in which colored teachers are employed.' George W. Biddle was principal of the male department and Fanny Barbour principal of the female department of No. 9.

At the School Board meeting, Mr. Horn said the new colored School No. 9 on Carrollton avenue had opened with about 600 pupils, depleting another school. The teachers in the male department were George W. Biddle, principal, Garrison D. Trusty, Roberta Sheridan, Nellie Anderson and Mollie Taylor; in the female department, Fannie Barbour, Nannie Groomes, Gertrude Deaver, Violet Thompson and Fannie McCabe.

Describing a political meeting held under the auspices of the Republican clubs of the twenty-second ward, the Sun listed the clubs present in bodies as the Central, Maister, Remington, Wellington, Homestead, Enterprise Colored and Waverly Colored Republican Clubs. The meeting was called to order by Mr. A. Warfield Monroe.

In the Sun's June 1900 list of pupils promoted from the city's grammar and primary schools, the colored-school section ends with 'School No. 115: Herbert Scott,' following lists for Schools No. 110 and No. 113.

In the School Board's list of citizen visitors assigned to each school, the Sun printed: School No. 115, Merryman's lane near York road, Dr. A. G. Hoen and George E. Leight. The list appears under the heading 'Visitors Announced' in a report of the board's meeting.
In the Sun's June 1901 promotions list, the colored schools entry reads 'School No. 115: Howard Scott, Arthur Washington, George Williams,' followed on the next line by 'Lizzie Jackson, Eva Thomson.'

The Sun identified the contralto of the First Presbyterian Church choir, whose resignation over a rumor about her race it had reported the previous Tuesday, as Constantia B. Brown, a teacher in School No. 115 (colored) at York road and Merryman's lane. A letter from a teacher stated she was teaching in a colored school with a colored faculty and was recognized by the other teachers as a colored teacher. The paper said she was a daughter of Dr. H. J. Brown, the colored politician, of 426 North Gilmor street, formerly of the Custom House and a delegate to the Republican National Convention that renominated Grant. Her mother told a reporter she had gone out of the city for an indefinite time.

Building Inspector Preston, arguing against the School Board's plan for portable schools, listed school buildings that in a few years at most must be torn down or abandoned. The list includes 'No. 115, Merryman's lane, near York road, a ramshackle old building' and 'Branch of No. 115, Barclay street, near Merryman's lane, ready to tumble down.' He called for a million-dollar loan from the Legislature to build ten needed schools.

Describing children's flower and plant shows organized by the Sunshine Section, the Sun reported that the remaining schools in the group, 'School 51 at Waverly, 50 at Homestead, and 115, colored, at Waverly,' would hold their plant shows that afternoon. Mrs. George W. Sadtler, president of the Mothers and Teachers' Union, and Mrs. A. K. Rogers and Mrs. Frank Beck would judge the white schools, and Mrs. John T. Graham the display at School 115. Miss Irene Dysart, chairman of the Sunshine Section and drawing teacher of the group, chaired the arrangements.

In the June 1905 list of pupils promoted to the Colored High and Training School, Group K, the Sun printed: 'School 115: Robert Ashby, Lucy Crigler, Florence Gittings, Annie Johnson, Lydia Jones, Laura Payne, Hattie Robinson, Margaret Scott, Bertha Williams, Adella Woodson.'

Reporting a School Board meeting, the Sun said the board decided to open two additional night schools for white pupils (School 83 and School 76) and that 'another night school for colored pupils will be opened at School 115, Merryman's lane, near York road.'

The Afro-American reported that a night school would be started at School 115, Merryman's Lane, Waverly, on Monday, in response to a petition of a large number of residents of that vicinity. Prof. Howard E. Young was to be the principal.

Among new school buildings planned for the Mayor and City Council, the Sun listed one-story frame and galvanized iron portable buildings costing $1,300 each, including one at School 115, at Merryman's lane near York road. In the same item, three one-story portable buildings of wood and galvanized iron were to be erected at School No. 51 on York road near Merryman's Lane, after plans by Architect B. B. Owens, to be built by P. J. Cushen.

An Afro-American list of the city's colored night schools for the season includes School No. 115, Merrymans Lane, Waverly, alongside the Colored High School at Pennsylvania avenue and Dolphin street and Schools 101, 106, 112 and 113.

A school-by-school building safety report printed in the Sun listed: 'No. 115, Frame building; unsafe for school.' and 'No. 115 (Annex), Unsafe; frame house with carpenter shop in first story.' The same list called No. 112's rented annex unsafe because it was over a paint store and No. 118 an old can shop.

A large rafter fell in the portable school adjacent to School 115 on Merryman's lane, and the Sun said that if the children had not been out of the room a number would probably have been killed or seriously injured. It was the second time a rafter had fallen in a portable school, the other at Lakewood avenue and Fayette street. Building Inspector Preston wrote School Board President Semmes recommending that all portable schools be abandoned until properly inspected and repaired.

In an account of a picnic to raise money to renovate Howard Chapel M. E. church, the Afro-American listed participants including lawyers C. C. Fitzgerald and W. Ashbie Hawkins, Prof. Joseph H. Lockerman, principal of the Colored Training School, and 'Mr. Howard E. Young, vice principal of School No. 115, of Baltimore.' The proceeds were $40.50.

The Afro-American reported that closing exercises for School No. 115, Waverly, were held Wednesday night with a musical and literary program by the students. Vice Principal John W. Woodhous introduced Group Principal Harry T. Pratt, who conferred eighth grade certificates on William I. Williams, James Wesley Powell, Thomas H. Mack, John Matthews, Drunell L. Owens, Ella May Owens, Katherine Robertson, Margaret Robertson, Margaret Robinson, Beatrice A. Howard, Mary E. Earls, Bertha M. Thompson, Helen A. Conner and Florence M. Turner.

The Afro-American's notice of the colored night schools says that outside the High School and School 106 only the studies of the first eight grades were given, on Monday, Wednesday and Friday nights, and lists the locations, including School No. 115, Merryman's Lane, Waverly, and the Mount Street School.

The Afro-American reported that the closing exercises of School No. 115 were held Thursday evening at Antioch Baptist Church, with songs and a play, 'Mistress Penelope,' and an address 'full of good advice' by Mr. W. Ashbie Hawkins. Certificates went to Hattie Booze, Alice Collins, Elizabeth Matthews, David Gordon, Samuel Owings, Samuel Banks, William McKinley Smith and Charles Anderson. Mr. J. W. Woodhouse was principal.
An Afro-American list of colored night schools opening for the season named Schools No. 101, 106, 112 and 113, and added: 'A night school may also be opened at School 115, Waverly.'

On complaint of Elisabeth Gilman, daughter of the late Johns Hopkins president Daniel C. Gilman, the Board of Public Safety detailed Health Commissioner Gorter and Building Inspector Stubbs to inspect Public School No. 115, Merryman's lane, west of York road, a colored school. Writing for the Baltimore Committee on the Negro Problem, Gilman said: 'It is a fire trap; it is unsanitary, and the water supply from the winter hydrants is a menace,' and that the group of buildings should be changed or the pupils moved, adding that there were 227 pupils. The Sun noted it was a frame building already complained of, and that Health Department and State Board of Health officials had pronounced it in bad condition several months earlier.

In an Afro-American report of a meeting on care for delinquent colored children, 'J. W. Woodhous, principal of School No. 115, urged that the delinquent child be cared for at the public expense.' William H. McAbee, principal of School No. 100, urged a School Board school for delinquents, preferably in the country, and Rev. L. Z. Johnson of Madison Street Presbyterian Church also spoke.

The Afro-American reported that the seventh and eighth grades of School No. 115, accompanied by their teacher, Mr. J. W. Woodhouse, visited the Maryland Steel Company's plant at Sparrows Point on Wednesday afternoon. A guide furnished by the management explained all points of interest, and after leaving the mills the party visited the public school, where they were entertained by the faculty and pupils.

An Afro-American front-page history of the colored schools said that when School No. 9 was completed, 'Mr. George Biddle was appointed as head of the male department and Miss Fannie Barbour, head of the female department.' Among the teachers of that school still engaged in the profession in 1914 were Fannie Barbour, George Biddle, Nannie Grooms, Annie Waters and Roberta Sheridan.

A school-by-school list of building conditions printed in the Maryland Suffrage News records: 'School No. 115, Merryman's lane near York road, Totally unfit building; no change in conditions since last year.' Neighboring Waverly-area white schools on the same list (No. 55 at Chestnut avenue and 37th street, No. 57 at Church avenue near Merryman's lane) were faulted for drainage, toilets and fountains.

At a special School Board meeting the committee on architecture proposed names of people of African descent for six colored schools. The board adopted Frederick Douglass for No. 100, Benjamin Banneker for No. 113 (the pupils' top vote), and Paul Laurence Dunbar for No. 111, but balked at 'Crispus Attucks' for School No. 115: Colonel Deems called Attucks 'anything but a rabble rouser' and Dr. Bibbins said he was highly respected among colored people, but the board refused the name and asked the committee to look further for School No. 115. Commissioner Biggs had urged names like 'Bunker Hill' instead; Dr. Delevett defended the colored race's right to its own heroes.

A front-page Afro-American survey of overcrowded colored schools, prompted by the School Board's push for a $1,500,000 loan, said: 'School No. 115 at Waverly is badly in need of adequate quarters, and the same could be given easily if the segregation law did not prevent the school authorities from turning over the schoolhouse nearby on Greenmount avenue.' It added that School No. 113 at Federal and Carter streets was greatly overcrowded.

In the Afro-American's account of Frederick Douglass Day exercises in the city's colored schools, 'Mr. Clarke L. Smith spoke at School 115, Waverly,' while Rev. P. C. Neal spoke at the Dunbar School, Rev. C. G. Cummings at the Banneker School and S. S. Booker at the Teachers' Training School.

The Afro-American reported that Miss Roberta Sheridan, 'one of the first colored teachers in the local public schools,' died at her home, 1441 N. Carey street, the previous Sunday night after a very brief illness. Born in Baltimore county, she was appointed to the first corps of teachers of old School No. 9 at Carrollton and Riggs avenues in 1889. About a quarter of a century earlier she had married George W. Biddle, was later divorced and allowed to resume her maiden name, and returned to teaching; at her death she was on the faculty of School No. 108, South Caroline street. She was survived by her mother, Mrs. Arietta Sheridan, and a daughter, Miss Hester Maud Biddle.

The Afro-American's school-by-school opening report lists 'School 115, Merryman Avenue and York Road. J. W. Woodhous, principal. Enrollment 320.' The same list names George Biddle as principal of School 118 (enrollment 400) and Edna Grooms among new teachers at School 116.

In the Afro-American's list of 1919 graduates by school, the School 115 entry reads: 'Dallas Roosevelt Carter, Robert Lee Curtis, Virginia Octavia Anderson, Jequetta Goode, Ida Celestia Harris, Bertha Erdine Winston.'

A front-page roundup of the opening of Baltimore's colored schools. It reports that last-minute repairs and painting in the High School and in School 115, Merryman avenue and York road, J. W. Woodhous principal, delayed the formal opening of those schools until the next Monday. The enrollment table lists School 115 at 320 pupils in 1918, with the 1919 figure left blank because the school was not yet opened.

In an Afro-American list of proposed colored school improvements and their costs, the item for Waverly reads 'School 115, Merryman's Lane, lot and addition $100,000.' Other items include a new School 112 at Calhoun and Laurens streets and a plan to turn the Western High School building over to the Colored High School.

The students of Public School No. 115, for colored boys, Merryman lane and York road, were painting their own building. The Board of School Commissioners furnished the paint and the boys did the work under the direction of H. M. Gross, principal of the school.

In the Sun's June 1920 promotion list, the School No. 115 entry names Harry Alexander Collins, Robert Wesley Johnson, Lloyd Elrich Curtiss, Gladys Rebecca Norris, Agrada Francis Deaver, Francis Elizabeth Collins, Gertrude Louise Brown, Iantha Stokes and Ruby Carter.

The Afro-American's fall school report lists 'School 115, Merryman's Lane near York Road, John H. Woodhouse, principal, 206 pupils. New building planned.' The same list gives George W. Biddle as principal of School 118 in the 1200 block of Argyle Avenue, enrollment 507.

The Proctor Needle Club, recently organized by the pupils of School No. 115, was given a luncheon at the home of Mrs. Louise Martin, Merryman avenue and Talbott street. Guests included Mrs. Bertha Proctor, for whom the club was named, and Sadie Steen, Gladys Deaver, Anna Day, Rebecca Lockhart, Nettie Lockhart, Hortense Allen, Enoa Jackson and Frances Anderson.

The Afro-American printed the school survey commission's ratings of each colored school building. The entry for Waverly reads: 'SCHOOL 115: Dangerous, unsanitary and totally unfit building. Should be abandoned at earliest possible moment.' The same page reports that a committee led by Mrs. John L. Hitchens, chairman of the colored citizens' committee, with Mrs. William Bauernschmidt (white) of the Public School Association and Councilman William L. Fitzgerald, was inspecting the colored school plant and cooperating with the Survey Commission.

In a feature on milk served to pupils in Baltimore's colored schools, the Afro-American reported that at School 115, Merryman's Lane, Principal Howard M. Gross and his assistants stopped the pupils from work ten minutes before recess so they could drink their milk, the teachers guiding them to get the most nourishment and do things in a sanitary way.

The Afro-American printed the rosters of more than 200 boys entered in its schoolboy baseball league at Druid Hill Park. The School 115 team, Merryman's Lane and York Road, is listed under D. C. Creditt, principal, with players Spencer Nash, Albert Giddings, Tilton Stokes, Samuel Harris, Garland Harris, Leonard Page, Clarence Booze, Harry Johnson, Frank Gibson, Tero Pride, Oliver Read, James Winder, Roger Middleton, Edward Anderson, Warfield Davis and George Contee.

In the Afro-American's June 1922 list of graduates, 'School No. 115, Henry W. Ebb, Prin.' lists boys Warfield Davis, Rodger Middleton and Spencer Nash, and girls Hortense Alton, Dorothy Amos, Grace Amos, Annie M. Anderson, Maggie Carter, Emma Downey, Lucy Elliott, Helen Morris and Elsie Wimbish. 'The closing exercises will be held Thursday evening, June 2[9], at 8 o'clock, in Mt. Zion Baptist Church, Barclay street, near Thirty-second street.'

In the Afro-American's list of children winning prizes in a Frederick Douglass essay or picture contest, the School 115 entries are 'Lelia Wilson, Grade 7B, 3203 Barclay street' and 'Agnes Clarke, 8B, 318 W. 28th St.'

A school-system report replying to Fire Department charges of unsafe conditions in city schools described 'School No. 115, Merryman avenue: One-story frame building school except for one room on second floor.
