Outside covered stairway.' The report took the cited schools in order and noted new structures elsewhere had interior fireproof stairways.

Under 'School 115, Merryman's Lane, York Rd., Mr. Wm. H. Proctor, principal,' the Afro-American reported plans for Educational Week: a Parents'-Teachers' meeting on Tuesday evening at Mt. Zion Church, a demonstration lesson by Mr. Lewis Wilson, 5th grade teacher, and an Open House the next week to which all parents were invited.

Under 'School 115, Merryman's Lane, York Rd., Mr. J. W. Woodhouse, principal,' the Afro-American reported that the sixth grade would present a Christmas playlet for the Parent-Teachers' Club on Thursday at Antioch Baptist Church, with Miss Viola Jones as directress. The Parent-Teachers' Club had presented the school with a piano. Mr. Wm. H. Proctor was teacher-in-charge.

A brief in the Afro-American's public-schools page announced a Parents'-Teachers' meeting at School 115 the next Tuesday evening, under Mr. W. H. Proctor, teacher-in-charge, at Merryman's Lane and York Road.

The Parent and Teacher Club of School 115 presented a musical and literary program on Thursday evening, April 10, before a large audience that crowded Mt. Zion Baptist Church, Barclay street, near 31st street. Features included Negro spirituals by the Glee Club of School 100 under Miss Alma Kelly and a solo by Miss Carrie Smith of School 100, and each class of School 115 was represented on the program.

An Afro-American historical installment on the colored schools recorded that in 1895 there were 206 teachers of colored children, 172 white and 34 colored. Twenty-four colored teachers were at the colored school at Carrollton and Riggs avenues, 12 under principal George W. Biddle and 12 under Miss Fannie Barber, and 'the remaining 10 colored teachers were in "Annex schools," schools that were formerly in Baltimore county, but which had been brought into the city through annexation,' among them one near Calverton and Edmondson avenues under George B. Murphy and one on the Frederick Road under Miss Annie O. Waters.

School 115 held an exhibition of pupils' work on May 22 and 23. The manual training department under Mr. J. C. Briscoe showed handicraft, and the girls demonstrated cookery and domestic arts under Mrs. Edith Spriggs and Miss Katherine Fletcher; a large group of parents, teachers and former pupils visited. Miss Aurelia Diggs and Miss Genevieve Fletcher had charge of the pupils in the Play Festival at Druid Hill Park, and the Parent-Teacher Club was to elect officers at its monthly meeting.

In its report of a School Board meeting, the Afro-American said the Parent-Teacher Club of School 115, Merrymans Lane, York Road, presented through a delegation a petition signed by 600 parents and citizens asking for a new school building for the children of that section. The petition was referred to a special committee for study and report.

Under Mr. William H. Proctor, teacher-in-charge, and Mr. John W. Woodhouse, principal, the Afro-American reported that the School 115 Parent-Teachers Association met at Antioch Baptist Church, where its arrangements committee reported on a conference with the Board of School Commissioners about a new building. Plans were made for a Shoe Fund for the benefit of the pupils, and each class held its own Hallowe'en celebration.

The pupils of Public School No. 115 (Merryman Ave. near Greenmount Ave., Wm. H. Proctor, teacher-in-charge) gave a Christmas program on Friday, December 19, 1924, at Antioch Baptist Church, 35th Street and Old York Road, under the Parent-Teacher club. Proceeds went to complete a shoe fund recently begun. Mr. James Grandison, president of the club, worked with Mr. Proctor and the teachers on the concert.

The School Board secretary read a letter from James Grandison, president of the Parent-Teachers' Association of School 115, stating that the city had cut 32nd Street through from Barclay to Homestead, placing one of the portables of School 115 almost at the curb and requiring that building's removal. He wrote that the children could not attend School 113 at Federal and Carter streets because the distance was too great, and asked that the white School 52 at Oak and 24th Streets, then with only 180 pupils and 'in the colored neighborhood,' be turned over to colored children. The board referred the matter to the Board of Superintendents.

Under 'School 115, Merryman's Lane, J. W. Woodhous, principal,' the Afro-American gave enrollment to date as 301. Under the direction of Mrs. Johns, Miss Wicks and Mr. Wilson, morning programs had resumed, each class taking charge of the opening exercises with Bible readings, recitations, dramatizations and songs.

A front-page Afro-American story said Baltimore was paying tribute to George W. Biddle, 'oldest public school-teacher,' retired on pension the previous week by the School Board after his years of service, 37 of them in the city schools. Born in South Baltimore 72 years earlier and privately schooled, he was given his first school in Carroll County at 20, then transferred to Kent County, 'and later to Baltimore County and Waverly. He became a part of the City System when Waverly was incorporated with Baltimore.' He was the first colored principal in the city when School No. 9 on Carrollton avenue was turned over to colored people, taught in seven schools, and for the past 12 years was principal of the Argyle avenue school. School 118's faculty gave him a reception at the Community House and the Principals' Association presented a gold watch. He quoted Dr. J. H. N. Waring: 'Graduates of Mr. Biddle's school are the best prepared students who come to our high school,' and called Fannie Barbour the best teacher in the city and the first colored person to pass the city teachers' examination.

In an Afro-American list of people treated (the headline context was not captured), the entries include 'William Datcher, 17, 3205 Barclay; Samuel Brown, 17, 3211 Barclay; Hosey Dutcher, 15, 3205 Barclay.'

In a list of school staff appointments, the Sun reported that Milton E. Branch, of 813 North Calhoun street, was appointed teacher in charge of School No. 115 '(formerly School No. 113A).' The same list shows George Albert Wright, of 3232 Barclay street, appointed vice-principal in charge of School No. 126.

An Afro-American list of the city's colored schools and heads gives 'School 115, Merryman Lane, near York Road, Milton E. Branch, teacher-in-charge.' The same list names H. Milton Gross as principal of School 114-A and Robert A. Proctor as teacher in charge of School 127.

An Afro-American listing of the city's colored schools includes 'School No. 115, at Merryman's Lane near Greenmount Avenue.' An editor's note in the same list remarks that the directory gave no official name for School No. 122, commonly called the Samuel Coleridge Taylor School.
In the Afro-American's weekly death list, an entry reads 'Datcher, Pearl, 8, 3205 Barclay-st.'

Two late-1930s Sun classified 'situations wanted' ads came from 3205 Barclay st., the Datcher address: on 18 August 1937, 'CHAUFFEUR (colored) wishes position. 3205 Barclay st.'; and on 15 March 1939, 'GIRL (colored) wants work of any kind. 3205 Barclay st.'

Paid death notice: on November 29, 1938, George W. Biddle, the beloved brother of Grant E. Biddle, died at his late residence, 1326 North Calhoun street. Cumberland, New York and Washington papers were asked to copy. The funeral was set for Saturday at 2 P.M. from Sharp Street Methodist Episcopal Church, Dolphin and Etting streets.

The Afro-American's front-page obituary called George W. Biddle the first colored principal of a Baltimore public school and, until his retirement in 1926, the oldest teacher in the system. He was 84 and had been a teacher and public figure for fifty-two years; the board retired him in 1926 at 72. Educated in private schools, he first taught in Carroll County at 20, and also taught in Kent and Baltimore counties 'and in Waverly.' The paper wrote: 'It was while teaching at the Waverly school he became a part of the Baltimore system by the incorporation of that section as a part of the city.' When School No. 9 on Carrollton Avenue was turned over to colored people he became its principal, the first colored principal to head a school in the city; he taught in seven schools and spent his last twelve active years as principal of the Argyle Avenue School.

The Afro-American reported that Lewis Gwynn, principal of School No. 115, addressed the P.-T.A. of School 101 at its regular Tuesday meeting on 'Knowing Your Child.' Mrs. Bertha Lee sang a solo, and principal Elmer A. Henderson presided in the absence of Mrs. Nathaniel Peck.

Describing a $8.3 million school loan program to go before voters, the Sun said 'School No. 115, with five classrooms for 198 Negro pupils on Merrymans lane, near York road, is to be replaced with a six-room fireproof building costing $90,000.' The story noted that providing adequate facilities for Negro pupils was a particularly difficult problem.

Bettye Murphy's profile of Samuel Richard Owings, principal of Robert Brown Elliott School No. 104 at Carey and School streets, says the Owings family moved to Waverly after his third year of school and that he completed his elementary training at School No. 115, Merryman's Lane, where John W. Woodhous was principal. From 1912 he worked for Dr. Howard Kelly, white, to help his widowed mother; he graduated from high school in 1916 and the teachers' training school in 1919, earned a B.S. from Columbia in 1933, and succeeded Mrs. Rodman as principal. He was superintendent of the Grace Presbyterian Sunday School and a member of the NAACP.
In a list of salaries set for colored school staff, the Afro-American reported that Henry N. West, teacher in charge of the Merryman Lane School No. 115, would receive $1,900.

In the list of registration places for the February 1942 wartime draft registration, Local Board No. 8 (Guilford Avenue and 28th Street) included 'School No. 115, Thirty-second and Barclay streets,' along with Schools 52 and 53.

The Sun announced shoe-exchange 'swap-shops' at three places, including Public School No. 115, a Negro school at Brentwood avenue and Merryman's lane. Shoes in poor condition, or that had been worn by children with ringworm, and correctional shoes, would not be accepted for exchange.

A Sun survey of 53 of the city's 105 portable schoolrooms found three schools entirely portable and used for Negro children, one standing since 'at least 1909' per its principal. Public School No. 115, Negro elementary school at Merryman's lane near Greenmount ave., consisted of three buildings with six classrooms, only four used, for 214 students. Mrs. Florence Gloster, Negro principal, pointed out improper lighting, lack of sufficient exits and ventilation, and need for painting, said 'These are permanent buildings' with no plans for reconstruction as far as she knew, and explained that windows in one room were boarded up 'as a safeguard against air raids.'

The Afro-American's rundown of portable colored schools reported: 'School No. 115, Merrymans Lane near York Road, Mrs. Florence G. Gloster, principal. Four portable classrooms used by 214 children; floors worn, paint dulled; lights could be improved; buildings run down from age; coal stoves in use; toilets and drinking water installed in separate unit.'

A front-page Afro-American list of open houses at colored schools scheduled Thursday-night open house at School No. 115, Merryman's Lane near York Rd., along with School No. 131 on Druid Hill Ave. and School No. 152.

The Evening Sun reported that of 44 school buildings Dr. Strayer's survey of a quarter century earlier had advised abandoning, 21 still stood in use, and eight he had recommended for immediate abandonment, using terms like 'fire trap,' 'dungeon-like' and 'not fit for housing schoolchildren,' were still being used. School No. 115, Merrymans lane, is one of the eight listed, alongside the Alicia Crossland School, Lafayette School, Wendell Phillips School and Schools 123, 124 and 128. A table on the same page lists 'No. 115, Merrymans' among buildings rated unsatisfactory.

In an Afro-American survey of how Black riders were treated on city transit, a principal of School No. 115 on Merryman's Lane, Mrs. Susie Cordery of 2415 McCulloh St., said she had to take a taxi to get to work on time because of crowds on the No. 8 car, and was often among the 'standing army' passed by half-empty cars on her way home.

In the Afro-American's marriage license column, entries include 'BROWN-ATKINS, Clinton P., 28, 3211 Barclay St.; Willie M., 28' and 'NERO-DATCHER, Symiel, 64, widower; Dora A. L., widow, 573 Laurens St.' Another entry lists 'TURNER-FAIDLEY, Joseph C., 18, 2448 Brentwood Ave.; Alma R., 17.'

A photo caption says models of animals made of wire and papier mache by pupils of the Opportunity Class of School No. 115 on Merryman's Lane near York Rd. were placed on display in the office of the Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals. Sidney Collins, a member of the class, is shown with a 'tiger.' Mrs. Susie Cordery was principal.
Reporting School Board appointments, the Afro-American said that among teachers-in-charge named at the session were Delmas Milbourne to School No. 115 and Wilfred Seaborne to School No. 154.

The Afro-American's fall enrollment roundup reported: 'School 115, Merryman's Lane near York Rd. Enrollment, 120, some 30 more pupils yet to enroll. Bellman Milbourne has been made teacher-in-charge.' In the same roundup Mrs. Anna Datcher is listed among new teachers at School No. 122, Preston St. near Pennsylvania Ave.

In a numbered list of school construction projects proposed for a city loan, item 9 is 'Replacement for School 115 (Merryman's lane near York road), $560,000.' Other items include a Northwest Baltimore colored junior high and replacements for the Stowe School (118) and Tubman School (114).

Reporting on a new school-plant directory rating 191 schools and annexes (63 satisfactory, 43 unsatisfactory, the rest fair), the Sun printed the list of schools in the lowest category, rated obsolete or on inadequate sites and lacking every facility, 'with their locations and the dates of their construction.' The list includes 'School No. 115, Merryman's Lane near York road, 1889.'
In a schedule of community speakers, the Sun listed for March 20 Miss Irene Olson of the State Department of Public Welfare at School No. 115, York road and Merryman lane, at 2 P.M.

Parents at overcrowded School No. 144 (Mosher st. and Wheeler ave., over 900 pupils in space for 320) objected to a plan by assistant superintendent Houston Jackson to bus about 200 intermediate pupils to School No. 115 and School No. 155. The Afro said a survey of colored schools found three vacant rooms at School No. 115 and two at No. 155. Parents objected that the schools were too far away (No. 115 'is on Merryman's Lane near York Road'), that busing was risky, that families would be split, and that 'the two schools in question are portable buildings.'

In an item on boys who won a theatre contest drawing, the Afro-American identified Kenneth Parnell, 11, as the son of Mr. and Mrs. Herbert Parnell of 3228 Barclay st. and a pupil at School 115; he had filed his contest coupon at the theatre the previous Sunday.
In the city's list of polling places for the 1954 primary, the 21st precinct (apparently of the 12th Ward) votes at 'School No. 115, Merryman's Lane & 32nd St.'

Lula Jones Garrett's guide to Baltimore's first integrated school year said all city schools were now open to all pupils, but listed School No. 115, Merryman's Lane nr. York Rd., among 'Districted Schools,' where crowding meant boundary lines were set over which pupils might not cross. Under 'Waverly Open To All' the same guide listed Waverly School No. 51 at 34th and Frisby Sts., the formerly white Waverly school.

Opening a series on Baltimore schools, Gwinn Owens wrote that in 1921 Dr. George D. Strayer of Columbia's Teachers College urged eight buildings abandoned immediately, and that 33 years later four were still in use, including 'No. 115, Elementary School, Merryman's lane near Greenmount avenue, where "temporary" buildings have been in use for 35 years, and where the children cross an open yard to use the toilets.' A photograph captioned 'Twice Berated, But Still Used' shows the frame School No. 115, which Strayer had called 'not fit for the housing of school children' and a 1951 Board of Education survey called 'unsatisfactory' and 'obsolete'; the caption says two additional buildings behind it, built for 'temporary' use 35 years earlier, were still in use.

In the Evening Sun's 'Baltimore Schools' series, a photograph is captioned: 'Across the yard to the washrooms. These portables on the left were built "temporarily" 35 years ago for School No. 115 on Merryman's lane. The small building on the right now houses the toilets and washrooms. Children must cross the yard to get to them.' The accompanying article notes that with the end of segregation many of the oldest and most outmoded schools were in Negro districts, and quotes superintendent Dr. John H. Fischer and building director William E. Lehr on the building program.

The Sun reported that the first open parking lot to be financed partly with city funds, and the first under the city's off-street parking program designed to serve a neighborhood rather than downtown, got final approval from the Off-Street Parking Commission. 'It will be located in the 3200 block of Barclay street, in the west part of the Waverly business section.' The city agency agreed to loan $70,000 toward the purchase of eleven tracts of land and for clearing, grading and surfacing them, under a contract between the city and the Waverly Merchants Parking Lot, Inc., which was furnishing 40 per cent of the cost; the Board of Estimates still had to approve.

In a roundup of Off-Street Parking Commission actions, the Evening Sun reported that 'a request for condemnation of four houses in the 3200 block Barclay street, to complete the land needed for a parking lot for Waverly merchants, was rejected today on the ground that all the property owners had not been offered high enough prices without condemnation.' The commission indicated that if the Waverly Merchants Parking Lot, Inc., offered more money and still could not obtain the properties, the decision could be reconsidered.

In an Afro-American item about a contest prize winner, Mrs. Hugo Oliver Taliaferro of 2648 Bloom St. was described as the mother of three boys: Leslie, 14, a Clifton Junior High student, and Delano, 12, and Oliver, 8, 'both of whom attend School No. 115.' Her husband was a trades helper at Bendix Radio Corporation.
A Sun television listing for the school-hours program 'It's an Original' gave the topic 'Gift Wrappings' and the teacher as 'Mary Bowman, of School No. 115.'

The School Board heard a delegation headed by Solomon Liss, city councilman from the Fourth district, asking to be allowed to buy the building and acquire the land of School No. 115, on Merryman lane near Greenmount avenue. Liss, representing the Waverly Business Men's Association and the Waverly Improvement Association, said the property was wanted to provide parking in a business area, called the school 'an eyesore and a disgrace,' noted it had been called unfit for use as long ago as 1921, and called it 'one of the poorest pieces of property in the system.' Board president Curlett agreed the building 'should not be used' but cited the problem of preventing split school shifts, and said the proposal to sell would be given serious consideration.

Donald Bremner reported that, in the second use of its condemnation power, the Off-Street Parking Commission ordered court action to acquire property for a 126-car parking lot in the western part of the Waverly business district, 'to be built in the 3200 block Barclay street.' The project, approved in January 1956 as the first city-financed open lot and the first to serve a neighborhood district, hit a snag when owners of four of the nine needed properties refused to sell. The City Council passed a condemnation ordinance in October; two owners later accepted the price, 'but two held out. They were "very hostile" and declared they would not sell to the city.'

The Afro-American's back-to-school story listed old schools still in service, including 'No. 115 on 32nd St. near Greenmount Ave.; a frame building that was blasted several years ago by City Councilman Sol Liss as "a disgrace and unfit for habitation by children."' A photograph captioned 'Still In Use' shows 'Elementary School No. 115 at 32nd St. near Greenmount Ave. Built as a temporary structure after World War One, the building is still in use.' The photo shows a two-story frame building behind two one-story frame classroom buildings with chimneys, behind a chain-link fence on a corner.

A legal notice dated October 18, 1957, invited sealed bids to the Board of Estimates for 'construction of a parking lot for the Waverly Merchants Parking Lot, Inc., 3212 Greenmount Avenue,' due November 6, 1957. The notice was signed for Waverly Merchants Parking Lot, Inc., by David S. Hyman, Engineer.

Lula Jones Garrett's column described a surprise party at the Morgan Park home of Mr. and Mrs. Clarence Roberts, hosted by the art department of School No. 181, honoring Ruth Taylor Johnson on her retirement after 37 consecutive years in the Baltimore schools. Johnson recalled her first assignment in 1920 'under Principal John Woodhous at School No. 115 in Waverly,' then eleven years as supervisor of art in elementary schools, and later teaching at Schools 112, 106, Dunbar, 137 and 181. Her sister, Alma Thomas, drove her to the party.

In an Afro-American report of School Board appointments for the term February 1 to June 30, 1958, 'Mrs. Katherine Crabbs was appointed teacher-in-charge of the Shop Center School No. 115, with an increase in basic salary of $370.'

In the Afro-American's list of School Board appointments for the 1958-59 year, 'Miss Katherine Crabbs was named teacher in charge of School No. 115.' The same item names demonstration teachers and other assignments.

A legal notice dated June 5, 1959, invited sealed proposals to the Board of Estimates for 'the construction of Venable Junior High School, Thirty-fourth and Frisby Streets,' with bids due June 24, 1959.
In a list of school administrative appointments effective September 1, 1959, the Sun named 'Katherine Crabbs at Junior High School No. 115' among new vice-principals.

In a front-page Afro-American story on the sudden death of a Mr. Carter (called 'Jimmy' by intimates), the survivors listed include his mother, Mrs. Susan Slowe Carter, 99, of 817 N. Wolfe St., and 'Mrs. Susie Cordery, who retired as vice principal of School 116 last year.'
Reporting the school building program, the Sun said plans called for completion in June 1960 of the $441,600 Venable Junior High School at Thirty-fourth and Frisby streets.
An Afro-American calendar listing for June 9, 1960, included an event at 'Venable Junior High School No. 115, at the school, 32nd St., near Greenmount Ave., 1 p.m.'

The Sun reported that three new schools would open the next day to ease enrollment pressure: the Hayes Elementary School at Monument street and Central avenue, the Venable Junior High School at Frisby and Thirty-fourth streets, and the Patterson Senior High School at 100 North Kane street.

The Afro-American reported that pupils of Venable Junior High School had moved in September into a new two-story brick building at 34th and Frisby Sts., built for $441,600 for 260 pupils. 'This beautiful new building replaces three old frame buildings which were located on 32nd St.,' the paper said, adding that the school was then 'a girls opportunity school.' Principal Katherine Crabbs said: 'There is a contrast entirely in buildings, but our program was just as fine in the old building. We were inadequately housed there, but the philosophy and spirit is the same in either building.' A photo caption says the new structure 'replaces frame huts.'

After a contested hearing before the Board of Municipal and Zoning Appeals, the Donnelly Sign Company withdrew its application to erect two illuminated billboards at 3201 Barclay St. Homeowners led by Mr. and Mrs. Edgar Somerville of 3220 Barclay St. argued the signs would depreciate their old residential area 'known as Govans.' Atty. Juanita Jackson Mitchell told the board 'that the site had been residential until five years ago when the City Council, over the strong protest of the residents, condemned the dwellings on the east side of the 3200 block Barclay St. to create an off street parking lot for the Waverly Merchants Association,' and asked councilmen to honor promises of no further commercialization. Rae E. Payne of 3026 Barclay St., in his home 55 years, protested for himself and for the Mt. Zion Baptist Church, at 32nd St. and Barclay, of which he was trustee; William Wells of 3226 Barclay St., owner of the Wells Printing Company, also objected, and the North Baltimore Protective Association, with counsel James H. Brown Jr., joined the residents. Councilmen Peter Angelos and Henry Hergenroeder appeared in support of the homeowners.
A front-page Afro-American photo row of new principal appointments shows 'Miss Betty Williams, To Eastern High,' alongside Dr. Joel Carrington, to New Walbrook High.

Isaac Rehert's Sun profile of Betty Williams, then administrative assistant to the Region 5 superintendent, said that in February 1970, after 126 years of its existence, she became Eastern High School's first black principal, after serving as vice-principal at Northwestern High. 'She had grown up in Waverly, only a few blocks away from Eastern, where she was known affectionately in the neighborhood as Miss Betty.' She had spent 16 years in the system, rising from substitute first-grade teacher to department head, special assistant and vice-principal; she recalled that 'they wanted a woman and they had to have somebody who was black,' and described restoring order after unrest at the all-girl school. She kept on her desk a plaque with a poem by Lucille Clifton.

Larry Perl reported that Mayor Stephanie Rawlings-Blake and schools CEO Andres Alonso broke ground on Tuesday, June 5, 2012, at Ellerslie Avenue and East 33rd Street for a $25 million replacement for Waverly Elementary/Middle School, due to open in 2014. The article notes the Waverly school had survived aging buildings, lack of resources and racial segregation, and that 'at one time, the old School No. 115 was ranked as the worst "colored school" in the city,' according to Joan Stanne, a local historian and community and school volunteer. Former Waverly principal Lou Franz, 86, who retired in 1989, attended.

Danae King reported on the opening of Schoolhouse Garden, attended by about 50 people on Monday night (July 7, 2014), which the Sun said 'now commemorates the space where Williams' school used to be, at Brentwood Avenue and Merryman Lane.' Betty Williams, 90, who attended grades one through six at Colored School 115 from 1929 to 1935 and retired in 1982 as principal of Eastern High School, recalled running through a lane between two of the school's buildings that children thought was haunted. Historian JoAnn Robinson, retired from Morgan State, said the school, built in 1888, was declared unfit in the 1920s but stayed in use because of 'the feeling that black children weren't deserving of anything better'; it was torn down in the 1950s after Brown v. Board. Waverly Main Street director Jermaine Johnson called the garden an 'homage,' Councilwoman Mary Pat Clarke spoke, and Civic Works COO Earl Millett said owners of surrounding buildings had begun fixing them up; the lot had been rubble- and trash-filled, and the work was funded by the community, alumni and a state grant.

A Sun community calendar item noted the deadline to reserve a bus seat for the fourth annual Charm City Farm and Garden Tour on Aug. 16, 2014, 'highlighting community gardens, including Schoolhouse Garden in Waverly.'

A Sun calendar item announced that Waverly Main Street was sponsoring a Garden Party fundraiser 'at the new Schoolhouse Garden, 427 1/2 Merryman Lane,' at 6 p.m. on Saturday, billed as a farewell to summer with food and a bar, $10 per person.

A 30 October 2012 appeal posted in the Waverly Improvement Association Facebook group by Doug Mowbray says a partnership of Waverly Main Street, Civic Works and the CAN artists' Collective was turning the vacant lot at Merryman Lane and Brentwood Avenue into the School House Garden. More than 100 volunteers had put in 300 hours removing 25 tons of rubble. About $30,000 was needed for landscaping and artwork; Parks and People Foundation grants provided seed money and Waverly Main Street was receiving $20,000 in State Community Legacy funds. Current and former residents of the historic African American blocks whose relatives attended Public School 115 had begun collecting donations; checks went to Waverly Main Street, Inc., 3124 Greenmount Avenue.

Delegate Regina T. Boyce (43rd District) posted thanks to Phi Beta Sigma Fraternity, located on Waverly Main Street, for cleaning 'our precious School House Garden'. She described it as on the lot at E. 32nd Street, Brentwood Avenue and Merryman Lane, in memory of Colored School #115 (1888-1950s), which served African American children in grades 1-6 from the immediate area. Photos show volunteers bagging weeds on an overgrown lot.

No source found places any relative of Thurgood Marshall on Brentwood Avenue, Talbot Street or Barclay Street, or names a Marshall concrete contractor in Waverly. Find a Grave lists the justice's paternal grandparents Thorney Good Marshall (1849-1915) and Annie E. Robinson Marshall (1858-1948) and uncles and aunts Mary E., William Canfield (his father), Thoroughgood G. (a Pullman porter waiter, 1886-1952), Anna Belle Burns, Cyrus Wesley Sr. (1891-1961), Thomas Roy Sr. (1894-1949) and Margaret B. Tucker, all born in Baltimore; none of the memorials gives an occupation in concrete or a Waverly address. The documented Marshall household was in West Baltimore at 1632 Division Street (uncle Fearless Williams's house). The MSA colored business directories show concrete and cement contractors (e.g., Stoker Stanley, C. T. Parker) but no Marshall contractor in the excerpts seen.

The Maryland State Board of Education's 17th annual report lists Baltimore County colored schools for the year ending June 30, 1883. The teacher list includes 'Geo. W. Biddle' and 'Roberta B. Sheridan'. Aligning the school and district columns puts Biddle at Colored School No. 3, District 9 (the district that contained Waverly) and Sheridan at School No. 2, District 1. The report does not name the school's location, so it does not prove that Biddle's school was the Waverly one.

The state reports for 1874-1888 give Baltimore County colored schools only by number and district, never by place name. For 1885 the District 9 colored schools were taught by Jno. H. Camper (School 1) and Carrie L. Cooke (School 2), and Biddle no longer appears. 'Waverly' turns up in these reports only for the white Waverly High School (School 12, District 9).

The 1880 state report says the summer class for colored teachers was conducted by 'Jos. S. Whittington, Principal of the Waverly High School' at the Howard Normal School in Baltimore each July. In 1903 the same Jos. S. Whittington was the group principal over School No. 115 (see the 1903 Polk entry).

After the 1888 annexation, the Board of School Commissioners listed the county school properties the city bought. Item 9 reads: 'School house and lot, on Merryman's lane, at Waverly, subject to a ground rent of $50 per annum', bought for $750. The white Waverly school was a separate purchase, 'School house and lot in fee, at Waverly', for $14,000.

The superintendent's 1888 report lists crowded annexed-district schools. It says: 'Annex Colored School No. 1. The building occupied by this school contains only two rooms occupied by three teachers with their classes.'

The 1889 Inspector of Buildings report lists 'Annex Colored School No. 1, Merryman's Lane. Roof painted and closets repaired.' The same list has 'Annex School No. 5, Merryman's Lane', a white annex school.
The school board's 1889 report says: 'Annex Colored School No. 1 has two class-rooms and three teachers.' This 'necessitates the use of one room by two teachers.'
The public-schools appendix of R.L. Polk's 1890 Baltimore directory lists the annex schools. One entry reads 'No 1 (colored) Merryman's la nr York rd, Waverly, Annie O Waters.'

The school board's 1890 report says that 'during the fall, portions of houses were rented for branches of Annex No. 2 and Annex Colored No. 1, both at Waverly'. The 1890 rent list shows 'Annex Colored No. 1, Merryman's lane and York road', at $108 a year.

The board's 1891 report has a heading 'Colored Schools No. 8 and Annex Colored School at Waverly'. It says both schools are crowded and several classes of each are in rented rooms. It adds that 'a large number of colored children in that part of the city' attend no public school, and it repeats a request for a new building between the two schools.
The annex-schools list in Polk's 1891 directory reads 'No 1 (colored) Merryman's la nr York rd, Waverly, Etta M Hyatt, 731 Gorsuch av.' The 1892 directory repeats 'Etta M Hyatt'.

Ordinance No. 73, approved May 4, 1892, told the Mayor, Comptroller and school board president to buy a lot 'somewhere between Colored School No. 8, corner of Bond and Chew streets, and Annex Colored School No. 1, Waverly'. It appropriated $10,000 for the lot and $20,000 for a building, to be called Colored Primary School No. 10. The new school was finished in 1895 at Girard Avenue and Sherman Place.

The board's 1892 report says 'Annex Colored School No. 1 occupies two buildings, each furnishing insufficient and unsatisfactory accommodation.' It hoped a new building authorized for the northeast would relieve the problem.

The board's 1893 report says 'the rented rooms used by Annex Colored School No. 1 were relinquished'. New rooms were 'secured in the church on Merryman's lane, near the York road', and the change took place early in October 1893. The 1893 rent list shows 'Annex Colored No. 1, Merryman's lane' at $120 a year.

The 1895 school report says 'Annex Colored School No. 1 occupies two buildings, one rented, neither well suited for school purposes, on Merryman's lane'. The 1896 report repeats this, adds 'Waverly', and says the school 'is in need of suitable accommodations.'

The city's 1897 list of school employees, under 'Annex Colored School No. 1', names Heber E. Wharton of 2019 Division street as colored principal at $900 a year. The assistants were Frances L. Murphy (First Grade, $504), Sarah K. Jackson (Second and Third Grade, $432) and Sallie B. Hatchett (First and Second Grade, $432). Jane Lewis was janitress at $156 a year plus $20.75 for fires.

From 1897 the board's rent lists show 'Annex Colored No. 1, Barclay street, near Merryman's lane', at $120 a year. The ground rent of $50 on the city-owned lot is listed separately as 'Annex School, Colored, No. 1, ground rent'.

The 1898 report says the school 'occupies two small buildings a short distance apart, neither of which is suitable'. It says the school needs better facilities. In 1899 the board wrote that 'it is necessary to erect a house for the use of the school.'

The city's 1900 rent list contains 'School No. 115, Barclay street, near Merryman's lane', the rented branch formerly listed under Annex Colored No. 1. The 1900 Inspector of Buildings report still calls the main building 'No. 1 Colored Annex School, Merryman's Lane and York Road'. It calls it 'an old frame building' with defective floors and 'only one' water closet 'for the entire school'.

The 1901 Inspector of Buildings report, under 'No. 115 School, Merryman's Lane, near York Road', says 'the digging of a well has added much to the bettered conditions at this school.' The school was whitewashed, and painting and general repairs were planned for the next year.
Polk's 1901 public-schools list reads 'Colored School No 115, Merryman la nr [York rd], Heber Wharton, vice-prin.'

Sanborn's 1902 Baltimore volume 3, sheet 348, shows a single 1-story building labelled 'ANNEX COLORED SCHOOL. HEAT STOVE. NO LIGHTS.' It stands mid-block just south of Merryman Av., behind the house lots on the east side of Barclay St. with a 10-foot alley between, and west of Talbot St. Two small outbuildings stand behind it, and two 2-story dwellings at 12-14 Merryman Av. stand to the east. Further south, on the west side of Talbot St., the sheet shows 'MT ZION BAPT. CHURCH. HEAT STOVE. LIGHTS KEROSENE. 12' TO EAVES.'

The 1903 Inspector of Buildings report lists, among new additions, 'School No. 115, Merryman's lane, 2' classrooms. It describes it as 'a two-story frame addition, more or less temporary in character' that 'will be heated by stoves'. The cost table shows 'No. 115 new addition 1,063 60'. The board's 1909 ten-year review repeats 'School No. 115, Merryman's lane, addition 2 classrooms 1903'.

Polk's 1903 school list groups 'Schools Nos 54, 51, 53, 50, 52, 115' as Group K, with 'Jos S Whittington, Prin'. The entry reads 'Colored School No 115, Merryman la nr York rd, Branch Barclay nr Merryman's la, Heber E Wharton, vice-prin.' The next page lists 'Colored School No 103, Stricker c Mulberry ... Geo W Biddle, vice-prin.'
Polk's school lists for 1904, 1905, 1906, 1907, 1908 and 1909 read 'Colored School No 115, Merryman la nr York rd, Branch Barclay nr Merryman's la, Howard E Young, vice-prin.'
The Evening Schools report dated Dec. 31, 1907 says three night schools opened that year. One was 'the third at Waverly (No. 115) employing three teachers.'

The 80th annual report (1908) says a lot behind School No. 115 was rented in July. It 'binds on the west side of Talbot Street 75 feet' and is 60 feet deep, at $75 a year. 'The old dwelling corner Barclay Street and Merryman's Lane, rented as an annex to School No. 115, was vacated in November', saving $120 a year. Twelve portable buildings went up in summer 1908, including 'School No. 115 - Two portables.'
The 81st annual report (1909) lists buildings with classroom stoves to be removed. It gives 'No. 115' with 8 stoves.

Polk's 1912 school list reads, in garbled OCR, 'Colored School No [115], Merryman la nr York rd. Branch Barclay nr Merryman la. John W Woodhouse, head asst.' The 1912 alphabetical list has '*Woodhouse John W, tchr, h 537 Presstman.'

The 1914 Directory of the Public Schools of Baltimore lists School No. 115, 'Merryman's Lane near York Road', with 'Teachers, 6; Pupils, 216.' The staff were John W. Woodhouse, Principal (7th & 8th), Pattie H. Eubanks (3rd), Camilla H. Gwathney (2nd), Martha E. Henson (4th), Tiola Jones (1st) and William H. Proctor (5th & 6th).

The 1914 directory's 'Location of Schools' gives 'No. 115 - Merryman's Lane, near York Road', reached by 'York Road car to Merryman's Lane, one square west.' It also lists 'No. 115 Branch - Barclay Street, near Merryman's Lane.'

The Health Department's 1914 report on medical examination of schools has a table, 'Review of Defectives in Colored School No. 115, by Dr. A. K. Bond and Miss V. B. Lorentz'. It lists small numbers of eye, scalp (pediculosis), adenoid and tonsil defects found and cured.

Sanborn's 1915 Baltimore volume 7, sheet 717, shows 'PUBLIC SCHOOL No. 115 (NEGRO) HEAT: STOVES NO LIGHT.' It is a long frame building, 1-story at the north and 2-story at the south with a stair, plus two 1-story frame buildings (the 1908 portables) and a small outbuilding. The lot runs south from Merryman Av., between a 10-foot alley behind the Barclay St. houses (3201-3223 Barclay) and Talbott St. on the east. Further south on the west side of Talbott, the sheet shows 'MT. ZION BAPTIST CHURCH (NEGRO) HEAT: STOVES, LIGHT: GAS. 10' TO EAVES', 1-story, with dwellings at 3106-3114 Talbott below it.

Polk's school lists give: 1917 and 1918, 'Colored School No 115 - Merryman's la nr York rd, John W Woodhouse, prin'. 1920, 'H Milton Gross, Principal'. 1922, 'Henry W Ebb, Principal'. 1923, 'No 115 Merryman's Lane nr Greenmount av, Harry T Pratt, Principal.'

The 1921 Strayer survey's recommendations for School No. 115 give a 'School building score, 94' on the Strayer-Engelhardt score card, among the lowest in the city. The school had 2 classrooms in portables. The survey estimated the district's population would grow about 35% and was 'about 95% white voters 1920', with 9% of census children colored. It recommended 'A new building on a new site located nearer the population served.'

Table LX, 'Suggested chronological order of replacement of inadequate elementary schools for colored children', puts No. 115 first in Group I of the 'Immediate replacement program'. On p. 37, No. 115 is among the colored schools ranking lowest on toilets, lighting, fire protection, water supply, heating and structure. Most of those schools 'rank lower than the lowest thirty' of the white elementary schools. Table LVIII (p. 308) lists 'School 115 (94)' among replacements.

Strayer Table XI gives School No. 115 a total enrollment in June 1920 of 283. It had 2,843 square feet of playground, 10.0 square feet per pupil. Table XVII says 77 of its children were housed in portables.

Drawings in the city school-plant microfilm show 'Plumbing Apparatus, School No. 115, Merrymans Lane Near York Road', Commission No. 566, dated Sept. 6, 1921 and revised Oct. 5, 1921. They were prepared by James Posey, consulting engineer, 11 E. Pleasant St. The plot plan shows a new girls' and boys' toilet building, the 'present toilets', 'portable bldg' units, the main building on Merryman's Lane, an alley, and Talbot Street.

The 1924-25 directory lists No. 115, Merryman's Lane near York Road, with Principal John W. Woodhouse of 537 Presstman St. ('also in charge of School No. 113'), 'Teachers, 9; Pupils, 353', grades I to VI. In 1925-26 it had 9 teachers and 307 pupils, grades I to VI. The 1925 directions read 'Greenmount Avenue and Thirty-first Street, half block west, one block north', or 'Greenmount to Merryman Avenue, half block west.'

The 1926-27 directory lists 'No. 113-A - Formerly School No. 115, Merryman's Lane, near York Road'. Principal John W. Woodhouse and teacher-in-charge Hammond J. Briscoe had 7 teachers and 288 pupils, grades I to VI. It stayed 113-A (annex of Banneker School No. 113) through 1930-31, with teachers-in-charge John W. Grinage (1927: 7 teachers, 304 pupils) and George E. Simms (1928: 6/306; 1929: 6/310; 1930: 7/310).

From 1931-32 the directory again lists 'No. 115, Merryman's Lane, near York Road' with a teacher-in-charge. Milton E. Branch had 5 teachers and 271 pupils in 1931 and 5/254 in 1932. Charles W. Harris had 5/272 in 1933, 5/257 in 1934, 6/251 in 1935 and 5/237 in 1936. Lewis M. Gwynn had 5/226 in 1937 and 5/198 in 1938. Grades were I-VI or I-V.

In 1939-40 and 1940-41, Acting Vice-Principal Edward L. Murray of 2303 Druid Hill Ave. had 5 teachers and 207 pupils, then 6 and 266. Henry N. West was teacher in charge in 1941-42 (6/270). Florence G. Gloster was in charge in 1942-43 (6/266) and 1943-44 (3/190), grades I to VI.

Susie C. (once 'M.') Cordery of 2415 McCulloh St. was teacher in charge from 1944-45 through 1950-51. In 1944 there were 3 elementary teachers with 153 pupils plus 1 special-education teacher with 21, for a total of 4 and 174. Totals were 4/172 in 1945, 4/156 in 1946, 4/168 in 1948, 4/147 in 1949 and 4/160 in 1950. From 1948 the entry lists grades I to VI and an 'Opportunity Class', with telephone Chesapeake 9410.

Delmas Milbourne of 2610 W. Lafayette Ave. was teacher in charge in 1951-52 (3 teachers, 122 pupils), 1952-53 (3/115) and 1953-54 (3/123), grades I to VI. The address was still 'Merryman's Lane, near York Road (18)'.

A Department of Education plat titled 'School No. 115, Physical Quantities', dated 5/29/37 (file 14-2-7, drawing PS 32), measures the main building at 2,005 sq ft and the auxiliary at 2,755 sq ft. It lists 1,923 sq ft of concrete and 3,006 sq ft of cinders as hard play surface. The deed lot 'A' fronts 42 ft 8 in on Merryman's Lane, 120 ft east of Barclay beyond a 10-ft alley. The ground to the south toward 32nd St. and Brentwood is labelled 'Occupied by school No. 115 not shown on deed plat' (about 92 ft 6 in by 65 ft).

In the No. 115 drawings is a plat dated April 2, 1931 (drawing 423, file 6-3-7). It shows the triangular block bounded by 33rd St., Merrymans Lane and Brentwood Avenue, with lot dimensions and notes on the widening of the northeast side of Merrymans Lane. Its purpose is not stated on the sheet.

Table 15 of the board's 119th report lists 'Future Projects for Which Loan Funds Will be Required (Construction Priority Not Determined to Date)'. One is 'Replacement for No. 115, Merryman's Lane', estimated at $560,000.

The 1928 Sanborn volume 6, corrected to May 1951, sheet 654, shows 'PUBLIC SCHOOL No 115' mid-block between E. 32nd St. (south) and Merryman Av. (north-east). A 10-ft alley lies behind the houses at 3201-3227 Barclay St. on the west, and the Brentwood Av. line on the east. It has a long main building, 1-story at the north end and 2-story (24 ft) at the south, a small 2-story stair element, a W.C., a rear dwelling 'R. 417 Merryman', and two 1-story (12 ft) buildings near 32nd St. marked 'CHEM. EXTGRS'. The original 1928 printing labels the same buildings 'SCHOOL No. 113A, HEAT: STEAM, LIGHTS: ELECTRIC'.

A page from the city's School Plant Directory (dated July '52) for 'No. 115, Elementary School, Merryman's La., near York Rd.' gives Date of Constr. 1889, Material Frame, Rating in the 1951 School Facilities Survey 'Unsatisfactory', and Defects 'Obsolete.' It lists 4 classrooms and no auditorium, gym, cafeteria, library, shop or laboratory. The site was 0.23 acre (10,197 sq ft): building 4,706, floor space 6,578, play space 4,429. Its three photos are captioned 'Main structure, on Merryman's Lane', 'Two portables on 32nd Street', and 'East and south faces of buildings, at Brentwood and 32nd Street respectively.'

From 1954-55 the directory gives the address as '32nd St. near Greenmount Ave. (18)', no longer Merryman's Lane. Wilfred Seaborne of 2604 Longwood St. was teacher in charge in 1954 (4 teachers, 124 pupils) and 1955 (3/99), grades I to VI. In 1956-57 Vernon Press of 2403 Mosher St. was teacher in charge, and no counts are given.

In 1957-58, No. 115 at 32nd Street near Greenmount Avenue is a 'Shop Center' with Mrs. Katherine Crabbs of 10 Wade Ave. as teacher in charge. In 1958-59 it is 'No. 115 - Junior High ... Special Curriculum Only'. In 1959-60 it is 'No. 115 - Venable Junior High, 32nd Street near Greenmount Avenue', with Crabbs as Vice-Principal-in-Charge. The elementary school is no longer listed at the site.

The board's 123rd report says planning committees worked on '115 Junior High (Venable)'. Table 71, 'Buildings in the Planning Stage June 30, 1958', lists '115 Venable Junior High School (7.312D-5), 34th and Frisby Streets, 7 classrooms, cafeteria'.

The 1961-62 directory lists 'No. 115 - Venable Junior High, Frisby and 34th Streets (18)', Special Curriculum Only, with Mrs. Katherine Crabbs as Vice-Principal-in-Charge. No school is listed at 32nd Street near Greenmount any longer.

Ordinance No. 502 (Council No. 885), approved Nov. 25, 1960 by Mayor J. Harold Grady, authorized the City Comptroller to sell the city's parcel at the northwest corner of 32nd Street and Brentwood Avenue. It fronts 63 ft 9 in on 32nd St. and runs 212 ft 11 in north along the 10-ft alley to the southwest side of Merryman Lane, then 42 ft 8 in along the Lane, then back to Brentwood. 'Said property being no longer needed for public use.'

Ordinances No. 664 and No. 665, approved June 14, 1974, condemned and opened, then condemned and closed, the 160-ft stretch of Brentwood Avenue from 32nd Street north to Merryman Lane. They follow plats 319-A-23 and 319-A-23A, filed March 13-14, 1974. This merged the former school parcel with the land east of it.

A Maryland State Archives exhibit page calls the site 'The Waverly School', or Annex School No. 1, on Merryman's Lane near York Road. It cites a 1945 Sanborn (MSA SC 1427-1328) showing the school on the block of Merryman's Lane, Greenmount Ave., 32nd St. and Brentwood Ave., and says the block is now a parking lot. It also claims 'Baltimore City expanded its borders in 1918, encompassing the land'.

The National Park Service's 2023 historic context 'Civil Rights in Baltimore, Maryland, 1831-1976' says that in 1888 Baltimore school officials appointed Roberta B. Sheridan to Annex Colored School No. 1 in Waverly, at Brentwood Avenue and Merryman Lane, one of the city's first Black public school teachers alongside Nannie B. Grooms and principal George W. Biddle. It says protests over the exclusion of Black teachers continued until Sheridan was hired in the fall of 1888. A footnote says the school was later known as Colored School 115, was torn down in the 1950s, and is remembered by Schoolhouse Garden, opened in 2014 by Waverly Main Street and Civic Works.

The Waverly Main Street Historic District nomination says School No. 115, part of the 'Colored District' of Baltimore, operated from 1889 until well into the 1950s, its classrooms wooden portables with unheated toilets, and that most children walked to it and remembered it fondly. It quotes alumna Dolores Parker that 'black teachers provided a quality of instruction that no white teacher could duplicate' and former teacher Betty Williams that 'authorities didn't really care if black children attended school or not.' Its source is 'Memories of "The Other" Waverly Public School on Merryman Lane and 32nd Street,' The Charles Villager, Winter 2007, p. 1.

Michelle Belco's 1977 Waverly history for the Commission for Historic and Architectural Preservation says the merchants' lot 'at the southeast corner of 32nd and Barclay, was the site for School Number 115 and 115A, which were the Waverly school for Negro children.' The two numbers match the main school and its Barclay Street branch recorded from 1903. The lot actually lies on the northeast side of that corner, and Mount Zion Baptist Church, which Belco places across the street, stood on the southeast side, so 'southeast' is probably a slip. Her separate line that 1903 school records list it as the Colored High and Training School is unlikely: that school was downtown.

A city-directory abstract in a 2021 environmental site report lists 3200 Brentwood Avenue as 'Public School 113 A' in 1930, 'School No 115' in 1942 and 'Shop Center PS No 118 A' in 1958. The 1930 listing matches the Sun's 1931 note that No. 115 had been run as No. 113A, an annex of the Banneker school, and the 1958 listing matches the Afro's 'Shop Center School No. 115'. The same abstract names households on Merryman Lane in 1920-42 (Bond, Childs, Braxton, Martin, Truehart, Bundy, Shakespere) without giving race.

In its school estimates report the Sun recorded that 'the charges against Annex colored school No. 1 at Waverly of disorderly conduct by the pupils and inefficiency in the teachers were unsustained.' It is the first record found of the school by its city name after annexation.

The Sun reported that 'Annex colored school No 1 was taught by colored teachers until it became necessary to take the teachers to No. 9,' and that the rules required all colored schools established after May 1889 to be staffed by colored teachers. It records why Biddle, Sheridan and Grooms left Waverly in 1889.

Arguing for a new colored school, the Sun reported that 'a large number of colored people live near the old northern boundary of the city, some of their children attending No. 8 and some attending Annex No. 1. A large portion of the children do not attend any school, because of the distance and inadequate accommodations of both schools named.'
Baltimore Beat's 2026 picks name Pete's Grille, 3130 Greenmount Ave, for breakfast sandwiches: 'the homiest diner spot in Baltimore', in Waverly near the farmers market.

The Sun's 'Colored Educator Dead' reported that Prof. Heber E. Wharton, principal of Group Y of the colored public schools and president of the Baltimore Educational Association, died about 9 p.m. on Monday 2 May 1910 at Provident Hospital after an appendicitis operation. He had been in the Baltimore schools about 15 years and for several summers lectured at the Institute for Colored Youth at Cheyney, Pa., helping train teachers for the South. He left a widow, Pauline, and four young children, Constantia, Hermione, Pauline and Heber E. Jr. The Afro-American ran a tribute, 'The Departure of Heber E. Wharton', the following Saturday.

An Afro-American front-page obituary of a Mr. Murray, a member of the Colored High School's first graduating class (1889), says Murray 'succeeded the late Heber E. Wharton as the principal of School 113, then Girard avenue.' This places Wharton, after his years at School 115, at the head of the Banneker school that later ran No. 115 as its annex (113-A).

Under 'Principal's Sister Dies at Parole, Md.', the Afro reported the death of Mrs. Mary E. Paxton, daughter of the late Rev. Americus Woodhouse, long a member of the Baltimore Conference of the A.M.E. Church, and sister of John W. Woodhouse. She died at a sister's home in Parole and was to be buried at Sparks, Md. Woodhouse was School 115's principal (and later head of No. 113 with 115 as its annex) from about 1911 to 1925.

Ruth Edith Taylor Johnson, a retired Baltimore art teacher, died on Sunday 21 August 1988 at Good Samaritan Hospital, aged 87. A Baltimore native, she earned her teaching certificate from Coppin Normal School in 1919 and later a bachelor's degree from Morgan. She began as an art teacher in the city schools in 1919, later supervised elementary art, and taught art at Dunbar Senior High before retiring in the early 1960s. Her husband, Baltimore physician Dr. Louis A. Johnson, died in 1965.

Delmas D. Milbourne, a retired Baltimore city school administrator, died on Thursday 25 June 1981 at the Veterans Administration Hospital, aged 73. A native of Deal Island, he moved to Baltimore with his family in 1912, graduated from Douglass High School, attended Coppin Normal School, earned a degree in education from Morgan State, and later a master's and doctoral study at New York University. He spent 45 years as a teacher and administrator, was principal of seven schools, and retired in 1975 as principal of Lexington Terrace Elementary School No. 19. He served three years in the Army in World War II as a staff sergeant and was a member of Grace United Presbyterian Church for 50 years.

Henry N. West, a retired city elementary school principal, died on 23 September 1982 at Good Samaritan Hospital, aged 67. Born in Baltimore and raised in Cumberland, he graduated from the normal school that became Coppin State and held a bachelor's degree from Morgan State and a master's from New York University. He taught for 10 years, then was a principal at city elementary schools for more than 30 years, retiring in 1978 as principal of Commodore John Rogers Elementary. His wife, the former Melissa Evelyn Nixon, died in 1971. In 1970 the Evening Sun listed 'Henry N. West ... school principal' on Verda Welcome's Fourth District ticket for the House of Delegates.

Samuel R. Owings Sr., a retired school principal, died on Friday 27 June 1986 at Old Court Convalescent Home, aged 88. A Baltimore native, he received a teaching certificate from Coppin in 1919 and bachelor's and master's degrees in education from Columbia. He began teaching in city elementary schools in 1920, became a vice principal six years later, led several schools, and retired in 1962 as principal of Charles Carroll of Carrollton School No. 139. He served Grace United Presbyterian Church for 45 years, including as an elder, trustee and Clerk of Session, and was elected a delegate to the Presbyterian general assembly in 1932. His first wife, the former Marie Stokes, died in 1954.

Agrada Deaver Diggs, a former schoolteacher active in civic affairs, died on Wednesday 10 December 1980 at a daughter's home, aged 76. A native of the Govans area, she graduated from what are now Dunbar High School and Coppin State College and as a young woman taught in elementary schools in Berryville, Va. For her last 20 years she held several offices in the Hoes Heights Community Association in the Waverly area. Her husband, George A. Diggs, a retired postal worker, had died 10 years earlier. A Mass of Christian Burial was at All Saints Church.
In the Sun's June 1922 list of Colored High School graduates, the 1922 vocational-course group ends with 'Bertie Erdine Win[ston]'. She had graduated from School 115 in 1919 as Bertha Erdine Winston.

The Sun's June 1916 list of Colored High School graduates includes, under the two-year vocational course, 'Drunell [Owens], dressmaking.' Drunell L. Owens received a School 115 eighth-grade certificate in June 1911.

Planning a 50th reunion for the June 1923 class of Douglass High School, the committee printed the names of classmates it could not locate, including 'Iantha Bernice Stokes.' Iantha Stokes was on School No. 115's June 1920 list of pupils promoted to high school.

The Afro's Eastside column named Mrs. Celeste Hughes its 'Good Neighbor of the Week.' A Baltimore native who had lived on the Eastside most of her life, a widow with three married daughters and an active member of St. Matthews Methodist Church, she 'was educated at School No. 115 and Morgan State College' and catered small parties and weddings.

The Baltimore Messenger's Community page ran a photo of volunteers planting sunflower seeds on the site of the old Colored School No. 115 on Merryman's Lane, where Civic Works had added hydrangeas, paving stones, mulch, fruit trees and silhouettes of children and teachers. About 50 people attended Monday's ceremony, and Councilwoman Mary Pat Clarke said, 'Instead of looking at a littered lot, you're looking at a legacy.'

The 1890 Polk directory, the third after annexation, lists a cluster of residents marked with the colored asterisk on numbered Talbott Street (Nos. 4 to 34) and on Merryman's Lane near the York road. Among them: Wm Anderson, lab, 14 Talbott; Nelson Brown, lab, 26 Talbott; Jane R. Griffin, laund, 4 Talbott; Frank Hall, hostler, 13 Talbott; Lee Harris, farmer, 16 Talbott; Michl Johnson, lab, 10 Talbott; Thos Lennox, lab, 22 Talbott; Jas B. Pinkett (printed Finkett), lab, 6 Talbott; Milton Sales, lab, 28 Talbott; Jas H. Walker, lab, 24 Talbott; John W. Blair and Jacob Jackson, 11 Merryman la; Fredk Gordon, 19 Merryman la; Robt C. Marshall, janitor, 5 Merryman la; Geo E. Dorsey, Oden Hawkins, Chas Warner, Alice Wheatley and Annie Green on Merryman la.

In 1891 and 1892 the colored-marked entries on Merryman's Lane run from No. 1 to No. 23: Brown William and George Wm H and Hawkins Wood at 1; Barnes Samuel L. at 4 Merryman av; Marshall Robt C. at 5; Wright Alfred, Hamilton Wm H. and Jones John at 7; Dorsey Geo E. and Jones Thos U. at 9; Johnson Fredk J. and Johnson Wm at 11; Wright Allison at 13; Bibb Jas N. and Bibb Robt at 15; Gould Jordan at 17; Gordon Fredk at 19; Dudley Frank W. at 21; Braxton Wm at 23. Most are listed as laborers. In 1892 Shiloh (A. M. E.) Church is listed at Merryman la corner of Barclay.

Fisher Trueheart (also Truehart, Truheart), a colored laborer, is at 14 Merryman Avenue in the 1901, 1909, 1912 and 1915 directories. In 1920 he owned his house free of mortgage, aged 58, with wife Sarah and son-in-law James Powell. The 1930 census lists him at 414 Merryman's Lane, aged 70, owner, with Sarah, 50; in 1940 he was at 417 Merryman Lane, a 70-year-old widower renting at $22.

Alfred Wright, colored laborer, is at 7 Merryman Lane in 1891-92 and at 3230 Barclay ext from 1901; the 1920 census shows Alfred and Ella M. Wright owning 3230 Barclay free of mortgage. Oden (Odin) Hawkins is on Merryman Lane in 1890 and at 21 Merryman Lane in 1892, then at 3218 Barclay ext from 1901 to 1905. Samuel L. Barnes, at 4 Merryman Avenue in 1891, is at 3220 Barclay ext in 1901-1903.

The 1901 directory is the first to use 3200 numbers on 'Barclay ext'. Every 3200-block entry found carries the colored asterisk and all are on the even (west) side: Geo F. Bragg, carp, and Mary Bragg, dressmaker, 3200; Rev. John W. Scott, 3204; Burley Mayo, 3206; Richd Thompson, driver, 3208; Abraham Gray, 3212; Danl Scott, 3214; Chas C. Gray, 3216; Oden Hawkins, 3218; Saml Barnes, 3220; Nathan Spellman, 3224; John W. Alton, porter, 3228; Alfred and Wm A. Wright, 3230; Mary Bennett, 3232; Preston Archer and Wm D. Griffin, 3234. Talbott (Nos. 2 to 137) and Merryman av (Nos. 1 to 19) remain largely colored, including Fisher Trueheart, lab, 14 Merryman av, and Mt. Zion (Bapt.) Church, Talbott near Merryman.

From 1903 to 1913 the east (odd) side of the 3200 block of Barclay, the row in front of School 115, is listed without race marks: Renteo H. Rykens, farmer, 3201 (1903); Jacob G. Hartzell, motorman, and Martha Graham, 3203 (1904-07); Dennis H. Dorsey, motorman, 3205 (1904-06); the Weckesser family (Geo F., printer; John F., confectioner and baker; Mrs. Annie C.), 3207 (1903-1915); Alfred T. Hopkins, then Cyrene J. Simmons, carpenter, 3209; Otto Gaertner, Jas S. Dixon, painter, 3211; the Haislip family, 3213-3225; Geo W. Eckstein, paver, 3215 (1903-1913); Frank Gardler, painter, 3217; Jacob Burkhardt, watchman, 3219; John T. Smith, 3221; Isaac G. Roberts, then Edwd J. Eckard, then Samuel Miller, grocers, at the corner, 3227. In the same years the even side (3200-3238) is marked colored throughout.

The corner store at 3227 Barclay (Merryman Lane end) passed from Isaac G. Roberts (1903) to Lavinia B. and Edwd J. Eckard (1904-05), to Samuel Miller (1906-1918), to Herman (Hyman) Paris (1920-21) and to Hyman Bass (1923); none carry the colored mark. The 1920 census lists Hyman Paris, 37, white, Yiddish-speaking, immigrant of 1904, 'grocery man', with wife Tillie and three children. At the 32nd St end, Chas Glaser (1920-21) and Louis Baylus (1921) ran a grocery at 3200 Barclay; Harry Asch, white, was a grocery clerk there in 1940 and proprietor of his own grocery in 1950.

The 1912 directory lists '*Smith Wm E Rev, h 3203 Barclay', the earliest colored-marked entry found on the odd side of the 3200 block. Rev. Gaines B. Lockhart is listed at 3241 Barclay in 1912 and 3240 Barclay in 1915 before moving to 3205.

Between 1914 and 1917 the white families on the odd side leave (Chas Schuldt, carpenter, 3215, and Mrs. Annie Weckesser, 3207, are among the last, 1914-15). By 1917 the entries carry the colored asterisk: Emmett Spiers, lab, 3201; Mrs. Martha E. and Edna M. (dressmaker), 3203; Rev. Gaines B. Lockhart, 3205; Jeremiah Moten (Morton), lab, 3207; Annabel Fortune, teacher, 3209; Frank J., waiter, 3211; Chas H. Nash, lab, 3221; Robt H., lab, 3225. Samuel Miller's grocery at 3227 carries no mark.

Jeremiah (Jerry) Morton is at 3207 Barclay from 1917; in 1920 he owned it, a 49-year-old quarry laborer, with wife Louise, stepson Emmanuel Taylor, 26, a minstrel singer, and grandson John E. Heath, 6. In August 1929 John Heath, 15, of 3207 Barclay was reported missing by Mary Heath and thought to be in Washington. Jerry Morton, 59, of 3207 Barclay died in 1935. In 1940 his widow Louisa rented the house at $22 a month and did cleaning. In 1948 Mrs. Louisa Moton of 3207 Barclay asked the Afro to find her son Emanuel Taylor, who had left Baltimore 20 years earlier and was last heard from in Detroit. Louiza Morton, 70, died in December 1949. In 1951 the house was advertised as a renovated 'Colored Bargain' cottage, six rooms, $300 to $500 down (Stevens Realty). John and Bessie Lattimore lived there in 1950.

William H. Roach owned 3209 Barclay by January 1920 (37, butler, mortgaged), with wife Bertha B., a laundress. Son Calvin Roach wrote to the Afro from 3209 Barclay as a Douglass High student in 1924; in 1940 Calvin T., 29, and his wife Sarah R. were both public school teachers living with his parents, and the house was valued at $1,500. William H. Roach Jr. was fined $10 for disorderly conduct in 1944 and married in 1950. Bertha B. Roach died on 1 November 1952; friends were received at her home, 3209 Barclay, and services were held at First Baptist Church, Caroline and McElderry streets, with burial in Mount Calvary Cemetery. In October 1956 the City Council authorized condemnation of 3209.

Clinton Brown (written Clifton in 1920) owned 3211 Barclay from at least 1920, when he was a 28-year-old auto chauffeur with wife Martha and son Samuel, 6. A colored chauffeur advertised for work from 3211 Barclay in 1924. Samuel L. Brown, of 3211 Barclay, took out a marriage license with Ruth A. Carter in 1932. Waverly business men, led by their attorney Solomon Liss, asked the Off-Street Parking Commission (chairman William G. Ewald) to condemn the last four parcels needed for a 120-car lot in the 3200 block of Barclay street. They had spent three years buying property, but four of eleven owners refused to sell. Liss said the four pieces 'were all homes occupied by their owners' and that the business men sought condemnation reluctantly because it meant moving residents from their homes. Theodore Frank was president of the Waverly Business Men's Association. Liss, just elected to the City Council, said he would withdraw from the negotiations.

The Off-Street Parking Commission gave preliminary approval to an open lot on Barclay street just west of the Waverly shopping district. 'The Waverly project involves clearing the entire 3200 block of Barclay street. There are eleven properties and the applicants for the city loan now control seven of them.' Owners of the other four were 'not willing even to discuss their sale' and condemnation was to be started. The next day the Evening Sun reported the commission would use condemnation 'where necessary and where justifiable,' its first use beyond minor skirmishes.

The commission gave final approval to the Waverly lot, called historic as the first open lot financed partly with city funds and the first to relieve parking in a neighborhood shopping district. 'The operators of the lot will be the Waverly Merchants Parking Lot, Inc. The city will put up $15,000 of the $25,000 cost.'

The commission declined for now to start condemnation for the Waverly lot, saying 'all means of getting the four remaining properties have not been exhausted.' 'In one case, for instance, the highest offer yet made is a price equal to the appraised value.' If the merchants offered more and still could not buy, the decision would be reconsidered.

The City Council Judiciary Committee held a two-hour hearing on the ordinance to condemn four properties, 'Baltimore's first case involving condemnation of residential property for an off-street parking project,' and gave 'the home owners and Waverly merchants two more weeks to negotiate.' Chairman Solomon Liss (D., Fourth) said if they could not agree 'we (the Council committee) will take it from there.' 'Testimony showed that offers of $7,000 have been made for each of the properties and that the tax assessments on them range from $2,200 to $3,000 each.' The merchants' group had bought or controlled seven of eleven properties.

'The City Council approved and sent to the Mayor a precedent-setting ordinance providing for the condemnation of four houses to make way for an off-street parking project. The dwellings are located at 3207, 3209, 3211 and 3219 Barclay street.' A group of business men had bought seven other homes in the block; 'The owners of the four remaining dwellings have refused to sell.' The ordinance directed the comptroller to negotiate and to bring condemnation proceedings if no agreement was reached. An Evening Sun editorial the next day called it a 'first' and said the commission was lending $70,000 toward the purchase and leveling of eleven Waverly properties.

'An 8-year neighborhood community improvement effort will culminate in the Waverly Merchants Association opening tomorrow a 109-car, $117,000 parking lot on Thirty-second street west of Greenmount avenue.' The association of 35 merchants from Thirty-first to Thirty-fifth streets on Greenmount began its 'Park and Shop' plan eight years earlier with nine members; the lot measured 210 by 150 feet. 'Meanwhile, among other things, the city had to pass an ordinance condemning the area for a parking lot.' Mayor D'Alesandro and Traffic Commissioner Henry Barnes were to attend.

An Evening Sun table of state and city subsidies to parking projects lists '3201-3221 Barclay Street' with an assessment of $61,530 (60 per cent of total cost) and an assessed value at acquisition of $29,200. The story explains that title is held by the Mayor and City Council during the loan, so no real-estate tax is collected, and that the operators take title when the loan is repaid.

The Sun reported that the Waverly Merchants Parking Lot, Inc., had bought the Barclay street properties in October 1957 for roughly $88,500 with a $60,200 low-interest city loan, 'knocked the houses down and built the parking lot,' bought an additional piece 'at 32d street and Brentwood avenue for $20,000' in November 1960, paid off the loan in March 1973, and the same month sold the land to Luck Dome, Inc., the company of hotel developer Simantov S. Capon, for $165,000. Harvey L. Miller, vice president of the Waverly Merchants Association, said 'Our interest was not in making a profit'; Stanley L. Adler, president, said they got back 'a little more than their investment.' A 12-story hotel was planned on the triangle of Barclay, 32d and Merryman lane.

The Sun reported that developer Samintov Capon had abandoned the hotel and that 'the Waverly Merchants Parking Lot, at 32d and Barclay streets and Merrymans lane, will be auctioned to the highest bidder Thursday.' A 1979 Evening Sun column by Grenville B. Whitman of the ad hoc Anti-Hotel Committee ('AHAH') recalls the 1973-74 fight, a 'People's Auction' on the lot, and the result 'No Sale'; by June 1979 a bill before the City Council provided 'for the city to purchase the lot and turn it into a municipal metered parking area, with a brick wall, trees, bushes, and landscaping.'

The root of title that 3117's deeds recite: its lot begins at a post at the northwest corner of 'the whole Coffield tract'. Deed of Assignment, Baltimore County Liber J.H.L. 43, folios 548 to 550 (MSA CE 62-43; read in full on the scan). Samuel H. Tagart (so spelled in the text and the signature; the 1988 deeds' 'Taggert' is a misreading), of the City of Baltimore, trustee, to George C. H. Coffield, dated January 31, 1865, acknowledged that day before Gideon Herbert, J.P., and recorded February 10, 1865 (Jno. H. Longnecker, clerk). It recites a decree of the Circuit Court for Baltimore County, sitting in equity, dated April 14, 1864, in William Tagart, complainant, against Elizabeth Baden and others, defendants, appointing Tagart trustee to sell the property; his sale of it to Coffield on July 5, 1864 for $1,525; and payment in full. For $5 recited, Tagart assigns 'all that lot or parcel of Ground' in Baltimore County on the east side of the York Turnpike Road: beginning at a stone on the east side of the road, north 1 degree west 12 perches along the road, south 88 degrees east 9 perches, south 7 1/2 degrees west 4 perches, south 15 degrees west 11 perches and thence to the beginning, containing 103 perches (about 28,000 square feet). No tract name is given. No 22 folio 164 &c', and that Thomas Rutter Junior, by indenture also of Feb. 7, 1795, sold him 'all that part of Merryman's Lot' within bounds it repeats (beginning at a stone in the first line of the land, north 59 degrees west 11 perches, north 41 degrees east 8 perches 14 feet, south 54 degrees east 9 perches to the first line of Merryman's Lot, and a straight line back: one half an acre), cited as 'Liber W.G. No 22 folio 165 &c'; Wilmans 'hath agreed to sell and convey the two above described pieces or parcels of Land' to Hackett. Deed, Baltimore County Court land records, Liber W.G. 72, folios 460 to 462 (MSA CE 66-122; read in full on the scan, which holds pages 460 to 463; the top of 460 is the end of an unrelated Stewart and Falls deed to William McCreery, and the foot of 462 opens Charles Carroll of Carrollton to Thomas Hillen). James Edwards and Abraham Van Bibber, of Baltimore County, to John Whitely, of the City of Baltimore, dated Jan. 2, 1802, for $333.33 current money of the United States. It recites Grant and Moale's deed to Edwards and Van Bibber 'recorded among the land records of Baltimore County Court in liber W.G. No. 65 folio 444 &c', conveying 'that part of a tract of Land situate in Baltimore County called Huntington that is distinguished on a plat thereof by the numbers ninety eight, ninety seven, ninety five and ninety six containing by estimation fourteen acres a quarter and twenty square perches', and John Hackett and Jane his wife's release of dower to them (W.G. No. 65 folio 442 &c). It then conveys to Whitely, in fee, 'all that part of the above mentioned part of a tract of Land called Huntington which is contained within the following metes and bounds': beginning at a stone on the north side of 'the road leading from Joseph Merryman's to the City of Baltimore', 'being the beginning of a lot of Ground part of said tract assigned by Jesse Brown to said Whitely', running from that stone north 84 1/2 degrees east 41 1/2 perches to 'the York Turnpike road', thence bounding on that road south 9 3/4 perches to 'the aforesaid part of said tract assigned by Jesse Brown to said Whitely', and thence bounding on that part to the beginning: one acre and one quarter more or less, with buildings and improvements, to Whitely, his heirs and assigns forever, with warranty and further assurance. Signed Jas. Edwards and Abm. Van Bibber (seals) in the presence of Geo. Gould Presbury and Thos. B. Hodgkin; receipt for $333.33 the same day; acknowledged Jan. 2, 1802 before Presbury and Hodgkin, Ruth wife of James Edwards and Mary wife of Abraham Van Bibber examined apart and releasing dower; received to be recorded Feb. 26, 1802 and recorded that day (Wm. Plat and descriptions, read from the Archives' public PDF of MSA C2843-15 (132 pages; Superior Court (Baltimore City) Survey Papers, the Bouldin surveyors' Envelope No. 15). Walker and John Smith before Wm Hollins says the parcel 'was sold originally in one body to William Jackson, Christopher Walker and James Byass' and was then parcelled out, and confirms the plat and certificate as binding on them. Folio 503 &c'; and 'the last mentioned moiety' (Elizabeth's) 'was granted and conveyed unto the said Harry Dorsey Gough by a certain Thomas Bond Onion and Elizabeth his wife' by indenture of Feb. 24, 1790, recorded in 'Liber W.G.
