Deed, Baltimore County Court land records, Liber W.G. 156, folios 50 to 54 (MSA CE 66-206; read in full on the scan Jeff saved, pages 49 to 54; page 50 opens with the end of an unrelated deed, Williams and others, received for record June 5, 1820, and page 54 closes with the opening of another, Courtenay to Courtenay). The Tract Index (MSA CE 15-1, p. 519) lists it as 'Jackson &c to Wilson', 12 1/2 a. 18 1/4 Pr, at 156/50; the folio was first misread as 30, and pages 29 to 34 of this liber hold other deeds. Three parties, dated April 21, 1820: the President and Directors of the Mechanics Bank of Baltimore (the first part, signing by James Mosher, President, with the corporate seal); William Jackson, of the City of Baltimore, merchant (the second part); and Thomas Wilson, of the City of Baltimore, merchant (the third). It recites (1) Gough and Prudence's deed to Jackson 'on or about the thirteenth day of January 1803', 'recorded ... in Liber W.G. No. 74 folio 337', whose lot begins 'at a stone on the north west side of a road laid out by' Gough 'at the north east corner of a lot then or lately belonging to Stephen P. Wante' and was 'laid out for fourteen acres and three quarters of an acre' (the courses are those of row 726:mdlr-wg74-337-gough-jackson-1803); (2) Jackson's deed of March 18, 1819 to the Bank (Liber W.G. No. 150 folio 371), made to secure a $9,000 'accommodation' on paper drawn by Jackson and endorsed by John Brice, the Bank's cashier, with power for the Bank's president to sell after thirty days' public notice in two Baltimore daily papers; and (3) that Jackson had agreed to sell Wilson part of the lot. For $7,000 paid by Wilson to the Bank and $1 to Jackson, the Bank and Jackson convey to Wilson, in fee, 'all that part of the aforesaid tract ... called Huntington' beginning at the beginning of the whole lot Gough conveyed to Jackson; north 40 degrees east 16 3/10 perches to the end of the first line of the whole lot; then on its second line north 36 1/2 degrees west 51 perches 15 feet 8 1/10 inches to 'the piece or parcel of land conveyed by the said William Jackson to Elisha E. Russell'; thence on that parcel south 57 1/2 degrees west 9 6/10 perches and north 35 1/2 degrees west 35 2/10 perches to the third line of the whole lot, at 9 perches and a fraction from its beginning; then on that third line south 39 1/2 degrees west 27 9/10 perches to its end; and by a straight line to the beginning: 'twelve Acres two roods and Eighteen perches and one fourth of a perch' (12a 2r 18 1/4p), more or less, 'except the part thereof conveyed by the said William Jackson to Elisha Russell by deed ... on or about the thirteenth day of March one thousand eight hundred and eleven ... Liber W.G. No. 112 folio 467'. Jackson warrants against himself and his heirs. Signed 'James Mosher Prest.' and 'William Jackson' (seals) in the presence of Nath. Knight and Peter Galt; acknowledged April 21, 1820 before Knight and Galt, justices of the peace, by Mosher for the Bank and by Jackson, Mary Jackson his wife relinquishing dower; received to be recorded June 5, 1820 and recorded and examined the same day (Wm Gibson, clerk). What it settles: the Tract Index's 1820 'Jackson &c to Wilson' is William Jackson's lot of 1803, less the piece he sold Elisha E. Russell in 1811 (W.G. 112/467, the index's 'Jackson to Russell'), passing to Thomas Wilson through the Bank that held it in trust; the 14 3/4 acres less about 2 acres 21 3/4 perches is the 12a 2r 18 1/4p. As the courses read, the Russell piece is at the north-west end of the lot, away from Gough's road. What it does not settle: the grantee is Thomas Wilson, merchant, and nothing read here ties him to James Wilson (whose estate's trustees included a Thomas J. Wilson), so it is not shown to be a source for the James Wilson estate's ground; and the deed names no street. Why it is filed on 3028: it is the later history of Jackson's lot, one of the four 1803 lots filed on 3028 (726:mdlr-wg74-337-gough-jackson-1803), which Bouldin's 1844 survey puts at the toll gate; this deed does not itself place the lot on a street, so the placement stays probable.

Deed, Baltimore County Court land records, Liber B No. Q, folios 502 to 507 (MSA CE 66-36; read in full on the scan Jeff saved, pages 502 to 508; the top of 502 is the end of an unrelated deed acknowledged April 15, 1768, and the foot of 507 opens another, Bond and Fell to Christie, May 12, 1768). Two instruments, a pair: (1) A lease for a year, 'made the 12th day of February 1768', Achsah Carnan, of Baltimore County, widow of John Carnan deceased and daughter of Colonel Charles Ridgely, to John Ridgely and Charles Ridgely Junior, both of the Town of Baltimore, for five shillings sterling, of 'that part of a tract of land ... called Taylors Purchase' (600 acres, conveyed to her by her father), 'all that tract or parcel of land called Huntington ... containing four hundred and Seventy five Acres more or less as per the Certificate thereof returned into his Lordship's Land Office at Annapolis in the name of the aforesaid John Carnan deceased and the said Achsah Carnan on or about the twenty Ninth day of September Seventeen hundred and fifty Seven', and 'that part of a tract of land called Ridgely's whim' (500 acres, also from her father), for a term of one year at a pepper corn, so that the Ridgelys could take a release. Witnesses Benjamin Rogers and Wm Asquith; Lord Baltimore's alienation fine, 3 pounds 3 shillings on the 1,575 acres, received by John Boyd for the Agent; recorded May 30, 1768 (B. Bordley, clerk). (2) The release, headed 'Achsah Carnan to John & Charles Ridgely in Trust', 'made the 13th day of February 1768', for ten shillings sterling and 'the advancement and maintenance of her children and other relations and for the setting and establishment of the lands and tenements', to the Ridgelys and their heirs and assigns, of the same three tracts, to the uses declared: to Achsah for her natural life without impeachment of waste; then, as to Huntington and Ridgely's Whim, one full moiety to Prudence Carnan 'and the heirs of her body lawfully to be begotten' and, failing such issue, to Elizabeth Carnan, and the other moiety to Elizabeth 'and the heirs of her body' and, failing such issue, to Prudence; failing both, to Charles Ridgely Carnan her son and the heirs of his body; then to her sons and daughters born after a later marriage, in order; then to John Robert Holiday her son; then, for a moiety, to Achsah and Deborah Ridgely, daughters of John Ridgely, in turn; and failing all, to the right heirs of Achsah Carnan forever. Taylors Purchase is limited separately in much the same family order, ending with Elizabeth and Susannah Gooding and then the right heirs. Signed 'A Carnan' (seal) in the presence of Benjamin Rogers; receipt of ten shillings Feb. 13, 1768; acknowledged that day before Benjamin Rogers and Wm Asquith, two of his Lordship's justices; recorded June 4, 1768 (B. Bordley, clerk). What it settles: the recital in all four of Gough's 1803 deeds ('indenture ... the thirteenth day of February 1768 ... Liber B Number Q Folio 503') is this release. What differs: the recital says the trustees were to let the daughters and their lawful issue enjoy a moiety each 'forever'; the release limits each moiety to the daughter 'and the heirs of her body', with remainders over, so the daughters took estates in tail, not (on the face of the deed) in fee. Whether those entails were barred, or ended, before Gough's 1790 and 1803 deeds is not shown by anything read. Prudence Carnan is the Prudence who joins Gough's 1803 deeds. The deed names no street, house or lot; it conveys the whole 475-acre Huntington and two other tracts. Why it is filed on 3028: it is a link above Gough's four 1803 deeds (726:mdlr-wg74-327-gough-smith-1803, -330-, -334- and -337-), which Bouldin's 1844 survey puts at the toll gate; it conveys the whole tract and names no street, so the placement stays possible.

Deed, Baltimore County Court land records, Liber W.G. E.E., folios 157 to 159 (MSA CE 66-80; read in full on the scan Jeff saved, pages 156 to 161; the top of 157 is the end of a different deed, Thomas Bond Onion alone to Gough of the same day, for 700 pounds, whose first page is not pulled; the foot of 159 opens James Calhoun to Alexander Gallagher, Feb. 25, 1790). A margin note beside the deed's title reads 'See Liber W.G. No. 102 folio 33'. Thomas Bond Onion of Baltimore County and Elizabeth Onion his wife to Harry Dorsey Gough of the same county, dated Feb. 24, 1790, for 1,400 pounds, receipt acknowledged. They convey 'all that undivided Moiety of a Portion a part of a Tract of Land called Ridgelys Whim heretofore conveyed to a certain Achsah Holliday mother to the aforesaid Elizabeth Onion by a certain Charles Ridgely Grandfather to the said Elizabeth Onion for five hundred acres more or Less', one moiety of which Achsah Holliday 'by the name of Achsah Carnan' had conveyed 'to and for the use of the said Elizabeth Onion and the heirs of her Body with sundry remainders over'; and 'all that undivided Moiety of a Tract or Parcel of Land called and known by the name of Huntington ... containing four hundred and seventy six acres of Land more or Less as per Certificate and Patent thereof in the name of John Carnan and Achsah his wife', of which one moiety was likewise conveyed by Achsah Carnan 'to the use and behoof of the said Elizabeth Onion then Elizabeth Carnan and the heirs of her Body with sundry remainders over as will appear by a Reference to said Deed'. With it go all the Onions' rights 'to all Debts Contracted and yet unpaid heretofore arising on the sale of the said Lands with the Interest accruing thereon and all arrearages of Rent', to Gough, his heirs and assigns forever, with the Onions' covenants of further assurance and warranty. Signed Thomas Bond Onion and Eliza Onion (seals) in the presence of Standish Barry and Saml Vincent; receipt of 1,400 pounds the same day; acknowledged Feb. 24, 1790 before Jas. Calhoun and Geo. Gould Presbury, Elizabeth examined apart and out of her husband's hearing; received to be recorded and recorded that day (Wm Gibson, clerk). What it settles: the instrument every 1803 Gough deed cites as 'W.G. Number E.E. folio 157' is this one, and it is how Elizabeth's moiety of Huntington reached Gough, who already held Prudence's through his wife. It says Huntington was 476 acres where the 1768 settlement says 475, and it recites that deed's limitations to Elizabeth 'and the heirs of her body with sundry remainders over' while conveying in fee, so it does not itself show that the remainders were barred. The sale of 'the said Lands' for which debts were 'yet unpaid' is not explained on these pages. The same pages show a second Onion deed of the same day, Thomas Bond Onion alone to Gough for 700 pounds, covering 'the aforesaid Tracts or parcels of Land' and Onion's own 'Estate Right Title Interest and Demand' in them (the end of it, on 156 to 157, is read; its first page, probably W.G. E.E. 155, is not). The 1803 deeds do not cite it. Why it is filed on 3028: it is a link above Gough's four 1803 deeds (726:mdlr-wg74-327-gough-smith-1803, -330-, -334- and -337-), which Bouldin's 1844 survey puts at the toll gate; it conveys the whole tract and names no street, so the placement stays possible. Update Oct. 12, 2026: two more pages are read. (1) W.G. E.E. 155, the opening of the same-day Onion-alone deed (700 pounds), is on the scan Jeff saved (MSA CE 66-80, pages 153 to 155): it conveys Onion's right in 'two hundred acres of Land lying in Baltimore County being part of a Tract of Land Called Thompsons Choice' and in 'another Tract or Parcel of Land being part of a Tract of Land Called Heathcotes Cottage' (123 acres), neither of them Huntington; the note above that it covers 'the aforesaid Tracts' should be read as those tracts, not as Huntington and Ridgely's Whim. (2) W.G. 102/33 (June 6, 1809), the deed the margin note points to, is read: the Onions reconveyed the moiety in fee to Gough's executors because 'doubts are entertained' whether the 1790 deed passed the fee simple (726:mdlr-wg102-33-onion-carroll-gough-1809).

Mortgage, Baltimore City land records, Liber S.C.L. 4353, folios 213 to 215 (MSA CE 168-4361; read in full on the scan, pages 211 to 215). Giuseppe Palladi and Adele Palladi, his wife, of the City of Baltimore, to The First Mortgage Bond Homestead Association Incorporated, dated March 13, 1925, securing $3,700 current money, 'part of the purchase price of the hereinafter described property', the Palladis being members who had subscribed to 36 shares of Series 'A' stock: a principal note due two years after date with 6 percent interest, and eight further notes of $55.50 (the interest) payable at 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18, 21 and 24 months, in gold coin. The mortgaged property is 'those two lots or parcels of ground ... located in block No 3855 and being now known as No 2958 Greenmount Avenue', 'the same two lots of ground described in an assignment of even date herewith and recorded or so intended to be immediately prior hereto ... conveyed to the said Mortgagors by Albert C Brandt and Alice E Brandt his wife': the first lot for the residue of the term, renewable forever, subject to the annual rent of $65, payable in half-yearly instalments on March 1 and September 1, the second in fee simple. Signed Giuseppe Palladi and Adele Palladi, witness O. P. Baker; acknowledged March 13, 1925 before O. Parker Baker, Notary Public, Harry B. Lease, Baltimore County Court land records, Liber A.W.B. 354, folios 371 to 373 (MSA CE 66-404; read in full on the scans Jeff saved, pages 369 to 372, with 373 on the earlier scan; the top of 371 and all of 370 are the end of an unrelated deed, Maurice and Catharine Barrett of Galway to George Brown, recorded July 10, 1845). It is the paired instrument of the deed of the same day, A.W.B. 354/374 (row 46070), and carries the 373 tail that ends in a covenant to renew. Made Nov. 9, 1844 between Sarah Biays, Henry N. Bowerman and Elizabeth Bowerman, Walter T. Allender and Hannah Jane Allender (of Baltimore City), Jacob Hoke and Nancy Hoke, Henry Hammond and Frances Hammond (of Harford County), of the first part; John W. Stump of Harford County and Philip G. Biays of Montgomery County, 'Trustees under the deed or Indenture hereinafter referred to', of the second part; and David Mumma of Baltimore County, of the third. They lease him, for 99 years from the day before the date (the term runs from Oct. 1, 1844) at a clear yearly rent of $15.75, payable on the first of October, 'to the said Sarah Biays for and during her natural life and after her death to the said Elizabeth Bowerman, Hannah Jane Allender, Nancy Hoke, and Frances Hammond', 'all that piece or parcel of Land or ground, Situate and lying in Baltimore County ... Beginning for the same on the East Side of the York Turnpike Road, at the Corner formed by the East side of the York Turnpike Road and the South Side of a Lane known as the Quaker Lane', then north 2 1/2 degrees east 66 feet 8 inches along the east side of the turnpike 'to the Lot of ground Leased by Sarah Biays and others to Abraham H. Becker', east 16 6/10 perches on that lot to the line of 'the Quaker Lot', south 16 1/4 degrees west 59 feet 'to Quaker Lane', and along the lane to the beginning. 'It being a part of the Land or ground which by Indenture bearing date the Eleventh day of April One thousand Eight hundred and twenty two, and recorded among the Land records of Baltimore County aforesaid in Liber W.G. No 165 folio 492 &c was granted and Conveyed by John McFadden to the above named John W. Stump and Philip G. Biays, In Trust for the said Sarah Biays Wife of James Biays now deceased, for and during the term of her natural life, and after her death, to be Conveyed to the aforesaid Elizabeth Bowerman, Hannah Jane Allender, Nancy Hoke, and Frances Hammond, (Children of the said James and Sarah Biays)'. The covenants (on 372 and 373): Mumma pays the rent and all taxes and assessments; the lessors may re-enter if the rent is 60 days unpaid and expel him if a year in arrears; they covenant quiet enjoyment; and, on 373, on payment of $10 and at the end of the term the parties 'shall and will' make him a lease 'for other ninety nine years', 'renewable and renewed from time to time forever'. Signed S. Biays, H. N. Bowerman, E. Bowerman, Walter T. Allender, Hannah J. Allender, J. Hoke, Nancy Hoke, Henry Hammond, Fanny Hammond, Jno. W. Stump, Philip G. Biays and David Mumma; acknowledged Nov. 9, 1844 (Baltimore City) and May 29, 1845 (Philip G. Biays, Montgomery County); recorded July 10, 1845 (A. W. Bradford, clerk). What it settles: the 1822 McFadden (McFadon) deed is Liber W.G. 165 folio 492, and it was a trust deed for Sarah Biays, widow of James Biays (d. 1822), for life and then for her four daughters, the same four couples who sell Mumma the south-west lot by the deed of the same day. Mumma took two parcels from them on Nov. 9, 1844: the 94 square perches in fee on the WEST side of the turnpike, at the south-west corner of the lane toward Gilmor's (354/374), and this lot on the EAST side, at the south-east corner by the Quaker Lane, as a 99-year lease at $15.75, renewable forever. Abraham H. Becker held an adjoining leased lot to the north, and the 'Quaker Lot' lay to the east. What it does not settle: which present parcel the east-side lot is (the 66 feet 8 inches of frontage and the 'Quaker Lane' are the clues; it is on the opposite side of the turnpike from 3010 to 3020, so it is not that chapter's ground); whether the Quaker Lane is the same lane as the one toward Gilmor's; and the later history of the lease. Update Oct. 12, 2026: the McFadon deed of trust is now read at W.G. 165/492 (719:mdlr-wg165-492-mcfadon-trust-stump-biays-1822), $7,700, April 11, 1822, in trust for Sarah Biays and then her four daughters.

Deed, Baltimore City land records, Liber S.C.L. 3459, folios 372 to 373 (MSA CE 168-3467; read in full on the scan Jeff saved, pages 371 to 375; the deed opens at the foot of 372 under the index heading 'Clara Butzler, Deed to Albert C Brandt &c'). The first of the five scanned pages, 371, and the top of 372 are the end of the deed that fed it (next row). Clara Butzler, unmarried, of Baltimore City, to Albert C. Brandt and Alice E. Brandt, his wife, 'as tenants by the entireties the survivor of them their assigns and the heirs personal representatives and assigns of the survivor', dated Oct. 9, 1919, for five dollars and other valuable considerations: 'all those two lots of ground situate in Baltimore City'. (1) The first begins on the west side of the York Road 402 feet 9 1/2 inches north of the northwest corner of Twenty-Ninth Street, at the centre of a partition wall, runs 14 feet north on the road to the centre of another wall, 100 feet west (parallel with Twenty-Ninth Street) to the west side of a ten-foot alley, 14 feet back along the alley 'with the use thereof in common with others', and 100 feet east: the lot 2958's 1925 and 1960 deeds describe word for word. (2) The second begins at 416 feet 9 1/2 inches 'at the end of the first line of the lot of ground described in a lease from James Keelty to James F. Bowersox dated August 24 1907 and recorded among the Land Records of Baltimore City in Liber S C L No 2363 folio 423', runs north on the west side of the York Road 'six and forty four hundredths feet' (the later deeds say 'eight feet, more or less') to 'the northernmost outline of the land described in a deed from William T. Wilson and wife to the said James Keelty dated January 11 1907 and recorded ... in Liber R O No 2302 folio 43', 36 feet 7 inches west along that line to the south side of Thirtieth Street, 63 feet 5 inches farther west along the street to the west side of the alley, 10 1/2 inches south along it to the end of the second line of the Keelty lease, and 100 feet east to the beginning. The deed says it is 'the same property which by deed bearing even date herewith and recorded or intended to be recorded ... was granted conveyed and assigned by Alice E. Brandt, trustee et al, to the said party hereto of the first part'. The first lot is held for 'all the residue of the term of years yet to come and unexpired therein with the benefit of renewal thereof forever subject to the payment of the annual rent of Sixty five dollars payable semi annually on March and September first'; the second 'in fee simple'; the household furniture and utensils in the house pass with the buildings. Butzler covenants special warranty and further assurance. Witness J. Milton Brandt; signed Clara Butzler (seal); acknowledged Oct. 9, 1919 before J. Milton Brandt, Notary Public, Baltimore City; received for record Oct. 10, 1919 and recorded the same day ('Sent for Stephen C. Little, clerk'); a Grantee index stamp reads 'Dec. 13 1919'. What it settles: the $65 rent is the rent of the 1907 lease from James Keelty to James F. Bowersox (S.C.L. 2363/423), so Keelty was the original ground-rent lessor and the lease dates from August 24, 1907; the lot and its metes are the same in 1919, 1925 and 1960, except that the second lot's frontage reads six and forty-four hundredths feet here and eight feet more or less later. Butzler was a one-day link: she took the property from the Brandts' own family and trust and sold it to Alice and Albert Brandt as tenants by the entireties the same day, taking back a $1,700 mortgage (third row). J. Milton Brandt witnessed and notarized every instrument, and is the broker of the 1924 advertisement and the attorney in the mortgage. What it does not settle: the lease itself (S.C.L. 2363/423 is not pulled), who built the house and when (the 1907 lease is the earliest date for the lot as a leasehold; the row of about 1900 is the National Register's), the 1917 trust deed's terms, and the date of the 'long' rent's extinguishment. The ground behind the $65 rent, as these pages recite it: William T. Wilson and his wife to James Keelty, deed of Jan. 11, 1907 (Liber R.O. 2302 folio 43); James Keelty to James F. Bowersox, lease of Aug. 24, 1907 (Liber S.C.L. 2363 folio 423), the lease of the first lot, so Keelty was the ground-rent lessor; and James Keelty and wife to Alice E. Brandt (formerly Alice E. Bowersox), in trust for the lives of James F. Bowersox and Mary E. Bowersox his wife and the survivor, remainder to Alice E. Brandt, Archibald Bowersox and Clarence V. Bowersox in fee simple, deed of Oct. 3, 1917 (Liber S.C.L. 3159 folio 384), which the pages cite for the second lot. None of the three is pulled. Mary E. Deed in the 'Assignment' printed form, Baltimore City land records, Liber M.L.P. 9546, folios 143 to 145 (MSA CE 168-9554; read on the scan Jeff saved, pages 142 to 146: 142 is the end of the Weber and Plack deed, the row above; 146 is the release, below). Elizabeth McC. West, of Baltimore City, to Max Silen, of the same city, Aug. 2, 1954, 'five dollars and other good and valuable considerations': 'all that lot or parcel of ground situate in the City of Baltimore' described by courses on the east side of Greenmount Avenue, beginning 'at the end of the first line of the firstly described lot of ground in the deed from J. Holliday Riepe (Single) to James M. Sinclair and Ena M. Sinclair his wife dated March 1, 1927 and recorded ... in Liber S.C.L. No. 4707, folio 12', at 'the point formed by the intersection of the East Side of said Greenmount Avenue sixty-six feet wide as established by the City of Baltimore Topographical Survey Commission as directed by Section 2 of Ordinance No. 129 of the Mayor and City Council of Baltimore approved December 3, 1898 and the North West Side of Old York Road', 58 feet 4 inches north along Greenmount and back by three lines (the Sinclair lot's fourth, third and second lines reversed) to the beginning; 'The improvements thereon being known as No. 3011 Greenmount Avenue. The courses in the above description are all referred to the True Meridian established by the City of Baltimore Topographical Survey Commission.' 'Being the same lot of ground described in a Deed from Henry John Weber and wife and Raymond H. Plack and wife, to the said Elizabeth McC. West, whereby the within leasehold was created, bearing even date herewith.' To hold to Max Silen, his personal representatives and assigns, 'for all the residue of the term of years yet to come and unexpired therein, with the benefit of renewal forever; subject to the payment of the annual rent of Sixty-Six ($66.00) Dollars, payable in equal semi-annual installments on the second days of February and August in each and every year'. Special warranty. Signed Elizabeth McC. West; witness Phyllis J. Smith; acknowledged Aug. 2, 1954 before Phyllis J. Smith, Notary Public, Baltimore County; recorded Aug. 2, 1954 at about 1:02 P.M. (M. Luther Pittman, clerk). What it settles: the lot's lines are tied to the 1927 Sinclair deed (S.C.L. 4707/12, Riepe to Sinclair, March 1, 1927, loaded in Jeff's browser and not yet downloaded); the improvements are 'No. 3011 Greenmount Avenue'; Max Silen (d. 1971, row 42365) took the leasehold; and the ground rent was $66 a year, owed to whoever held the reversion after the 1954 Weber and Plack deed. What it does not settle: who held the reversion and the $66 rent from Aug. 2, 1954 (the Silen family later held both lots in fee, but when the rent was merged is not shown), and the price.

Release, Baltimore City land records, Liber M.L.P. 9546, folio 146 (MSA CE 168-9554, last page of the scan; a stamp on the margin reads 'GRANTEE OCT 28 1954'; Law Offices of J. Calvin Carney, 3 East Lexington Street, on the printed form). The Belair Road Building and Loan Association, Incorporated, 'whereas all the covenants of the hereinafter described Mortgage have been performed, and the whole sum of money and interest secured thereby has been paid', releases to Henry John Weber and Lillian F. Weber, Adam H. Weber and Virginia Weber, and Raymond H. Plack and Doris E. Plack, 'all that lot of ground and premises known as 3011 Greenmount Avenue described in a mortgage from [them] to the said body corporate, dated June 19th, 1954, recorded ... Liber M.L.P. No. 9513 folio 64, free and clear from the operation of said Mortgage'; J. Calvin Carney appointed attorney to acknowledge it. Signed for the association by J. David Lassahn, President (corporate seal); witnessed by Elizabeth McC. West; acknowledged Aug. 2, 1954 before Elizabeth McC. West, Notary Public, Baltimore City, by J. Calvin Carney; recorded Aug. 2, 1954 (M. Luther Pittman, clerk). What it settles: the three owners, the Webers and the Placks, borrowed on 3011 on June 19, 1954 (M.L.P. 9513/64, not pulled) and the loan was paid off the same day the lot was leased to West and the reversion sold, Aug. 2, 1954, i.e. the sale of the lot and the closing of the mortgage were one transaction; that the lot had a street number, '3011 Greenmount Avenue', before it passed to the Silens; and that Elizabeth McC. West is the lessee of the same-day lease (row above) and also the witness and notary on this release, three roles on one day. What it does not settle: the amount of the mortgage (not recited here) and the price. Update Oct. 13, 2026: the mortgage this release discharges is read (720:mdlr-mlp9513-64-weber-plack-belair-mortgage-3011-1954): June 19, 1954, $10,000, recorded June 24, 1954 (M.L.P. 9513/64).

Deed, Baltimore City land records, Liber M.L.P. 9566, folios 459 to 460 (MSA CE 168-9574; read on the scan Jeff saved, pages 458 to 462; 458 is the acknowledgment of an unrelated Johnson and Boone mortgage to the Provident Savings Bank, Aug. 25, 1954; 461 and 462 are the Obrecht deed, next row; a margin stamp on 459 reads 'GRANTEE OCT 15 1954'). John E. Minor, of Baltimore County, to Max Silen, of Baltimore City, Aug. 25, 1954, 'five dollars and other good and valuable consideration': the lot 'Beginning for the same on the east side of Greenmount Avenue (formerly the York Turnpike Road) at a point distant 190 feet 7 inches southerly from the 2 mile stone located on the east side of Greenmount Avenue in front of the Waverly Methodist Episcopal Church lot, said point of beginning being also 267 feet 2 inches southerly from the north side of a 4 foot alley-way called Bateman's Alley, and running thence southerly bounding on the east side of Greenmount Avenue 14 feet, thence easterly at right angles to Greenmount Avenue 42 feet 4 inches to the westernmost side of the Old York Road, thence northeasterly bounding on the westernmost side of the Old York Road 15 feet 2 1/2 inches and thence westerly by a straight line 48 feet 3 inches to the place of beginning. The improvements thereon being known as No. 3013 Greenmount Avenue.' 'BEING the same lot of ground and premises which were transferred and conveyed to the said John E. Minor from Charles F. Obrecht and wife, by Lease dated 20th December, 1943 ... Liber M.L.P. No. 6544, folio 521, creating a one cent ground rent, if demanded, bearing date of December 20th, 1943', to hold 'for all the residue of the term of years yet to come and unexpired therein, with the benefit of renewal forever; subject to the payment of the annual rent of One Cent ($.01), if demanded'. Special warranty. Signed John E. Minor (seal), witness Charles F. Obrecht; acknowledged Aug. 25, 1954 before Charles F. Obrecht, Notary Public, Baltimore County; recorded Aug. 25, 1954 (M. Luther Pittman, clerk). What it settles: 3013 Greenmount (the 14-foot lot a few feet north of the Waverly Methodist Episcopal Church lot, measured from the two-mile stone and from Bateman's Alley) came to Max Silen in two steps three weeks after he took 3011 (Aug. 2, 1954): the leasehold from John E. Minor on Aug. 25 (this row) and, the day before, the fee and the penny rent from the Obrechts to Samuel G. Silen (next row). John E. Minor's leasehold dated from Dec. 20, 1943, when he deeded the fee to the Obrechts and took back a 99-year lease at one cent, a sale-leaseback; Charles F. Obrecht witnessed and notarised this deed; he was the grantor of the reversion to Samuel G. Silen the day before. What it does not settle: the 1943 deed and lease (M.L.P. 6544/521, not pulled), why Minor sold the fee in 1943 and kept the lease, and the price. Update Oct. 15, 2026: a month after this deed the one-story store at 3013 was razed (permit 169771, Sept. 23, 1954; 720:bca-brg48-permit-card-3013-greenmount-1954-1957).

Deed of ground rent, Baltimore City land records, Liber M.L.P. 9566, folios 461 to 462 (MSA CE 168-9574, the last two pages of the scan Jeff saved; the foot of 462 is the end of the pages pulled, so the signatures, the acknowledgment and the recording stamp are on 463, not pulled; a margin stamp on 461 reads 'GRANTEE OCT 15 1954'). Charles F. Obrecht and Alice F. Obrecht, his wife, to Samuel G. Silen, Aug. 24, 1954, 'five dollars and other good and valuable considerations': the 3013 lot with the same description as in the Minor deed (row above), 'being the same lot of ground and premises which were transferred and conveyed to the said Charles F. Obrecht and Alice F. Obrecht, his wife, in fee simple, by Deed dated December 20, 1943 ... Liber M.L.P. No. 6544, Folio 521, from John E. Minor and Edythe Minor, his wife', and 'which by original lease, dated the 20th day of December, 1943 ... was demised and leased by Charles F. Obrecht and Alice F. Obrecht, his wife, unto John E. Minor, his personal representatives and assigns, for the term of Ninety Nine (99) Years, renewable forever, at and for the annual rent of One Cent ($.01), payable yearly, if demanded, on the 20th day of December'. 'To Have and To Hold the above granted property and particularly the aforesaid rent payable out of said lot, and the reversion thereto, unto the said Samuel G. Silen, his heirs and assigns forever, in fee simple; subject, however, to the estate, terms and interest of the said lessee, his representatives and assigns, under said lease.' Special warranty. What it settles: Samuel G. Silen (who later co-owned both lots with Irvin Silen, rows 39577 to 39581, 42365) bought the reversion and one-cent rent of 3013 on Aug. 24, 1954 and Max Silen bought the leasehold the next day (row above), so one family held both estates from Aug. 25, 1954; the Obrechts held the reversion for eleven years, from Dec. 20, 1943. Update Oct. 13, 2026: the Dec. 20, 1943 instruments that created the one-cent lease and this reversion are read (720:mdlr-mlp6544-521-minor-obrecht-sale-leaseback-3013-1943): Minor sold the lot to Obrecht, Obrecht leased it back at one cent and Minor mortgaged it back for $1,000 (released Feb. 18, 1946).

Deed, Baltimore County Court land records, Liber W.G. 102, folios 33 to 35 (MSA CE 66-152; read on the scan Jeff saved, pages 32 to 36; 32 is the end of a Howard to Cross lease and 36 opens a Pierpoint deed; the margin note beside the 1790 deed in W.G. E.E. 157 reads 'See Liber W.G. No. 102 folio 33', which is how this page was found). Index heading 'Thomas B. Onion & wife, Deed to James Carroll & Prudence Gough'. The recitals: Charles Ridgely, on or about Dec. 27, 1753, conveyed to his daughter Achsah Holliday and her heirs Huntington and a part of Ridgely's Whim (Liber B.B. No. 1 folio 210); Achsah married John Carnan, survived him, and by lease and release of Feb. 12 and 13, 1768 conveyed an undivided moiety of Huntington and of that part of Ridgely's Whim to John Ridgely and Charles Ridgely the younger, to her use for life and then to her daughter Elizabeth Carnan 'and to the heirs of her Body and for default of such heirs to the use of sundry other persons in remainder' (the release is read as B Q 503, filed on this property); Elizabeth married Thomas Bond Onion, and by their joint indenture of Feb. 24, 1790, for 1,400 pounds, assigned to Harry Dorsey Gough 'all the said Elizabeth's undivided half part of the said Tracts of land and all the Estate right and title of her and her said Husband therein and thereto' (W.G. E.E. 157); Gough then died, having by his will devised 'the said two moieties of Ridgelys Whim and Huntington to his Executors James Carroll and Prudence Gough of Baltimore County and their heirs in trust to sell and convey the same or such parts thereof as they should deem proper and to hold all such parts thereof as they should not so sell and convey in trust for Sophia Carroll daughter of the said Harry Dorsey Gough during her life and after her death in trust for such Children as she should leave living at the time of her death and their heirs in equal portions' (with the issue of a dead child taking its parent's share). Then: 'And whereas doubts are entertained whether the said Indenture from the said Thomas Bond Onion and Elizabeth his wife be sufficient and operative in law to pass the fee simple Estate of and in the Lands aforesaid and therein mentioned to the said Harry Dorsey Gough and the said Thomas Bond Onion and Elizabeth have therefore agreed to execute these presents for the purpose of conveying to the said James Carroll and Prudence Gough and their heirs a good and indefeasible Estate in fee simple of and in the said lands to and upon the trusts herein before and in the said Will recited and expressed.' 'Now This Indenture made on this sixth day of June in the year of our Lord one thousand eight hundred and nine' between Thomas Bond Onion and Elizabeth his wife of the one part and James Carroll and Prudence Gough of the other, for one dollar, they 'grant bargain sell release and confirm' to Carroll and Prudence Gough and their heirs 'all the said above described premises' with the reversion and remainders, to hold in trust 'to sell and convey in fee simple all such parts thereof as they or the survivor of them may think proper, and to receive the Purchase money therefor and to apply and dispose of it as in the said Will is directed', and for Sophia Carroll and her children as the will provides. Signed Tho. B. Onion and Eliza Onion (seals); acknowledged June 6, 1809 before Geo. Gould Presbury and Saml. Vincent, Elizabeth examined apart from her husband; received to be recorded June 10, 1809 and recorded the same day (Wm. Gibson, clerk). What it settles: the question the 1768 release and the 1790 deed left open (whether Elizabeth Carnan's moiety, limited to 'the heirs of her body' with remainders over, passed to Gough in fee) was raised in 1809 in terms: 'doubts are entertained', and the Onions, the only grantors to the deed, gave a confirmatory deed in fee to Gough's executors to remove them; the Carnan moiety therefore reached Gough's executors by a second route in June 1809. What it does not settle: whether the sundry remaindermen under the 1768 limitation joined or were barred (the deed names no one but the Onions), and whether the 1809 deed cured the title of buyers who had already bought from Gough and Prudence under the 1803 deeds (Jackson, Biays, Smith: W.G. 74/327, 330, 334, 337): it does not mention them, and its trust is for the unsold remainder.

Deed, Baltimore County Court land records, Liber W.G. 112, folios 467 to 469 (MSA CE 66-162; read on the scan Jeff saved, pages 466 to 471; 466 and the top of 467 are the end of Michael Warner's deed to the Vestry of St. Peter's Church, Oct. 27, 1810, unrelated; the instruments of 469 to 471 are the next two rows and Russell's deed of trust). Index heading 'William Jackson, deed to Elisha E. Russell'. William Jackson 'of the City of Baltimore in Baltimore county and State of Maryland Merchant' to Elisha E. Russell 'of the City County and state aforesaid Master Mariner', March 13, 1811, for 'four thousand Dollars lawful money of the United States': 'all that part of a tract of Land situate and lying in Baltimore County aforesaid and near to the said City of Baltimore called Huntington', 'Begining for the same part at a stone placed at the End of the north thirty six and a quarter degrees West ninety and one quarter perches line of that part of said tract which was on the thirteenth day of January Eighteen hundred and three conveyed by Harry D. Gough and wife to the said William Jackson', running 'bounding on said line reversely South thirty six and one quarter of a degree East thirty Eight perches and three tenths of a perch' (about 632 feet), then south 57 1/2 degrees west 9.6 perches, north 35 1/2 degrees west 35.2 perches 'until it intersects the second line of that part of said tract conveyed by Harry Dorsey Gough and wife to the said William Jackson at the distance of nine perches and sixtenths of a perch from the beginning stone', and on that line to the beginning, 'containing' a blank (the acreage was left unfilled in the record). With the buildings and improvements, 'the reversion and reversions remainder and remainders rents issues and profits', to Russell, his heirs and assigns forever; special warranty and further assurance. Signed Wm. Jackson (seal); acknowledged March 13, 1811 before two justices of the peace (Sam. H. Gatchell and Matthew Bennet), Mary Jackson, his wife, relinquishing dower; received to be recorded April 5, 1811 and recorded the same day (Wm. Gibson, clerk). What it settles: that William Jackson's 1803 lot (W.G. 74/337, 14a 3r) was already being cut by 1811, to a master mariner, for $4,000 (roughly 2 acres by the courses, 38.3 by 9.6 perches, my estimate; the sum is large for that, and the 'buildings' words are boilerplate); that Jackson was described as a merchant of the City while the 'tract of Land called Huntington' was still in Baltimore County; and that the beginning stone is the end of the 90 1/4-perch first line of Gough's deed to Jackson, so Jackson's 1803 courses are the frame for this strip. What it does not settle: where on the ground (the courses are tied to Jackson's deed, not to a road or a street), the area (blank), and whether the strip was ever built on. Russell borrowed against it the next day (a deed of trust to George I. Brown and William S. Hollins, March 14, 1811, $4,735 owed on account, opening on 471; not filed). Update Oct. 14, 2026: Russell put both lots in trust with Brown & Hollins the next day to secure $4,735 (726:mdlr-wg112-471-russell-trust-brown-hollins-1811). Update Oct. 14, 2026: this lot reached James Wilson on July 4, 1823, through the City Bank and James McCormick Jr. (726:mdlr-wg168-653-mccormick-james-wilson-russell-lots-1823).

Deed, Baltimore County Court land records, Liber W.G. 112, folios 469 to 471 (MSA CE 66-162; read on the scan Jeff saved; index heading 'James Biays, deed to Elisha E. Russell'; 471 then opens Russell's deed of trust to Brown and Hollins, not filed). James Biays 'of the City of Baltimore in Baltimore county and State of Maryland Merchant' to Elisha E. Russell, master mariner, March 13, 1811, for 'five hundred dollars lawful Money of the United States': 'all that piece or parcel of Land part of a tract of Land called Huntington', 'Beginning for the same part at a stone standing at the north East Corner of William Jacksons lot part of said tract and running thence and bounding on said Jacksons Lot South thirty six and an half degrees East eight and a half perches thence north thirty nine and three quarter degrees East twenty six perches and seven tenths of a perch to a road leading to Joseph Merryman's [the surname is written cramped, 'Meeryman's' or 'Moorymans'] thence bounding on said road north fifty eight and a half degrees West Eight and a half perches to the End of the north thirty nine and a half degrees East twenty four perches line of said James Biays's part of said tract and thence bounding on said line to the place of begining containing one Acre and forty seven perches of Land more or less'. With the buildings and improvements, the reversion and remainders, to Russell and his heirs; Biays's special warranty and further assurance. Signed Jas. Biays (seal), witness Matthew Bennet; acknowledged March 13, 1811 before two justices (Sam. H. Gatchell and Matthew Bennet), Sarah Biays, his wife, relinquishing dower; received to be recorded April 5, 1811 and recorded the same day (Wm. Gibson, clerk). What it settles: James Biays sold a small piece (1 acre 47 perches) of his Huntington ground to the same buyer, on the same day and recording, as William Jackson's strip, so Russell assembled roughly 3 1/2 acres of Huntington in March 1811 (my estimate from the courses) on the common line between the two men's lots; the Biays piece touches the north-east corner of Jackson's lot and a road 'leading to Joseph Merryman's', so the ground lies along a lane to the Merryman house (the lane's name is not given: this is the 'Merryman's Lane' question in the Edition 2 open list, and it fits a lane running from the turnpike toward the Merryman farm, not necessarily 33rd Street); and that Biays described himself in 1811 as 'of the City of Baltimore'. What it does not settle: which of Biays's 1803 lots (W.G. 74/330, the first lot of 1a 1r 7p; or W.G. 74/334, the second, 7a 2r 33p) the piece came from, the position on the ground, and whether the 1811 road is the lane that later became Vineyard Lane, Gilmor Lane or Merryman's Lane. Update Oct. 14, 2026: Russell's deed of trust of the next day is read in full (726:mdlr-wg112-471-russell-trust-brown-hollins-1811): this lot runs to 'a road leading to Joseph Merryman's'. Update Oct. 14, 2026: this lot reached James Wilson on July 4, 1823 (726:mdlr-wg168-653-mccormick-james-wilson-russell-lots-1823); the 1823 deed calls the road 'a road leading from Joseph Merrymans house to the turnpike road leading from the City of Baltimore towards York town'.

Mortgage, Baltimore County Court land records, Liber W.G. 141, folios 46 to 47 (MSA CE 66-191; read on the scan Jeff saved, pages 45 to 50; 45 is the end of an Adam Waltemeyer to Dr. Allen Thomas deed, 47 below the mortgage and 48 to 50 are other deeds: Bryson to Dorsey, 1815, and a Carrere mortgage to the Bank of the United States). Index heading 'James Biays, Mortgage to John W. Stump'. James Biays of the City of Baltimore to John W. Stump of the same place, Dec. 23, 1816, 'for and in consideration of the sum of thirty four hundred dollars current money of this State due and owing by the said James Biays to the said John W. Stump and for the better securing the payment thereof': 'All the following lots or parcels of land situate on or near the York Turnpike road in Baltimore County': (1) 'all that part of a tract of land called Ensors Inspection which was conveyed by James Edwards of Baltimore County to the said James Biays by deed bearing date on or about the third day of November ... one thousand eight hundred and four ... Liber W.G. No. 83 folio 371'; (2) 'all that part of one other tract of land called Huntington containing seven acres two roods and thirty three perches more or less which was conveyed to the said James Biays by Harry Dorsey Gough and Prudence his wife by deed bearing date on or about the thirteenth day of January ... eighteen hundred and three ... Liber W.G. No. 74 folio 334'; and (3) 'all that lot or part of the aforesaid tract of land called Huntington which was conveyed by Dorathy Brown executrix of Jesse Brown [containing two acres and fifteen sixteenths of an acre] to the said James Biays by deed of assignment bearing date on or about the second day of September Eighteen hundred and nine ... Liber W.G. No. 104 folio 48'. To hold to Stump, his heirs and assigns, 'in the same right and estate as he the said James Biays held and enjoyed the same provided nevertheless that if the said James Biays shall on or before the twenty third day of December Eighteen hundred and eighteen well and truly pay or cause to be paid unto the said John W. Stump his heirs executors administrators or assigns the aforesaid sum of thirty four hundred dollars and Interest thereon then this deed and every thing therein contained shall cease and be null and void'. Signed Jas. Biays (seal), witnesses John Hanna and S. H. Gatchell; acknowledged Dec. 23, 1816 before S. H. Gatchell and Matthew Bennet; received to be recorded May 21, 1817 and recorded the same day (Wm. Gibson, clerk). What it settles: that the 7a 2r 33p Huntington lot Gough sold Biays in 1803 (W.G. 74/334, row 726:mdlr-wg74-334-gough-biays-second-lot-1803) was whole and in his hands in December 1816, as security for $3,400 owed to John W. Stump (a John W. Stump is a trustee of the McFadon trust in 1822 and a grantor in the 1844 Mumma deed: the same name, probably the same man, so Stump would be a long-time Biays creditor and co-trustee); that Biays then also held an Ensor's Inspection lot from James Edwards (1804, W.G. 83/371, a new hop) and a 2-acre-and-fifteen-sixteenths Huntington lot bought from Jesse Brown's executrix on Sept. 2, 1809 (W.G. 104/48, a second new hop). The mortgage does not list the 1a 1r 7p 'first lot' (W.G. 74/330) or any piece of the 1811 Russell sale (W.G. 112/469), so those had left his hands by 1816 (an inference from what the mortgage lists). What it does not settle: whether Biays paid in 1818 (no release is among the pages read) and where the three parcels lie on the ground. Update Oct. 13, 2026: the third parcel, 'two acres and fifteen sixteenths of an acre ... deed of assignment ... Liber W.G. No 104 folio 48', is read in its 1847 sale: Walter T. Allender, trustee, to John Leitzinger, June 10, 1847, a leasehold under Gough's lease to Jesse Brown (W.G. 54/156), bounded by the York Turnpike on the west and the Old York Road on the east, 35 perches long (A.W.B. 381/475, 720:mdlr-awb381-475-allender-trustee-leitzinger-huntington-leasehold-1847). It lies EAST of the turnpike, between it and the Old York Road. Update Oct. 13, 2026: the Edwards deed this mortgage cites is read (714:mdlr-wg83-371-edwards-biays-1804, W.G. 83/371, Nov. 3, 1804).

Deed, Baltimore City land records, Liber S.C.L. 5328, folios 111 to 112 (MSA CE 168-5336; read on the scan Jeff saved, pages 111 and 112: it opens at the foot of 111 under the index heading 'William H Flayhart Jr &c, Deed to' with the number 100, and ends on 112 above an unrelated assignment of mortgage, West North Avenue Savings and Loan to Welsh Construction Company; the first lines on 111 after the heading are cut off in the scan, so the grantee names and the consideration are read from the habendum and the recital). William H. Flayhart Jr. and Catherine B. Flayhart, his wife, of Baltimore City, dated Oct. 5, 1932: the 3020 corner lot with the same description as the deed of the same day to them (36 feet on the west side of Greenmount Avenue from the south side of Vineyard Lane, formerly Gilmor Lane, 76 feet 4 inches west, 38 feet north, 76 feet 6 inches east, 'the improvements thereon being known as No 3020 Greenmount Avenue'). 'BEING the same lot of ground which by deed of even date herewith and intended to be recorded among the Land Records of Baltimore City immediately prior hereto was conveyed by the said Charles T Leight and wife to the said Grantors.' To hold 'unto and to the proper use and benefit of the said Charles T Leight and Ella B Leight his wife as tenants by the entireties their assigns the survivor of them and the survivors heirs and assigns in fee simple'. Special warranty and further assurance. Signed William H. Flayhart Jr. and Catherine B. Flayhart (seals), witness Lennox B. Clemens; acknowledged Oct. 5, 1932 before Lennox B. Clemens, Notary Public; recorded Oct. 7, 1932 at 2:41 P.M. (Stephen C. Little, clerk), one minute after the deed to the Flayharts (2:40 P.M.). A grantee-index stamp on the facing page reads 'MAR 22 1935'. What it settles: the two deeds of Oct. 5, 1932 are one transaction: Charles T. Leight, who held 3020 alone after his mother Susan's death, conveyed it with his wife Ella to Charles's daughter Catherine and her husband, and they conveyed it straight back to Charles and Ella as tenants by the entireties; the Flayharts held title for the minute between the two recordings. That is why the 1953 deed to the Rashbaums (row 42211) recites 3020 as 'conveyed by William H. Flayhart, Jr. and wife to Charles T. Leight and Ella B. Leight ... S.C.L. 5328, folio 111', and why Charles T. Leight, widower, could sell it in 1953. It is the same device as the 3010 lot's pass through Lula Smith the year before (rows 46089 and 46090). What it does not settle: the consideration, and why the pass-through was made (the deeds do not say). Update Oct. 13, 2026: the two 3020 parents recited in S.C.L. 5328/110 are read: W. Harry Holmes to Susan and Charles T. Leight, May 1, 1919, a straw round trip (S.C.L. 3361/216, 719:mdlr-scl3361-216-holmes-susan-charles-leight-1919), and Mary Clemens, widow, to them, June 9, 1924, merging the $9 rent (S.C.L. 4210/380, 719:mdlr-scl4210-380-mary-clemens-leight-3020-merger-1924).

Deed, Baltimore City land records, Liber J.F.C. 2008, folios 87 to 89 (MSA CE 168-12326; the scan Jeff saved opens on 89, the last page of this deed, so the parties' opening, the consideration and the list of lots are on 87 and 88, not pulled; pages 90 to 92 are the next deed, the row below, and 93 is an unrelated cancellation of a lease). Read on 89: the habendum, 'unto and to the proper use and benefit of the said Straw Man, Inc., it's successors and assigns ... in fee simple'; the special-warranty covenants; signed Jerome Silbiger and Lillian Silbiger (seals), witnessed by Melvin C. Paul; acknowledged Dec. 28, 1965 before Melvin C. Paul, Notary Public, whose address is typed under his signature as 2958 Greenmount Avenue; recorded Dec. 28, 1965 at 2:10 P.M., Liber J.F.C. 2008 page 87 (James F. Carney, clerk). That it conveys 2958 and the other ten lots is read from the next deed, whose last line recites 'a Deed of even date herewith and recorded or intended to be recorded among the Land Records of Baltimore City immediately prior hereto was granted and conveyed by Jerome Silbiger and Lillian Silbiger, his wife unto Straw Man, Inc.' What it settles: the Silbigers, who held 2958 by the 1960 and 1961 deeds as tenants by the entireties, deeded it with ten other lots to a corporation named Straw Man, Inc. Mortgage, Baltimore City land records, Liber S.C.L. 5497, folios 148 to 149 (MSA CE 168-5505; read on the scan Jeff saved to the foot of 149: the end of the mortgage, its acknowledgment and its recording stamp are on 150 and after, not pulled; index heading 'Fletcher L Vinson Mtge To R Benson Phelps', with a margin note 'Order filed 3/13/35' in a later hand). Fletcher L. Vinson of Baltimore, mortgagor, to R. Benson Phelps, mortgagee, dated Dec. 18, 1934, securing $1,000.00 'for money this day loaned and advanced', repayable $350.00 at four years, $350.00 at five and $350.00 at six, 'with interest on all of said payments at the rate of 6% per annum payable semi-annually', anticipation permitted on interest days. He grants and assigns the 15-foot lot of 3015 'for all the residue of the term of years yet to come and unexpired therein with the benefit of renewal thereof from time to time forever subject to the payment of the annual rent of one hundred and twenty ($120.00) dollars', with a power of sale under Chapter 123 of the Laws of Maryland of the January session of 1898 and Article LXVI of the Code of 1904, E. The 1944 buy-back (row 42030, about $2,000 by stamps) paid Phelps for the rent. What it does not settle: the rest of the mortgage, when it was released, and the $1,000's relation to the 1934 price of the lot ($3,600 on Sept. 18, 1934, S.C.L. 5481/414).

Lease, Baltimore City land records, Liber R.O. 1728, folios 284 to 286 (MSA CE 168-1736; read on the scan Jeff saved, pages 283 to 287: 283 is the end of a Maryland Building and Loan Association deed of two Milton Avenue lots; 287 is Jane C. For 99 years from the date, rent sixty dollars 'in even and equal half yearly instalments accounting from the fifteenth day of April' 1898, over and above taxes; distress; re-entry if the rent is sixty days in arrear and, at six months or a year, as if the lease 'had never been made'; on ten dollars as a renewal fine the lessors to give a new 99-year lease on the same rent 'so that the demise hereby created may be renewable and renewed from time to time forever'. Signed Augustus D. Clemens Junior, Mary Clemens and Jacob H. Aull, witness John J. Dunn; acknowledged April 14, 1898 before John J. Dunn, Justice of the Peace; recorded the same day (Robert Ogle, clerk). What it settles: the lot 123 ft 5 in to 156 ft 5 in south of the two-mile stone, 33 ft on the avenue, is the lot of 3019, and the lease the 3017 description bounds itself on ('the southwest corner of the lot leased by Augustus D. Clemens, Jr. and wife to Jacob H. Aull', 1909, 1951, 1961 and later) is this one: it was made April 14, 1898, four days before the Fink deed for the 14-foot lot to the south of 3015. Clemens Jr. leased the 3019 ground at $60 a year and deeded Henry D. Konig the rent the same day (next row, R.O. 1728/286); the whole is cut from Shepard G. Deed, Baltimore City land records, Liber R.O. 1728, folios 286 to 287 (MSA CE 168-1736; read on the scan Jeff saved: the deed opens at the foot of 286, just under the acknowledgment and recording stamp of the Aull lease, and ends on 287, where an unrelated assignment, Jane C. Rowe to William L. Batchelor, begins). Index heading 'Augustus D Clemens Jr &c Deed to Henry D Konig'. Augustus D. Clemens Jr. and Mary Clemens, his wife, of Baltimore County, to Henry D. Konig of Baltimore City, April 14, 1898, 'in consideration of one thousand dollars', in fee simple: the same 33-foot lot of the Aull lease, 123 feet 5 inches south of the two mile stone, 'Being a part of the ground described in a deed from Shepard G Miller to said Augustus D Clemens Jr dated December 20th 1897 and recorded ... Liber R O No 1710 folio 153 &c', 'Together with the improvements thereon ... and especially the clear yearly rent of sixty dollars issuing out of said lot by virtue of a lease thereof from said Augustus D Clemens Jr and wife to Jacob H Aull of even date herewith and intended to be recorded prior hereto', to hold 'in fee simple subject to the leasehold interest created by the above mentioned lease but with the right to collect' the rent, payable half-yearly on the 15th of April and October. Special warranty. Signed Augustus D. Clemens Junior and Mary Clemens, witness John J. Dunn; acknowledged April 14, 1898 before John J. Dunn, Justice of the Peace; recorded the same day (Robert Ogle, clerk). What it settles: Clemens Jr. leased the lot at $60 and sold the right to the $60 for $1,000 (6 percent) to Henry D. Konig on the same day, so the reversion of 3019 was Konig's from April 14, 1898. This is the common Baltimore pattern (lease out, sell the rent) and it is what the 1934 Vinson and Norris deeds do again at 3015. What it does not settle: how the rent ended, and what became of Konig's reversion.

Deed, Baltimore City land records, Liber R.O. 1710, folios 153 to 154 (MSA CE 168-1718; read in full on the scan Jeff saved, pages 151 to 155: 151 to the top of 153 are Joseph Peters's mortgage to the Loyola Perpetual Building Association; the deed opens on 153 under the index heading 'Shepard G. Miller Deed to Augustus D. Clemens Jr' and ends at the top of 154; 154 and 155 are Clemens's mortgage, next row). Sheppard G. Miller, unmarried, of Baltimore City, to Augustus D. Clemens Jr. of Baltimore County, Dec. 20, 1897, 'fifty three hundred dollars', his heirs and assigns forever in fee simple: 'all that lot of ground situate in Baltimore city', 'Beginning for the same on the East side of the York Turnpike Road at the Southwest corner of a lot of ground formerly belonging to William Baden and running thence bounding on said York Turnpike Road South six degrees west two hundred and fourteen feet' [the next words are cut at the page edge in the scan], north 89 degrees east 8 feet 6 inches to the northwest side of the Old York Road, 'thence bounding on the Northwest side of the Old York Road two courses and distances viz North thirty one and one half degrees East ninety nine feet and North twenty one and one half degrees East ninety five feet to a post at the Southeast corner of the lot formerly belonging to William Baden and thence bounding thereto North sixty one degrees West eighty two feet to the place of beginning. Being the same lot described in a deed from William H Bayless trustee to said Shepard G. Miller dated September 2nd 1896 and recorded ... Liber R.O. No 1637 folio 49 &c'. With the improvements; special warranty. Signed Shepard G. Miller (seal), witness John J. Dunn; acknowledged Dec. 20, 1897 before John J. Dunn, Justice of the Peace; received for record Dec. 20, 1897 at 3:50 P.M. and recorded the same day (Robt. Ogle, clerk). What it settles: the 'Keller' of the 1902 Rahe deed and of Corridor's earlier rows is Shepard G. Miller (spelled Sheppard on the page), and his deed is at R.O. 1710/153, not 1710/105; it is the parent ground of the 1898 Fink deed (3013), the Aull lease and Konig deed (3019), and the Rahe deed of 1902 (3015) and the 3017 lot, each of which says it is 'a part of the ground conveyed by Shepard G. It is a wedge between the turnpike and the Old York Road, 214 feet on the turnpike, bounded north by William Baden's former lot, and its first line is about 75 feet longer than the 139 feet 6 inches from the north line of 3019 to the fork (arithmetic from the stone-measured distances of the 1898 deeds, so the Miller ground probably ran about 75 feet north of the Aull lot, taking in the lots now numbered above 3019: an inference). Miller is 'unmarried' here and 'widower' in the 1898 recitals. Clemens paid $5,300 and mortgaged the same ground the same afternoon (next row). It also names the first source back: William H. Bayless, trustee, to Miller, Sept. 2, 1896 (R.O. 1637/49), a new hop. What it does not settle: whose trust Bayless executed (William Baden's former lot adjoins it on the north and the 1889 plat letters the tip 'Miss Tredway, Jno. T. Ensor Guardian'), and how much of the ground north of 3019 Clemens kept. Update Oct. 13, 2026: the 'Bayless, trustee' source it recites is read (720:mdlr-ro1637-49-bayless-miller-1896, R.O. 1637/49): a trustee's deed under the Circuit Court decree of June 25, 1896 in Miller v. Harrison (Alice M. Harrison and N. Waldo Harrison, defendants), the sale of July 27, 1896 at $4,950. It recites no earlier deed and no County instrument.

Mortgage, Baltimore City land records, Liber R.O. 1710, folios 154 to 155 (MSA CE 168-1718; read in full on the scan Jeff saved; index heading 'Augustus D. Clemens Jr &c Mtge to Loyola Perptl Bldg Ass', index 92). Augustus D. Clemens Jr. and Mary Clemens, his wife, of Baltimore County, to the Loyola Perpetual Building Association of Baltimore City, Dec. 20, 1897: Clemens, a member, has received 'an advance of Four thousand dollars on thirty two shares of stock standing in his name being the full par value' of them 'when fully paid up and completed'; they grant 'all that lot of ground' beginning on the east side of the York Turnpike Road at the southwest corner of the former William Baden lot, south 6 degrees west 214 feet 'with irregular depth to the Old York Road', 'Being the same lot described in a deed from Shepard G. Miller to said Augustus D Clemens Jr dated of even date herewith and intended to be recorded prior hereto', to hold in fee simple, provided that if the mortgagors perform the covenants the mortgage is void; they covenant to pay 25 cents a week as dues on each of the 32 shares and 15 cents a week on each as interest or premium until the shares are paid up, to pay ground rents, taxes and assessments, and to keep the improvements insured for at least $2,500; with a decree to be passed under Sections 692 to 704 of Article 4 of the Public Local Laws on three consecutive months' default. Signed Augustus D. Clemens Junior and Mary Clemens (seals), witness John J. Dunn; acknowledged Dec. 20, 1897 before John J. Dunn, Justice of the Peace, Francis P. K. Walsh, the Association's President, swearing the consideration; recorded Dec. 20, 1897 at 3:50 P.M. (as read; the Miller deed carries the same time) and the same day (Robt. Ogle, clerk). What it settles: Clemens bought the Miller ground with building-association money: $4,000 of the $5,300 price came from the Loyola Perpetual Building Association, secured on the same ground, and Mary Clemens signed with him; that is the first lien on the ground from which he then cut 3011 to 3019 in 1898 to 1903 (the Aull lease, the Konig rent, the Fink and Rahe deeds, the Willis lease). What it does not settle: how the mortgage was released or divided as the lots were sold (none of the 1898 deeds mentions it).

Deed, Baltimore City land records, Liber R.O. 1637, folios 49 to 50 (MSA CE 168-1645; read in full on the scan Jeff saved, pages 47 to 51: 47 and 48 are other instruments, a Herring mortgage and Slonaker's assignment to Kendall; the deed opens on 49 under the index heading 'William H. Bayless Trustee Deed to Shepard G. Miller', a later hand noting 'grantee 11-10-96', and ends on 50, where a Safe Deposit and Trust Company release to Frank W. Trimble follows). William H. Bayless of Baltimore City, trustee, to Shepard G. Miller of the same city, Sept. 2, 1896. It recites a decree of the Circuit Court of Baltimore City dated June 25, 1896, passed in a cause between Shepard G. Miller, complainant, and Alice M. Harrison and N. Waldo Harrison, defendants, appointing Bayless trustee with authority to sell 'the real estate in the proceedings in said cause mentioned'; that he sold it, 'after complying with all the previous requisites of the decree', on or about July 27, 1896 to Miller 'for the sum of forty nine hundred and fifty dollars'; that the sale was reported to, ratified and confirmed by the court and the purchase money paid; and that the decree authorizes him to execute the deed. The property: 'Beginning for the same on the east side of the York Turnpike Road at the southwest corner of the lot belonging to William Baden', south 6 degrees west 214 feet on the turnpike, north 89 degrees east 8 1/2 feet to the west side of the Old York Road, north 31 1/2 degrees east 99 feet 'to a post', north 21 1/2 degrees east 95 feet 'to a post at the southeast corner of Wm Badens lot', and north 61 degrees west 82 feet to the beginning (the courses of the Miller to Clemens deed of Dec. 20, 1897, which was written from this one). For $5 Bayless grants Miller, his heirs and assigns, the property 'and all the right title interest and estate of the parties to the aforesaid decree both at Law and in equity in and to the same'. Signed William H. Bayless, trustee (seal), witness Robert C. Rhodes; acknowledged Sept. 2, 1896 before Robert C. Rhodes, Justice of the Peace; received for record Sept. 2, 1896 at 2 o'clock P.M. and recorded the same day (Robt. Ogle, clerk). What it settles: Miller did not buy the ground at arm's length from an owner; he was the complainant in a suit against Alice M. Harrison and N. Waldo Harrison and bought the property at the trustee's sale the court ordered (in a suit where the complainant takes the property, the usual shape is a foreclosure or a creditor's bill, but the deed does not say which, and it does not say what the Harrisons' interest was). The $4,950 sale price is $350 below the $5,300 Miller took from Clemens fifteen months later, and the deed names no earlier owner, no earlier deed and no County instrument: the Miller to Clemens deed's 'R.O. 1637/49' is a trustee's deed, not a chain of title. The tract's County-era title therefore has to be reached through the Harrisons (how Alice M. and N. Waldo Harrison came to hold it) or through William Baden's adjoining lot (the northern neighbour, named in both deeds as 'the lot belonging to William Baden'), not through this deed. What it does not settle: the Harrisons' source, the nature of the suit (the equity papers and docket), and whether Miller held a mortgage on the ground; the grantee-index stamp 'grantee 11-10-96' is a later indexing note, not a second recording. The 1889 plat's 'Miss Tredway, Jno. T. Ensor Guardian' is not mentioned here, so the Tredway link (row 42366) is not supported by this deed.

Deed, Baltimore County Court land records, Liber W.G. 160, folios 580 to 581 (MSA CE 66-210; read on the scan Jeff saved, pages 580 to 584: the foot of 580 is the end of a Rogers, Donaldson and Emory deed to Richard Caton, acknowledged Aug. 8, 1821; this deed opens in the lower half of 580 under the index heading 'Samuel Moale & James Biays Deed to John McFadon' and ends on 581; the next deed, row below, follows it on 582). Samuel Moale, trustee for the sale of the property in a Chancery decree of Feb. 2, 1819 (John Bolte, J. and E. Schultze, Rudolph Wagler and others, complainants, against James Biays, defendant), and James Biays, of Baltimore City, to John McFadon, April 26, 1821. The decree ordered a sale of the ground Biays had mortgaged to Bolte on Feb. 4, 1813; Moale sold it at public auction at Patrick Allison's auction room on July 28, 1819, in lots shown on a plat made for the sale. This deed conveys Lot No. 1, 'part of a tract of Land called Ensors Inspection': 'Beginning for the same at a Stone marked B it being the beginning of the Ground mortgaged by the said James Biays to John Bolte', running north 40 1/2 degrees east 27 perches 'to the York Turnpike Road', then southerly on the turnpike about 34 perches (the figure reads thirty-four and a half) until it meets a line the clerk wrote as 'the Green line' of the whole mortgaged ground, and back along that line to the stone, 'Containing one acre three quarters and thirty Square perches'. Biays was the highest bidder for it at $1,450, subject to the dower of his wife Sarah Biays, and directed Moale to convey it to McFadon, which Biays joins in doing. Signed Saml Moale, trustee, and Jas. Biays (seals), witnesses R. H. Moale and John F. Harris; acknowledged April 26, 1821 before two justices; received to be recorded Aug. 14, 1821 (Wm. Gibson, clerk). What it settles: McFadon's first source for the ground his 1822 deed of trust describes is read. The lot-1 beginning stone 'B' is the beginning stone of McFadon's 1822 trust ground (W.G. 165/492, row 46094), so Lot No. 1 and the 1822 ground start at the same stone and the same first line (north 40 1/2 degrees east to the York Turnpike), which crosses the road. The courses (from the stone on the south-east side of the lane, 27 perches north-east to the turnpike, then south along it) suggest Lot 1 lies on the west side of the turnpike, south of the toll-gate lane, where the 1844 Mumma lot (A.W.B. 354/374, row 46070) is; that is an inference from the courses, not a statement in the deed. Why the five lots came to McFadon: James Biays bought Lot 1 at the sale of his own mortgaged ground and assigned the bid; the other lots are in the next deed. What it does not settle: where on the modern grid any lot lies; the figure after 'thirty four and a half perches' is not certain. Update Oct. 13, 2026: the mortgaged ground is read (719:mdlr-wg122-133-biays-bolte-mortgage-1813): stone B stands 'on the south east side of a road leading from the land of Hugh Thompson into the york turnpike road at or near the gate', the road later called Gilmor Lane; the ground was the 'Walker's Tavern' parcel, conveyed to Biays by Christopher Walker about July 14, 1809 (W.G. 104/46). Update Oct. 17, 2026 (archive lead): the Archives' chancery index lists the Bolte suit as S512-1-501 (Aug. 30, 1816, John Bolte, John E. Schultz, Rudulph Vogelar v. James Biays, 'Mortgage foreclosure on Ensors Inspection', accession 17,898-450-1/3, 1/35/5, Chancery Record 109 p. 354); an outside addendum's 'S512-501' is a truncation of that ID. Not read (719:msa-leads-ensors-inspection-s512-1-501-c295-3272-2026-10-17).

Deed, Baltimore County Court land records, Liber W.G. 160, folios 582 to 584 (MSA CE 66-210; read on the scan Jeff saved: it opens on 582 under the index heading 'Samuel Moale Deed to John McFadon' and ends on 584, where an Isaac Green mortgage to John Cugle follows). Samuel Moale, trustee in Bolte et al. v. Biays, to John McFadon, April 26, 1821, the second of the pair (the first, Lot No. 1, is the row above). Lot No. 2, 'part of a tract of Land called Ensors Inspection' and so numbered on the trustee's plat: 'Beginning for the same at a Stone standing at the end of the north sixty nine degrees west thirty five perches line of the Land mortgaged by James Biays to John Bolte ... and for the corner of a Lot of Ground belonging to the Quaker Society and running south fifteen degrees west twenty two perches and nine tenths of a perch to Henry Starrs lane thence bounding on said lane south eighty four degrees west fifteen and a half perches to the York Turnpike Road thence northerly bounding on said road' [to the stone, the line continued across the page edge], 'Containing three acres and twenty Square perches of Land more or less with the Tavern and other improvements thereon erected', sold to McFadon, by the bid of Edward Perine, for $3,000, 'subject to the right of Dower of Sarah Biays' and 'to a County road that runs as it is said through a corner of this Lot to intersect the York Turnpike road'. Lot No. 3 ('Beginning ... north sixty nine degrees west two perches from the Stone the beginning of Lot number Two', north 32 degrees east 12 perches, north 67 degrees west 21 perches to a lot owned by Captain Chaytor, and so back along the first line of the mortgaged ground to the turnpike, 8 perches 'to Lot number Two'): 'one acre two quarters and sixteen Square perches ... with the brick building and two frame buildings on the road which are subject to a lease of twenty-two years (as read) from the twenty sixth day of May eighteen hundred and nineteen and at thirty two dollars each per annum', sold by the bid of William Bromwell Junior for $1,400, subject to dower, to that lease and 'to a County road that runs as it is supposed through the front of this Lot to intersect the York Turnpike road'. Lot No. 4 (six acres two quarters and thirty-four perches, bounded by Captain Chaytor's lot, a 'Grant's addition', Lot 3 and the first line of the mortgaged ground) and a further parcel of Lot 4 and Lot 5 (nine acres one quarter and twenty perches, with 'a claim set up to Lot number five by Robert Gorsuch Esq.') were sold to McFadon 'subject to the several claims and supposed incumbrances before particularly mentioned', the prices not certain on the page; the deed then conveys 'all those aforegoing Lots pieces and parcels of Land numbers Two, Three, Four and Five' together to McFadon, his heirs and assigns forever. Signed Saml Moale (Trustee); acknowledged April 26, 1821 before two justices; received to be recorded Aug. 14, 1821. What it settles: the five parcels McFadon's 1822 trust deed says Moale conveyed to him in two deeds of April 26, 1821 are Lots 1 to 5 of the ground Biays mortgaged to Bolte, sold at a Chancery sale on July 28, 1819; they lie in Ensor's Inspection, the east-side lots (2 to 5) bounded by the Quaker Society's lot, Henry Starr's lane, Captain Chaytor's lot, 'Grant's addition' and a County road that crosses the turnpike frontage, with a Tavern on Lot 2 and a brick building and two frame buildings on the road on Lot 3. That is a lead for the east-side lots at the fork, not a placement: the deeds name no street, no modern lot and no number, and the 1897 and 1896 deeds of the Miller ground (R.O. 1710/153, 1637/49) do not cite them. What it does not settle: whether the 'County road' of Lots 2 and 3 is the Old York Road, where Henry Starr's lane and the Quaker lot were, and the prices and exact bounds of Lots 4 and 5. Update Oct. 13, 2026: the 'Quaker Society' lot that bounds Lot 2 also appears in 1847 as 'the Quaker Lot' on the south-east of Jacob Aull's 2 a 29 P bought from the four Biays couples (A.W.B. 381/479, 720:mdlr-awb381-479-bowerman-aull-bond-1847), beside the Vestry's lot and Leitzinger's 77 1/2 perches (A.W.B. 381/477, 720:mdlr-awb381-477-bowerman-leitzinger-1847): the same name on the same Biays ground. Same lot, not proved. Update Oct. 17, 2026 (archive lead): the case is S512-1-501 in the Archives' chancery index (Chancery Record 109 p. 354); Moale's sale plat of July 28, 1819 may be in that file. Not read (719:msa-leads-ensors-inspection-s512-1-501-c295-3272-2026-10-17).

Deed, Baltimore County Court land records, Liber A.W.B. 359, folios 136 to 137 (MSA CE 66-409; read on the scan Jeff saved, pages 136 to 140: the top of 136 is the end of a different instrument; it opens under the index heading 'John W. Stump Trustee Deed To Nancy Hoke &c' and ends on 137 above Samuel Griscom's grant of a right of way to Thomas Galloway; 138 to 140 are other instruments). John W. Stump, surviving trustee, 'of Harford County' [struck, 'now of the City of Baltimore' interlined], to Nancy Biays (now the wife of Jacob Hoke), Frances J. Biays (now the wife of Henry Hammond), Elizabeth Biays (now the wife of Henry N. Bowerman) and Hannah Jane Biays (now the wife of Doctor Walter T. Allender), Oct. 28, 1845. It recites McFadon's deed of trust of April 11, 1822 (W.G. 165/492) to Stump and Philip G. Biays, for Sarah Biays for life and then for her four daughters; that Philip G. Biays and Sarah Biays are both dead; and that Stump executes the deed 'for the more fully and completing the object and intent of the trust'. For $5 he conveys to the four daughters, their heirs and assigns, 'all that part of a tract of Land situate lying and being in Baltimore County ... commonly called or known by the name of Ensors Inspection', by the same metes as the 1822 deed ('Beginning ... at a Stone standing on the South East side of a road leading from the land of Hugh Thompson into the York Turnpike near the gate the said stone being marked with the letter B', north 40 1/2 degrees east to the turnpike 'and with the same course across the said road to the distance of ninety four perches and three quarters of a perch from the beginning', the Foster to Walker line of 'on or about the fourth March 1800', south 59 east 41 perches, south 19 west 9 1/4, and so on to the Quaker Society's lot and Henry Starr's lane and James Biays's lot), 'being the same land which was by two several Indentures bearing date respectively on the twenty sixth day of April in the year Eighteen hundred and twenty one Conveyed in five several parcels by Samuel Moale to the said John McFadon' (W.G. 160/580 and 582). Signed Jno. W. Stump; acknowledged Oct. 28, 1845 before G. D. Spencer and T. Hanson Belt, justices of the peace of the City; received Nov. 5, 1845 at 10 minutes before 10 A.M. and recorded the same day (Wm. A. W. Bradford, clerk). A later margin note beside the index heading ('W. T. Allender, 6 [?] May 184[?]') is not read. What it settles: the trust of 1822 was executed on Oct. 28, 1845, after Sarah Biays's death (after the 1844 Mumma deed, which she signed) and Philip G. Biays's: the four daughters took the whole ground in fee. The partitions that follow in the Tract Index (Hoke, Hammond, Bowerman and Allender to Wilson, Leitzinger, Heavey and Brady, A.W.B. 381 to 404, 1847 to 1848) are their sales, so the Biays-heirs ground passes to the people on the 1844 to 1849 plats and in the deeds on file (Wilson, Mumma, Allender to Brady) from here. What it does not settle: where any of the later lots lie. Update Oct. 13, 2026: Allender, one of the four sons-in-law who took under this deed, sold Samuel Brady 19 a 38 P of Ensor's Inspection on Nov. 30, 1848 (A.W.B. 404/533), by a trustee's deed under his own 1847 Chancery suit against William Jackson and others; it recites the 1801 to 1804 Biays deeds (714:mdlr-awb404-533-allender-brady-1848). Update Oct. 13, 2026: the four couples' first small sales under this deed are read: John Leitzinger, 8 1/2 and 77 1/2 square perches, June 10, 1847, $500 (A.W.B. 381/477, 720:mdlr-awb381-477-bowerman-leitzinger-1847), and Jacob Aull, 2 a 29 P by bond of conveyance of May 1, 1847 (381/479, 720:mdlr-awb381-479-bowerman-aull-bond-1847); both recite this deed (A.W.B. 359/136). Update Oct. 14, 2026 (late): the daughters sold James Wilson the 85-perch triangle at the turnpike and Gilmor's Lane in 1847 (725:mdlr-awb382-43-hoke-biays-daughters-james-wilson-toll-gate-triangle-1847).
