Deed, Baltimore County Court land records, Liber A.W.B. 404, folios 533 to 535 (MSA CE 66-454; read in full on the scan Jeff saved, pages 533 to 537: the top of 533 is the end of another instrument; the deed opens on 533 under the index heading 'Walter T. Allender, Trustee, Deed to Samuel Brady' and ends on 535, where a lease follows and runs on to 536; 537 holds a second lease). Walter T. Allender, of the City of Baltimore, trustee, to Samuel Brady of Baltimore County, dated Nov. 30, 1848. It recites a cause 'lately depending in Baltimore County Court sitting as a Court of Equity wherein Walter T. Allender the above named trustee and wife were Complainants and William Jackson and others were defendants', in which it was 'on or about the Second day of April ... eighteen hundred and forty seven' decreed that the property be sold and Allender appointed trustee; that on May 1, 1847 he sold at public auction the land described, Samuel Brady the highest bidder at $6,700; and that the sale was reported to and ratified by the Court of Chancery. For $1 Allender conveys 'all that piece or parcel of land being part of the tract of land called Ensors Inspection': 'Beginning for the same at a Stone heretofore planted on the West side of the Baltimore and York Turnpike road marked J.B. on one side and E. on the other which said Stone stands on the Second line of the land conveyed by James Edwards to James Biays on the third day of November ... eighteen hundred and four', north 86 degrees west 36 4/10 perches to another stone marked J.B. and E., south 35 1/2 degrees west 17 1/10 perches to a white oak, south 53 degrees west 5 1/2 perches, north 45 degrees west 29 1/2 perches to a stone on the east side of a road two perches wide, 'being the beginning of the land conveyed by Samuel Smith and others to James Biays' on May 30, 1801, then on that road north 42 3/4 degrees east 72 perches, south 81 degrees east 27 perches to the Baltimore and York Turnpike Road, and 'running and bounding on said road south three and one half degrees west fifty three and one half perches to the beginning, Containing Nineteen acres and thirty eight square perches'. It is 'the land conveyed by Samuel Smith and others to James Biays' (May 30, 1801, W.G. 67/447), 'also the land conveyed by James Maydwell to James Biays' (Sept. 26, 1801, W.G. 67/63 as read; the Tract Index has 67/62), 'also the land conveyed by John Gorsuch to William Jackson and others in trust' (May 10, 1803, W.G. 76/243), 'also the land conveyed by James Edwards to James Biays' (Nov. 3, 1804, W.G. 83/371, the folio written 381 and corrected above), 'and also a part of the land conveyed by Christopher Walker to James Biays' (March 9, 1801, W.G. 66/519), 'the greater portion of the above described land being also the land conveyed by James Biays to William Jackson and others in trust by deed dated the fourth day of February ... eighteen hundred and two' (W.G. 72/319), with the buildings and improvements, to Brady, his heirs and assigns forever. Signed Walter T. Allender, trustee (seal), witnessed by two men whose names read as Henry F. Friese and John J. Snyder; acknowledged Nov. 30, 1848 before two justices of the City, who are the same two names that witness it; received to be recorded Dec. 1, 1848 at about 12:07 P.M. (as read) and recorded the same day (Wm. A. W. Bradford, clerk). What it settles: the Tract Index entry 'Allender to Brady, 19 a. 38 Pr., A.W.B. 404/533' is this deed, and it is the first County instrument that puts a Brady on a named tract west of the turnpike: Samuel Brady bought, at a Chancery sale in 1847 brought by Walter T. Allender and his wife (presumably Hannah Jane Biays Allender, one of the four Biays daughters of the 1822 trust, though the deed does not name her) against William Jackson and others, 19 acres 38 perches of Ensor's Inspection which James Biays had assembled between 1801 and 1804 (five County deeds, all named by liber and folio) and put in trust for Jackson in 1802. The ground has 53 1/2 perches (about 882 feet) of frontage on the west side of the turnpike. Why it is filed on 2958 as probable and not verified: the deed names no street, no lot and no neighbour on the turnpike; the placement rests on the west side of the turnpike, the frontage, and the 1877 plan's 'Saml. Brady Est.' on the west side south of the toll gate (Edition 2, ch. 04), and the identity of this Samuel Brady with the mayor (1789 to 1871, the Brady Mansion at 2900 Greenmount) is not stated in the deed ('of the County'). What it does not settle: the 1801 to 1804 deeds themselves (not pulled; W.G. 66/519 is the Walker to Biays deed Bouldin abstracts), where the beginning stone lies, and how Brady's 19 acres became the 'about 8 acres on the York road' of his will. Update Oct. 13, 2026: the Chancery suit that produced this sale (Allender and wife v. William Jackson and others, decree April 2, 1847, sale May 1, 1847) also sold John Leitzinger the Huntington leasehold east of the turnpike, between it and the Old York Road, for $587.50 (A.W.B. 381/475, 720:mdlr-awb381-475-allender-trustee-leitzinger-huntington-leasehold-1847). Deed, Baltimore County Court land records, Liber A.W.B. 381, folios 477 to 479 (MSA CE 66-431; read in full on the scan Jeff saved, pages 477 to 481: the top of 477 is the end of another instrument, see below; this deed opens on 477 under the index heading 'Henry N. Bowerman, wife & others, deed to John Letzinger' and ends on 479, where the second instrument, the Aull bond, begins). Dated June 10, 1847; acknowledged the same day before John W. Stump and J. Hanson Bell, two Justices of the Peace for the City, each wife examined apart from her husband; the $500 receipted on p. 478 and the deed received to be recorded June 14, 1847 at 2 p.m. (P. A. W. Bradford, Clerk). Grantors: Henry N. Bowerman and Elizabeth his wife, Walter T. Allender and Hannah Jane his wife (both of Baltimore), Jacob Hoke and Nancy his wife and Henry Hammond and Frances his wife (both of Harford County): the four couples who took the Biays ground under the trustee's deed of Oct. 28, 1845 (A.W.B. 359/136, row 46130), which the deed recites twice by liber and folio. Grantee: John Leitzinger (the clerk writes Letzinger; the Tract Index has Leitzinger). Price $500. The deed conveys 'all that part of Ensor's Inspection' within two parcels. First parcel: begins on the east side of the York Turnpike Road at the south-west corner of a parcel 'now owned by the said Letzinger', runs along the turnpike south 5 1/2 perches, then 3/10 of a perch to the west side of the Old York Road, up the west side of the Old York Road (north 30 1/2 degrees east, distance not legible) and closes on a 3 1/10-perch line (the record writes East for that last course; it must be West to close): 8 1/2 square perches, a wedge between the two roads. Second parcel: begins at the north-west corner of the lot the same parties conveyed to the Vestry of St. John's Church by a deed of Sept. 27, 1844, runs on the east side of the road north 32 1/2 degrees east 8.2 perches, south 81 1/4 degrees east 10.4, south 17 degrees west 6.3 to the corner of the Church Lot, and back along it north 87 1/2 degrees west about 12 perches: 77 1/2 square perches. Together 86 square perches, which is the Tract Index's 'Bowerman to Leitzinger, 8 1/2 Pr. + 77 1/2 Pr., 381/477' (row 46123). What it settles: the Tract Index entry is this deed; the four couples were selling the Biays ground in small lots by June 1847; the deed puts a wedge between the turnpike and the Old York Road inside Ensor's Inspection. At the wedge's south end the two roads are 3/10 of a perch (about 5 feet) apart, and its turnpike side is 5 1/2 perches (90 ft 9 in), with an area of 2,314 square feet: the shape and place of the fork's tip. Thompson's 1889 ward plat gives the tip lot at the fork 88 ft on the York Road (chapter 06), the same order, which is suggestive and nothing more. Leitzinger already owned ground that touches the wedge's north-west corner; the instrument that ends at the top of p. 477 is a $1 conveyance from Walter T. Allender, trustee, to Leitzinger with rent or tax language ('over and above all deductions for taxes and assessments'), whose opening is on p. 476 or earlier and is not pulled. What it does not settle: which lots today are these. The deed names no street, no lot number and no neighbour that can be tied to the 1889 plat; nothing read links the wedge to 3011 or 3013, or the second parcel to any property, and whether the Vestry's 'Church Lot' of 1844 is the ground of 3009 (property 718, where the church's cornerstone was laid April 22, 1847) is not shown. Next: the beginning of the Allender-to-Leitzinger instrument (A.W.B. 381/476, or earlier), the Vestry's deed of Sept. 27, 1844, and the chain from Leitzinger forward (City or County grantor index under Leitzinger, 1847 to 1888). Bond of conveyance, Baltimore County Court land records, Liber A.W.B. 381, folios 479 to 481 (MSA CE 66-431; read in full on the scan Jeff saved: the bond begins at the foot of 479 under the index heading 'Henry N. Bowerman, wife & others, Bond of Conv. to Jacob Aull' and ends on 481, where an unrelated instrument, George L. Melleman's assignment to George Phelan dated June 14, 1847, begins and is not read). It is not a deed. The four couples of the Leitzinger deed (Bowerman, Allender, Hoke, Hammond, with wives) bind themselves to Jacob Aull for $1,500, dated May 1, 1847, to convey him 2 acres 29 square perches 'part of the Land which was conveyed by John W. Stump Surviving trustee to Elizabeth Bowerman and others' on Oct. 28, 1845 (A.W.B. 359/136, row 46130). The price was $750: Aull paid $250 on delivery of the bond (receipted May 1, witnessed by J. Hanson Bell) and gave two $250 notes at nine and eighteen months, 'the amount of purchase money yet due'; the $1,500 penalty is twice the price. Until the deed is made he takes the rents and profits. Acknowledged June 10, 1847 before Stump and Bell with the wives examined apart, and received to be recorded June 14, 1847 at 2 p.m., the same time as the Leitzinger deed. The lot begins on the east side of the Old York Road at the end of the 8.2-perch line of the lot 'purchased from the parties by a certain John Letzinger' (the second parcel of the Leitzinger deed, so Aull's ground is immediately north of it), runs along the road north 21 1/4 degrees east about 10 perches, south 77 1/4 degrees east about 27 perches to 'the outline of the Land belonging to the heirs of James Biays' (the four daughters, as heirs of James and Sarah Biays), south 28 1/4 degrees west 16.9 perches to 'the Quaker Lot', along the north line of the Quaker Lot north 66 1/4 degrees west about 5 perches to its north-west corner, north 81 1/4 degrees west about 9 perches to the north-east corner of the Vestry's lot, and by Leitzinger's lot north 17 degrees east 6.3 perches and north 81 1/4 degrees west to the beginning (the tenths of several perch distances are hard to read in the scan and are not given here). What it settles: the County side of the ground east of the Old York Road in June 1847, in order from the south: the Vestry's lot (deed of Sept. 27, 1844), Leitzinger's 77 1/2 perches, Aull's 2 acres 29 perches; the Biays heirs' ground on the east; and 'the Quaker Lot', the Quaker Society's lot that the 1821 Moale deeds also name on the east boundary of Lot 2 beside Henry Starr's lane (row 46129): the same name on the same ground, so the 1847 parcels lie in or beside the ground of Moale's Lots 2 to 5 (Tavern, brick building), which the chapter for 3011 and 3013 carries as an unproven lead. What it does not settle: where any of this lies on today's grid, or whether it touches 3011. The Tract Index lines read (row 46123) list no Aull deed, so the deed that completed the bond was either not entered under this tract's name or not found. Next: the Aull deed (grantor index under Bowerman, Allender, Hoke or Hammond, 1847 to 1849), the Vestry's 1844 deed, and a plat. Update Oct. 13, 2026: Leitzinger's lot 'purchased from the parties herein first above mentioned' is the second parcel of the Bowerman deed (720:mdlr-awb381-477-bowerman-leitzinger-1847); his other ground, the 2 a 15/16 Huntington leasehold between the turnpike and the Old York Road (whether it adjoins these parcels is not shown), came from Allender as Chancery trustee on the same day (A.W.B. 381/475, 720:mdlr-awb381-475-allender-trustee-leitzinger-huntington-leasehold-1847). The Grantee Index 1848-49 (CE 32-17 p. 24) lists it as 'Aull, Jacob from Henry N. Bowerman &c, lot on York road 2a 29P'.

Trustee's assignment, Baltimore County Court land records, Liber A.W.B. 381, folios 475 to 477 (MSA CE 66-431; read in full on the scan Jeff saved, pages 473 to 476 plus a second copy of 476; 473 is the end of a release, Hertzog to Hahn; 474 and the top of 475 an assignment of a Jefferson Street lease, Humphreys to Baer; this instrument opens at the foot of 475 under the index heading 'Walter T. Allender, Trustee, Assignt to John Letzinger', fills 476 and ends at the top of 477, where the Bowerman deed to Leitzinger follows). Dated June 10, 1847; acknowledged the same day before John W. Stump and J. Hanson Bell; received to be recorded June 14, 1847 at 2 p.m. (P. A. W. Bradford, Clerk). Allender, appointed trustee by the Baltimore County Court sitting in equity (decree of April 2, 1847, in the suit Walter T. Allender and Hannah Jane his wife v. William Jackson and others, the suit that also sold Samuel Brady 19 a 38 P west of the turnpike, row 46149), advertised and sold at auction on the premises on May 1, 1847; John Leitzinger was the highest bidder at $587.50 with interest, paid it in full, and the sale was ratified in June (the day is blank). The trustee assigns Leitzinger 'all that part of a tract of Land called Huntingdon', 2 acres and 15/16 of an acre: it begins in the middle of the York Turnpike where the first line of the parcel named first in 'a Lease from Harry Dorsey Gough and Prudence his wife [and] Job Merryman to Jesse Brown', recorded W.G. 54/156, crosses the road; runs along that line south 82 degrees east 15.9 perches to a stone on the west side of the Old York Road; down the old road south 7 3/4 degrees west 30.7 perches; south 79 1/2 degrees west 11.7 perches to the middle of the York Road; and straight back to the beginning. It is a leasehold: the unexpired term of Gough's lease, renewable forever, which Dorothy Brown, executrix of Jesse Brown, assigned to James Biays on Sept. 2, 1809 (W.G. 104/48), at a yearly rent of 4 pounds 8 shillings 1 penny currency (about $11.75), over and above taxes and assessments. The Biays heirs' side (the four daughters, who are the Bowerman, Allender, Hoke and Hammond couples of the Leitzinger deed) is cleared of all claim by the decree. What it settles: (1) the 'W.G. 104/48' that Biays's 1816 mortgage to John W. Stump recites as the third parcel (row 46103; 'two acres and fifteen sixteenths of an acre') is this lot, and W.G. 54/156, which the Tract Index carried as an unread instrument, is the Gough lease behind it (Gough and Prudence with Job Merryman to Jesse Brown): the County chain of the ground between the turnpike and the Old York Road is Gough's lease (W.G. 54/156; its date is not recited), Jesse Brown, Brown's executrix to James Biays in 1809, the Chancery sale of 1847 in the suit Biays's daughters and their husbands brought, Leitzinger. (2) Where it lies: a strip between the York Turnpike (west, the middle of the road) and the Old York Road (east), 15.9 perches wide at its north line and 11.7 at its foot, and some 35 perches (about 570 ft) long: the ground between the two roads, in Huntington, east of the turnpike. The same-day Bowerman deed to Leitzinger (row 46151) puts an 8 1/2-perch Ensor's Inspection wedge at the very tip of the fork (the roads 3/10 of a perch apart at its south end, 3.1 perches apart at its top) 'at the south west corner of a parcel of land now owned by the said Letzinger'. Whether that parcel is this leasehold is not shown, and the widths argue against it unless the old road bends: this lot is 11.7 perches wide at its foot, the wedge only 3.1 at its top, so some ground lies between them (about 24 perches at a 20 degree opening, my estimate from the courses). All the ground is Leitzinger's by June 1847 either way, in three pieces: the tip, the lot above it that he already owned, and this leasehold. What it does not settle: which of today's lots (3011, 3013, 3015, 3017 or others) lie in either piece, because the deed names no street or neighbour that reaches the 1889 plat; the lengths along the turnpike (about 570 ft for this lot and 91 ft for the wedge) and the widths are the evidence to hold against the lot frontages in the City chains. Next: Leitzinger's own deeds out (grantor index CE 33 for 1847 to 1849 and the County sales after), the Biays heirs' 1845 deed (A.W.B. 359/136), the original lease (W.G. 54/156) and the Chancery file Allender v. Jackson (the plat and the report of sale). Update Oct. 13, 2026: the Vestry's deed of Sept. 27, 1844, the head of the Church Lot, is T.K. (A.W.B.) 349 folio 45, entered January 1845 in the Grantor Index (718:mdlr-ce33-15-p50-bowerman-vestry-st-johns-tk349-45). Update Oct. 14, 2026: the 1809 assignment is read (720:mdlr-wg104-48-dorothy-brown-biays-huntington-leasehold-1809): 2 15/16 acres between the centre of the turnpike and the west side of the Old York Road, 30.7 perches along the old road, under Gough and Job Merryman's 1798 lease to Jesse Brown, £4 8s 1d. Update Oct. 14, 2026: Litzinger bought the fee and rent of this leasehold from Oliver P. and Araminta Merryman in 1865 (720:mdlr-jhl46-149-oliver-merryman-litzinger-brown-lease-fee-1865). Update Oct. 16, 2026 (Litzinger deeds): the parcel the wedge deed starts from is not this leasehold: it is Litzinger's 1841 land from John W. Stump and others (T.K. 315/188), recited with the wedge in his 1864 deed to John W. Treadway (G.H.C. 39/499), the 214-ft parent lot of 3011 to 3019. This leasehold lies north of it: Litzinger cut it into the Blum half-acre (J.H.L. 45/362, 1865; fee 1871, E.H.A. 70/80), John H. White's half-acre (J.H.L. 48/502, 1866) and Jacob Aull's north 260 ft (J.H.L. 46/520, 1865), all read.

Index entry, Baltimore County Land Records, Grantor Index 1844 to 1845 (MSA CE 33-15, page 50, 'Bo cont'd', read on the scan Jeff saved, pages 50 to 59; the grantor index lists every deed by the first-named grantor, with the grantee, the kind of instrument, a one-line description and the liber and folio). Under January 1845: 'Bowerman, H. N.; Bowerman, Elizabeth &c' to 'Vestry of St. John's Church, Huntingdon, Balto. County', 'Deed', 'Lot of ground on the York Road', folio 45; the liber is a ditto mark under the 349 of the line above, so T.K. 349 folio 45 (the T.K. and A.W.B. books are one series: the Mumma deed that the 1912 turnpike deed cites as 'T.K. 354' is A.W.B. 354/374). The 1847 deed of the same four couples to John Leitzinger names 'the Lot of Ground conveyed ... to the Vestry of St Johns Church by deed bearing date the 27th September 1844' as the Church Lot at the head of his 77 1/2-perch parcel and at the foot of Jacob Aull's 2 a 29 P (rows 46151 and 46152 on 3011): this entry is that deed, dated Sept. 27, 1844 and entered in January 1845, so the Vestry's own title comes from the Biays couples, the grantors of the Stump trustee's deed of Oct. 28, 1845 (A.W.B. 359/136, row 46130); the order is odd (the lot was conveyed a year before the trustee executed the 1822 trust) and is what the deed itself should explain. What it settles: the Church Lot is a private deed of a lot on the York Road to the Vestry from the Biays couples (the 1844 federal sale of the Barracks to the Gibsons, which the National Register form describes, is a separate conveyance). What it does not settle: whether the lot is the present ground of St. John's at 3009 (the parish's first services were in 1843 to 1844 and the cornerstone was laid April 22, 1847, which fits), and which road 'the York Road' is. The deed, T.K. 349 folios 45 to 49 (MSA CE 66-399), is loaded in Chrome for Jeff to save and is not read. Update Oct. 13, 2026: the deed is read (718:mdlr-awb349-45-biays-couples-vestry-st-johns-1844): Sept. 27, 1844, $1,200, one acre, 209 by 208 ft on the east side of the York Turnpike, from the McFadon trust ground, recorded Jan. 31, 1845.

Deed, Baltimore County Court land records, Liber T.K. (A.W.B.) 349, folios 45 to 47 (MSA CE 66-399; read in full on the scan Jeff saved, pages 45 to 49: the deed opens at the foot of 45 under the index heading 'Sarah Biays & others, deed to The Vestry of St. John's Church, Huntingdon, Baltimore County', fills 46 and ends with its acknowledgments on 47, where Benjamin Hart's deed to Lemuel Wetherell follows; 48 and 49 are other instruments). Dated Sept. 27, 1844. Grantors: Sarah Biays, Henry N. Bowerman and Elizabeth, Walter T. Allender and Hannah Jane, Jacob Hoke and Nancy, Henry Hammond and Frances and John W. Stump (all of Harford County), and Philip G. Biays of Montgomery County: the life tenant, her four daughters and their husbands, and both trustees of the McFadon trust, so the whole interest is conveying. Grantee: the Vestry of St. John's Church, Huntingdon, Baltimore County. Price $1,200. The lot: begins 200 feet from the north side of 'a lane known as the [Gerker?] Lane' (the name is hard to read), runs east at right angles with the York Turnpike 209 feet, north parallel with the turnpike 208 feet, west at right angles 209 feet and south binding on the turnpike 208 feet to the beginning: 'one acre more or less' (209 by 208 feet is 43,472 square feet, 0.998 acre), 'part of the ground conveyed by John McFadon to John W. Stump and Philip G. Biays in trust' on April 11, 1822 (W.G. 165/492, row 46094). To the Vestry and their successors 'to be for ever kept and used as and for the site of a Protestant Episcopal Church', with covenants of further assurance. Acknowledged in Baltimore on Sept. 27, 1844 before J. Hanson Bell and O. P. Merryman, two Justices of the Peace (the wives examined apart); Philip G. Biays acknowledged in Montgomery County on Oct. 9, 1844 before Richard Ricketts and Wm. S. Beckwith, certified by John A. Carter, clerk of that court; received to be recorded Jan. 31, 1845 at 10 minutes before 5 p.m. and recorded the same day. What it settles: the church ground is a one-acre lot that fronts the York Turnpike on its east side, cut from the McFadon trust ground that the 1822 deed names Ensor's Inspection, for $1,200 (the sum Scharf gives; the $12,000 in the National Register form and the Gibson family's purchase belong to the Barracks, the old federal building, which this deed does not mention). It is the 'Church Lot' of the 1847 Leitzinger deed and Aull bond (rows 46151, 46152): their parcels begin at its corners. Its west side binds on the turnpike for 208 feet, its north line is 209 feet (12.6 perches), and a lane lies 200 feet south of its south-west corner. What it does not settle: the lane's name and place on today's grid, and whether the present ground of 3009 is exactly this acre (the parish held the church, cemetery and rectory as separate pieces in 2023). Update Oct. 14, 2026 (night): the Bouldin papers hold a St. John's vestry list folded with a June 1844 survey of 20,000 sq ft by the eastern gate post (718:msa-c2843-15-p77-st-johns-huntingdon-vestry-list-gate-post-lot-1844), and Bouldin's notes of Apr. 19, 1847 give the church lot as '208 feet square' beside the Leitzinger wedge (718:msa-c2843-15-p106-bouldin-field-notes-1847-04-19).

Deed, Baltimore City Superior Court land records, Liber S.C.L. 3692, folios 300 to 301 (MSA CE 168-3700; read in full on the scan Jeff saved, pages 300 to 305: the deed opens at the head of 300 under the index heading 'Lulie H. Wallace, deed to James M. Sinclair' and ends at the top of 301; the instruments after it on 301 to 305, Parks to Levy, Levy's mortgage, Ripple to Ripple and Bachmann's mortgage, are unrelated). Dated Jan. 6, 1921 and acknowledged the same day in Washington before the notary Alfred H. Mori; received for record Jan. 18, 1921 and recorded the same day (Stephen C. Little, Clerk). Grantor: Lulie H. Wallace, a widow of Washington. Grantee: James M. Sinclair. Price $1,250. The lot: begins on the east side of the York Turnpike 204 ft 7 in south of the two-mile stone in front of the Waverly Methodist Episcopal Church lot (281 ft 2 in south of the north side of Bateman's Alley, a four-foot alley), runs south along the turnpike 58 ft 4 in to the south-west corner of the whole ground of which it is a part, north 89 degrees east 8 ft 6 in to the north-west side of the Old York Road, up that side north 31 1/2 degrees east 66 ft, and west 42 ft 4 in to the beginning. It is, word for word in its measurements, the 'firstly described' 3011 lot of the 1995 deed (S.E.B. 4810/135) and the 1954 mortgage (M.L.P. 9513/64). 'Being the same lot of ground which by lease dated April 18th 1898 and recorded ... in Liber R.O. No. 1730 folio 92 &c. was demised by Augustus D. Clemens Jr. and wife to Jacob H. Aull for the renewable term of ninety nine years', rent $75 a year in half-yearly installments on May 1 and November 1; Wallace's title is the deed of William Hall Wallace to her dated April 1, 1907 (R.O. 2320/441). She conveys 'especially the right to collect the rent', in fee, to Sinclair 'to the end and intent that the leasehold interest created by the lease aforesaid shall be forever merged and extinguished': the leasehold was already Sinclair's, so the sale of the reversion ended the ground rent in 1921. What it settles: the chain behind the Sinclair holdings of the tip: Clemens Jr. leased the 3011 lot to Jacob H. Aull on April 18, 1898 (the day of the Clemens-to-Fink deed of the 3013 lot, R.O. 1729/241); the leasehold passed to Sinclair by Clemens's 1906 assignment (R.O. 2292/410, loaded for Jeff, not read) and the reversion, by way of William Hall Wallace and Lulie H. Wallace, in 1921: the 'Lulie H. Wallace's deed of the 3011 reversion' of the chapter's hop list. It also shows the lessee of 1898, Jacob H. Aull, bore the name of the Jacob Aull who bought the 2 a 29 P north of Leitzinger from the Biays couples in 1847 and 1848 (rows 46152 and the 1848 deed): a son or grandson is likely and no document read says so. The $75 rent of 1898 ended with this merger. The $66 rent on 3011 that every deed from 1954 to 2017 carries is a different, later lease (made Aug. 2, 1954, row 46095), and the 1927 deeds treat 3011 as fee simple (row 46110). What it does not settle: how the ground came to Clemens Jr. (the Miller deed of 1897 and the Baden, Tredway and Ensor lines remain the route above him) and where the rent of 1921 to 1927 went after the Sinclairs' 1927 pass-through (rows 46110, 46111). Update Oct. 14, 2026: the reversion's earlier holders are read: Clemens to Lulie H. Wallace (Apr. 18, 1898, the end of the deed on R.O. 1730/92, probable), Lulie to William Hall Wallace (Aug. 11, 1898, R.O. 1748/566), and back to Lulie (Apr. 1, 1907, 720:mdlr-ro2320-441-william-hall-wallace-lulie-wallace-3011-reversion-1907). The 1898 Aull lease is read (720:mdlr-ro1730-92-clemens-aull-lease-3011-1898): $75, May and November.

Trustees' deed, Baltimore City Superior Court land records, Liber R.O. 2290, folios 225 to 227 (MSA CE 168-2298; read in full on the scan Jeff saved, pages 225 to 230: the deed is 225 to 227, where Harvey's mortgage to the trustees begins and runs on through 230 and beyond, not pulled beyond 230). Dated Nov. 22, 1906; acknowledged the same day before the notary Harry L. Drake; received for record Nov. 22, 1906 at 1:35 p.m. and recorded the same day (Robt. Ogle, Clerk). Grantors: Richard H. Woollen, Howard P. Sadtler and S. Procter Brady, trustees; grantee James W. Harvey. Price $200,000: the deed recites the sale of Oct. 17, 1906, its ratification by the Circuit Court, and $30,000 paid, the $170,000 balance being secured by Harvey's mortgage of the same day. The decree it recites is NOT the Feb. 21, 1895 decree in Brady v. Sadtler that Corridor carries: it is a decree of May 23, 1899 in a cause between 'Martha A. Woollen et al., plaintiffs, and Nannie H. Stump et al., defendants' (Docket A 51-1899), by which the Court 'assumed jurisdiction of the trust created by the twelfth clause of the will of Samuel Brady, deceased' and appointed these three trustees to sell. The tract: bounded by Hunter Alley (west), the centre line of 28th Street, the centre line of Guilford Avenue, the centre line of 29th Street, the road formerly Gilmor Lane (the present Vineyard Lane) and an irregular line along the outline of the Brady land on W. H. Shipley's plat of March 1889 (the 1877 plan's 'Saml. Brady Est.') to 26th Street, a block of land between York Road and the lane, with the York Road frontage from 29th Street to 51 feet south of 28th Street among its edges. It excepts 'the seven brick houses on the York road' (built by John W. S. Brady on the land immediately adjoining the tract on the north, facing the York Road, with their land) and 'the lot at the northwest corner of York road and Twenty-ninth Street fronting fifty feet on York road'. Title: Gilmor to Samuel Brady, Apr. 24, 1849 (A.W.B. 412/283); Walter T. Allender, trustee, to Samuel Brady, Nov. 30, 1848 (A.W.B. 404/533, the Chancery sale read as row 46149: so the County deed the 2958 chapter reads is the root of this tract); Francis E. Yewell and wife to John W. S. Brady, trustee, Nov. 11, 1896 (R.O. 1647/561); and the Peabody Heights Company to the trustees, Feb. 24, 1906 (R.O. 2212/510). What it settles: (1) the 1906 sale of the Brady tract is the deed the Old Oriole Park dossier listed as an open item; it is to James W. Harvey, not 'Harvey & Son', and the price is $200,000. (2) The Brady estate sold in 1906 was in the hands of Woollen, Howard P. Sadtler and S. Procter Brady under the 1899 decree: Charles Herbert Sadtler and the 1895 decree are not named. (3) The ground behind the Allender-to-Brady deed (A.W.B. 404/533) was still the Brady estate's in 1906, with the 'seven brick houses on the York road' just north of it: the row of about 1900 that the 2958 chapter carries as an inference. (4) 'Gilmor lane' is the old name of Vineyard Lane, the lane at the corner of 3026. What it does not settle: which of the seven brick houses are today's 2900 block lots (the deed gives no numbers); the 1895 decree itself (Brady v. Sadtler), which is not recited; the 1899 decree's papers (Docket A 51-1899, Baltimore City Superior Court equity). Update Oct. 13, 2026: the first of the four title deeds recited here is read (2332:mdlr-awb412-283-gilmor-brady-1849): William Gilmor and wife Louisa A. to Samuel Brady, Apr. 24, 1849, A.W.B. 412/283, part of Huntington beginning at the large red oak, 12 acres 2 roods 19 1/5 perches, $3,500, recorded Apr. 28, 1849. The recital's date, book and folio are right. Update Oct. 14, 2026: both deeds it recites are read: Yewell to John W. S. Brady, 1896 (half the bed of Gilmor's Lane north of 29th, formerly Holmes, Street; 714:mdlr-ro1647-561-yewell-brady-trustee-gilmor-lane-bed-1896) and the 1906 exchange with the Peabody Heights Company between Calvert Street and Guilford Avenue (714:mdlr-ro2212-510-brady-trustees-peabody-heights-exchange-1906), which names the cause as Martha A. W. Woollen et al. v. Nannie H. Stump et al. Neither touches the Greenmount frontage.

Purchase-money mortgage, Baltimore City Superior Court land records, Liber R.O. 2290, opening at folio 227 and running through 230 (MSA CE 168-2298, pages 225 to 230; the mortgage continues past 230, so its acknowledgment, recording stamp and any release are not read). James W. Harvey, the buyer, mortgages the whole tract back to the three trustees for the $170,000 balance of the price: two notes, $10,000 due Oct. 17, 1907 without interest, and $160,000 due Oct. 17, 1909 at 5 percent from Oct. 17, 1908. He may prepay and have land released at the capitalization of $3.50 a front foot until 2,000 front feet are paid for and $3.00 after that, the front measured along Guilford Avenue, Barclay Street and the York Road to the centre lines of the blocks on 'said plat' (the W. H. Shipley plat of March 1889); the $10,000 note does not count toward the releases. The mortgage names the sale 'ratified on or about the 22nd day of November 1906'. What it settles: how the Brady estate was sold in lots: Harvey paid $30,000 down and bought the whole $200,000 tract on credit, with a release schedule by front foot, so that lots sold on from Harvey (such as Hanlon's, the same day, R.O. 2290/355) could be freed from the trustees' lien by paying the per-foot price; this is the mechanism behind 'Hanlon is sole owner' and the Harvey resales of 1907. What it does not settle: the release of Hanlon's lot (no release is on the pages pulled), the mortgage's later folios and the sale of the remainder of the tract.

Deed, Baltimore City Superior Court land records, Liber R.O. 2290, folios 355 to 356 (MSA CE 168-2298 p.355 to 360; the deed opens at 355 under the index heading 'James W. Harvey &c, deed to Edward Hanlon' and ends on 356, where the next instrument, Goldstein to Stockdale, begins; 357 to 360 are other deeds and mortgages of Nov. 22, 1906). Dated Nov. 22, 1906; acknowledged the same day before a notary; received for record Nov. 22, 1906 at 3:40 p.m. (two hours after the trustees' deed to Harvey, recorded at 1:35 p.m.) and recorded the same day (Robt. Ogle, Clerk). Grantors: James W. Harvey and his wife Maude T. Harvey; grantee: Edward Hanlon; price: 'five dollars and other valuable considerations', no sum. The lot: begins where the west side of the York Road meets the centre line of 29th Street, runs west along that centre line 390 ft 9 in to the east side of Barclay Street and 33 ft more to Barclay's centre, south along Barclay's centre line 541 ft to a point 40 ft 10 in south of the south side of 28th Street, east by a straight line 423 ft 9 in to the west side of the York Road, and north along the York Road 549 ft 3 in to the beginning: a block of ground of about 549 ft by 424 ft (roughly 5.3 acres by my count of the courses). It is 'part of the whole tract' the trustees sold Harvey the same day. What it settles: Ned Hanlon took the ballpark lot on Nov. 22, 1906, the same day as Harvey's purchase, not on Nov. 27 as the dossier and Corridor row 11603 have it, and the deed states no price (the roughly $50,000 is the newspapers' figure); the grantee is 'Edward Hanlon'. The Brady-Sadtler-Hanlon chain of the Old Oriole Park dossier is therefore closed at the deed: Brady estate trustees (R.O. 2290/225) to Harvey to Hanlon, all Nov. 22, 1906, and the lot lies south of the centre line of 29th Street, running down the York Road past 28th Street to 40 ft 10 in beyond it; the Harvey mortgage's release schedule at $3.50 a front foot (row on this property) is how Hanlon's lot would have been freed. What it does not settle: which ball ground this is on the ground (the 1901 American League Park, Oriole Park IV, or the grounds of the later park): the deed names only streets, York Road, Barclay Street, 28th and 29th Streets; the release of Hanlon's lot from the trustees' mortgage; and Hanlon's 1908 and 1909 transactions with the White syndicate and the Sadtler estate.

Deed, Baltimore City Superior Court land records, Liber M.L.P. 9513, folios 61 to 63 (MSA CE 168-9521; read in full on the scan, pages 61 to 63; page 61 is typed 'No Consideration'). Dated June 19, 1954, acknowledged the same day, recorded June 24, 1954 (M. Luther Pittman, Clerk). Elizabeth McC. West conveys Henry John Weber (of Baltimore County), Adam H. Weber and Raymond H. Plack (of Baltimore City), as tenants in common, in fee simple, the same 3011 lot by the same courses. Deed, Baltimore County Court land records, Liber A.W.B. 382, folios 30 to 32 (MSA CE 66-432; read in full on the scan Jeff saved, pages 30 to 34: the deed opens at the top of 30 under the index heading 'Jacob Hoke & wife & others, Deed to William T. What it settles: (1) the second of the two Wilson deeds that Keelty's lease-origin deed of 1907 recites (row 46084 begins 'at the end of the south forty six degrees east twenty two and four tenths perch line of the land described in a deed from Walter T. Allender Trustee et al to William T. Wilson senior dated January 19th 1848 ... A.W.B. No. 391 folio 169', and refers to 'the north 81 degrees west 27 perch line of the Allender deed'): both lines are read here word for word, so the 2958 lot's County title is now two deeds on the page rather than a recital. (2) The piece is 'lately sold' to Wilson in the 1847 deed (previous row): the May 1, 1847 auction came before the June 10, 1847 deed, and the Allender deed was only delivered in January 1848. The 1848 land and the 1847 land share their line of south 46 degrees east, 22.4 perches, ending on the turnpike. (3) Allender, as trustee under the one decree of about Apr. 2, 1847, sold more than this piece on May 1, 1847: the Brady deed of Nov. 30, 1848 (A.W.B. 404/533, rows 46124 and 46149) recites the same decree and the same auction day, with Samuel Brady the bidder at $6,700, so the Brady tract and the Wilson piece were two lots of one Chancery sale, deeded ten months apart. What it does not settle: the cause papers (Allender v. Jackson, not online), which would say what was being divided; the first deed on 168 (to James Wilson, the Gough ground of 1803), which is not read; and why Scott, not Wilson, bid. Update Oct. 14, 2026: the defendant 'William Jackson' is very probably the trustee (or his heirs) of James Biays's 1802 trust for Sarah Biays and her children (W.G. 72/319, read: 714:mdlr-wg72-319-biays-trust-sarah-biays-1802), which held Walker's 3 3/8 acres; the four Biays daughters were the children who took the remainder at Sarah's death, so the Chancery sale cleared the trustee's legal title (inference).

Deed, Baltimore County Court land records, Liber W.G. 66, folios 519 to 521 (MSA CE 66-116; read in full on the scan Jeff saved, pages 519 to 523: the deed opens at the foot of 519 under the index heading 'Christopher Walker, Deed to James Biays', after the end of George Foss's assignment of a leasehold to Benjamin Mason, and ends on 521, where Leah Knysly's deed to Peter Frank begins). Dated Mar. 9, 1801, acknowledged the same day before Abraham Van Bibber and Richard Britton, with Patience Walker, the grantor's wife, releasing her dower; received for record May 4, 1801 and recorded the same day (Wm. Gibson, Clerk). Christopher Walker, of Baltimore County, sells James Biays, of Fells Point, 'all that part of a Tract of land ... called Ensors inspection' for $900 current money. The bounds: beginning at a stone north 43 3/4 degrees east 62 perches from 'a bounded red oak tree said to be the Beginning tree of a Tract of land called Huntington'; north 43 3/4 degrees east 24 perches along 'a Road leading to intersect the York Turnpike Road'; south 47 1/4 degrees east 22.4 perches 'to a stone standing in the York Road'; along the road south 1 degree west 30 perches; south 75 degrees west 3.7 perches; north 28 degrees west 1 perch to a stone; north 9 1/2 degrees west 27.2 perches; south 75 1/2 degrees west 18.3 perches; and by a straight line to the beginning; 3 3/8 acres. No ground rent, no lease: an outright sale in fee, no prior title recited. What it settles: (1) the 1848 Allender deed to Wilson (previous rows) names this deed as the source of its land ('a part of the land conveyed by Christopher Walker to James Biays by the deed above referred to') and its second line, south 46 degrees east 22.4 perches to the turnpike, is the second line of this one (south 47 1/4 degrees east 22 4/10 perches 'to a stone standing in the York Road': the same line, the bearing read 47 1/4 degrees in 1801 and 46 in 1848). So the Wilson-Keelty-2958 lots are ground James Biays bought of Walker in 1801. (2) This is the Biays purchase the Spear deed of May 30, 1801 (next row) adjoins: the Spear land ends 'at the end of the last line of a parcel of land conveyed by Christopher Walker to the said James Biays'. (3) The land is fixed to the tree each deed calls the beginning tree of Huntington (a 'bounded red oak' here and in the Spear deed, a 'large red oak' in Gilmor's deed to Samuel Brady, A.W.B. 412/283): very probably one tree, so Ensor's Inspection and Huntington are tied together here. What it does not settle: how Walker got the 3 3/8 acres (no title is recited), where the red oak stood in terms of a present street, and what the 'Road leading to intersect the York Turnpike Road' became (Gilmor Lane, the later Vineyard Lane, is a candidate, not a reading). Update Oct. 13, 2026: Walker's own deed is read (719:mdlr-wg63-161-foster-walker-1800): John Foster to Christopher Walker, Mar. 4, 1800, 29 acres from a stone 62 1/2 perches north 42 east of the Huntington red oak; the 1801 parcel begins at that stone and closes on Foster's last two courses, so it is the south-western corner of Walker's 29 acres. Update Oct. 14, 2026: within a year Biays put this land into a trust for his wife Sarah for life, then their children (Feb. 4, 1802, W.G. 72/319, read: 714:mdlr-wg72-319-biays-trust-sarah-biays-1802), with William Jackson, Levin Jones and John Smith as trustees. The 1847 Chancery case that sold part of it to Wilson was against 'William Jackson and others'.

Deed, Baltimore County Court land records, Liber W.G. 67, folios 447 to 451 (MSA CE 66-117; read in full on the scan Jeff saved, pages 447 to 451: the deed opens at the foot of 447 under the index heading 'Samuel Smith & Margaret his wife, and others, Representatives of the late William Spear deceased, Deed to James Biays', after the end of a lease from William Morgan to Nathaniel Brown, and ends on 451, where Mary Ross's assignment to Robert Carter begins). Dated May 30, 1801, acknowledged the same day before W. Winchester, an associate justice of the County Court, the four wives examined apart from their husbands; received for record June 19, 1801 and recorded the same day (Wm. Gibson, Clerk). Grantors: Samuel Smith and Margaret, William Patterson and Dorcas, William Lee Forman and Jane, Joseph Spear and Barbara, 'the Daughters of William Spear deceased, late of Baltimore County, merchant'; grantee James Biays, merchant; price $790. The land: 'that part of a tract ... called ... Ensors Inspection' beginning 'at a Bounded Red oak tree (the Beginning of a tract ... called Huntington)'; south 47 degrees east 29 1/2 perches; north 50 degrees east 5.6 perches to a bounded white oak; north 33 3/4 degrees east 38 perches; north 70 degrees east 0.7 perch to the southwest corner of 'a Lot of ground which formerly belonged to John Gorsuch now the property of the said James Biays'; along that lot north 5 degrees 6 minutes west 27.1 perches 'to a stone standing at the end of the last line of a parcel of Land conveyed by Christopher Walker to the said James Biays'; along Walker's land north 52 1/2 degrees west 7.1 perches to the southeast side of a road, and along the road to the beginning; 9 7/8 acres. The title of the Spear daughters is not recited. What it settles: (1) James Biays had, by June 1801, assembled three adjoining pieces east of the Huntington red oak: the Gorsuch lot (not read here), Walker's 3 3/8 acres (previous row, bought Mar. 9, 1801) and these 9 7/8 acres of the Spear estate (May 30, 1801), all of Ensor's Inspection. (2) The Spear parcel starts at the very tree the Walker parcel is measured from (Walker's beginning stone is 62 perches north 43 3/4 east of it), and it closes on the end of Walker's last line, so the two fit together along a stone. (3) This is the Biays deed of the 'Brady route' of the next-hops list (W.G. 67/447); the others, 67/63, 76/243, 83/371 and 72/319, are not read. What it does not settle: how the Spear daughters took the land (William Spear's will or estate, not recited); the Gorsuch lot; and how the ground passed from Biays to Brady (the Brady title instead runs Gilmor 1849, A.W.B. 412/283, Huntington, and Allender 1848, A.W.B. 404/533, Ensor's Inspection). Update Oct. 14, 2026: William Spear also sold John Foster ground about Oct. 4, 1786, the source of Foster's 1800 sale to Walker and of the Walker's Tavern ground Biays bought in 1809 (719:mdlr-wg104-46-walker-biays-tavern-1809): both the Spear-heirs land and the tavern ground at the gate descend from William Spear. Update Oct. 14, 2026: the 9 7/8 acres went into James Biays's trust for Sarah Biays and their children on Feb. 4, 1802 (714:mdlr-wg72-319-biays-trust-sarah-biays-1802). Update Oct. 14, 2026 (night): the Spear title is probably Job Garretson's deed to William Spear of Feb. 3, 1781, 46 acres of Ensor's Inspection from a Huntington tree (714:msa-c2843-15-p68-garretson-spear-ensors-inspection-1781). Update Oct. 15, 2026: the grandchild's share followed on Oct. 24, 1801 (714:mdlr-wg72-226-nicholas-spear-heir-biays-ensors-inspection-1801): Philip N. and Mary Nicholas, John Spear's only child, for $20, the same courses; 'N 5.6 W' is 5 degrees 6 minutes.

Deed in trust, Baltimore City Superior Court land records, Liber S.C.L. 2445, folios 42 to 43 (MSA CE 168-2453; read in full on the scan Jeff saved, pages 42 to 46: the deed opens at the foot of 42 under the index heading 'James F. Bowersox &c, Deed to Alice E. Bowersox, Trustee' and ends on 43, after the end of a deed of the same date, John Novak and wife to Shepherd and Eliza D. Owens, a Hoffman Street leasehold). Dated Aug. 1, 1908, acknowledged the same day before Robert H. Carr, a Justice of the Peace (as read); received for record Aug. 25, 1908 at about half past three in the afternoon and recorded the same day (Stephen C. Little, Clerk). The grantors, James F. and Mary E. Bowersox, who took the lease of the 14-foot lot from James Keelty on Aug. 24, 1907 (R.O. 2363/423, row 46085), convey it for $1 to Alice E. Bowersox as trustee (she is also one of the five beneficiaries named), 'the owners of a certain lot of ground ... which is occupied by them and their children as a home', so that 'no interest therein can be conveyed by those having interests therein during the lifetime of said grantors except by joint consent'. The lot is described by the 1907 courses (402 ft 9 1/2 in north of the northwest corner of 29th Street and the York Road, 14 ft on the avenue, 100 ft to a ten-foot alley) and named 'the same lot of ground described in a lease from James Keelty, bachelor, ... dated August 24th 1907 ... R.O. No. 2363 folio 423'; it is held 'subject to the payment of the annual ground rent of sixty-five dollars payable on the first day of March and September'. The use: during the lifetime of James F. and Mary E. or the survivor, 'for the use and benefit of the family now constituted', named as James F., Mary E., Alice E., Archibald and Clarence V. Bowersox; after both parents' deaths, to the children absolutely, 'as tenants in common share and share alike'. Special warranty only. What it settles: the missing 1908 step of the Edition 2 chain, which had only the recital in the Butzler deed of 1919 (S.C.L. 3459/370, row 46082): the Bowersoxes put the leasehold into a family trust less than a year after Keelty's lease, with the trustee being the Alice who appears as 'Alice E. Brandt (formerly Bowersox)' in the 1917 and 1919 deeds (rows 46087 and 46082). It also settles who the beneficiaries were: five named family members, of whom the three children are Alice, Archibald and Clarence V. The restraint on alienation ('except by joint consent') is consistent with the 1919 deed to Clara Butzler being signed by the whole family (trustee, father, the children and their spouses). What it does not settle: to whom the $65 rent was owed (the deed holds the lot 'subject to' it and says no more; the Armour deed of 1932, S.C.L. 5289/183, next row, shows the reversion was by then Sarah Stanley Armour's); and the exact minute of recording.

Deed, Baltimore City Superior Court land records, Liber S.C.L. 5289, folios 183 to 186 (MSA CE 168-5297; read in full on the scan Jeff saved, pages 183 to 187: the deed opens in the middle of 183 under the index heading 'Sarah Stanley Armour &c, Deed to Henry Gerwig', after the end of a mortgage, and ends at the top of 186 with the acknowledgment taken at Cobourg, Ontario, and the recording stamp; 186 and 187 hold two later instruments, Cook and Jones, administrators of Marian J. M. Sims, to William L. Carter for a Vine Street leasehold, and Carter's mortgage back to the Adonis Building and Loan Association). Dated Mar. 12, 1932; acknowledged at Cobourg, County of Northumberland, Province of Ontario before T. K. Creighton, notary public; received for record Mar. 14, 1932 at 1:20 p.m. (Stephen C. Little, Clerk). Grantors: Sarah Stanley Armour (formerly Sallie H. Stanley) and her husband George Armour, of Cobourg; grantee Henry Gerwig, of Baltimore City, 'heretofore adjudged a lunatic', with William F. Gerwig as his committee ('Ex Parte in the matter of Henry Gerwig', Circuit Court No. 2 of Baltimore City, Docket 28 A folio 308), who by the Court's order of Mar. 10, 1932 was authorized to invest $4,516.67 of his funds in 'the four lots of ground hereinafter described together with the four annual ground rents issuing and payable thereout'. The four lots, all leasehold reversions: (1) 'No 2958 York Road', 14 by 100 ft, 402 ft 9 1/2 in north of the northwest corner of 29th Street, 'the same lot of ground described in a Lease from James Keelty to James F Bowersox and wife dated August 24th 1907 ... R O No 2363 folio 423', rent $65 a year, March and September, 'and BEING ALSO the same lot of ground described in a Deed from James G Stanley Trustee to the said Sarah Stanley Armour (she being therein named as Sallie H Stanley ...) dated November 4th 1908 ... SCL No 2460 folio 398'; (2) 4418 Wrenwood Avenue, $65 (Baltimore County lease of 1914); (3) 3624 Parkdale Avenue, $75 (1927 lease); (4) 502 East Lynn Street, $66 (1926 lease). The deed conveys each lot 'in fee simple ... subject however to the respective leasehold estates and terms of years' and the right to the four rents. What it settles: (1) who held the reversion, and so the $65 ground rent, of 2958 from late 1908 until 1961, as far as this deed goes: Sallie H. Stanley, by a trustee's deed of Nov. 4, 1908 (S.C.L. 2460/398), three months after the Bowersox trust and fourteen months after Keelty's lease; then Sarah Stanley Armour (the same woman, married, living at Cobourg, Ontario) until Mar. 1932; then Henry Gerwig, bought by his committee for his estate. (2) The fifteen grantors of the merger deed of July 15, 1961 (J.F.C. 1134/578, row 46088, which does not say who they were) are presumably Henry Gerwig's heirs: the 1965 lot list (next row) names the first grantor as Jacob F. Gerwig, widower, 'et al'. On that reading the reversion ran Keelty (before 1908) to a trustee, James G. Stanley, to Sallie H. Stanley (Armour), to Gerwig, to Gerwig's heirs, to the Silbigers, where it merged with the leasehold. (3) 2958 York Road is the first of four ground-rent lots bought together by a committee for a lunatic's estate, a purchase of four rents, not of four houses. What it does not settle: how the reversion went from James Keelty to James G. Stanley, trustee, before 1908 (S.C.L. 2460/398, not yet read); and who Henry Gerwig's heirs were beyond the names in the 1961 deed. Update Oct. 14, 2026: the gap is closed (714:mdlr-scl2460-398-stanley-trustee-sallie-stanley-1908): James Keelty sold the reversion to James G. Stanley, trustee, on Sept. 26, 1907 (R.O. 2371/148), and the trustee conveyed it to Sallie H. Stanley by court order on Nov. 4, 1908.

The opening pages of the Silbigers' deed to Straw Man, Inc., Baltimore City Superior Court land records, Liber J.F.C. 2008, folios 87 to 89 (MSA CE 168-12326, pages 85 to 88 on the scan Jeff saved: 85 and 86 are a different instrument, Straw Man, Inc.'s assignment of a Falls Road leasehold back to Jerome Silbiger, dated and recorded Dec. 28, 1965 at 2:11 p.m. (J.F.C. 2008/85); 87 and 88 are the deed's first two pages; 89 and the next deed were read earlier, rows 46105 and 46106). The deed, a printed fee-simple form stamped 'No title search performed, No consideration necessary' and 'Transfer tax not required', is dated Dec. 28, 1965; the grantee index is stamped Mar. 18, 1966. Jerome and Lillian Silbiger convey Straw Man, Inc., 'its successors and assigns', in fee simple, eleven lots 'described as follows' by their title deeds: Abbotston Street (three houses, one lot), 515 and 514 East 25th Street, 1762 Carswell Street, 2702-04 Harford Road, 1765 Abbottston Street, 2958 Greenmount Avenue, six concrete garages in the rear of Paine Street (marked 'unlocated' in the margin), two Falls Road lots and 2700 Harford Road. 'Lot #7' reads: 'the same lot of ground described in a Deed dated December 30, 1960 ... JFC 1004, Folio 488 ... granted and conveyed by Guiseppe Palladin ... unto the said Jerome Silbiger and Lillian Silbiger. See also Deed dated July 15, 1961 ... JFC 1134, Folio 578 ... granted and conveyed by Jacob F. Gerwig, widower, et al ... extinquishing said ground rent. The improvements thereon being now known as 2958 Greenmount Avenue.' Lots 5, 9 and 11 are subject to Equitable Trust Company mortgages and lot 10 to a Yorkridge Federal Savings and Loan mortgage; 2958 has no mortgage recited. What it settles: (1) row 46105 was 'probable' because the deed's lot list had not been read: Lot 7 now names 2958 Greenmount by number, so the Silbiger-to-Straw-Man deed of 2:10 p.m. does convey 2958 and is verified. (2) The deed repeats, in 1965, the two instruments that built the Silbigers' title: the 1960 purchase of the leasehold from Guiseppe Palladin (spelled here 'Palladin', 'wife', so the typed word after the name may be a slip for 'and wife'; the 1960 deed itself, row 46072, names Guiseppe and Adele Palladi) and the 1961 purchase of the reversion from Jacob F. Gerwig, widower, 'et al', 'extinquishing said ground rent': the merger of the ground rent is stated in the Silbigers' own deed. (3) Jacob F. Gerwig, widower, is the first-named grantor of the 1961 deed; the surname matches Henry Gerwig's, who bought the reversion in 1932 (S.C.L. 5289/183, previous row), which is the reason to read the 1961 grantors as his heirs. What it does not settle: why the Silbigers, whose eleven lots were not all mortgaged, put them through a corporation for a minute (the 2:10 and 2:11 p.m. stamps; a 'straw man' deed of this kind presumably turned the husband and wife's tenancy by the entireties into Jerome's sole ownership, and row 46107 puts the lots back into the entireties in 1969: an inference from the pattern, not a statement in the deeds); and the incorporation of Straw Man, Inc. Update Oct. 14, 2026: Straw Man, Inc. also appears in 1954, conveying 3014 Vineyard Lane to Harry W. and Bertha J. Hoover (M.L.P. 9509/244, recited in 1117:mdlr-jfc877-28-hoover-bordley-lease-1960): a conveyancing straw company used across Waverly, not the Silbigers' own (an inference).

Deed, Baltimore County Court land records, Liber A.W.B. 412, folios 283 to 285 (MSA CE 66-462; read in full on the scan Jeff saved, pages 283 to 287: the deed opens at the foot of 283 under the index heading 'William Gilmor & Wife, Deed to Samuel Brady', after the end of a trust deed of John Glenn, trustee, and William Broadbent; it ends on 285, where William F. Johnson and others' deed to Walter T. Allender, for two Baltimore City lots at Chester and Pratt Streets and Duncan Alley, begins; 286 and 287 are later pages of that deed and others). Dated Apr. 24, 1849, acknowledged the same day before Henry F. Friese and John I. Snyder, Justices of the Peace, Louisa A. Gilmor examined apart from her husband; received Apr. 28, 1849 at 10 a.m. and recorded the same day (A. W. Bradford, Clerk). William Gilmor and his wife sell Samuel Brady, of Baltimore County, for $3,500, part of 'a tract of land called Huntington': beginning at 'a large red Oak tree, being the beginning tree of a resurvey called Huntington Surveyed the Sixteenth day of May Seventeen hundred and Ninety four'; south 47 1/4 degrees east 50 perches; south 15 3/4 degrees west 9 perches 17 links; south 41 1/4 degrees west 21 perches; north 80 1/4 degrees west 16 perches; north 48 3/4 degrees west 40 perches 10 links 'until it intersects a thirty foot road'; north 40 1/2 degrees east along that road 39 perches 5 links to the beginning; 12 acres 2 roods 19 1/5 perches. Title: John I. and Samuel I. Donaldson, trustees, and Eliza H. Emory, to Gilmor by a deed of June 9, 1845 (A.W.B. 355/275). What it settles: (1) the first of the four title deeds the Brady trustees' deed of 1906 names (row 46168: 'a deed from William Gilmor and wife to Samuel Brady dated April 24th 1849 and recorded ... A.W.B. No 412 folio 283'): the date, the book and the folio of the 1906 recital are right. (2) Samuel Brady's Huntington purchase of 1849 ($3,500, 12.6 acres) and his Ensor's Inspection purchase of Nov. 30, 1848 from the trustee Allender (A.W.B. 404/533, 19 a 38 P, $6,700, row 46149) were two separate tracts; they are two of the four title deeds of the 1906 sale, and the Huntington part came from Gilmor, not Allender. (3) A possible origin of the name of 'Gilmor Lane' (the later Vineyard Lane, called Gilmor's in the 1906 and 2006 deeds): Gilmor owned land on a thirty-foot road from 1845; the deed itself names no lane, so this is an inference, not a reading. (4) The 'large red oak ... beginning tree of a resurvey called Huntington' here is, very probably, the 'bounded red oak' that Walker's and the Spear heirs' parcels of 1801 are measured from (W.G. 66/519, 67/447), so Brady's 1849 land and the 1801 Biays land hang from one tree; the deeds do not say it is the same tree. What it does not settle: what Donaldson and Emory held (A.W.B. 355/275, not read), whether the 'thirty foot road' is the York Road-to-lane road of the 1801 and 1848 deeds, and which parts of Gilmor's twelve acres lie in the ball ground of 1906 (the 1906 deed says it covers 'all of the land belonging to the estate of Samuel Brady').

Deed, Baltimore City Superior Court land records, Liber M.L.P. 5874, folios 532 to 533 (MSA CE 168-5882; read on the scan Jeff saved, pages 532 to 536: 532 holds the partial release that precedes the deed and the deed's opening, 533 the rest of the deed and the Mosers' mortgage, 534 to 536 the mortgage's later pages and the next instruments). Dated Nov. 23, 1938, acknowledged the same day before a notary (Gershil Moss); recorded Nov. 25, 1938 at 12:02 p.m. (M. Luther Pittman, Clerk). James M. Sinclair and Ena M. Sinclair, his wife, convey Simon Moser and Helena J. Moser, his wife, 'as tenants by the entireties', in fee simple, for $5 and other considerations, 'No 3013 Greenmount Avenue': 190 ft 7 in southerly from the two-mile stone in front of the Waverly Methodist Episcopal Church lot, 267 ft 2 in southerly from Bateman's Alley, 14 ft on the avenue, 42 ft 4 in east, 15 ft 2 1/2 in northeast along the Old York Road, and 48 ft 3 in west, the courses of every later deed; it is 'the same lot of ground which by Deed dated March 1st 1927 was granted and conveyed by J. Holliday Riepe to the said Grantors ... S.C.L. 4707 folio 12'. Special warranty only. On the same page and recorded one minute before: The Waverly Building Association of Baltimore County's partial release of Nov. 10, 1938 (signed by its vice-president, Henry Joesting Jr.) frees 'that lot of ground and premises secondly described' in the Sinclairs' mortgage of Apr. 15, 1930 (S.C.L. 5109/220) and 'thirdly described' in their mortgage of Apr. 7, 1934 (S.C.L. 5419), 'the property hereby intended to be released being known as No 3013 Greenmount Avenue', reserving the association's lien on the other lots in the mortgages. After the deed (533): the Mosers' $2,000 purchase-money mortgage of the same lot to Sara K. Sykes, Nov. 23, 1938, six percent, in ten notes (three of $250 at 18, 24 and 30 months, one of $1,250 at three years, and six interest notes). What it settles: (1) the 1938 deed behind the Moser deed of 1943 (row 46173, 'M.L.P. 5874/532') is read: Sinclair sold 3013 to the Mosers on Nov. 23, 1938, with Sinclair's title being the Riepe deed of 1927 (row 46111). (2) The Sinclairs had mortgaged the lots to the Waverly Building Association three times, May 1929, Apr. 15, 1930 and Apr. 7, 1934, and the 1938 release freed 3013 from the last two while the association kept its lien on the other lots (presumably 3011 among them): the full release of all three mortgages was not given until June 21, 1954, two days after the Sinclair children's deed to Weber (M.L.P. 9513/53 and 54, 3011, row 'Sinclairs to Weber'). (3) The Mosers' purchase was financed: a $2,000 purchase-money mortgage of the same day, then a $5 sale to Minor in Dec. 1943 and the sale-leaseback that followed (rows 46173, 46162). (4) The Sinclairs held 3013 from Feb. 7, 1919 (Holmes to Sinclair, row 46161) through the Riepe round trip of March 1927 (rows 46110 and 46111) until this sale in 1938, and kept 3011 until their heirs sold it in 1954. What it does not settle: the price (stated only as $5 and other considerations; the Mosers' mortgage calls its $2,000 'part of the purchase price'); who Simon Moser was (the 1943 deed, row 46173, is his sale to John E. Minor); and the folio of the 1934 mortgage (the 1938 and 1954 releases print it differently). Update Oct. 14, 2026: the 1930 and 1934 Sinclair mortgages are read (720:mdlr-scl5109-220-sinclair-waverly-bldg-mortgage-3011-3013-1930, 720:mdlr-scl5419-571-sinclair-waverly-bldg-mortgage-four-lots-1934); the 1930 one carries a margin note pointing to this liber and folio. The cited 1929 mortgage is not at S.C.L. 5005/541 (720:negative-scl5005-541-545-no-sinclair-1929-mortgage).

John Foster sells Christopher Walker 'all that part of tract of Land called ... Ensors Inspection', 29 acres, for five pounds sterling: beginning at a stone north 42 degrees east 62 1/2 perches 'from a bounded red oak standing in an old field being a bounded tree of Huntington'; north 42 east 117 perches to a stone in a line of 'Grants Addition'; south 59 east 41 perches; south 27 west 13 perches to 'Loveless Addition'; along it north 58 west 3, south 52 west 38, south 58 east 20 and south 7 west 7 perches to the tract 'Darby'; along it north 66 west 36 perches to a bounded tree; south 15 west 53, south 26 1/2 west 16, north 8 west 27 1/2 and south 75 1/2 west 18 1/2 perches; and straight to the beginning. What it settles: (1) the source of Walker's ground, which the 1801 deed to Biays (row 46179) and the 1813 Bolte mortgage (row below) both cut from: the Walker-to-Biays 3 3/8 acres of 1801 begin 62 perches north 43 3/4 east of the same red oak and close on two courses that are this deed's last two (north 9 1/2 west 27.2 and south 75 1/2 west 18.3 perches in 1801, north 8 west 27 1/2 and south 75 1/2 west 18 1/2 here), so the 1801 parcel is the south-western corner of these 29 acres; and the Bolte mortgage of 1813 runs to 'the end of the north forty two degrees east one hundred and seventeen perch line mentioned in the deed from said Foster to said Walker'. (2) Ensor's Inspection here adjoins Grants Addition, Loveless Addition and Darby (Darley Hall), the neighbours the 1754 certificate and the Hopkins plates name. What it does not settle: Foster's own title (none recited) and the Nicholas Foster deed above it (its land is on page 160, not pulled). Update Oct. 14, 2026: Foster's title, which this deed does not recite, is named in Walker's 1809 deed to Biays: 'by the said Foster purchased from William Spear by Deed on or about the fourth day of October' 1786 (719:mdlr-wg104-46-walker-biays-tavern-1809).

Mortgage, Baltimore County Court land records, Liber W.G. 122, folios 133 to 136 (MSA CE 66-172; read in full on the scan Jeff saved, pages 133 to 137: the top of 133 is the end of a Frederick County deed of John Dudderar to Conrod Dudderar, recorded the same day; the mortgage opens at the foot of 133 under the index heading 'James Biays Mortgage To John Bolte', ends on 136 with the list of notes, and is followed by an Ann Carson and Peter Green assignment to Henry Harrod of a Fells Point lot). Dated Feb. 4, 1813, acknowledged the same day before Saml. H. Gatchell and Matthew Bennet, witnessed by John Hanna; recorded Feb. 9, 1813 (Wm. Gibson, Clerk). James Biays, merchant, owes John Bolte, merchant, $13,930.73 on eighteen notes of Jan. 1, 1813 drawn in favour of and endorsed by John Hanna (at 7, 9 and 11 months, the amounts listed on 136), and mortgages him 'All that part ... of the tract ... called "Ensors Inspection" on which is situated the tenement called "Walker's Tavern"', part of Foster's land sold to Christopher Walker: beginning at 'a stone standing on the south east side of a road leading from the land of Hugh Thompson into the york turnpike road at or near the gate', marked B; north 40 1/2 east along that road to the turnpike and on across it, 94 3/4 perches in all, to the stone at the end of the 117-perch line of the Foster deed; then south 59 east 41, south 19 west 9 1/4 to a stone on the east side of a branch, [south] 59 west 3, south 51 west 38, south 59 east 20, south 6 west 17 3/4 and north 69 west 35 perches to a stone at the corner of a lot of 'the quakers society'; south 15 west 22.9 perches to Henry Starr's lane; south 84 west 19 1/2 perches to 'a lot now owned by said Biays'; and along that lot to stone B. Biays had it of Walker by a deed of about July 14, 1809 (W.G. 104/46, not read). What it settles: (1) the mortgage that the Chancery decree of Feb. 2, 1819 in Bolte et al. v. Biays foreclosed and Samuel Moale sold in lots in 1819 (rows 46128 and 46129): Moale's Lot 1 begins 'at a Stone marked B it being the beginning of the Ground mortgaged by the said James Biays to John Bolte', and Lot 2 at 'the end of the north sixty nine degrees west thirty five perches line', with the Tavern; every course of those two deeds is here. (2) The road from Hugh Thompson's land is Gilmor Lane: the 1901 Wood lease and the 1896 Dodson deed call Gilmor Lane 'also called a road leading from the lands of Hugh Thompson into the York Turnpike Road', so stone B stands on the south-east side of the lane, and by its courses the mortgaged ground takes in the south-west corner of the turnpike and the lane (the later 3010 to 3020, Moale's Lot 1 of 1821) and runs across the road to the east. (3) The Walker's Tavern ground came to Biays from Walker in 1809 (W.G. 104/46), out of Foster's 29 acres of 1800 (row above). What it does not settle: the 1809 Walker deed itself; the Chancery papers and the trustee's plat of the five lots; and who John Hanna and the other complainants (the Schultzes and Rudolph Wagler) were. Update Oct. 14, 2026: Walker's 1809 deed is read (719:mdlr-wg104-46-walker-biays-tavern-1809): $6,000, the same courses; Walker was an innkeeper in possession of the tavern; Foster had bought of William Spear about Oct. 4, 1786.

The deed recites that by an agreement of July 9, 1814 James Biays had agreed to give Benjamin Collins of Baltimore County a lease for 99 years renewable forever of 'a certain lot of Ground part of a tract of land called Ensors Inspection lying and being on the east side of the old York Road, running and bounding on said Road two hundred feet running thence Easterly to the line on the plat called Gorsuchs regulation', and that Collins conveyed his interest to William Gray as trustee on Sept. 13, 1817. Gray, as trustee, assigns McFadon for $60 the lot and the residue of the term 'Granted or to be Granted by the said James Biays with the benefit of renewment forever', subject to the yearly rent (not stated) and the agreement's covenants. What it settles: (1) the Tract Index's '1819, Gray to McFadon, 149/635' (row 46122) is not a sale of fee: it is the assignment of a promised Biays lease of a 200-ft lot on the EAST side of the old York Road, bounded east by a line on a plat called 'Gorsuch's regulation'; so the McFadon trust ground of 1822 (W.G. 165/492, 'at or near the gate' and across the turnpike) was not the Gray lot, and the trust's two named sources remain the Moale deeds of 1821. What it does not settle: where the 'old York Road' frontage lies against today's streets (the 'old York Road' is presumably the later Old York Road, east of the turnpike at the 3011 fork, but no distance from a known point is given); the rent; and whether the promised lease was ever executed by Biays.

Dated Nov. 3, 1804; acknowledged Dec. 3, 1804 before Geo. Gouldsmith Presbury and Sam W. Lee; received Jan. 24, 1805 and recorded the same day (Wm. Gibson, Clerk). James Edwards sells James Biays, for $1,000 (the receipt below the signature names 'five shillings current money' as the full consideration, a discrepancy on the page), part of Ensor's Inspection: beginning on the west side of the York Turnpike in the first line of the part Joseph Ensor conveyed to Richard Dick, 'now owned by the said James Edwards'; south 1 degree west along the road 22.8 perches 'until it intersects a line drawn south eighty eight degrees east from a stone marked J.B. upon one side and E upon the other'; north 88 west 36.4 perches 'to another stone marked J.B. upon one side and E upon the other'; north 34 east 4 perches 2 ft 7 in to the part James Maydwell conveyed Biays; north 83 east 33 perches to the second line of Dick's part; along it 'reversely along the old main road' north 1 east 17 perches; and back along Dick's first line. What it settles: (1) the 'stone marked J.B. on one side and E. on the other' at which Samuel Brady's 1848 deed begins (A.W.B. 404/533, row 46149: 'which said Stone stands on the Second line of the land conveyed by James Edwards to James Biays on the third day of November ... eighteen hundred and four', then 'north 86 degrees west 36 4/10 perches to another stone marked J.B. and E.') is this deed's: the second line runs 36.4 perches west between the two J.B. and E. stones, so Brady's tract of 1848 begins on the Biays-Edwards line and its first course is that line. (2) It is the Edwards deed Biays's 1816 mortgage to Stump cites (row 46103, on 3028) and one of the six Biays deeds the Brady deed recites. (3) The parcel fronts the turnpike for 22.8 perches (about 376 ft) and also bounds 'along the old main road', so two roads ran here in 1804. The end of Susan's deed (216) shows its second lot: 20 ft on the east side of Barclay Street at the north side of Waverly Avenue, 110 ft deep, which Charles T. What it settles: (1) the recited 1919 'assignment from W Harry Holmes dated May 1st 1919 ... S C L No 3361 folio 216' (S.C.L. 4210/380, row below) is read, at 3361, not the '3561' of the Edition 2 hop list (S.C.L. 3561/216 was pulled and holds 1920 Bartlett Avenue instruments: row '719:negative-scl3561-216'). Update Oct. 14, 2026: the opening of Susan Leight's deed to Holmes is read (719:mdlr-scl3361-215-susan-leight-holmes-1919): the corner, 'Known as No 3020 Greenmount Avenue', came to Henry and Susan Leight from Louis W. Deed, Baltimore County land records, Liber J.B. 96, folios 352 to 355 (MSA CE 62-96, the Circuit Court series; read in full on the scan Jeff saved, pages 352 to 356: the top of 352 is the end of Patrick H. and Rosa B. Walker's deed to Isaac H. Matthews, recorded May 8, 1876 at 4 p.m.; this deed opens at the foot of 352 under the heading 'David T Mumma and others, Deed To Abraham G Mott' and ends on 355 to 356 with acknowledgments; 356 then opens a Martinet and Chesapeake Bank release to John Moul). Dated Apr. 10, 1876; acknowledged in Baltimore City Apr. 10, 1876 before John T. Gorsuch, J.P., and in Adams County, Pennsylvania on Apr. 3, 1876; recorded May 8, 1876 (Jno. Bacon, Clerk). The grantors are the heirs of David Mumma, late of Baltimore County: his children Sarah Pennington (wife of Ross T.), David T. Mumma (and Georgia), Eugenia L. Gabler (and Lewis), Margaret Mumma Matthews, John J. Mumma, Edward W. Mumma (and Sarah, of Adams County, Pa.) and Julia Clowes (and Norris A., of Pittsburgh). By his will of May 31, 1857 (filed June 1857), Mumma left the parcel and 'the yearly rent of thirty two dollars issuing there out' to his wife Julia Ann for life, then to the children; she has died. For $533.33 they convey Abraham G. Mott in fee the parcel 'at the south west intersection of the York Turnpike Road and the Road leading ... towards the Lands of Mrs Gilmor and Mrs Biays': south 3 1/4 west 6.3 perches along the turnpike, west 17 perches to a free stone on the east side of the lane, north 42 1/2 east 9.6 perches and south 85 1/2 east 11 perches to the beginning, 94 square perches. It is the ground Mumma leased on Jan. 21, 1846 'to Jo[seph] D. Nicoll for the renewable term of ninety nine years' at $32 a year (Feb. 1 and Aug. 1), recorded, the deed says, 'in Liber A.W.B. no 372 folio 23[4]'; Mott already held the leasehold, by a deed from Samuel Hamilton Caughy of Oct. 4, 1860 (Baltimore County Liber G.H.C. No. 30 folio 473). The rent is conveyed 'to the end and intent that the said yearly rent of thirty two dollars ... shall henceforth be merged and extinguished'. What it settles: (1) the 'bought out' original rent of R.O. 1619/244 (row 46196): Mott bought the Mumma reversion and the $32 rent in 1876 for $533.33, which is the rent capitalized at 6 percent, and so held the 94 perches in fee, subject only to Nicoll's 1848 sub-lease of the corner to Leicht at $9. (2) The 1846 lease's terms, never read because the cited folio is empty (rows 46071 and 46201): 99 years renewable, $32 a year, to a lessee written here as 'Jo[seph] D. Nicoll' (the 1848 sub-lease names John D. Nicoll). The 1876 deed repeats the citation 'A.W.B. 372 folio 23[4]', so two independent recitals agree on a folio that does not hold the lease. (3) The 94 perches are exactly the two lots of the later deeds: 6.3 perches on the turnpike is 103 ft 11 2/5 in, the 36 ft of the corner lot (3020) plus the 67 ft 11 2/5 in of the 3010 lot; 17 perches west is the 280 1/2 ft depth of the 1896 Dodson deed. So the 1844 Mumma deed (A.W.B. 354/374, row 46070) is the 3010-3020 ground and nothing more. (4) The Mumma family: David Mumma's will of 1857 and the seven children, two in Pennsylvania. What it does not settle: the Caughy deed of 1860 (G.H.C. 30/473) and the leasehold's path from Nicoll to Caughy; the will itself. Update Oct. 14, 2026: Mott's leasehold is read (719:mdlr-ghc30-473-caughy-mott-1860, G.H.C. 30/473): Caughy assigned it to him on Oct. 4, 1860 for $3,300; Caughy had it from Frederick Gabler (Aug. 14, 1854), and Nicoll had cut two sub-leases from it, to Franklin Wilson (Feb. 7, 1847, $7, A.W.B. 378/206) and to Lorentz Leicht (1848, $9); Caughy bought Wilson's back in 1855. Update Oct. 14, 2026: the $533.33 is the buyout price written into the 1846 lease itself (719:mdlr-awb372-23-mumma-nicoll-lease-1846): the $32 rent capitalized at 6 percent, raised from $500 by words inserted before signing. Mott was exercising the lessee's redemption right, not paying a market price. Correction to the pointer above: Nicoll's sub-lease to Franklin Wilson is dated Feb. 27, 1847 (A.W.B. 378/206), not Feb. 7.

Deed, Baltimore City Superior Court land records, Liber J.B. 1422, folios 568 to 570 (MSA CE 168-1430; read on the scan Jeff saved, pages 568 to 572: the top of 568 is the Loyola Perpetual Building Association's partial release to Augustus D. Clemens Jr. of a lot in his and Mary Clemens's mortgage of June 10, 1892 (J.B. 1398/170), recorded Dec. 6, 1892 at 1:25 p.m.; this deed opens below it under the heading 'Abraham G Mott & Wife, Deed to Richard S Dodson &c' and ends on 570, where Mollie E. Bond, Clerk). Abraham G. and Mary E. Mott sell Richard S. Dodson and John M. Griffith, as tenants in common, for $1,500, the 94 square perches at the south-west corner of the turnpike and the road toward 'the lands of Mrs Gilmor and Mrs Biays' (the courses of the 1876 deed), 'the same lot ... conveyed to the said Abraham G Mott by Samuel Hamilton Caughy by a deed of assignment dated October 4th 1860 ... Deed, Baltimore County Court land records, Liber W.G. 104, folios 46 to 47 (MSA CE 66-154; read in full on the scan Jeff saved, pages 46 to 50: the top of 46 is the end of John Tessier's lease to Stephen Farall, acknowledged Sept. 16, 1809; this deed opens in the lower half of 46 under the heading 'Christopher Walker Deed To James Biays' and ends on 47). Dated and acknowledged July 14, 1809 before Sam. H. Gatchell and Thos. Cole, Patience Walker examined apart; received Sept. 16, 1809 and recorded the same day (Wm. Gibson, Clerk); the margin is marked 'paid'. Christopher Walker, 'of Baltimore County Innkeeper', sells James Biays, merchant, for $6,000, the part of Ensor's Inspection 'which Land said Walker is now in the actual possession of and on which is situated the Tenement called Walkers Tavern', part of the land Foster sold Walker about Mar. 4, 1800, which, by an interlined clause, Foster 'purchased from William Spear by Deed on or about the fourth day of October in the year Seventeen hundred and eighty six'. The courses are word for word those of Biays's 1813 mortgage to Bolte (row 46192): from stone B on the south-east side of the road from Hugh Thompson's land (Gilmor Lane) 'at or near the Gate', north 40 1/2 east across the turnpike 94 3/4 perches to the end of Foster's 117-perch line, around to the Quaker lot, Henry Starr's lane and a lot already Biays's, and back to B. What it settles: (1) the Walker's Tavern deed the 1813 mortgage recites is read, at $6,000: the biggest single purchase in the Biays assembly at the gate, and the ground that Moale sold in lots in 1821 (Lot 1 at stone B, Lot 2 with 'the Tavern'), part of which became the McFadon trust ground and in 1844 the Mumma lot (3010 and 3020). (2) Foster's title came from William Spear, about Oct. 4, 1786: the same Spear whose four daughters sold Biays the 9 7/8 acres in 1801 (row 46180), so both the Walker ground and the Spear-heirs ground at the gate descend from William Spear. (3) Walker was an innkeeper in possession: the tavern at the gate was his before 1809. What it does not settle: the Spear-to-Foster deed of 1786 (no liber given); 'a Lot at present owned by said Biays' on the west, probably the 1801 Walker lot or the Spear lot (an inference).
