Assignment, Baltimore County land records, Liber G.H.C. 30, folios 473 to 474 (MSA CE 62-30, the Circuit Court series; read in full on the scan Jeff saved, pages 473 to 477: the top of 473 is the acknowledgment of a William and Sarah D. B. Pole indenture, recorded Oct. 20, 1860; this deed opens below under the heading 'Samuel Hamilton Caughy, Assignment to Abraham G. Mott' and ends on 474). Dated and acknowledged Oct. 4, 1860 before Wm. H. Hayward, J.P. of Baltimore City (certified by Geo. E. Sangston, Clerk of the Superior Court); recorded Oct. 22, 1860 (Geo. H. Carman, Clerk). Samuel Hamilton Caughy, of Baltimore, assigns Abraham G. Mott, for $3,300, the 94 square perches at the south-west corner of the York Turnpike and 'the Road leading therefrom towards the lands of Mrs. Gilmore and Mrs. Biays' (the courses of the 1844 Mumma deed and the 1876 deed), held for the rest of the term renewable forever, subject to the clear yearly rent of $32 and to Lorentz Leicht's sub-lease, with the right to collect its rent. Caughy's title: Frederick Gabler assigned him the leasehold on Aug. 14, 1854 (H.M.F. 9/447, a folio of the book before its 1866 re-recording; row 719:negative-hmf9-447-reconstituted-volume), subject to the $32 rent and to two sub-leases by 'John D. Nicholl': one of Feb. 7, 1847 to Franklin Wilson at $7 a year (A.W.B. 378/206) and one of Feb. 29, 1848 to Lorentz Leicht at $9 (A.W.B. 394/156); Franklin Wilson assigned his sub-lease to Caughy on Apr. 5, 1855 (H.M.F. 11/305). What it settles: (1) the lessee's side of the 1846 Mumma lease from Nicoll to Mott: Nicoll, then Frederick Gabler (by 1854; the step from Nicoll to Gabler is not recited), then Caughy (1854), then Mott (1860), who bought the fee and the $32 rent from Mumma's heirs in 1876 (row 46204). (2) Nicoll had cut TWO sub-leases out of the 94 perches: the corner to Leicht (36 ft, the later 3020) and a second parcel to Franklin Wilson at $7 a year in February 1847, a year earlier. Caughy bought Wilson's sub-lease back in 1855, so in 1860 only the Leicht sub-lease was outstanding, which is why every later deed knows only the $9 rent. Lease, Baltimore County land records, Liber A.W.B. 372, folios 23 to 26 (MSA CE 66-422; read in full on the scan Jeff saved, pages 23 to 27: the top of 23 is the end of a Peter Rose to Enoch Holl lease, acknowledged Nov. 2, 1846 and recorded Nov. 3; this lease opens at the foot of 23 under the heading 'David Mumma, Lease to John D. Nicoll' and ends on 26 with its recording line). Dated and acknowledged Jan. 21, 1846, before R. Middleton and a second justice whose name reads like Wm. McTilton; recorded Nov. 3, 1846 at 11 a.m. (A. W. Bradford, Clerk), more than nine months after signing. David Mumma leases John D. Nicoll, both of Baltimore County, the 94 square perches at the south-west corner of the York Turnpike and the road toward Mrs. Gilmore's and Mrs. Biays's lands (the courses of the 1844 deed, A.W.B. 354/374, which the lease says was recorded July 10, 1845), for 99 years from Jan. 20, 1846, renewable forever on a $5 fine, at $32 a year from Feb. 1, 1846, paid $16 each Feb. 1 and Aug. 1. Two covenants matter: Nicoll must build 'a good and sufficient dwelling house' on the lot within one year, at his own cost; and Mumma must release the rent and convey the fee whenever Nicoll or his assigns pay $533.33 plus arrears. The clerk notes that the words 'and thirty three' and 'thirty three cents' were inserted before the lease was signed, so the buyout was first written as $500. What it settles: (1) the head lease that the 1847 and 1848 sub-leases, the 1860 Caughy deed and the 1876 Mott deed all rest on is found and read, at folio 23. The earlier search at '372/234' (folios 233 to 242, two negative pulls) was looking at a bad citation: the 1847 sub-lease cites it correctly as 'Liber A.W.B. 372 folio 23 &c.', and the 1848 '234' is probably '23 &c.' misread or miscopied (an inference). (2) The 1876 price is the lease's own buyout figure: $533.33 is the $32 rent capitalized at 6 percent, and Mott paid exactly that to Mumma's heirs (row 46204). He was exercising the redemption right written in 1846, not paying a market price. (3) The building covenant gives the first documented plan for a house on the lot: Nicoll was bound to have a dwelling up by January 1847 (a promise in the lease, not proof that it was built). (4) The arithmetic of the deal: Mumma paid $250 for the 94 perches in November 1844 (row 46070) and fourteen months later had a rent whose buyout value was $533.33, a little over twice his price (an observation from the two documents). What it does not settle: whether the house was built, and the step from Nicoll to Frederick Gabler, who held the lease by 1854.

Lease, Baltimore City Superior Court land records, Liber R.O. 2037, folios 211 to 213 (MSA CE 168-2045; read in full on the scan Jeff saved, pages 211 to 215: the top of 211 is the Waverly Building Association of Baltimore County's release, Oct. 5, 1903, of the mortgage Clemens Jr. and his wife gave it on Jan. 9, 1903 (R.O. 1995/142), signed by Henry C. Dated and acknowledged Oct. 1, 1903 before Chas. J. Fox, notary of Baltimore County, who witnessed it; recorded Oct. 6, 1903 at 1 p.m. (Robert Ogle, Clerk), with the release and the Fink deed. Augustus D. Clemens Jr. and Mary, of Baltimore County, lease Joseph J. Willis, of Baltimore City, the lot 156 ft 5 in south of the two-mile stone in front of the Waverly Methodist Episcopal Church, at the south-west corner of the 1898 Aull lease (R.O. 1728/284): 19 ft 2 in on the turnpike to Charles M. Term 99 years from the date, renewable forever on a $10 fine; $54 a year, half-yearly from Oct. 1, 1903, clear of taxes; re-entry after 60 days, forfeiture after six months. Deed, Baltimore City Superior Court land records, Liber R.O. 2037, folios 213 to 215 (MSA CE 168-2045; read on the scan Jeff saved). Dated and acknowledged Oct. 5, 1903 before Chas. J. Fox, notary of Baltimore County; recorded Oct. 6, 1903 at 1 p.m. (Robert Ogle, Clerk). Augustus D. Clemens Jr. and Mary Clemens, of Baltimore County, convey Mary K. Fink, of Baltimore City, in fee, for $1,733, two lots 'in the Village of Waverly': first, the 3017 lot (the courses of the Willis lease), part of Shepard G. Miller's 1897 deed (R.O. 1710/153), 'especially the clear yearly rent of fifty-four dollars' under the Willis lease of Oct. 1, 1903, subject to the leasehold; second, a lot on the east side of the turnpike 23 ft 7 in wide, between a lot Clemens leased Joseph J. Willis on Jan. 9, 1903 (R.O. 1995/231) and one he leased Leonard P. Eisinger and wife on May 4, 1903 (R.O. 2011/211), running 160 ft to Old York Road, which Henry W. Fox, trustee, had conveyed Clemens in fee on Jan. 9, 1903 (R.O. 1995/230). Special warranty. What it settles: (1) who bought the 3017 ground rent: Mary K. Fink, four days after the lease, recorded the same hour. From her it went to Leopold Lehmann (deed of Sept. 17, 1907, R.O. 2369/13, recited in M.L.P. 7060/156), then by his will to Mary C. Lehmann, to the Sinclairs in 1946 and the Vinsons in 1951, where it merged. (2) Clemens was creating rents and selling them: a lease, then the rent sold the same week. (3) Joseph J. Willis took a second Clemens lease in January 1903, elsewhere on the turnpike, where the gap to Old York Road is about 160 ft. The second lot's place on the avenue is not fixed by this deed. Mary K. Fink may be of the family of William L. Fink, who bought 3013 from Clemens in 1898 (R.O. 1729/241): the deed does not say. What it does not settle: the price split between the two lots (at 6 percent the $54 rent is worth $900, an inference) and where the second lot lies. Update Oct. 14, 2026: Fink to Lehmann is read (721:mdlr-ro2369-13-mary-fink-lehmann-3017-rent-1907): Sept. 17, 1907; Mary K. Fink's title as recited includes a deed from Estella Fink of July 31, 1907 (R.O. 2358/421).

Sub-lease, Baltimore County land records, Liber E.H.A. 59, folios 86 to 88 (MSA CE 62-59; read in full on the scan Jeff saved, pages 86 to 90; Edwin Eachus and wife's deed to Joseph F. Snyder follows on 88). Dated and acknowledged Mar. 2, 1868 before Wm. H. Bayzand, J.P. of Baltimore City, who witnessed it (certified by George Robinson, Clerk of the Superior Court, the same day); recorded Aug. 6, 1868 (Edward H. Ady, Clerk). The margin heading reads 'Sub Lease to'. George C. H. Coffield leases George Vandyke Smith, both of Baltimore County, the 79-ft lot at the north end of the Coffield tract: beginning on the turnpike 125 ft 6 in north of the tract's beginning (J.H.L. 43/548), a point four feet north of 'the two story house erected on the lot next adjoining on the south', then N 2 E 79 ft to the tract's north-west corner post, S 85 1/2 E 140 ft 6 in to Old York Road, S 19 1/2 W 78 ft 6 in, N 86 1/4 W 119 ft. Term: 'all the rest and residue save one year' of Coffield's own term, renewable forever on a $10 fine by a new sub-lease 'reserving ... a reversion of one day'; rent $150 a year from Mar. 1, 1868, clear of taxes; re-entry after 60 days, forfeiture after one year. Buyout: only 'within thirty days after the expiration of ten years' (March 1878), on $2,500 and arrears, Coffield to assign the lot free of the rent and subject 'to the yearly rent of one cent only'. What it settles: (1) the 1868 instrument is read and it is a SUB-lease: Coffield held the tract under a 99-year renewable lease at one cent a year (the 1865 Tagart deed), so the $150 rent was a sub-rent, carved under a one-cent ground rent whose lessor is still unknown. Every later 'fee' and 'reversion' of the $150 rent (the Schaeffer trust 1936, Crittenton, the 1988 merger) is Coffield's position: the one-cent leasehold plus the $150 sub-rent (an inference from the two deeds; no later deed read mentions the one cent). (2) The buyout was a single 30-day window in 1878 at $2,500 (the $150 at 6 percent) and was evidently not used, which is why the rent lived to 1988. (3) A two-storey house stood on the lot south of the 79 ft in 1868, the Bateman ground (3111). What it does not settle: how the sub-leasehold passed from Smith to Charles Hamilton by 1889, and the original one-cent lease. Update Oct. 14, 2026: confirmed in words by the 1887 assignment (742:mdlr-jws160-431-stump-peirce-150-subrent-1887), which calls this 'a certain sub-lease (the original rent being one cent)'. The $150 sub-rent was held by Mary J. Stump by 1886 and John H. Stump, who assigned it to Mary Louisa and William Edward Peirce in 1887. Update Oct. 16, 2026 (3117 batch 4): the passage from Smith toward Hamilton is now read in outline. Martin Kratt's assignment to Charles Hamilton of July 2, 1870 (E.H.A. 67/41, $500; 742:mdlr-eha67-41-kratt-hamilton-79ft-leasehold-1870) recites that Kratt held the term jointly with Joseph M. Cone by a deed of about May 8, 1869 (E.H.A. 62/262, grantor not named) and took Cone's interest by a deed of about July 30, 1869 (E.H.A. 63/71). Update Oct. 16, 2026 (3117 batch 5): E.H.A. 62/262 is read (742:mdlr-eha62-262-treadway-bruns-heise-cone-kratt-1869). Its grantors were John W. Treadway, John Bruns and William Heise, for $800 on May 6, 1869, and they held by an assignment of Oct. 14, 1868 from 'John C Smith' (E.H.A. 59/471, not read), seven months after this sub-lease; whether that is George Vandyke Smith miscopied or a second holder is open. Update Oct. 16, 2026 (3117 batch 6): E.H.A. 59/471 is read (742:mdlr-eha59-471-george-vandyke-smith-treadway-bruns-heise-1868). George Vandyke Smith himself assigned this sub-lease to John W. Treadway, John Bruns and William Heise on Oct. 14, 1868 for $325, reciting it ('leased or subleased to the said George Vandyke Smith by George C. H. Coffield'); the 'John C Smith' of the 1869 recital is a miscopy, very probably of the index heading 'John V. Smith' (inference). The leasehold side now runs deed by deed from Coffield to Hamilton.

Trustees' deed, Baltimore City Superior Court land records, Liber S.C.L. 5349, folios 127 to 128 (MSA CE 168-5357; read on the scan Jeff saved, pages 127 to 131: the top of 127 is the end of a Mortgage Guarantee Company assignment, recorded Feb. 24, 1933; this deed follows under the heading 'James L. Hennegan &c Trustees, Deed to The Eyring Realty Corp'). Dated and acknowledged Feb. 23, 1933 before Antoinette S. Gray, notary, who witnessed it; recorded Mar. 7, 1933 at 2:30 p.m. (Stephen C. Little, Clerk); $19 in federal stamps, which fits $19,000. Under a decree of the Circuit Court of Baltimore City of Oct. 21, 1932 in Erhard Eyring et al. v. The Miller Brothers Furniture Company, Incorporated, et al. (Docket 72-C folio 663), the trustees sold the leasehold on or about Nov. 21, 1932 to The Eyring Realty Corporation for $19,000; the sale was ratified and the money paid. The lot: 35 ft on Greenmount Avenue beginning 114.7 ft south of the south curb of 32nd Street, which is the north-west corner post of the Coffield tract, 204 ft 6 in north of its beginning (J.H.L. 43/548), 126 ft to Old York Road. It passes for the residue of the term, renewable, 'subject however to the payment of the annual rent of twelve hundred dollars'. What it settles: (1) the folio: 127, as the Hong-side papers say; the 1988 Crittenton deed's 'folio 727' is wrong (there is no folio 727 in this liber). (2) The date, Feb. 23, 1933, and the leasehold: Eyring bought the sub-leasehold under the $1,200 sub-rent, not the fee. (3) The suit behind the sale was brought by Erhard Eyring, of E. That this was a builder's claim for an unpaid contract is an inference: the deed does not say what the suit was for. What it does not settle: the equity file (Docket 72-C/663).

Trustee's deed, Baltimore City Superior Court land records, Liber S.C.L. 5669, folios 442 to 443 (MSA CE 168-5677; read on the scan Jeff saved, pages 442 to 446: the top of 442 is the end of Rhoda M. Weant's deed, recorded Oct. 30, 1936 at 10:30 a.m.; this deed follows, and John L. Long's deed to Home Friendly Insurance Co. begins on 443). Dated and acknowledged Oct. 28, 1936 (W. R. Hubner, vice president, before Chas. C. Reinhardt, notary); recorded Oct. 30, 1936 at 10:40 a.m. (Stephen C. Little, Clerk). The Safe Deposit and Trust Company of Baltimore, trustee under the will of Ellen M. Schaeffer of Baltimore City (will dated Sept. 20, 1926, Wills E.R.D. 158/519, with power of sale), conveys Florence Crittenton Mission, Incorporated, 'in fee simple', for $4,137.93, the $150 annual rent and reversion of the whole 79-ft lot, then 3113, 3115 and 3117 Greenmount Avenue and 3100 and 3102 Old York Road (the 1868 courses), 'which said annual rent is the special subject of this conveyance', subject to the leasehold. Title: Coffield's lease to Smith (E.H.A. 59/86) and Henry Bradley and wife's deed to Ellen M. Schaeffer of Oct. 27, 1908 (S.C.L. 2459/514). What it settles: (1) the fee-side hop before 1936 is named: Henry Bradley and his wife sold Ellen M. Schaeffer the $150 rent in October 1908, so the 71-year gap (Coffield 1865 to 1936) is now 1868 to 1908, Coffield to Bradley. (2) Ellen M. Schaeffer's will is dated 1926 and her trustee was the Safe Deposit and Trust Co., which sold under its power of sale. (3) The price, $4,137.93, is not the 6 percent figure ($2,500); it is about 27.6 years' purchase, a 3.6 percent yield (arithmetic). (4) The house south of the lot is a 'two story brick house' by 1936; the 1868 lease just says 'two story house'. What it does not settle: Coffield to Bradley (1868 to 1908), and the one-cent lease above Coffield's term, which this deed does not mention. Update Oct. 14, 2026: the 1908 deed is read (742:mdlr-scl2459-514-bradley-schaeffer-150-rent-1908): Bradley held the rent three days, from Edward S. Deed, Baltimore City Superior Court land records, Liber S.C.L. 5686, folios 215 to 216 (MSA CE 168-5694; read on the scan Jeff saved, pages 215 to 219: the top of 215 is the end of a Real Estate Investment and Finance Company deed recorded Dec. 30, 1936 at 2:45 p.m.; this deed follows, and the Eyring company's mortgage to the Eyring trustees begins on 216). Dated and acknowledged Dec. 30, 1936 before Raymond L. Henry, notary, who witnessed it; recorded the same day at 2:45 p.m. (Stephen C. Little, Clerk). Dorothy Dietrich, Wilhelmina Dietrich and Helen Dietrich Butler, of Baltimore City, convey The Eyring Realty Corporation, for $5 and other consideration ($19 in federal stamps), the $1,200 sub-ground rent and sub-reversion of 3117 (the 35-ft lot at the Coffield tract's north-west corner, 409 ft south of Gorsuch Avenue), 'to the end and intent' that it be merged in Eyring's leasehold, subject to the $150 rent. The sub-rent was created by 'a sub-lease from Lula S. Dietrich, widow, to Miller Brothers Furniture Company Incorporated dated March 3, 1928' (S.C.L. 4854/321), $1,200 a year quarterly; the grantors had it by 'a Deed from Wilhelmina Dietrich, Administratrix' of Apr. 27, 1931 (S.C.L. 5213/440). The same day Eyring Realty mortgaged the lot for $15,000 to Edward and Richard Eyring, surviving trustees under Erhard Eyring's will (Wills J.H.B. 181/6). What it settles: (1) the 1928 sub-lease is named: S.C.L. 4854/321, dated Mar. 3, 1928, made by Lula S. Dietrich as a widow, so John H. Dietrich was dead by March 1928. (2) The three grantors took through an administratrix's deed of 1931, very probably from Lula's estate, and are very probably her daughters (inference: the deed states no relationship and does not say whose estate Wilhelmina administered). (3) Erhard Eyring, the complainant of 1932, was dead by December 1936, and his estate financed the purchase. (4) It confirms the 1933 folio, 5349/127. What it does not settle: how the Dietrichs took the leasehold (the 1904 decree sale, Hamilton or Zoll), and the administratrix deed (S.C.L. 5213/440).

Corporate deed, Baltimore City Superior Court land records, Liber M.L.P. 7523, folios 422 to 424 (MSA CE 168-7531; read on the scan Jeff saved, pages 422 to 426). Dated May 3, 1948 and acknowledged that day by Edward Eyring, president, with Richard Eyring, secretary, who swore that the board (May 1, 1948) and the stockholders approved it; recorded July 28, 1948 at 10:50 a.m. (M. Luther Pittman, Clerk), with a sheet of federal documentary stamps. Under 'a plan of reorganization', The Eyring Realty Corporation conveys Eyring Realty Enterprises, Inc., for $5 and other consideration, 'all and singular the lands ... fee simple and leasehold properties, ground rents, reversionary estates' it owned in Baltimore City and Baltimore County, except stocks, bonds and notes: leaseholds subject to their rents, fee lots in fee. No lot is described, and the clerk marked it 'UNLOCATED'. What it settles: (1) the 1948 transfer is a blanket deed: it passes 3117 only because the company owned it, and it names no lot, no liber and no rent, so it cannot settle fee against leasehold for 3117 (the 1933 and 1936 deeds do: leasehold under the $150 rent until 1988). The 1988 Hong-side papers' 'fee simple' does not come from this deed. (2) Edward and Richard Eyring ran the company; Erhard Eyring had died by 1936. What it does not settle: the stamp total (not counted) and what else the company owned.

Trustees' deed, Baltimore City Superior Court land records, Liber J.F.C. 2079, folios 102 to 105 (MSA CE 168-12397; read in full on the scan Jeff saved, pages 102 to 106, which also hold the start of the purchase-money mortgage at 106). Dated June 1, 1966; acknowledged June 1 (the individual trustees, before Dorothy S. Weintraub) and June 6 (Maryland National Bank by J. Edward Macatee Jr., vice president, before Frances Elizabeth Brown); recorded June 7, 1966 at 1 p.m. (James F. Carney, Clerk). Janet E. C. Wurtzburger and Moses W. Rosenfeld, successor trustees, and Maryland National Bank, successor corporate trustee, under Tillie M. Wurtzburger's deed of trust of Dec. 13, 1940 (M.L.P. 6111/293), convey Harry B. Gorfine, surviving trustee under two deeds of trust of Dec. 30, 1948 from Myles Katz and wife (M.L.P. 7669/44 and /56), an undivided half under each, in fee simple, for $35,500, the apex lot: 36 ft 1/2 in on York Road north from Merryman's Lane, 42 ft back to the lane, 55 ft on the lane; 'known as 3200 and 3202 Greenmount Avenue'. Recited title: Elizabeth Ruth Samstag to Alan and Tillie M. Wurtzburger, joint tenants, Dec. 2, 1936 (S.C.L. 5678/406); Tillie's half into the 1940 trust; her resignation and Janet E. C. Wurtzburger's appointment (Dec. 13, 1941, M.L.P. 6254/433); Alan's half into the trust (Aug. 1, 1962, J.F.C. 1326/16); Alan's death about Feb. 20, 1963; Rosenfeld named successor (Apr. 26, 1961, J.F.C. 1696/562); Maryland National Bank named (Dec. 10, 1965, J.F.C. 2014/51); and the 1926 party-wall agreement with J. What it settles: (1) the Katz trusts took the corner in June 1966 by purchase, $35,500, as the 1976 deed recites (row 42333's reading is right). (2) The Samstag name question: the 1936 grantor is 'Elizabeth Ruth Samstag', so the 1924 'Ruth E.' and the 1926 and 1936 'Elizabeth R.' are one woman, Frederick H. Samstag's wife. (3) The Wurtzburger tenure is now read step by step, 1936 to 1966, with the trust's successor trustees. (4) The mortgage was larger than the price because it also covered a second lot (on Frederick Road at Warwick Avenue, from an 1890 deed, J.B. 1283/277). What it does not settle: what the Katz trusts were for (the 1972 papers name the beneficiaries) and the S.C.L. 5678/406 deed itself.

Two trust instruments, Baltimore City Superior Court land records, Liber R.H.B. 2927, folios 593 to 595 (resignation) and 596 to 598 (designation) (MSA CE 168-13245; read in full on the scan Jeff saved). Katz and Morris Fiddle accept on July 6, 1972 and declare themselves satisfied with Gorfine's accounts. What it settles: (1) the trusts' beneficiaries (Alan R. Katz; Barbara K. Gerstley) and why Arthur H. Katz could deed the corner as 'successor trustee' in 1976 (R.H.B. 3415/175). (2) Gorfine was still the owner of record on the 1977 DHCD roster after he had resigned, a stale roster entry. (3) The papers do not describe 3200: the margin indexes other property (Block 107, 1900 Edmondson Avenue, and Block 4163), so the trusts held several Baltimore properties. What it does not settle: the 1948 deeds of trust themselves (M.L.P. 7669/44 and /56) and how Arthur H. Katz is related to Myles Katz (not stated).

Assignment, Baltimore County land records, Liber E.H.A. 74, folios 321 to 322 (MSA CE 62-74; read on the scan Jeff saved, pages 321 to 325: the top of 321 is the end of Joseph Low's deed to John Atkinson Jr. of half of a lot No. 21, acknowledged Mar. 16, 1872 before Mark Mellor, J.P., and recorded Mar. 21; this deed opens at the foot of 321 under the heading 'Elizabeth D. Huff, Assignment to James E. Sinclair' and ends on 322, where George W. Eyler's deed to Sallie A. Hoshall begins). Dated and acknowledged Mar. 6, 1872 before Frank Lewis, J.P. of Baltimore County, who also witnessed it; recorded Mar. 22, 1872 (Edward H. Ady, Clerk). Elizabeth D. Huff assigns James E. Sinclair, both of Baltimore County, for $2,500, 'part of a tract called Huntington': beginning at the intersection of the York Turnpike 'agreeable to Baker's survey' and 'the road now called Merryman's Lane leading to Van Bibber's Mill', ten perches (165 feet) up the York Road, then square across to the lane, which closes the lot. It is the land Andrew Brown assigned her on Apr. 9, 1866 (J.H.L. 48/236), and passes for the rest of 'the original Lease', subject to its yearly rent (neither lease nor rent is named). What it settles: (1) the first of the three sources the 1884 Sinclair-to-Harris deed cites (W.M.I. 141/407, row 23723) is read, and it names the TRACT: Huntington, the first tract name reached for the 3200 block. (2) The lot is a triangle at the fork of the York Road and Merryman's Lane, 165 feet on the road, which is the 3200 apex and the frontage north of it (an inference from the description; 3200-3202 is the 36-foot apex lot). (3) It was a leasehold: Sinclair bought a term under an older ground lease, through Andrew Brown (1866). The 1873 Wilson deed (J.B. 84/387) bounds its own lot on 'the old division fence between Brown's lot and said Wilson's land', which is this lot's north line (an inference). (4) Huff is the family of 'Residence late A. J. Huff, 1815, west side York Road, near Merryman's Lane' (Aull, Old Land Marks no. 21): probable. What it does not settle: the original lease (its lessor, date and rent), the Brown deed of 1866, and how the fee was cleared before Sinclair sold to Harris in 1884. Dated and acknowledged Mar. 6, 1872 before Frank Lewis, J.P. of Baltimore County, who also witnessed it; recorded Mar. 22, 1872 (Edward H. Ady, Clerk). Elizabeth D. Huff assigns James E. Sinclair, both of Baltimore County, for $2,500, 'part of a tract called Huntington': beginning at the intersection of the York Turnpike 'agreeable to Baker's survey' and 'the road now called Merryman's Lane leading to Van Bibber's Mill', ten perches (165 feet) up the York Road, then square across to the lane, which closes the lot. It is the land Andrew Brown assigned her on Apr. 9, 1866 (J.H.L. 48/236), and passes for the rest of 'the original Lease', subject to its yearly rent (neither lease nor rent is named). What it settles: (1) the first of the three sources the 1884 Sinclair-to-Harris deed cites (W.M.I. 141/407, row 23723) is read, and it names the TRACT: Huntington, the first tract name reached for the 3200 block. (2) The lot is a triangle at the fork of the York Road and Merryman's Lane, 165 feet on the road, which is the 3200 apex and the frontage north of it (an inference from the description; 3200-3202 is the 36-foot apex lot). (3) It was a leasehold: Sinclair bought a term under an older ground lease, through Andrew Brown (1866). The 1873 Wilson deed (J.B. 84/387) bounds its own lot on 'the old division fence between Brown's lot and said Wilson's land', which is this lot's north line (an inference). What it does not settle: the original lease (its lessor, date and rent), the Brown deed of 1866, and how the fee was cleared before Sinclair sold to Harris in 1884. Deed, Baltimore County land records, Liber J.B. 84, folios 387 to 389 (MSA CE 62-84; read in full on the scan Jeff saved, pages 387 to 391: the top of 387 is the end of another indenture, recorded Dec. 31, 1873; this deed follows under the heading 'Thomas J. Wilson, Trustee, Henry R. Wilson, Trustee, Deed to James E. Sinclair', and Margaret Slater and others' deed to John Daniel Ahles of part of 'Lukes Adventure' begins on 389). Dated and acknowledged Oct. 24, 1873 before John P. Maddox, J.P. of Baltimore City, who witnessed it (certified Dec. 30, 1873 by George Robinson, Clerk of the Superior Court); recorded Dec. 31, 1873 (John Bacon, Clerk). The Wilsons, with David S. Wilson, as trustees under James Wilson's will, leased Sinclair the lot for 99 years on Oct. 1, 1872 (E.H.A. 77/361). Sinclair paid $800 and the arrears and so was entitled to have the rent extinguished; David S. Wilson being absent from the county, the Circuit Court of Baltimore City (William C. Wilson and others v. David S. Wilson and others) ordered on Oct. 23, 1873 that Thomas J. and Henry R. Wilson deed the reversion alone. The lot, 'adjacent to the village of Waverly': on the west side of the turnpike, 150 ft south of the line of the north end wall of a stone house on a lot lately leased to J. H. Hartman and 475 ft south of Wilson Street, at the south-east corner of Lot No. 7 conveyed to P. P. Pendleton; west 200 ft to the centre of a 20-ft alley; south 22 1/2 ft to the north-east side of Merryman's Lane; south-east 30 ft along the lane 'to the place where the old division fence between Brown's Lot and said Wilson's Land formerly stood'; along that line south-east 175 ft to the turnpike; north 44 1/2 ft to the start. What it settles: (1) the second of the three sources the 1884 deed cites is read: the Wilson-estate lot is the one leased Sinclair in October 1872 (the Towson News item, row 5208) and bought outright in 1873 for $800 ($800 is $48 a year at 6 percent, an inference about the rent). (2) It lies just north of 'Brown's lot', the Huff lot (Andrew Brown to Huff 1866, Huff to Sinclair 1872), so Sinclair held the fork from the apex north: Brown's lot for 10 perches (165 ft), then the Wilson lot for 44 1/2 ft. (3) 3224, 181 to 196 ft north of the lane, falls inside the Wilson lot (165 to about 209 ft) if Brown's 10 perches are measured along the turnpike from the fork (probable, from the measurements; the 1884 lease's second lot begins 164 ft 8 in north of the lane, almost exactly 10 perches). If so, 3224's fee comes from the James Wilson estate, whose Huntington holding at the turnpike dates from 1802 and 1811. What it does not settle: the 1872 lease itself (E.H.A. 77/361), the Merryman deed, and the Wilson estate's title to this exact lot. Update Oct. 14, 2026 (late): the lease this deed ends is indexed: David S. Wilson and others, trustees, to James E. Sinclair, lease recorded Oct. 2, 1872, E.H.A. 77/361 (776:index-ce256-287-p143-wilson-trustees-1867-1872). Update Oct. 16, 2026 (J.B. 84/381 read): on Oct. 31, 1873, a week after this deed, Sinclair sold the north 30 ft of the Wilson lot to Mary F. Ridgely, $600, from the south-east corner of Pendleton's Lot 7 (J.B. 84/381, 768:mdlr-jb84-381-sinclair-ridgely-north-30-ft-of-wilson-lot-1873), recorded Dec. 31 just ahead of this deed at 387. Huff, both of Baltimore County, for $1,900, 'part of a tract of land called Huntington ... about two miles on the Baltimore and York Turnpike': beginning at the intersection of the turnpike and 'the road leading to Van Bibbers Mill now called Paradise Mill', ten perches up the road, then square across to the mill road. Deed of trust, Baltimore County land records, Liber W.G. 72, folios 319 to 324 (MSA CE 66-122; read on the scan Jeff saved, pages 319 to 323: the top of 319 is the end of William Brookes's assignment to John Shaw, acknowledged Oct. 12, 1801 and recorded Feb. 4, 1802; this deed opens lower on 319 and runs past 323, so its acknowledgment and recording stamp are not on the scan). Dated Feb. 4, 1802. James Biays, merchant of Baltimore City, for love and affection for his wife Sarah and their children and $1 from each trustee, conveys William Jackson, block maker, and Levin Jones and John Smith, master mariners, all of Baltimore City, three parts of Ensor's Inspection: (1) 9 7/8 acres beginning at 'a bounded red Oak tree (the beginning of a tract of land ... Called Huntington)', which runs to the south-west corner of 'a lot of Ground which formerly belonged to John Gosuch now the property of the said James Biays' and to the end of Walker's last line, from William Spear's representatives (May 30, 1801); (2) Walker's 3 3/8 acres beginning 62 perches north 40 3/4 east of the red oak, with a line south 47 1/4 east 22.4 perches to a stone in the York Road (Mar. 9, 1801, W.G. 66/519); (3) 2 1/4 acres at the northern end of a tract adjoining Biays's land, beginning near the second corner of James Maidwell's land, east 25 perches 'to the main road', south 10 east along it 14 perches 10 ft 4 in, then west 'through the Northern part of the orchard' (from Maidwell, Sept. 26, 1800, W.G. 67/62). The trustees are to let Sarah take the rents and profits for her own use for life, 'notwithstanding her Coverture', and at her death convey in fee to the children of James and Sarah then living, the issue of any dead child taking the parent's share, as tenants in common; failing children, to Biays's heirs. Biays covenants that he holds the land in fee simple without condition. What it settles: (1) both 1801 purchases behind 2958 (Walker's and the Spear heirs', rows 46179 and 46180) went into this trust within a year. (2) It explains the 1840s sellers: the four Biays daughters and their husbands were the children who took the remainder when Sarah died (she was dead by October 1845, row 46130). (3) It names the defendant of the 1847 Chancery case: the 1848 deeds out of the Walker land (to Wilson, row 46178) and to Samuel Brady (row 46149) were made under Allender and wife v. 'William Jackson and others', and William Jackson is the trustee named here (very probably the same man or his heirs; the 1848 deeds do not say). So the 2958 ground passed from Walker (1801) to Biays, into this trust (1802), out of it by the 1847 Chancery sale, and to William T. Wilson (1848) (the trust link is probable). (4) A lot 'formerly ... John Gosuch's' was already Biays's in February 1802; its conveyance into the same trust is W.G. 76/243 (row 714:mdlr-wg76-243-gosuch-trust-harkins-rest-1803). What it does not settle: the recording date (folio 324), and the 1847 Chancery papers.

Deed of trust, Baltimore County land records, Liber W.G. 76, folios 243 to 246 (MSA CE 66-126; read on the scan Jeff saved, pages 243 to 247: the top of 243 is the end of Thomas Rutter Jr.'s deed to Solomon Rutter, $6,000, acknowledged May 27, 1803; Henry Alexander's deed to Charles Conaway of part of 'Monzie' follows on 246). Dated and acknowledged May 10, 1803 before Rob. Gosuch and Geo. Gouldsmith Presbury, justices of the peace; John Gosuch signs by his mark; recorded June 7, 1803 (Wm. Gibson, Clerk). John Gosuch, son of Thomas, gentleman, conveys the three Biays trustees, for $1,200, a lot of Ensor's Inspection 'heretofore sold by a certain Job Garretson unto a certain John Harkin': beginning at a stone marked 'I.H. 1765' on the west side of 'the old main road', at or near where the given line of Ensor's Inspection crosses it, north 7 west 26 1/2 perches along the road to stone No. 2, south 26 west 18 perches 2 ft to No. 3, south 7 east 26 1/2 perches to No. 4, then straight back: 3 acres 'called by the Name of Harkin's rest'. Harkin conveyed it to Gosuch on Mar. 4, 1771 (Liber A.L. C, folio 231 as read; the letters are uncertain). It is held on the trusts of the 1802 deed: Sarah Biays's separate use for life, then the children of James and Sarah living at her death. What it settles: (1) the 'lot ... which formerly belonged to John Gosuch now the property of the said James Biays' in the 1802 deed is Harkin's Rest, and it joined the trust in 1803 (Biays had evidently bought it before February 1802; Gosuch conveyed straight to the trustees). (2) It gives the oldest dated mark found on this ground: a stone 'I.H. 1765', very probably John Harkin's initials (an inference), on the old main road where the Ensor's Inspection line crossed it. (3) The Biays holding west of the York Road in the 1802 to 1803 trust was four pieces: Spear's 9 7/8 acres, Walker's 3 3/8, Maidwell's 2 1/4 and Harkin's Rest, 3. Whether the 2958 lot lies in Walker's land (as the 1848 deed says) or reaches Harkin's Rest is not shown. What it does not settle: the Garretson-to-Harkin deed and the 1771 citation. Update Oct. 17, 2026 (County grantor index, Dick and Gorsuch): the County grantor index for Gorsuch finds no deed or mortgage by John Gorsuch of Thomas in 1778 to 1786 (CE 33-2 pp. 134-138, the whole Go run: only an estray notice, W.G. B/290; 714:index-ce33-2-p133-gorsuch-john-1778-1786). From 1787 to 1803 (CE 33-3 and 33-4) his only conveyances of Ensor's Inspection are A.A. 205 (1787, to James Edwards, index p. 151, recorded twelve folios after Maidwell's mortgage, A.A. 193; not read), the 1795 release to Maidwell (S.S. 231) and the 1803 deed of trust (76/243, 3 acres, which is Harkin's Rest, bought from Harkin in 1771, and not this lot). There is no Gorsuch deed to Biays, Walker, Maidwell or Dick in the index, and none between W.G. 53/197 (1798) and 73/72 (1802). So the 5 1/4 acres Gorsuch took from the Speagles in 1778 are not shown sold before the 1787 mortgage, and A.A. 205 is the best candidate for where they went (INFERRED: the index gives no acreage or road, and it could instead be another part of Ensor's Inspection, for example Richard Dick's part, which Edwards held by 1804). The lot that 'formerly belonged to John Gorsuch now the property of the said James Biays' in 1801 (rows 46180, 46685) therefore rests on a deed or contract not indexed under Gorsuch, or on A.A. 205 through Edwards. Next: W.G. A.A. 205 itself (MSA CE 66-76 p. 205; the scan on disk stops at p. 197), read against the 1778 courses (row 47038) and the Edwards deeds. (714:index-ce33-3-p151-gorsuch-john-1787-1797 and -ce33-4-p163-gorsuch-john-1798-1803.)

Deed, Baltimore County land records, Liber W.G. 67, folios 62 to 63 (MSA CE 66-117; only folio 63 and the following deeds were saved, pages 63 to 67: George Littig's Fells Point deed and lease of Apr. 17, 1800 and John Robert Holliday's deed to George Everhart of part of 'Gotham' follow). Folio 63 holds the end of James Maidwell's deed to James Biays of 'the aforesaid moiety of land': the covenant for further assurance, Maidwell's signature (written 'James Maywell'), witnesses Adam Gantz and Thomas Donovan, his receipt of $450 from Biays on Sept. 26, 1800, the acknowledgment that day before John Moale and Geo. A. Dunkel, justices, with Temperance Maidwell's private examination and release of dower, and the recording on Oct. 16, 1800 (Wm. Gibson, Clerk). What it settles: (1) the Maidwell purchase is dated (Sept. 26, 1800), priced ($450) and recorded (Oct. 16, 1800), and the 1802 trust deed's citation 'W.G. 67 folio 62' is right: the deed begins on 62. (2) The land is a 'moiety', a half share; the 1802 deed describes it as 2 1/4 acres at the north end of a tract adjoining Biays's land, east to 'the main road', with an orchard. What it does not settle: the description, the source of Maidwell's title and whose other half the 'moiety' was (all on folio 62, not pulled). Update Oct. 14, 2026: the start is read (714:mdlr-wg67-62-maidwell-biays-1800-start): 2 1/4 acres at the north end of Maidwell's tract of Ensor's Inspection, on the main road, through his orchard; no earlier title recited.

Lease, Baltimore County land records, Liber J.B. 86, folios 487 to 490 (MSA CE 62-86; read in full on the scan Jeff saved, pages 487 to 491: the top of 487 is the end of another instrument certified by the Clerk of the Superior Court of Baltimore City and recorded May 6, 1874 at 2 p.m.; Henry Bowerman and wife's deed to Eliza Bowerman of a St. Denis lot follows on 490). Dated Apr. 16, 1874; Margaret Hamilton acknowledged that day before Frank Lewis, J.P. of Baltimore County, and William Thomas Wilson before H. W. Snowden, J.P. of Baltimore City; recorded May 6, 1874 at 3:40 p.m. (John Bacon, Clerk). William Thomas Wilson, of Baltimore City, leases Margaret Hamilton, wife of Charles Hamilton, of Baltimore County, a lot on the west side of the York Turnpike beginning at the south-east corner of 'a lot of ground belonging, or supposed to, ... A. G. Mott' at a stone, 282 ft west along Mott's lot to a marked stone, 100 ft south to a stake, about 282 ft east to the turnpike, 100 ft north along it. His title: the will of his mother, Henrietta D. A. Wilson, probated by the Baltimore County Orphans' Court on Aug. 29, 1854 (the third digit of the year is faint). Term 99 years from the day before, renewable forever on a $10 fine; $325 a year from June 1, 1874, half-yearly; re-entry after 60 days, forfeiture after six months. Within five years she may buy the fee for $4,642.86 (the $325 at 7 percent), free of the rent but still bound by covenants against liquor saloons, houses of public entertainment, bone, glue and hair factories, butchers, public stables, tanneries, blacksmith shops and any nuisance. What it settles: (1) the citation carried for 'the lease from William Thomas Wilson to Eleanor Cross dated April 16th 1874' (the outline that bounds Keelty's 1907 ground on the north, row 46084) leads to a different lease of the same date: to Margaret Hamilton, of the 100 ft immediately south of Mott's lot (3010 to 3020; that lot began at Gilmor Lane). Wilson very probably made two leases that day, Hamilton's adjoining Mott and Cross's south of it, adjoining the later Keelty ground (an inference; the 1877 plan letters 'Chas. Hamilton' and 'Jno. C. Cross' together north of 30th Street with 'A. Mott', row 714:1877 plan). The instrument that ends at the top of folio 487, recorded at 2 p.m. the same day, is the first candidate for the Cross lease. (2) Henrietta D'Arcy Wilson's will was probated in 1854, so the life estate and power of appointment the Keelty deed describes had passed to William Thomas Wilson by then. (3) Wilson was creating rents at 7 percent with nuisance covenants in 1874. What it does not settle: the Cross lease itself and where on the avenue the two lots end. Update Oct. 14, 2026: the Cross lease is on folios 483 to 487, just before this one (714:mdlr-jb86-483-wilson-elenor-cross-lease-1874); the 2 p.m. instrument is a Myers deed to John C. Cross of a Western Homestead lot. The 1854 probate date is confirmed on that copy. Update Oct. 16, 2026 (3117 batch 6): Charles and Margaret Hamilton mortgaged this lease, with the 79 ft lot at 3113 to 3117 Greenmount, to John T. Ensor on Apr. 21, 1886 for $1,000 (Balt. Co. mortgage J.W.S. 121/373, read; 742:mdlr-jws121-373-hamilton-ensor-mortgage-1000-1886), where it is called a deed of assignment.

Deed, Baltimore City Superior Court land records, Liber R.O. 1647, folios 561 to 562 (MSA CE 168-1655; read on the scan Jeff saved, pages 561 to 565: the top of 561 is the William Street Permanent Loan and Savings Association's release to Henry Kawalske; William E. McCaffray, J.P., who witnessed it; recorded Nov. 12, 1896 in the morning (Robert Ogle, Clerk). Francis E. Yewell and Florence E., his wife, convey John W. S. Brady, 'surviving Trustee named in the last Will and Testament of Samuel Brady late of Baltimore County', for $5, 'the southeasternmost half part of the bed of Gilmors Lane from the centre of Twenty Ninth formerly Holmes Street to the prolongation northwesterly of the northeasternmost outline of the land bounding on said lane belonging to the estate of Samuel Brady deceased', in trust under the twelfth clause of Brady's will. Exchange deed, Baltimore City Superior Court land records, Liber R.O. 2212, folios 510 to 512 (MSA CE 168-2220; read on the scan Jeff saved, pages 510 to 514, a heavily speckled film; the Ninth West Columbia Building Association's release to John G. Delrick follows on 512). Dated and acknowledged Feb. 24, 1906 before T. Bayard Williams, notary; recorded Feb. 26, 1906 at 3 p.m. (Robert Ogle, Clerk). Richard H. Woollen, Howard P. Sadtler and S. Procter Brady, trustees of Samuel Brady's estate, and the Peabody Heights Company (Eugene Levering, president; J. Appleton Wilson, secretary) own adjoining tracts whose division line is 'the Southeast side of a former lane or road now called Gilmor Lane'. To make both more marketable they exchange four irregular lots so the line follows the city blocks: the trustees give Peabody Heights two lots at Calvert and 27th Streets and at Guilford Avenue and 28th Street; Peabody Heights gives the trustees two at Calvert and 28th Streets and at Guilford Avenue and 29th Street. The agreement was reported to the Circuit Court of Baltimore City in the cause administering the trust, 'Martha A. W. Woollen et al. vs Nannie H. Stump et al.' (docket and folio read as '59 A folio 512', uncertain on this film), and ratified. What it settles: (1) the 1906 Peabody Heights deed recited in R.O. 2290/225 is read: a boundary exchange west of the York Road, between Calvert Street and Guilford Avenue, nowhere near the Greenmount frontage. (2) The Brady trust case is Martha A. W. Woollen et al. v. Nannie H. Stump et al., and the trustees in 1906 were Woollen, Sadtler and S. Procter Brady. (3) In 1906 the old Gilmor Lane was the line between the Brady estate (south-east) and Peabody Heights (north-west). It adds nothing on whether 2958 was ever Brady land.

Deed, Baltimore City Superior Court land records, Liber J.F.C. 968, folios 290 to 291 (MSA CE 168-11286; read on the scan Jeff saved). Dated, acknowledged (before Norman P. Deeds, Baltimore City Superior Court land records, Liber S.C.L. 4728, folios 193 to 201 (MSA CE 168-4736; read on the scan Jeff saved, pages 192 to 201: 192 is the end of a Hahn and Coleman mortgage on Riggs Avenue). Three Swormstedt instruments, all recorded Apr. 27, 1927 at 2:30 and 2:35 p.m. (Stephen C. Little, Clerk). (1) Folio 193: Martha and Mary L. Swormstedt assign their brother Richard a mortgage of their father's estate (Mar. 30, 1927); it recites that Richard Swormstedt senior died on or about Aug. 28, 1913 (the day as read), will H.W.J. 116/331, leaving all to his wife Barbara C. Swormstedt for life, then their three children, and that Barbara died about Oct. 13, 1926. (2) Folios 194 to 198: the deed of Mar. 29, 1927 from Richard Swormstedt, of Douglas, Wyoming, and Martha and Mary L. Swormstedt, all unmarried, to Robert N. Baer, so that Baer might reconvey by the dividing deeds of Mar. 30, 1927, of eleven ground-rent lots. Six were Barbara's own (her will dated Apr. 7, 1924, probated Oct. 26, 1926, E.R.D. 156/455); the seventh was held by Barbara and Richard 'as tenants by the entireties'; four more were bought by her as trustee with his estate's money. The seventh is the 3010 lot: on the west side of the turnpike 36 ft south of a stone at the south-west corner of the turnpike and Gilmor Lane ('known as the road running between the lands of Mrs Gilmore and Mrs Biays and also called a road leading from the lands of Hugh Thompsons' into the York Turnpike Road'), 67 ft 11 2/5 in on the turnpike to Mary Clemens's south line, 215 ft west, 82 ft north to the lane, 53 ft on the lane, then around the Nicoll-to-Leicht sub-lease (cited 'A.W.B. 374/156', a slip for 394); its rent is $180 a year quarterly, February, May, August and November. Its source: 'a deed from John P. Clarke Executor &c to Richard Swormstedt and Barbara C. Swormstedt dated December 16th 1903' (R.O. 2050/46). Richard junior acknowledged in Converse County, Wyoming on Apr. 22, 1927; his sisters in Baltimore on Mar. 30 before Chas. H. Taylor. (3) Folios 198 to 201: a second deed of the same date to Baer of the lots devised by Richard senior's will (dated June 15, 1909): York Road at 23rd Street, Baltimore Street and Bouldin Street. What it settles: (1) how the Swormstedts held the $180 reversion on 3010: Richard and Barbara C. Swormstedt bought it from John P. Clarke, executor, on Dec. 16, 1903, two years after Mary Clemens created the rent; Barbara held it as survivor from 1913 and died in October 1926; her three children divided her estate through Baer in March 1927, and the 3010 rent went to Martha and Mary L. (row 46208). (2) Mary Clemens therefore sold the reversion to someone, or it passed through an estate, between October 1901 and December 1903: whose executor John P. Clarke was is the next question (R.O. 2050/46). What it does not settle: R.O. 2050/46 itself. Update Oct. 14, 2026: R.O. 2050/46 is read (719:mdlr-ro2050-46-duggan-executors-swormstedt-3010-rent-1903): John P. Clark and James B. Kailer were executors of Francis P. Duggan, who bought the $180 rent from Mary Clemens on Oct. 31, 1901 (R.O. 1928/238); the Swormstedts paid $3,000, the rent at 6 percent.

Assignment, Baltimore City Superior Court land records, Liber S.C.L. 4836, folios 513 to 514 (MSA CE 168-4844; read on the scan Jeff saved, pages 513 to 517). Dated and acknowledged Jan. 14, 1928 before Emma Roberts, notary, who witnessed it; recorded Jan. 17, 1928 at 10:51 a.m. (Stephen C. Little, Clerk), a minute after the Waverly Building Association's release of Wyman's 1927 mortgage (George E. Leight, president; Lennox B. Clemens, attorney) and a minute before the Wolfes' own mortgage. John E. Wyman, of Baltimore City, conveys William H. and Carrie Wolfe, for $5 and other consideration, the lot on the south-east side of Gilmor Lane: from the end of the second line of the 1896 Dodson-to-Mary Clemens deed (R.O. 1615/24), 75 ft east to the south-west corner of the Wood lot (the 1901 lease, R.O. 1928/77), 82 ft north along it to the lane, 125 ft back along the lane. It passes for the rest of the term, renewable forever, subject to $54 a year (April 15 and October 15). Wyman's title: Mary Clemens's deed of Apr. 21, 1919 (S.C.L. 3348/167). The same day the Wolfes mortgaged it to the Kennedy Hill Permanent Building and Loan Association for $910 on seven shares, 'part of the purchase price'. What it settles: (1) how the Wolfes held the Vineyard Lane lot behind 3010 that they deeded to Charles T. Leight in 1953 (row 46199): as a $54 leasehold from Wyman (1928), whose rent they bought out in 1937 (719:mdlr-scl5742-413-harding-wolfe-vineyard-lane-reversion-1937). (2) The Wolfes bought this lot two months after buying the 3010 leasehold with the Leights (Nov. 1927). What it does not settle: S.C.L. 3348/167 (how Mary Clemens conveyed a leasehold she had created, presumably her lessee Wood's interest come back to her; an open question). Update Oct. 14, 2026: S.C.L. 3348/167 is read (719:mdlr-scl3348-167-mary-clemens-wyman-vineyard-lane-1919): Mary Clemens to Wyman, Apr. 21, 1919, from Wood's 1903 assignment back to her.

Deed, Baltimore City Superior Court land records, Liber S.C.L. 5742, folios 413 to 415 (MSA CE 168-5750; read on the scan Jeff saved, pages 413 to 417: Rudolph M. Winterling's deed of 2335 Druid Hill Avenue is above it on 413, and Adolph H. Schlag's deed of a Harford Road lot to David W. Chertkof follows on 415). Dated July 14, 1937 and acknowledged that day in Northumberland County, Virginia before W. C. Blackwell, notary; witnessed by T. M. Spangler; recorded July 21, 1937 at noon (Stephen C. Little, Clerk). Rose I. Harding, widow, of Northumberland County, Virginia, conveys William H. and Carrie Wolfe, by the entireties, for $5 and other consideration, the Vineyard Lane lot (the courses of the 1928 Wyman deed) 'and particularly the aforesaid rent', 'to the end and intent that the reversion and aforesaid annual ground rent ... be forever merged and extinguished'. What it settles: (1) the Vineyard Lane lot's two estates: Mary Clemens leased it to Allen K. Wood on Apr. 17, 1902 at $54, six months after leasing him the 3010 lot at $180; the leasehold reached Wyman (1919) and the Wolfes (1928); the reversion went from Mary Clemens to James B. Guyton (how and when not shown) and to the Conways (1910), and merged in the Wolfes in 1937. (2) Allen K. Wood was the Clemenses' lessee for both lots behind the corner. What it does not settle: R.O. 1952/245 itself, how Guyton took the reversion, and S.C.L. 3348/167. Update Oct. 14, 2026: the 1902 lease is read and the rent went straight to Mary L. Conway for $900 the same day (719:mdlr-ro1952-245-mary-clemens-wood-lease-conway-rent-vineyard-lane-1902), so Guyton's 1910 deed to Rose I. and Mary L. Conway was very probably a straw for a joint tenancy (inference).

Lease, Baltimore City Superior Court land records, Liber R.O. 1730, folios 92 to 94 (MSA CE 168-1738; read on the scan Jeff saved, pages 92 to 96; the Maryland Building and Loan Association's deed of 1310 Milton Avenue to Ella Virginia Vander Horst follows on 94). Aull, of Baltimore City, the tip lot at the fork: from a point on the east side of the turnpike 204 ft 7 in south of the two-mile stone in front of the Waverly Methodist Episcopal Church lot (281 ft 2 in south of the north side of Bateman's Alley), 58 ft 4 in south to the south-west corner of the whole ground, N 89 E about 8 ft 6 in to the north-west side of Old York Road, N 31 1/2 E 66 ft along it, then 42 ft 4 in straight back; part of Shepard G. Mortgage, Baltimore City Superior Court land records, Liber S.C.L. 5419, folios 571 to 573 (MSA CE 168-5427; read on the scan Jeff saved, pages 571 to 575; the recording stamp is not on the pages read). The Sinclairs owe the Waverly Building Association of Baltimore County $1,913.29, repaid monthly at 6 percent, with the right to have the first lot released for $1,000, and mortgage it four lots: (1) 202 Homewood Terrace (from the Baltimore Discount Company, 1925, S.C.L. 4502/519), a leasehold at $180, also under a Home Owners Loan Corporation mortgage of the same day; (2) 3011 and (3) 3013, in fee; (4) a lot beginning on 'the fourth line of description in an Assignment from M. Estelle Bateman to The Provident Savings Bank', the centre line of an 8-ft alley, 28 ft 6 1/4 in east of Greenmount Avenue at the west side of a frame building, 24 ft south along it, 86 ft 6 in east to Old York Road, 24 ft 11 in north-east to the alley centre, 92 ft 8 in back: a one-cent leasehold ('the annual rent of one cent if demanded'). Lots 2 to 4 are the three of Riepe's 1927 deed (S.C.L. 4707/12). What it settles: (1) the 1934 Sinclair mortgage is read; with the 1930 one it accounts for the releases of 1938 and 1954. (2) The Sinclairs' third Riepe lot, the one-cent leasehold, lies behind a frame building on the Greenmount-to-Old York Road block, measured from an alley line named in the 1904 Bateman-to-Provident deed (R.O. 2062/398, row on 3111): it is Coffield-tract ground near 3105 to 3111, held at the tract's one cent (an inference about which lot; the deed gives no house number). What it does not settle: the exact place of the fourth lot and the recording date. Update Oct. 14, 2026: the fourth lot is placed: Provident Savings Bank assigned it to Sinclair on Mar. 26, 1920 and he assigned it back on July 9, 1934 (737:mdlr-scl5455-522-sinclair-provident-one-cent-lot-1934): ground behind the bank, from M. Estelle Bateman's 1904 assignment.

Executors' deed, Baltimore City Superior Court land records, Liber R.O. 2050, folios 46 to 48 (MSA CE 168-2058; read on the scan Jeff saved, pages 46 to 50; the Assurance Permanent Loan and Savings Association's release to Edmund T. Horner follows on 48). Dated and acknowledged Dec. 16, 1903 before Wilmer Emory, J.P., who witnessed it; recorded the same day about noon (Robert Ogle, Clerk). John P. Clark (written 'Clarke' in the 1927 recital) and James B. Kailer, executors of Francis P. Duggan of Baltimore City (will dated June 8, 1901, Wills S.R.M. 91/446, with power to sell this property), sold at private sale about Nov. 10, 1903, ratified by the Orphans' Court, to Richard and Barbara C. Swormstedt by the entireties, for $3,000, the $180 rent and reversion of the 3010 lot (the courses of the 1927 deeds). Duggan's title: Mary Clemens and husband's deed of Oct. 31, 1901 (R.O. 1928/238), 'being the Reversion or Ground Rent of $180.00', the same day as the lease to Allen K. Wood (R.O. 1928/77). What it settles: (1) whose estate John P. Clark served: Francis P. Duggan's. (2) Mary Clemens created the $180 rent and sold it the same day, as she did at 3017 (1903) and 3011 (1898): a builder's pattern of leasing a lot and selling the rent at once. (3) The executors' price is the rent at exactly 6 percent ($180 / 0.06 = $3,000). The 3010 rent chain is now read from its creation: Clemens (Oct. 31, 1901), Duggan (same day), his executors to the Swormstedts (1903), the 1927 partition, the Wolfes (1930), Leight (1950, merged). What it does not settle: R.O. 1928/238 itself (the rent deed of 1901, its price) and Duggan's dates. Update Oct. 14, 2026: the 1901 deed to Duggan is read (719:mdlr-ro1928-238-mary-clemens-duggan-3010-rent-1901): $3,000, the same 6 percent price.

Lease and deed, Baltimore City Superior Court land records, Liber R.O. 1952, folios 245 to 248 (MSA CE 168-1960; read on the scan Jeff saved, pages 245 to 249: Clarence C. and Minnie S. Deed, Baltimore City Superior Court land records, Liber R.O. 1730, folios 91 to 92 (MSA CE 168-1738; read on the scan Jeff saved, pages 88 to 92). Dated and acknowledged Apr. 18, 1898 before Wm. D. Wright, J.P., who witnessed it; recorded Apr. 25, 1898 (Robert Ogle, Clerk), just before the Aull lease on 92. The Clemenses convey Lulie H. Wallace, of Baltimore City, in fee, for $1,250, the 3011 lot 'in the Village of Waverly', subject to the Aull lease of the same day ($75 from May 1, 1898), 'and especially the clear yearly rent of seventy five dollars'. On folio 90 the Loyola Perpetual Building Association, two days earlier, released from Clemens's December 1897 mortgage (R.O. 1710/154) the reversion of the Aull lot, a lot Clemens held under a lease from Henry C. Huff and wife, and the lot Clemens sold William L. Fink in fee (3013), leaving the mortgage on the rest. What it settles: (1) the start of the Wallace deed, whose end was read on folio 92: the 3011 rent's first sale, $1,250, the rent at 6 percent, so the chain of the 3011 rent is read from creation to Sinclair's merger in 1921. (2) Henry C. Huff (later president of the Waverly Building Association, 1903) had leased Clemens a lot near the fork before April 1898, so Clemens held part of the Miller ground as a Huff lessee (inference from the release; the Huff lease is not read). Deed, Baltimore City Superior Court land records, Liber R.O. 2369, folios 13 to 14 (MSA CE 168-2377; read on the scan Jeff saved, pages 13 to 17; Monro Smith's assignment to Albert Ottilber follows on 14). Dated, acknowledged before Wm. H. Watson, J.P., and recorded Sept. 17, 1907 (Robert Ogle, Clerk). Mary K. Fink conveys Leopold Lehmann, in fee, for $5, the 3017 lot (156 ft 5 in south of the two-mile stone in front of the Waverly Methodist Episcopal Church lot, at the south-west corner of the 1898 Aull lease, R.O. 1728/284) 'and particularly the rent or reversion', subject to the Willis lease of Oct. 1, 1903 (R.O. 2037/211, $54). Her title as recited: 'a deed dated July 31st 1907 ... Liber R O No 2358 folio 421 ... from Estella Fink to said Mary K Fink'. What it settles: (1) the one unpulled deed in the 3017 rent chain is read: Fink to Lehmann, September 1907. (2) A second Fink, Estella, held the rent for a time between 1903 and July 1907 (how she took it from Mary K. is not recited: perhaps a straw or a family transfer, not shown). The chain now reads Clemens (1903), Mary K. Fink (1903), Estella Fink (to July 1907), Mary K. Fink, Leopold Lehmann (1907), Mary C. Lehmann, the Sinclairs (1946), the Vinsons (1951). What it does not settle: R.O. 2358/421 and the Finks' relationship to William L. Fink of 3013. Update Oct. 14, 2026: R.O. 2358/421 is read (721:mdlr-ro2358-421-mary-estella-fink-straw-3017-rent-1907): Estella Fink was a same-day straw, Mary K. to Estella and back, July 31, 1907. Update Oct. 17, 2026 (Fink deeds S.C.L. 2559/393 and 3126/290 read): Mary K. Fink is Mary Catherine Fink and Estella Fink her sister, two of the four children of William L. Fink of 3013 (will of Feb. 2, 1893; deed S.C.L. 2559/393, Feb. 9, 1910). The Finks' relationship to William L. Lease, Baltimore County land records, Liber J.B. 86, folios 483 to 487 (MSA CE 62-86; read in full on the scan Jeff saved, pages 481 to 486, the stamp on 487 read earlier). Dated Apr. 16, 1874, acknowledged the same day by Elenor Cross before Frank Lewis, J.P. of Baltimore County, and by William Thomas Wilson before H. W. Snowden, J.P. of Baltimore City; recorded May 6, 1874. William Thomas Wilson leases Elenor Cross, wife of John C. Cross, of Baltimore County, a lot on the west side of the York Turnpike beginning at the south-east corner of 'the lot of ground leased by Indenture of even date herewith to Margaret Hamilton', 282 ft west along it, 35 ft south, about 282 ft east to the turnpike, 35 ft north along it; title from his mother Henrietta D. A. Wilson's will, probated Aug. 29, 1854 (the year is clear on this copy). Term 99 years renewable forever on a $10 fine; $113.75 a year from June 1, 1874 (June and December); buyout within five years at $1,625, the rent at 7 percent, as in the Hamilton lease; the same nuisance covenants. Above it (folios 482 to 483), recorded at 2 p.m. the same day, is Thomas and Sarah Ann Myers's deed to John C. Cross of a lot on Jefferson Street in the Western Homestead, part of 'Ensors Inspection', merging a $45 rent (Fox to Cross lease of 1867, E.H.A. 57/219): another Cross holding, not this lot. What it settles: (1) the Cross lease the Keelty deed bounds on is read: 35 ft directly south of the Hamilton lot, which is 100 ft directly south of A. G. Mott's lot. So from Mott's south-east corner on the turnpike the frontage runs Hamilton 100 ft, Cross 35 ft, then Keelty's ground (about 118 ft) and the 2944 to 2958 row (arithmetic from the three instruments; where 30th Street was cut through is not stated in any of them). (2) Henrietta D. A. Wilson's will was probated Aug. 29, 1854: confirmed. (3) The 1874 leases of the Wilson frontage at Waverly all carry the same 7 percent buyouts and nuisance covenants. What it does not settle: whether the Cross lot became fee, and where 30th Street falls in these lines.

Deed, Baltimore County land records, Liber W.G. 67, folio 62 (MSA CE 66-117; read on the scan Jeff saved, pages 60 to 62; the end is on 63, read earlier, row 46254). John O'Donnell's lease to Peter Ealer of a Water Street lot in the city is on 60 to 62 above it. Dated Sept. 26, 1800. James Maidwell, of Baltimore City, sells James Biays, of the same place, for 450 Spanish milled dollars or £168 15s Maryland currency, 2 1/4 acres 'in the northern extremity of a tract of land lying in Baltimore County adjoining the land of the said James Biays being part of a tract of land called Ensors inspection': from near a stone at the second corner of Maidwell's land, N 76 1/2 E 25 perches 'to the main Road, or as near to it as elder surveys will permit', S 10 E along the main road 14 perches 10 ft 4 in, then S 88 W 'thro the northern part of the Orchard' to the tract's first line and along it to the start, 'no more nor no less'; with general warranty. No source of Maidwell's title is recited. What it settles: (1) the Maidwell deed is now read in full: the land was the north end of Maidwell's own tract of Ensor's Inspection, fronting the main road (the York Road), with an orchard; Biays already owned the land next to it in September 1800, before the 1801 Walker and Spear purchases (so Biays had an earlier holding, not identified). (2) The 'moiety' of folio 63 is this 2 1/4-acre part. What it does not settle: Maidwell's title and Biays's earlier land. Update Oct. 14, 2026 (late): a lead for Maidwell's title: John Gorsuch (son of Thomas) to James Maidwell, a release dated Feb. 14, 1795 of part of Ensor's Inspection, reciting Maidwell's deed to Gorsuch of Feb. 26, 1787, begins at the foot of W.G. S.S. 231 (seen on the scan of the 1795 Merryman lease). Its N 76 1/2 E 25-perch line 'to the main road' and S 10 E course along the road are courses of this 1800 deed, so it is very probably Maidwell's title (inference); folios 231 to 235 are loaded for Jeff. Update Oct. 14, 2026 (later): the 1795 release is read (714:mdlr-wgss231-gorsuch-maidwell-release-ensors-inspection-1795): Maidwell held nine acres of Ensor's Inspection on the main road, mortgaged to John Gorsuch in 1787 (W.G. AA/193) and cleared in 1795; this 1800 deed's 2 1/4 acres were their northern tip, from stone M on the Garretson line. Update Oct. 17, 2026 (Maidwell to Edwards read): the rest of Maidwell's nine acres went to James Edwards, 2 1/2 acres on Mar. 25, 1801 (W.G. 66/123) and 3 acres on Sept. 11, 1804 (W.G. 82/206), the latter beginning at the J B stone at the south-east corner of this 2 1/4 acres (rows 714:mdlr-wg66-123-maidwell-edwards-2-5-acres-1801 and 714:mdlr-wg82-206-maidwell-edwards-3-acres-1804).

Deed, Baltimore City Superior Court land records, Liber M.L.P. 9274, folios 275 to 277 (MSA CE 168-9282; read on the scan Jeff saved). Dated and acknowledged Sept. 14, 1953 before Ralph C. Opening page of a trustees' deed, Baltimore County land records, Liber E.H.A. 65, folio 404 (MSA CE 62-65; read on the scan Jeff saved, pages 401 to 404; the deed continues on 405 to 407, on disk since September and filed in Corridor). It recites that 'a certain lot of ground on the west side of the York Turnpike Road known or formerly known as the gate house lot ... has been for sixty years or more in the possession under claim of title' of the company, and that by an indenture of May 14, 1844 (T.K. 341/328) 'the late Alexander Contee Magruder conveyed or intended to convey in fee to the late James Wilson of the City of Baltimore a certain' [tract, continued on 405]. What it settles: (1) the missing opening of the 1870 deed: the company had held the gate-house lot by possession since about 1810 or before, without a deed, and the Wilson trustees, heirs to Magruder's 1844 conveyance to James Wilson, gave it one (with folio 405's memorandum that Wilson held title for the company). (2) A new County hop above the toll-gate corner: Magruder to James Wilson, May 14, 1844 (T.K. 341/328). The gate-house lot is the corner at Gilmor Lane that the company sold Aull in 1912 for 3026 to 3032 (the 1912 deed recites a Wilson-trustee deed of July 5, 187-, E.H.A. 70/92, for 'all that property'; whether that is this deed's lot or a second lot is open). What it does not settle: T.K. 341/328 itself and E.H.A. 70/92. Update Oct. 14, 2026: Magruder's 1844 deed is read (725:mdlr-tk341-328-magruder-trustee-james-wilson-huntington-1844): $1,025 for 3 a 1 r 12 p of Huntington between Gough's road and the turnpike, sold as trustee under Philip G. Biays's 1826 deed of trust (W.G. 184/618). Update Oct. 14, 2026 (late): the gate-house lot itself went to the company by a separate deed of July 5, 1871 (725:mdlr-eha80-97-wilson-trustees-turnpike-first-toll-gate-house-lot-4-1871), Lot 4 of the Huntingdon plat, 57 ft at Gilmor's Lane; this 1870 deed's 50 ft lies north of the gate.

Deed of redemption, Baltimore City Superior Court land records, Liber M.L.P. 8123, folios 414 to 416 (MSA CE 168-8131; read on the scan Jeff saved). Dated June 13, 1950, acknowledged that day in Baltimore County before Howard F. Sieber, notary, for the trustee by A. F. Dempsey, vice president; recorded June 15, 1950 at 11:30 a.m. (M. Luther Pittman, Clerk). Francis X. Hooper's will (Baltimore County Wills W.J.R. 19/182; City J.H.B. 217/204) left a third to his widow Florence W. (2) It fixes the Hooper trust's documents: the will's two citations and the 1917 division. What it does not settle: nothing new upstream.

Division deed, Baltimore City Superior Court land records, Liber S.C.L. 3177, folios 132 to 136 and following (MSA CE 168-3185; read on the scan Jeff saved, pages 132 to 136, which end before the deed does; the Geiler mortgage ends at the top of 132). Dated Dec. 7, 1917. Francis X. Hooper, late of Baltimore County, left his estate a third to his widow Florence W. Hooper and two-thirds to the Mercantile Trust and Deposit Company of Baltimore and William Jenkins in trust; the widow and the trustees divide the real estate, the widow taking lots in Beaumont Park, Idlewylde and elsewhere in Baltimore County, the trustees taking, among others, 'all those four lots' on the west side of Greenmount Avenue 'formerly the York Turnpike Road' at Vineyard Lane 'formerly Gilmor Lane', beginning at the corner and at 15, 29 and 43 ft north of it (3026, 3028, 3030 and 3032). What it settles: (1) the Hooper division deed recited in the 1950, 1964 and 1967 deeds is read: the four Aull rents bought by Hooper in December 1912 ($4,500) went to his testamentary trust in 1917, which sold them one by one (3028 in 1945, 3026 in 1950, 3032 in 1964; 3030's rent was elsewhere by 1944, see 726:mdlr-mlp8386-70-interrante-podlich-3030-1951). What it does not settle: the folios after 136 and the recording date. Update Oct. 16, 2026 (late): the 3030 rent the Interrantes bought in 1944 (M.L.P. 6549/594, read) was a 1935 rent created by the Waverly Building Association of Baltimore County, which then held 3030 in fee; how the trust's 1912 rent on 3030 ended is not read. Update Oct. 16, 2026 (1935 read): the 1935 instruments are read (S.C.L. 5518/171 to 175, rows 47394 to 47396). The Waverly Building Association of Baltimore County took the 3030 leasehold by assignment from David McCoy and wife, July 8, 1932 (S.C.L. 5312/27), and the reversion by a deed from 'the Mercantile Trust Company of Baltimore et al Trustees', Feb. 18, 1935 (folio not given; very probably the Hooper trust selling the 1912 $66 rent, an inference), so the 1912 lease and rent met in the Association. On Feb. 25, 1935 it leased 3030 to Helen M. Bordley at $66, sold that new rent to Charles T. and Ella B. Leight for $1,100, and took the lease back from Bordley the same day (a straw, inference). Bordley's 1943 assignment to the Interrantes is M.L.P. 6513/139 (row 47397). Update Oct. 16, 2026 (5313/27 read): the McCoy assignment that the 1935 instruments cite as 'Liber S C L No 5312 folio 27' is recorded at S.C.L. 5313/27 (MSA CE 168-5321; Grantor Index 1932, row 47520), on a folio whose typed header reads '5312', corrected by hand to 5313. It is read (726:mdlr-scl5313-27-mccoy-waverly-bldg-assignment-3030-1932): David and Mary E. McCoy assigned the 3030 leasehold to The Waverly Building Association of Baltimore County on July 8, 1932 (recorded July 12) for $5 and other valuable considerations, subject to the 1912 rent of $66 due June 1 and Dec. 1; they held it by Mary A. J. Aull's assignment of Dec. 20, 1929 (S.C.L. 5076/70). No mortgage or default is recited. Update Oct. 16, 2026 (1929 and 1935 read): S.C.L. 5517/92 (MSA CE 168-5525, read; 726:mdlr-scl5517-92-hooper-trustees-waverly-bldg-redemption-3030-1935) is the deed of Feb. 18, 1935 by which Mercantile Trust Company of Baltimore and William Jenkins, trustees under Francis X. Hooper's will, on the Waverly Building Association's statutory notice to redeem, conveyed it the 1912 $66 reversion on 3030 for $1,100, 'to the end and intent that the leasehold estate created by the lease aforesaid shall be merged with the fee'. So the trustees of the 1935 recitals are Hooper's, and the 1912 lease and rent on 3030 merged in the Association by that deed, not by inference. S.C.L. 5076/70 and /71 (MSA CE 168-5084, read) show how the leasehold reached the McCoys: Jacob H. Aull's executors deeded it to his widow Mary A. J. Aull on Oct. 11, 1922 (S.C.L. 3918/495, recited), she assigned it to David and Mary E. McCoy on Dec. 20, 1929, and they mortgaged it the same day to the Waverly Building Association for a $3,120 purchase-money advance on 24 shares, released only on Mar. 15, 1951 (M.L.P. 8386/69). Their 1932 assignment to that lender was very probably in lieu of foreclosure [inference].

Assignment, Baltimore City Superior Court land records, Liber S.C.L. 3281, folios 596 to 597 (MSA CE 168-3289; read on the scan Jeff saved, pages 596 to 600). Interrante, by the entireties, from Helen M. Bordley (Sept. 30, 1943, M.L.P. 6513/139), and the reversion from Charles T. and Ella B. Leight (Jan. 7, 1944, M.L.P. 6549/554); Ida died, leaving Nicholas the fee. On folio 72, the same day, Podlich leases 3030 to Marie B. Pipitone for 99 years at $90 from Mar. 15, 1951: the lease recorded just before the deed of the rent (row 42198). What it settles: (1) the 3030 dark run is partly lit: by 1943 the leasehold was Helen M. Bordley's and the 1912 reversion was held by Charles T. and Ella B. Leight, the 3010 and 3020 family across the lane, who sold it in January 1944 (how the Leights took it from the Hooper trust is not shown). (2) Dr. Nicholas Interrante owned 3030 from 1943 to 1951 (rows 39349, 42015 to 42017 put him there). (3) The 1951 $90 rent is Podlich's creation. What it does not settle: M.L.P. 6549/554 (the Leights' title) and 6513/139 (Bordley's). Update Oct. 14, 2026: M.L.P. 6549/554, the cite this deed gives for the Leights' 1944 deed to the Interrantes, was pulled and holds other deeds recorded Jan. 12, 1944 (726:negative-mlp6549-554-not-leight-interrante-1944); the folio is probably miscopied. The $90 rent this deed created is still in the 2016 deed (726:mdlr-lga18376-272-bloom-substitute-trustee-3028-greenmount-llc-2016). Update Oct. 16, 2026: the 1944 Grantee Index (MSA CE 166-315, p.151) gives the Leight-to-Interrante deed of Jan. 11, 1944 as M.L.P. 6549 folio 594, not 554 (the 1951 recital miscopied it); M.L.P. 6549/594 is the next pull. Update Oct. 16, 2026 (late): M.L.P. 6549/594 is read (726:mdlr-mlp6549-594-leight-interrante-3030-rent-1944). It is a deed of reversion dated Jan. 7, 1944, for $1,100 and accrued rent, and the rent it conveys is not the 1912 Aull rent: it recites a new 99-year lease at $66 from the Waverly Building Association of Baltimore County to Helen M. Bordley of Feb. 25, 1935 (S.C.L. 5518/171), the Association's deed of the reversion to the Leights the same day (S.C.L. 5518/173), and Bordley's assignment to the Interrantes (M.L.P. 6513/139). How the Association came to hold 3030, and how the 1912 Aull leasehold and the Hooper trust's 3030 rent ended, are not read. Update Oct. 16, 2026 (1935 read): the 1935 instruments are read (S.C.L. 5518/171 to 175, rows 47394 to 47396). The Waverly Building Association of Baltimore County took the 3030 leasehold by assignment from David McCoy and wife, July 8, 1932 (S.C.L. 5312/27), and the reversion by a deed from 'the Mercantile Trust Company of Baltimore et al Trustees', Feb. 18, 1935 (folio not given; very probably the Hooper trust selling the 1912 $66 rent, an inference), so the 1912 lease and rent met in the Association. On Feb. 25, 1935 it leased 3030 to Helen M. Bordley at $66, sold that new rent to Charles T. and Ella B. Leight for $1,100, and took the lease back from Bordley the same day (a straw, inference). Bordley's 1943 assignment to the Interrantes is M.L.P. 6513/139 (row 47397). Update Oct. 16, 2026 (5313/27 read): the McCoy assignment that the 1935 instruments cite as 'Liber S C L No 5312 folio 27' is recorded at S.C.L. 5313/27 (MSA CE 168-5321; Grantor Index 1932, row 47520), on a folio whose typed header reads '5312', corrected by hand to 5313. It is read (726:mdlr-scl5313-27-mccoy-waverly-bldg-assignment-3030-1932): David and Mary E. McCoy assigned the 3030 leasehold to The Waverly Building Association of Baltimore County on July 8, 1932 (recorded July 12) for $5 and other valuable considerations, subject to the 1912 rent of $66 due June 1 and Dec. 1; they held it by Mary A. J. Aull's assignment of Dec. 20, 1929 (S.C.L. 5076/70). No mortgage or default is recited. Update Oct. 16, 2026 (1929 and 1935 read): S.C.L. 5517/92 (MSA CE 168-5525, read; 726:mdlr-scl5517-92-hooper-trustees-waverly-bldg-redemption-3030-1935) is the deed of Feb. 18, 1935 by which Mercantile Trust Company of Baltimore and William Jenkins, trustees under Francis X. Hooper's will, on the Waverly Building Association's statutory notice to redeem, conveyed it the 1912 $66 reversion on 3030 for $1,100, 'to the end and intent that the leasehold estate created by the lease aforesaid shall be merged with the fee'. So the trustees of the 1935 recitals are Hooper's, and the 1912 lease and rent on 3030 merged in the Association by that deed, not by inference. Aull on Oct. 11, 1922 (S.C.L. 3918/495, recited), she assigned it to David and Mary E. McCoy on Dec. 20, 1929, and they mortgaged it the same day to the Waverly Building Association for a $3,120 purchase-money advance on 24 shares, released only on Mar. 15, 1951 (M.L.P. 8386/69). Their 1932 assignment to that lender was very probably in lieu of foreclosure [inference].

Assignment, Baltimore County land records, Liber E.H.A. 62, folios 390 to 391 (MSA CE 62-62; read on the scan Jeff saved, pages 390 to 394; John P. and Mary Meyer's deed to Caroline Sutton follows on 391). Dated and acknowledged May 15, 1869 before Geo. McCaffray, J.P. of Baltimore City (certified by George Robinson, Clerk of the Superior Court); recorded May 18, 1869 (Edward H. Ady, Clerk). George C. H. Coffield assigns William Hammel, of Baltimore City, for $600, the south part of the Coffield tract on the east side of the turnpike: from a stone on the road 125 ft 6 in along it to the south line of the 1868 Smith lot (E.H.A. 59/86), about due east 140 ft to the tract's fourth line (J.H.L. 43/548), S 15 W along it, then straight back to the start; for the rest of the term, renewable, 'subject however to the payment of the yearly rent of one cent if demanded'. What it settles: (1) the Bateman ground's County source is read: Coffield split his tract in 1868 and 1869, the north 79 ft to Smith under a $150 sub-rent and the south 125 ft 6 in to Hammel outright at the tract's one cent, so 3105 to 3111 never carried a sub-rent. (2) From Hammel the ground went in two parts: the south end to the Methodist trustees by the 1872 sub-lease (737:mdlr-eha77-296-hammel-methodist-trustees-church-lot-1872) and the rest, 70 ft 6 in, to the Batemans. What it does not settle: how the Batemans took Hammel's part (the 1901 deed recites only this deed).

Sub-lease, Baltimore County land records, Liber E.H.A. 77, folios 296 to 299 (MSA CE 62-77; read on the scan Jeff saved, pages 296 to 300; the recording stamp is on a later folio, not read). Dated Aug. 31, 1872. William Hammel sub-leases nine trustees (Edward Mallalieu, Samuel Corby, Joseph J. Wheeler, John Prince, Edward P. Standiford, John T. Dellahunt, Joseph A. Bolgiano, John H. Brown and Robert H. Heyde; some names as read) the south end of his Coffield ground: from a stake on the east side of the turnpike 3 1/2 ft from the beginning stone of the Coffield-to-Hammel deed, 55 ft north along the road, 101 ft east to the fence on the west side of the Old York Road and 13 ft more to the deed's fourth line, 99 ft south-west along it in the old road's bed, then back about 97 ft. Term: the rest of Hammel's term less a year, renewable on a $1 fine; rent $165 a year (February and August) from Aug. 1, 1872; buyout $2,750 (the rent at 6 percent). In trust: the ground and 'the Church and Parsonage to be erected thereon' for divine worship of the Methodist Episcopal Church and a residence for its preachers stationed there. What it settles: (1) the 'Methodist trustees' 1872 sub-lease' named in the 1901 and 1902 Bateman deeds is read: a church lot of 55 ft at the south end of the Coffield tract, with a $165 sub-rent to Hammel. (2) The church and parsonage were still to be built in August 1872. This is very probably the Waverly Methodist Episcopal Church lot in front of which the two-mile stone stood, the stone every 3011 to 3017 description measures from (probable: the deed names no congregation, and Joseph A. Bolgiano is a Waverly name). (3) Of Hammel's 125 ft 6 in, 55 ft went to the church; 70 ft 6 in remained, the Bateman ground. What it does not settle: the congregation's name, the recording date, and whether the $165 rent was ever redeemed.

Two administrator's deeds, Baltimore City Superior Court land records, Liber R.O. 1896, folios 419 to 422 (MSA CE 168-1904; read on the scan Jeff saved, pages 419 to 423; the second continues on 422, not saved). (3) The Old York Road lot comes from a lease by John Litzinger in 1866, the name of the man who sold the Huntington fork lot at 3200 to Andrew Brown in 1834 (same man probable, not shown). What it does not settle: how James S. and Mary A. Bateman took the Hammel ground, and folio 422. Update Oct. 14, 2026: both cited instruments are read: the 1866 Litzinger lease to John H. White (737:mdlr-jhl48-502-litzinger-white-lease-1866: half an acre and 20 perches between the turnpike and the Old York Road at $120, from a P.
