Trustee's deed, Baltimore County Court land records, Liber T.K. 341, folios 328 to 330 (MSA CE 66-391; read on the scan Jeff saved, pages 328 to 332: Louis Regis Deluol's lease to James Quinn ends on 328 above it; David Hines and wife's deed to William O. Eichelberger follows on 330). Dated May 14, 1844; acknowledged that day in Anne Arundel County before Wm. Glover and J. M. Hunter, justices; recorded May 16, 1844 (Thomas Kell, Clerk). Alexander Contee Magruder, of Annapolis, trustee under a deed of trust of Nov. 7, 1826 from Philip G. Biays (W.G. 184/618) of two parts of 'Huntington' (3 a 1 r 12 p and 3 a 3 p) with power to sell, sells James Wilson, of Baltimore City, for $1,025, the first: 'part of a tract called Huntington', beginning at a stone at the end of the S 43 3/4 E line of the part Harry D. Gough and Prudence sold James Biays, 'which stone stands on the northwest side of a road laid out by the said Harry D. Gough'; S 40 3/4 W 41 1/2 perches along the Biays lot, N 38 1/4 W 10 perches to Joseph Thornburg's lot, N 49 1/2 E about 39 perches along it to the York Turnpike, S 3.7 perches along the turnpike to Gough's road, and along the road to the start: 3 acres 1 rood 12 perches, with buildings. What it settles: (1) the Magruder deed recited in the 1870 gate-house deed is read: James Wilson bought this Huntington parcel in 1844 from a trust Philip G. Biays had created in 1826, so the Wilson estate's ground at the toll gate comes from the Biays family through Philip G. Biays. (2) It is Huntington, bounded by Gough's road (the lane, later Gilmor and Vineyard Lane), the turnpike (only 3.7 perches, about 61 ft), a Biays lot (Gough to James Biays) and Joseph Thornburg's lot: a wedge running back from the turnpike at the mouth of the lane on its north side, which is where 3026 to 3032 and the toll-gate lot stand (an inference from the bounds; no deed ties a house to it). (3) The parcel came with buildings in 1844. (4) A new hop above it: Philip G. Biays's 1826 trust (W.G. 184/618). What it does not settle: the 1826 trust itself and who its beneficiaries were. Update Oct. 14, 2026: the 1826 trust is read (725:mdlr-wg184-618-philip-biays-trust-magruder-1826): Philip G. Biays bought both Huntington parcels from James Carroll the Elder and his sons on July 7, 1823 (W.G. 169/672) and put them in trust for his wife and children. Update Oct. 14, 2026 (late): James Wilson gave the Trustees of Huntingdon Chapel part of this ground, beside the Gate House lot, in 1849 (725:mdlr-awb423-290-james-wilson-huntingdon-chapel-church-lot-1849).

Deed, Baltimore City Superior Court land records, Liber R.O. 1928, folios 238 to 239 (MSA CE 168-1936; read on the scan Jeff saved, pages 238 to 242: Oliver H. Ebbert's assignment is above it on 238, and Howard W. Patton's deed to Willard F. Gore follows on 239). Dated, acknowledged before Chas. J. Duggan, of Baltimore City, for $3,000, the 3010 lot in fee 'and particularly the aforesaid rent ... and the reversion', subject to Allen K. Wood's 99-year lease of the same day at $180 (quarterly, February, May, August and November); part of the Dodson deed of 1896 (R.O. 1615/24). Distribution deed, Baltimore City Superior Court land records, Liber R.H.B. 2860, folios 136 to 138 (MSA CE 168-13178; read on the scan Jeff saved). Dated Nov. 17, 1971; acknowledged Nov. 8 in Broward County, Florida, and Nov. 12, 1971 in Baltimore; recorded Dec. 2, 1971 at 11:35 a.m. (Robert H. Bouse, Clerk); the margin reads 'Unlocated'. Ruth Realty, Inc. was dissolved on Aug. 1, 1969; at dissolution David W. Chertkof's revocable trust of Feb. 9, 1968 held half its stock and Annie Chertkof the other half; Annie died Sept. 13, 1969 and her estate took cash, the trust took the real estate. So the corporation's directors and trustees (Ethel Posnick, Helen Gimbel, Howard Chertkof, Jack O. Chertkof) and Annie's executors (Jack O. Chertkof, Ethel Posnick, Charles F. Stein Jr.) convey Jack O. Chertkof, surviving trustee, 'all that property described in a Deed from David W. Chertkof and wife dated November 1, 1960' (J.F.C. 969/476), and any other Ruth Realty property. What it settles: (1) the 1971 deed the 1974 sale recites is read: a family corporation unwinding, not a purchase. (2) The Chertkofs held 3105 to 3109 before 1960 in David W. Chertkof's own name and put it into Ruth Realty on Nov. 1, 1960, so the gap behind 3107 is now the Bateman heirs (after 1920) to David W. Chertkof (before 1960). What it does not settle: J.F.C. 969/476 (it should recite how Chertkof bought) and the Bateman-heirs sale. Update Oct. 14, 2026: J.F.C. 969/476 is read (737:mdlr-jfc969-476-chertkof-ruth-realty-1960): the Chertkofs bought 3105 to 3109 from M. Lillian and Charles A. Slade on Nov. 25, 1935 (S.C.L. 5580/582).

Deed of trust, Baltimore County Court land records, Liber W.G. 184, folios 618 to 620 (MSA CE 66-234; read on the scan Jeff saved, pages 618 to 622: Charles Worthington's lease to John Brooks ends on 618 above it; Isaiah Mankin's deeds to Henry Mankin follow). Dated and acknowledged Nov. 7, 1826 before Saml. Young and Tho. W. Griffith, justices of Baltimore City; recorded Feb. 27, 1827 (Wm. Gibson, Clerk). Philip G. Biays, gentleman, conveys Alexander Contee Magruder, counsellor at law of Annapolis, two parts of 'Huntington' (3 a 1 r 12 p and 3 a 3 p), as described in a deed of July 7, 1823 from James Carroll the Elder and his three sons, James Carroll Jr., Harry Dorsey Gough Carroll and Charles Ridgely Carroll, to Philip G. Biays (W.G. 169/672), in trust for his wife Jane Catharine Thomas Biays and their son Alexander Magruder Biays and any other children of the marriage, share alike for life, remainder to the survivor, with power to sell and apply the proceeds to them. What it settles: (1) the 1826 trust behind Magruder's 1844 sale to James Wilson is read, and it names the source: the Carrolls, heirs of Harry Dorsey Gough's estate (James Carroll was Gough's son-in-law and executor; Harry Dorsey Gough Carroll and Charles Ridgely Carroll his sons), sold Philip G. Biays both parcels in July 1823, after the 1818 to 1819 Carroll allotment of Gough's lands. So the toll-gate corner's chain runs Huntington, Gough (1790 to 1808), the Carroll heirs, Philip G. Biays (1823), the Magruder trust (1826), James Wilson (1844), the Wilson trustees and the turnpike company (1870s), Aull (1912), 3026 to 3032 (the first parcel's place at the corner is an inference from the 1844 bounds). (2) Magruder was evidently a family connection: the Biays son was named Alexander Magruder Biays. What it does not settle: W.G. 169/672 (the 1823 Carroll deed and its description) and where the 3 a 3 p second parcel lay. Update Oct. 14, 2026: the 1823 Carroll deed is read (725:mdlr-wg169-672-carroll-heirs-philip-biays-toll-gate-wedge-school-house-1823): lot 1 is the toll-gate wedge, bought by Christopher Walker under Gough's 1803 bond and plat, with a school-house lot excepted.

Deed of trust, Baltimore County Court land records, Liber W.G. 112, folios 471 to 473 (MSA CE 66-162; the first page was on disk, the rest saved by Jeff October 14, pages 472 to 474; John Armagost's deed of 'Stoddars Delight' follows on 473). Dated and acknowledged Mar. 14, 1811 before Edwd. Woodyear and Edwd. Aisquith, justices, with Elizabeth Russell's release of dower; recorded Apr. 5, 1811 (Wm. Gibson, Clerk). Elisha E. Russell, master mariner of Baltimore, conveys George I. Brown and William S. Hollins, merchants trading as Brown & Hollins, as joint tenants, both of the Huntington lots he had bought the day before, to secure $4,735 owed the firm: the strip from William Jackson's 1803 Gough lot (W.G. 112/467) and the 1 a 47 p from James Biays (W.G. 112/469), the latter bounded by Jackson's lot, 'a road leading to Joseph Merryman's' and James Biays's part of the tract. Whether that road is the later Merryman's Lane (33rd Street) or another track near the toll gate is not shown, so the lots are not yet placed. What it does not settle: whether Russell defaulted, and where on the road the lots lay. Update Oct. 14, 2026: both Russell lots reached James Wilson: McCormick's deed of July 4, 1823 (726:mdlr-wg168-653-mccormick-james-wilson-russell-lots-1823) conveys them course for course with a third parcel, from the City Bank of Baltimore (1820, W.G. 155/345); the Tract Index has Brown to the City Bank in 1817 (W.G. 141/81). Update Oct. 14, 2026 (late): the May 4, 1811 deed is read (726:mdlr-wg113-638-russell-brown-hollins-release-1811): Russell released his equity of redemption and conveyed both lots outright to Brown and Hollins for a $4,500 credit on the $4,735 debt; there was no trustees' sale.

Assignment, Baltimore County Court land records, Liber W.G. 104, folios 48 to 49 (MSA CE 66-154; on disk since October 13 in the Walker-to-Biays scan, pages 46 to 50, and read October 14). Dated and acknowledged Sept. 2, 1809 before J. Smith and Saml. H. Gatchell, justices; recorded Sept. 16, 1809 (Wm. Gibson, Clerk). Harry Dorsey Gough, Prudence Gough and Job Merryman leased Jesse Brown two lots of 'Huntington' on Apr. 16, 1798 (W.G. 54/156); Brown agreed to sell part to Christopher Walker, who sold his right to James Biays and witnessed this deed; Brown's widow and executrix Dorothy assigns Biays, for $1, 2 15/16 acres: from the centre of the York Turnpike where the lease's first line crosses it, S 82 E 15.9 perches to a stone on the west side of the Old York Road, S 7 3/4 W 30.7 perches along it, S 79 1/2 W 11.7 perches to the centre of the turnpike, and straight back; for the rest of the term, renewable forever, at £4 8s 1d a year on April 16. What it settles: (1) the 1809 assignment recited in Allender's 1847 sale to Leitzinger (row 46153) is read: the 2 15/16-acre Huntington leasehold lies between the York Turnpike and the Old York Road, about 506 ft along the old road, 15.9 perches (262 ft) across at the north line and 11.7 perches (193 ft) at the south: ground where the two roads run about 190 to 260 ft apart, which fits the stretch from about the 3100 block north rather than the fork tip at 3011, where they are under 50 ft apart (an inference from the widths; no house or street of the later city is named). (2) Job Merryman joined the 1798 lease as the lessee of a defective 1795 lease that he surrendered for GBP 100 paid by Jesse Brown (W.G. 54/156, read October 14), not as an owner. (3) Christopher Walker, who sold Biays the Ensor's Inspection lot in 1801, was also the go-between here. What it does not settle: where the 1798 lease's 11 acres lie and how the leasehold passed from Biays to Allender's 1847 sale. Update Oct. 14, 2026: the parcel's fee went to the leaseholder Litzinger in 1865 (720:mdlr-jhl46-149-oliver-merryman-litzinger-brown-lease-fee-1865): Gough's heirs to Charles R. Carroll, to Oliver P. Merryman (1859), to Litzinger, with the £4 8s 1d rent. Update Oct. 14, 2026 (late): the Jesse Brown lease cited in this chain was surrendered and re-granted in corrected form on Jan. 9, 1802 (720:mdlr-wg72-124-gough-jesse-brown-corrected-lease-1802), so by 1809 Brown held under the 1802 lease (inference).

Deed, Baltimore City Superior Court land records, Liber R.O. 1748, folios 566 to 567 (MSA CE 168-1756; read on the scan Jeff saved, pages 566 to 570; Daniel Donnelly's lease to Carl Kreuzberg follows). Dated and acknowledged Aug. 11, 1898 before Wm. D. Wright, J.P.; recorded Aug. 27, 1898 at 10 a.m. (Robert Ogle, Clerk). Lulie H. Wallace, widow, conveys William Hall Wallace, for $1,250, 'in pursuance of an order of the Orphans Court of Baltimore City passed on the 22nd day of July 1898 in the matter of the estate of William Hall Wallace an Infant', the 3011 lot in the Village of Waverly 'and especially the clear yearly rent of Seventy five dollars', subject to the Aull lease. What it settles: (1) the 1898 hop is read: four months after buying the rent, Lulie H. Wallace sold it at cost to William Hall Wallace, a minor, under a court order in his estate, so the rent was an investment of a ward's money (she was presumably his mother and guardian; the deed does not say). In 1907, of age, he deeded it back to her for $1 and love and affection (row 46267). What it does not settle: the relationship and the guardianship papers.

Two deeds, Baltimore City Superior Court land records, Liber R.O. 2358, folios 420 to 422 (MSA CE 168-2366; read on the scan Jeff saved, pages 421 to 425; the first begins on 420, not on the scan). Both dated and acknowledged July 31, 1907 before Wm. H. Watson, J.P.; both recorded Aug. 3, 1907 at 10 a.m. (Robert Ogle, Clerk). Mary K. Fink, single, conveys Estella Fink, single, the 3017 lot and its $54 rent (first lot of the 1903 Clemens deed, R.O. 2037/213); Estella conveys it straight back to Mary K. 'by Deed of even date herewith'. What it settles: Estella Fink was a straw, not an owner: the 1907 Lehmann deed's recital of 'a deed ... from Estella Fink' is this round trip, made seven weeks before Mary K. Fink sold to Leopold Lehmann, very probably to separate the 3017 rent from the second lot of the 1903 deed for the sale (an inference: the deeds give no reason). The 3017 rent chain is now read at every step: Clemens 1903, Mary K. Fink 1903 to 1907, Lehmann 1907, Mary C. Lehmann, the Sinclairs 1946, the Vinsons 1951. Update Oct. 17, 2026 (Fink deeds S.C.L. 2559/393 and 3126/290 read): Mary K. and Estella Fink, the 1907 straws, are two of William L. Fink's four children and co-owners of 3013 from 1910 (S.C.L. 2559/393; S.C.L. 3126/290): sisters passing the 3017 rent between themselves before the sale, not strangers.

Deed, Baltimore City Superior Court land records, Liber S.C.L. 2599, folios 429 to 430 (MSA CE 168-2607; read on the scan Jeff saved, pages 429 to 433; the Hendersons' mortgage to the Ashland Building Association follows). Dated and acknowledged July 30, 1910 before Wm. S. Gould, J.P.; recorded Aug. 4, 1910 at 1 p.m. (Stephen C. Little, Clerk). James B. Guyton, bachelor, conveys Rose I. and Mary L. Conway, as joint tenants, two ground rents and reversions: $30 on a lot on the north side of St. Joseph Street and $54 on the Vineyard Lane lot behind 3010 (the 1902 Wood lease courses), the same two lots Rose I. Conway had deeded him that day. What it settles: the inference in row 46273 is confirmed: Guyton was a straw, used so that Rose I. Conway could hold the rents jointly with Mary L. Conway (the $54 rent came to Mary L. Conway in 1902 and evidently passed to Rose before 1910; how is not shown). Mary L. Conway died about Oct. 5, 1916, leaving Rose (later Harding) as survivor (row 46263). What it does not settle: how Rose took the rent from Mary L. Conway, and the sisters' relationship.

Assignment, Baltimore City Superior Court land records, Liber S.C.L. 3348, folios 167 to 168 (MSA CE 168-3356; read on the scan Jeff saved, pages 167 to 171; Michael G. Kilchenstein's deed to Fred A. Rahe follows on 168). Dated Apr. 21, 1919, witnessed and acknowledged before Lennox B. Clemens, notary; recorded Apr. 24, 1919 at 10 a.m. (Stephen C. Little, Clerk). Mary Clemens conveys John E. Wyman the Vineyard Lane leasehold (the 1902 lease courses), subject to $54 a year; her title is Allen K. Wood's deed to her of Apr. 11, 1903 (R.O. 2027/364). What it settles: how the Vineyard Lane leasehold came back to Mary Clemens: Wood assigned it to her in April 1903, a year after taking it, so she held the leasehold while Mary L. Four instruments, Baltimore City Superior Court land records, Liber M.L.P. 6570, folios 338 to 342 (MSA CE 168-6578; read on the scan Jeff saved). All dated Mar. 7, 1944, acknowledged before John A. Lease, Baltimore County land records, Liber J.H.L. 48, folios 502 to 504 (MSA CE 62-48; read on the scan Jeff saved, pages 502 to 506: the top of 502 is the end of John H. White's deed to Henry Taylor, acknowledged May 9 and recorded May 14, 1866, conveying a lot subject to $120 a year, very probably this leasehold; Thomas A. Mellon's deed of a St. Denis lot follows on 505). Dated May 5, 1866, acknowledged by the Litzingers before Edward B. Freeland, J.P., and by White before W. H. Hayward, J.P.; recorded May 14, 1866. John and Elizabeth Litzinger lease John H. White for 99 years, renewable forever, at $120 a year (half-yearly, from March 1), redeemable after ten years for $2,000: from stone '1' on the east side of the Baltimore and Yorktown turnpike, S 84 1/2 E 9 21/25 perches (about 162 ft) to stone '2' on the west side of the Old York Road, N 10 3/4 E 10 17/25 perches (about 176 ft) along the old road to stone '3' at a corner of John O'Brian's lot, N 80 1/2 W 11 16/25 perches (about 192 ft) along it to stone '4' on the turnpike, and straight back; half an acre and 20 perches, part of the land a P. Merryman and wife deeded Litzinger on June 27, 1865 (J.H.L. 46/149). The first name is cramped at the line end and reads like 'Olivr': probably Oliver P. Merryman, the name 3224's 1884 deed recites as one of its sources (row 23723). What it settles: (1) the 1866 lease that the 1901 and 1902 Bateman deeds cite (rows 46289, 46222) is read: the Bateman Old York Road lot (40 ft on the old road from stone '2') is the south-east part of this half-acre. (2) Litzinger's title is a Merryman deed of 1865, not Huntington ground from Brown or Parks, so the ground between the two roads here came from the Merrymans (Merryman's Lot is the tract that lies north of Huntington: an inference, no tract named). (3) White assigned the leasehold to Henry Taylor within days (May 9, 1866), and Taylor gave it back in 1870 (E.H.A. 65/502). What it does not settle: J.H.L. 46/149 (the Merryman deed and its tract), and where O'Brian's lot and this half-acre sit against 3107 to 3117. Update Oct. 14, 2026: the Merryman deed is read (737:mdlr-jhl46-149-oliver-merryman-litzinger-brown-lease-fee-1865): Oliver P. Merryman, the 2 15/16-acre Jesse Brown lease parcel, from Charles R. Carroll (1859); White's half-acre was cut from it.

Two instruments, Baltimore County land records, Liber E.H.A. 65, folios 502 to 504 (MSA CE 62-65; read on the scan Jeff saved, pages 502 to 506; Franz Henry Boklage's deed of a Bear Creek farm to Christian Schorr follows on 505). (1) The end of Henry Taylor's deed back to John H. White of the leasehold White had assigned him in 1866 (J.H.L. 48/501), subject to the $120 rent; acknowledged Mar. 8, 1870 before Thos. H. Robinson, J.P.; recorded Mar. 24, 1870 (Edward H. Ady, Clerk). (2) Sub-lease dated Feb. 17, 1870, acknowledged that day before John B. O'Donnell, J.P., recorded Mar. 24, 1870: White sub-leases Christian Hunteman, for the residue of the term less one year, renewable forever, at $55 a year from Mar. 1, 1870, redeemable for $916.66 (the rent at 6 percent), a lot from stone '1' on the east side of the turnpike, 82 ft east, 22 ft north parallel with the turnpike, 82 ft west to the turnpike and 22 ft south along it; part of the 1866 Litzinger lease (J.H.L. 48/502), the whole subject to $120. The sub-rent pattern ($120 on the whole, $55 on a 22-ft piece) is the 1870s Waverly ground-rent ladder. Assignment and mortgage, Baltimore City Superior Court land records, Liber S.C.L. 3552, folios 81 to 83 (MSA CE 168-3560; read on the scan Jeff saved, pages 81 to 85). Both dated Mar. 26, 1920; the assignment acknowledged that day before Otto V. [Yursik], notary, and recorded Mar. 26, 1920 at 3 p.m. (Stephen C. Little, Clerk). The Provident Savings Bank of Baltimore, by Elisha H. Perkins, president, assigns James M. Sinclair, for $5 and other considerations, the easternmost part of the lot M. Estelle Bateman assigned the bank on Mar. 18, 1904 (R.O. 2062/398): from the centre line of an 8-ft alley (the bank lot's fourth line), 28 ft 6 1/4 in east of the turnpike and in line with the west side of the frame building on the lot, 24 ft south along that building, 86 ft 6 in east to the Old York Road, 24 ft 11 in north-east along it to the alley, and 92 ft 8 in west along the alley's centre line; for the rest of the term, renewable forever, at one cent. Sinclair mortgage the lot to the bank for $1,000 at $10 a month and 6 percent. What it settles: the 1920 sale behind row 46290 is read in its own words: a frame house stood on the back of the bank lot, the bank kept the front, and the line between them ran along the house's west wall, with a one-cent rent carried down from the Coffield tract. What it does not settle: who built the frame house (the Bateman house of the 1877 atlas sat on the turnpike front, not here).

Deed, Baltimore County Court land records, Liber W.G. 168, folios 653 to 657 (MSA CE 66-218; read on the scan Jeff saved: the Mayor and City Council's deed to Edward Denison ends above it on 653, and Henry Lenhart's assignment of a John Street lot follows on 657). Dated and acknowledged July 4, 1823 in Baltimore City before Fielder Israel and John T. Harris, justices, Elizabeth McCormick releasing dower; recorded Aug. 7, 1823 (Wm. Gibson, Clerk); the margin records delivery to 'Wm C Wilson' on Dec. 13, 1848, the year of James Wilson's will. James McCormick Jr. conveys James Wilson, for $7,000, three parcels of 'Huntington' (7 a 0 r 2 p in all, the Tract Index's '7 a 2 p'): (1) 2 a 27 p from the end of the N 36 1/4 W 90 1/4-perch line of the lot Harry Dorsey Gough sold William Jackson on Jan. 13, 1803, back along it 38.3 perches and round to his second line; (2) 1 a 47 p from the north-east corner of Jackson's lot, N 39 3/4 E 26.7 perches 'to a road leading to Joseph Merryman's'; (3) 3 a 2 r 8 p beside it, running to 'a road leading from Joseph Merrymans house to the turnpike road leading from the City of Baltimore towards York town' and along that road. All three came to McCormick from the City Bank of Baltimore on Mar. 15, 1820 (W.G. 155/345). What it settles: (1) parcels 1 and 2 are, course for course, Elisha E. Russell's two lots of 1811 (from William Jackson, W.G. 112/467, and from James Biays, W.G. 112/469), which Russell put in trust with George I. Brown and William S. Hollins (W.G. 112/471); the Tract Index has Brown to the City Bank in 1817 (W.G. 141/81), so the path is Russell, the Brown & Hollins trust, the City Bank, McCormick (1820), James Wilson (1823): James Wilson's estate held the Russell ground (the Brown-to-bank step and the trust sale are not yet read). (2) The road on which the Russell lots front runs from Joseph Merryman's house to the York Turnpike, so it is a cross road meeting the turnpike, not the turnpike itself. (3) The 1823 purchase is Huntington at the north corner of Jackson's 1803 lot; nothing in it names Wilson Street or Lots 16 and 17, so it is not yet shown to be the Lots 16-17 ground. What it does not settle: where Jackson's lot lies against the modern blocks (plotting W.G. 74/327 to 341 would place all three parcels). Update Oct. 14, 2026: the bank's deed to McCormick is read (726:mdlr-wg155-345-city-bank-mccormick-russell-lots-1820): $6,000 in 1820; George I. Brown had deeded the bank the lots in 1817 'in satisfaction of a debt' (W.G. 141/81, with a plat).

Deed, Baltimore County Court land records, Liber W.G. 169, folios 672 to 674 (MSA CE 66-219; read by a helper agent on the scan Jeff saved and checked; an assignment from William A. Ridgely ends above it and a sheriff's deed of 'Shillings Meadows' follows). Dated and acknowledged July 7, 1823 before Fielder Israel and Jas. B. Latimer, justices of Baltimore City; recorded Dec. 9, 1823 (W. Gibson, Clerk). James Carroll the Elder (Gough's executor, who had married Sophia, Gough's only child) and his three surviving sons convey Philip G. Biays, for $1, two Huntington lots whose price had long been paid but never deeded: (1) 3 a 1 r 12 p, under Harry Dorsey Gough's bond of about Jan. 15, 1803 to Christopher Walker and a plat of Jan. 13, 1803 'signed by William Jackson Jas Biays C Walker & John Smith' and lodged by Carroll in the County Court office: from the end of the S 40 3/4 E line of James Biays's lot, on the north-west side of 'a road laid out by the said Harry D Gough', along Biays's lot to Joseph Thornburgh's lot, along it about 39 perches to the York Turnpike, 3.7 perches down the turnpike to Gough's road and back along the road, excepting 'a School house' lot that Gough and Prudence had conveyed to trustees; (2) 3 a 3 p, sold by Carroll as executor to Walker on Mar. 8, 1809 at $200 an acre: from the point where the N 45 W line of 'Old Huntington' meets the Old York Road (a line run from a stone at the beginning of 'New Huntington' to two stones where a boundary stone once stood, shown to James Baker by Joseph Merryman and John Gorsuch), N 40 1/4 E 45 perches, N 82 1/2 W 24.7 perches to the Old York Road and back along it, subject to an old lease by Gough, Prudence Gough and Thomas B. and Elizabeth Onion to 'Charles Carline' (reading uncertain). Walker's rights passed to James Biays, then to John W. Stump, then to Philip G. Biays. The Carrolls' title is the wills of Harry Dorsey Gough and of Prudence Gough, 'who held in her own right an undivided moiety' of Huntington. What it settles: (1) the 1823 deed behind Philip G. Biays's 1826 trust and Magruder's 1844 sale is read: lot 1 is the toll-gate wedge (the same courses as 1844), bought by Christopher Walker under Gough's 1803 bond and plat, which is Cope's plat of Gough's 1803 lots (MSA C2843-15), signed by the buyers. (2) A school house stood on the wedge by 1823, on a lot Gough and his wife gave trustees; whether it is the later toll-house lot is not shown. (3) Prudence Gough's own half of Huntington is the Carnan daughters' share of the 1768 settlement, and the Carrolls are the heirs by both wills. (4) Lot 2 lies on the Old York Road at the 'Old Huntington' line, under an Onion-era lease. What it does not settle: the Gough deed to the school trustees, the 1803 bond itself, and the lease to Carline. Deed, Baltimore County Court land records, Liber W.G. 141, folios 81 to 85 (MSA CE 66-191; read by a helper agent on the scan Jeff saved, the date and plat checked). Dated and acknowledged Mar. 12, 1817 before Geo. Gouldth Presbury and Baltzer Schaeffer, justices (Esther Brown releasing dower); recorded May 23, 1817 (Wm. Gibson, Clerk). George I. Brown, merchant, sells the City Bank of Baltimore, for $12,000, three lots of 'Huntington' (7 a 0 r 2 p): Lot 1 (Jackson's strip of 1811) and Lot 2 (1 a 47 p, Biays's lot of 1811), which Elisha E. Russell conveyed Brown and William S. Hollins by a deed of about May 4, 1811 (W.G. 113/638), Brown holding by survivorship after Hollins's death; and Lot 3 (3 a 2 r 8 p), John Smith's lot from Gough of Jan. 13, 1803, which Dennis A. Smith conveyed Mary Allison in 1811 (W.G. 116/404) and Allison conveyed Brown on Feb. 26, 1817; Lot 3 runs to 'a road leading from Joseph Merrymans house to the Turnpike road' and to the centre of 'a road left open by William Jackson and James Biays'. Copied into the record is Jehu Bouldin's plat of Apr. 1, 1817, 'Three lots part of Huntington', at 10 perches to the inch, with 'Merryman's Road' along the north-east and 'Jackson & Biays's Road' running south-south-east from the lots; no turnpike, neighbours or north arrow are drawn. What it settles: (1) Russell's lots left him by an outright conveyance to his creditors Brown and Hollins in May 1811, two months after his deed of trust; the bank's 1820 deed calls the 1817 sale a settlement of Brown's debt, while this deed states $12,000. (2) The 1817 plat is the oldest drawing found of any of these lots, and it names two roads: Merryman's Road and the road Jackson and Biays left open. (3) The three lots, with the Smith lot, went bank (1817) to McCormick (1820) to James Wilson (1823). What it does not settle: W.G. 113/638 itself, and where the plat sits on the modern blocks (the Jackson-Biays road is the key). Update Oct. 14, 2026 (late): both deeds it recites are read: Russell to Brown and Hollins, May 4, 1811 (726:mdlr-wg113-638-russell-brown-hollins-release-1811), and Dennis A. Lease, Baltimore County Court land records, Liber W.G. 54, folios 156 to 160 and on (MSA CE 66-104; read by a helper agent on the scan Jeff saved; the renewal clause, signatures and recording are past folio 160). Dated Apr. 16, 1798. A three-party lease: Harry Dorsey Gough and Prudence Gough, Job Merryman, farmer, and Jesse Brown, tailor of Baltimore. The Goughs had leased Job Merryman two parcels of 'Huntingdon' on Aug. 6, 1795 (W.G. S.S. 227) for 99 years renewable at £16 11s 3d; that lease was defective (an unattested interlineation and obliterations), and Job, needing £100, surrendered it for that sum paid by Brown, and the Goughs re-granted it to Brown on the same terms. Parcel 1, 6 a 3 q 15 p: from a point 16 perches 6 ft S 46 1/2 E of a large stone at the corner of Joseph Merryman's land, S 82 E 59 3/4 perches to the York road, S 8 W 37 perches along it to 'a road left by the said Harry Dorsey Gough and wife', and along that road back. Parcel 2, 4 a 32 p, a quadrilateral off the end of the first lot's second course, also bounded by the Goughs' road. 11 a 7 p in all; rent £16 11s 3d on April 6. What it settles: (1) the 1798 lease behind the 1809 Brown-to-Biays assignment, the 1847 Allender sale and the 1865 Merryman deed is read: it is Job Merryman's 1795 lease re-granted, so Job was the outgoing lessee, not an owner. (2) The 1809 parcel (2 15/16 acres) starts where parcel 1's S 82 E line 'crosses' the later York Turnpike and runs to its end at the 'York road' of 1798, which is the Old York Road: so the turnpike, built after 1798, was cut across the lease, leaving most of parcel 1 west of it and the 2 15/16 acres between the two roads. (3) Joseph Merryman's land (Merryman's Lot) lay at its north-west corner. What it does not settle: where on the modern blocks (the 1801 Brown-to-Wheetley assignment and Whitely's to James Wilson, rows 46012 to 46014, are parts of the same lease, at 3200 to 3224 by the chapter's reading). Update Oct. 14, 2026 (late): the 1795 original (720:mdlr-wgss227-gough-job-merryman-lease-1795), this lease's end with Job Merryman's GBP 100 receipt (720:mdlr-wg54-160-jesse-brown-lease-1798-end-receipt) and the corrected 1802 re-grant (720:mdlr-wg72-124-gough-jesse-brown-corrected-lease-1802) are read: parcel 2's N 30 W, copied from 1795 into this lease, was corrected to N 50 W in 1802.

Procter Brady, trustees under the twelfth clause of Samuel Brady's will (the Circuit Court of Baltimore City took the trust under a decree of May 23, 1899 in Martha A. Woollen et al. v. Nannie H. Stump et al.), sell James Keelty, for $10,350 (sold Feb. 13, 1907, ratified), in fee: from the west side of the York Turnpike 206 ft 4 1/2 in north of the corner house at 29th Street, 'in the line of the south wall of the southernmost of seven houses heretofore erected on the lot', 95 ft 'more or less' north 'to the land belonging to the said James Keelty', 100 ft west to the west side of a 10-ft alley (its use in common reserved), and back; part of the lot Walter T. Allender, trustee, conveyed Samuel Brady on Nov. 30, 1848 (A.W.B. 404/533). No leases or rents are recited: the fee passes clear. What it settles: (1) the 2930 to 2942 row (seven houses) stood on Brady estate ground before Keelty bought it; he did not build it, and his October to December 1907 leases of 2930 to 2940 created new $60 rents on fee he held (704:mdlr-scl2394-467-keelty-fischer-six-rents-2930-2940-1907). (2) The Brady ground's north line is Keelty's own land, his January 1907 purchase from William T. Wilson (R.O. 2302/43): the Brady and Wilson grounds meet at the north end of the seventh house, 2942 (95 ft from 206 ft 4 1/2 in is about 301 ft 4 1/2 in; the built widths, 14 ft 5 in and six 14-ft lots, reach 304 ft 9 1/2 in, the 2942/2944 line, within the 'more or less'). (3) The Brady chain is now linked from the 1848 Allender trustee's deed to 2930 to 2942. What it does not settle: Samuel Brady's will and the 1899 equity papers, and who built the seven houses (between 1889, when the Brady trustees laid out 29th Street, and 1907). Update Oct. 17, 2026 (south call re-read): the Wilson-to-Keelty deed's closing call confirms from the north side what this deed says from the south: Keelty's ground ends on 'the north eighty one degrees west twenty seven perch line' of the Allender-to-Wilson deed, run reversely, 'indicated on the ground by a partition fence there situate', 450 ft more or less (714:mdlr-ro2302-43-wilson-keelty-1907), and that line is the north line of the Brady tract of 1848 ('south 81 degrees east 27 perches to the Baltimore and York Turnpike Road', 714:mdlr-awb404-533-allender-brady-1848). The deed measures nothing from Twenty-ninth Street, so the 2942/2944 point above is still inferred from the lot widths and this deed's 95 feet.

Hammond, Henry N. and Elizabeth Bowerman and Walter T. and Hannah Jane Allender (the wives the four daughters of James and Sarah Biays) sell James Wilson of Baltimore, for $705, in fee, 85 square perches of 'Ensor's Inspection': beginning at the intersection of the west side of the York Turnpike and the north side of 'a Road one perch and seven tenths of a perch wide running from the York Road by the residence of Mrs Gilmor and others', 1.7 perches north of the stone that begins David Mumma's 1844 lot (A.W.B. 354/374); N 84 W 11.1 perches along the lane to the lot Wilson had lately bought from Walter T. Allender, trustee; N 42 1/2 E 18 1/2 perches along that and Wilson's other land to the turnpike; and S 3 1/4 W 15.2 perches along the turnpike back: a triangle about 251 ft on the turnpike and 183 ft on the lane. Title: John McFadon's deed of Apr. 11, 1822 to John W. Stump and Philip G. Biays in trust for Sarah Biays for life, then the four daughters (W.G. 165/492), and Stump's deed as surviving trustee to the daughters of Oct. 28, 1845 (A.W.B. 359/136). No gate house, toll gate or turnpike company is named. What it settles: (1) the root the 1871 deed gives for the First Toll Gate House lot (Lot 4) is read: the lot is the south end of this 1847 triangle, its south-east corner the triangle's beginning at the lane and the turnpike (the 57 ft by 100 ft lot fits inside it, plotted). (2) So the 3026 to 3032 ground runs McFadon's 1822 trust for Sarah Biays, the daughters (1845), James Wilson (1847), the Wilson trustees to the turnpike company (1871) and Aull (1912). (3) It is a different deed from the same day's sale to William T. Wilson (A.W.B. 382/30, the 2958 side). What it does not settle: why the deed is silent about the toll house the company had held for decades (the 1870 deed's opening says James Wilson held the gate-house lot for the company under a memorandum). Update Oct. 14, 2026 (night): Bouldin's field survey of this triangle, Apr. 19, 1847, is read (725:msa-c2843-15-p106-bouldin-field-notes-1847-04-19).

Deed, Baltimore County Court land records, Liber A.W.B. 423, folios 290 to 291 (MSA CE 66-473; read by a helper agent on the scan Jeff saved; the courses close within about 3 ft). Dated, acknowledged (before John I. Snyder and Henry F. Friese, justices) and recorded Nov. 17, 1849 (A.W. Bradford, Clerk). James Wilson of Baltimore gives the Trustees of Huntingdon Chapel, a corporation under the 1846 general incorporation act (articles in Chattel Records A.W.B. 75/5), for $1, in fee and without conditions, the lot 'on part of which is built the Chapel known as Huntingdon Chapel', about two miles from the city: 'Beginning ... at a Stone now planted on the West side of the York Turnpike Road at the South East Corner of the Gate house Lot', a 20-ft-3-in strip running back some 150 ft to a block about 107 by 115 ft, 56.49 square perches in all; part of the Huntingdon land Alexander Contee Magruder, trustee, sold Wilson on May 14, 1844 (T.K. 341/328). No trustees or denomination are named. Plotted against the 1847 Hoke triangle, the chapel's turnpike frontage sits in the mouth of Gilmor's Lane, the strip roughly following the lane, the block west of the triangle. What it settles: (1) the 'Gate house Lot' is named in a deed by 1849, at the turnpike just north of the chapel strip, which the 1871 deed makes Lot 4 of the Huntingdon plat. (2) Huntingdon Chapel stood on the York Turnpike at the toll gate from 1849 (or before) until the 1873 exchange moved it to Waverly Avenue and Barclay Street. (3) The lane by Mrs. Gilmor's was probably the chapel's approach from the turnpike (inference: the two deeds' surveys differ by a wedge up to about 16 ft). What it does not settle: the chapel's denomination and trustees (the articles, A.W.B. 75/5) and when it was built. Update Oct. 14, 2026 (night): Bouldin's plat for this deed draws the 'Church' 43 ft 3 in by 27 ft 3 in, the size, bearing and place of the 'Old Stone Barn' on his 1844 plat for John Gibson: the chapel was probably the barn converted (725:msa-c2843-15-p69-old-stone-barn-huntingdon-chapel-1844-1849).

Lease and mortgage, Baltimore City Superior Court land records, Liber S.C.L. 2390, folios 425 to 428 (MSA CE 168-2398; read by a helper agent on the scan Jeff saved, the description, names and the Cook recital checked). Lease dated and acknowledged Dec. 6, 1907 before Calvin G. Chesnut, notary; recorded Dec. 7, 1907 (Stephen C. Little, Clerk). James Keelty leases Frank A. Lyons and Catherine Lyons, his wife, for 99 years renewable forever (renewal fine $10), at $60 a year in half-yearly payments counted from Nov. 1, 1907, the lot on the west side of the York Turnpike beginning 234 ft 9 1/2 in north of the south-east corner of the house at the north-west corner of the turnpike and 29th Street, 14 ft front by 100 ft deep: today 2934 Greenmount Avenue (the 1966 deed's same 234 ft 9 1/2 in). The lease names no house number, no alley, no building covenant and no redemption right, and recites no title (Keelty held the ground from the Brady trustees, R.O. 2319/497). The same day the Lyonses mortgaged the leasehold to the Merchants and Manufacturers Permanent Building and Loan Association for a $520 advance on four shares (folios 426 to 428; delivery note dated about Apr. 22, 1912); that mortgage recites the lot as 'conveyed by Henry E. Cook to Frank A. Lyons Et. Al.' by a deed of even date, a name the lease does not mention. What it settles: (1) 2934 began as the Lyons family's house: Frank A. Lyons (the stonemason and contractor of the 1915 and 1928 directories) and Catherine Lyons took it from Keelty on Dec. 6, 1907, five weeks after the Gent and Anderson lease of 2936; the Lyonses' line ran to Ann B. Lyons, whose 1953 and 1966 deeds are already read. (2) It is the 2934 lease the 1907 Keelty-to-Fischer rent sale recites (S.C.L. 2394/467): that cite is S.C.L., not R.O. (3) The mortgage's Henry E. Cook recital is unexplained: either Cook sold them the house (Keelty leasing the ground) or the clerk copied a form; it is an open question, not a finding. What it does not settle: how the $60 rent was redeemed or merged before 1953, and how the leasehold passed from Frank A. and Catherine to Ann B. Lyons. Update Oct. 15, 2026: the 1907 City grantor index shows no deed from Henry E. Cook to the Lyonses (703:negative-ce167-131-p264-no-cook-to-lyons-deed-1907); Cook's Dec. 7 assignment to Ida A. Bozman is at S.C.L. 2390/404, the same book, so the mortgage's Cook recital is probably carried over from another form.

Draft deed, in the Bouldin surveyors' Envelope 15 (MSA C2843-15, pages 15 and 16 of the public PDF; found in the full page-by-page sweep of Oct. 14, 2026 and checked on the page). An unsigned, undated draft 'made the __ day of __' 1821: James Carroll of Baltimore County to Philip G. Biays, for $2,000, the lot 'known and distinguished on a plat of Huntington by the number Seventy four', 3 acres 3 perches, beginning where the N 45 W line of 'Old Huntington' meets the Old York Road (the line run from a stone at the beginning of 'New Huntington' to two stones where a boundary stone, shown to James Baker by Joseph Merryman and John Gorsuch and 'planted under a Land Commission', once stood), N 40 1/4 E 45 perches, N 82 1/2 W 24.7 perches to the Old York Road and back along it. The facing sheet, in the same hand and headed 'pt of Huntington', is an 'And Also' parcel whose courses are, call for call, those of James Biays's Second Lot of Jan. 13, 1803 (7a 2r 33p, W.G. 74/334), to 'a Road left open by' Gough; the sheet ends there. The page is stamped '12th Ward, Envelope No. 1, Plat No. 23' by a later office. What it settles: (1) the 3a 3p parcel that the executed deed of July 7, 1823 (W.G. 169/672) conveys as its second lot, sold to Christopher Walker in 1809, was Lot No. 74 on a numbered plat of Huntington: the plat whose Nos. 95 to 98 Gough sold Henry Wilmans in 1794 (Q.Q. 164). (2) The Carrolls first drew the conveyance in 1821 at $2,000; the deed they executed in 1823 recites the price as long paid and takes $1. What it does not settle: why the Second Lot's courses were attached (James Biays held it in fee from 1803, so a confirmation is a guess), and where the numbered Huntington plat is.

(1) An unsigned sketch in Bouldin's hand, captioned 'John Gibsons Property' (page 69, with its pencil field note on page 75), draws the 1823 Carroll-to-Philip G. Biays ground at the York Road and Gough's road: the 'Gate House Lot', a strip 3 perches on the road and 6 3/4 perches deep at N 77 W, and, 5.3 perches N 82 W beyond its inner end, an 'Old Stone Barn' 2.6 by 1.6 perches (about 43 by 26 ft), its long side S 41 1/2 W. Bouldin's January 1844 plat of the same ground, docketed 'for John Gibson Esqr' (pages 81 to 82), hatches a 'Stone House' in that place. (2) Bouldin's Nov. 10, 1849 plat for James Wilson's gift to the chapel trustees (pages 83 to 85; the deed is A.W.B. 423/290) draws the 'Gate House Lot' along the chapel's entrance strip and a hatched 'Church' 43 ft 3 in by 27 ft 3 in, its long side on the S 42 W line, with the lot drawn around it at 40, 40, 40 and 32 ft. (3) Bouldin's field notes of June 10, 1846 (page 99) pass 'the N W Corner of the Stone Barn' 19.7 perches along the lane and note that 'The Lane is between Mumma's Stone and the gate House 1 7/10 p wide at the Turnpike road'. What it suggests: Huntingdon Chapel was the old stone barn, converted, or was built on its exact footing: the 1844 barn and the 1849 church are the same size within a foot, face the same way, and, plotted from the Gate House lot, fall within a few feet of each other (an inference from the drawings; no paper says the barn became the chapel). Certified copy of the 1757 Huntington resurvey certificate, with its plat, and an abstract booklet, in the Bouldin surveyors' Envelope 15 (MSA C2843-15, pages 92 to 102 and 119 to 129 of the public PDF; found in the full page-by-page sweep of Oct. 14, 2026, the patent endorsement and the Huntington courses checked on the page). The Western Shore Land Office's true copy of Mar. 6, 1810 (John Brewer, register; cost $5.75 with the plat) of the certificate of Nicholas Ruxton Gay, deputy surveyor: under a special warrant of renewment of Apr. 11, 1757, Huntington was resurveyed on Sept. 29, 1757 for John Carnan and Achsah his wife, taking in Huntington (granted to John Edwards for 135 acres; the copy's year reads 1748, apparently written over), Wilkinson's Folly (William Wilkinson, May 6, 1689, 89 acres), part of Edwards Lot (Moses Edwards, Oct. 13, 1704) and part of Edwards Enlargement (Moses Edwards, May 10, 1707), with 90 acres of vacant land: 475 acres in all, 'to be held of the mannor of Baltimore by the name of Huntington'. Huntington's own lines begin at its original beginning tree, 'also a bounded tree of the land called Merryman's lot', S 42 3/4 W 199 perches, SE 88, N 48 3/4 E 190, NE 60, NW 90 (155 acres); the whole runs on Ensor's Inspection, Darley Hall, Sheredine's Discovery, Merryman's Lot, Mount Royal and Jones Falls. Disallowed Aug. 1, 1758 for an unclear sixth course, amended and passed Mar. 3, 1760, approved by Governor Sharpe Feb. 10, 1761: 'Patent the 29th of September 1761 ... Recorded in Liber B C & G S No. 14 fol 295', rent 19 shillings sterling. A small booklet in the same envelope (pages 93 to 99) abstracts the same certificate with the patents of Ensor's Choice (1702), Ensor's Inspection (1734 or 1754 in that copy), Lovelace's Addition (1734), Gorsuch's Regulation (Nov. 9, 1759, bounding on 'Huntingdon as lately resurveyed for John and Achsah Carnan'), Grant's Addition (1722) and Gorsuch's Folly (1720), and Bouldin's notebook (pages 100 to 102) copies the resurvey's courses. What it settles: (1) the Huntington of every corridor deed is the Carnans' 475-acre resurvey of 1757, patented Sept. 29, 1761. The copy's 'Recorded in Liber B C & G S No. 14 fol 295' is where the certificate was recorded: the Land Office index cards give certificate B.C. & G.S. 14/295 and patent B.C. & G.S. 15/219, so 15/219 remains the patent to pull. The certificate itself was already read from the Archives (MSA S1190-2564, Edition 2 ch. 05); this is an 1810 copy of it, lodged with the Biays papers, and it agrees on the courses and the acreage. (2) It is the land Achsah Carnan settled in 1768 (B.Q. 503) on her daughters Prudence (Gough) and Elizabeth (Onion), a moiety each. (3) Huntington's first tree is also a Merryman's Lot tree: the two tracts met there, and the 1802 Wilson deeds name them together. What it does not settle: where the resurvey's lines fall on today's grid. The copy's 1748 for the original Huntington grant is a copyist's slip: the Archives' certificate reads 1688.

Certified copy of the 1757 Huntington resurvey certificate, with its plat, and an abstract booklet, in the Bouldin surveyors' Envelope 15 (MSA C2843-15, pages 92 to 102 and 119 to 129 of the public PDF; found in the full page-by-page sweep of Oct. 14, 2026, the patent endorsement and the Huntington courses checked on the page). The Western Shore Land Office's true copy of Mar. 6, 1810 (John Brewer, register; cost $5.75 with the plat) of the certificate of Nicholas Ruxton Gay, deputy surveyor: under a special warrant of renewment of Apr. 11, 1757, Huntington was resurveyed on Sept. 29, 1757 for John Carnan and Achsah his wife, taking in Huntington (granted to John Edwards for 135 acres; the copy's year reads 1748, apparently written over), Wilkinson's Folly (William Wilkinson, May 6, 1689, 89 acres), part of Edwards Lot (Moses Edwards, Oct. 13, 1704) and part of Edwards Enlargement (Moses Edwards, May 10, 1707), with 90 acres of vacant land: 475 acres in all, 'to be held of the mannor of Baltimore by the name of Huntington'. Coloured plat, in the Bouldin surveyors' Envelope 15 (MSA C2843-15, page 130 of the public PDF; found in the full page-by-page sweep of Oct. 14, 2026 and checked on the page). An unsigned, undated plat of James Biays's whole holding at the York Turnpike, each purchase washed yellow and lettered with its deed: on the south-east side of a 'Road 2 ps wide' (S 42 3/4 W 86 perches from the turnpike), the Ensor's Inspection pieces, John Gorsuch's lot ('Surveyed Septr 17th 1799'), Maidwell's (W.G. 67/62), Christopher Walker's (Mar. 9, 1801), the Spear heirs' 9 7/8 acres (May 30, 1801) and Edwards's (1804, with the 'J.B' and 'E' stones); on its north-west side, in Huntington, William Jackson's lot, 'James Biays Lot 7 A. 2 R. 33 P.', 'Philip G Biays Lot 3 A. 1 R. 12 P.' and Joseph Thornburgh's lot, up to 'Merrymans Road'; east of the turnpike, the Old York Road. Later additions at the turnpike (a lane between a lot marked 'D M', David Mumma's of 1844, and a small piece whose figures are those of the April 1847 survey) date its use to the 1840s; two small buildings stand on the 2-perch road. What it settles: (1) it is the one map of the Biays ground as a whole: the 1799 to 1804 Ensor's Inspection purchases and the 1803 Gough lots lie on the two sides of one road, the 2-perch road 'leading to intersect the York Turnpike Road' of the Walker deed, with the Huntington lots between it and Merryman's Road. (2) Philip G. Biays's 3a 1r 12p (the 1823 Carroll lot, the toll-gate wedge) is drawn between James Biays's Second Lot and Thornburgh's lot, fronting the turnpike, where the 1823 deed puts it. What it does not settle: its date and maker (Bouldin's additions are in pencil and ink over an older plat), and which of the drawn buildings is the stone barn of 1844.

Deed, Baltimore County Court land records, Liber W.G. 72, folios 226 to 230 (MSA CE 66-122; read by a helper agent on the scan Jeff saved, the grant and courses checked; the scan stops in the Virginia governor's certificate, so the recording entry on folio 231 is not read; the Jarman mortgage above it was recorded Jan. 26, 1802). Dated Oct. 24, 1801. Philip Norborne Nicholas, attorney at law of Henrico County, Virginia, and Mary his wife, 'the only surviving Child of John Spear late of Baltimore County ... Merchant deceased, who was the only surviving son of William Spear', sell James Biays, for $20, their 'undivided part share' (the fraction is not stated) of 9 7/8 acres of Ensor's Inspection: from the bounded red oak at the beginning of Huntington, S 47 E 29 1/2, N 50 E 5.6 to a white oak, N 33 3/4 E 38, N 70 E 0.7 perches to the south-west corner of the lot 'which formerly belonged to John Gorsuch now the property of the said James Biays', N 5 degrees 6 minutes W 27.1 perches along it to the stone at the end of the last line of Christopher Walker's parcel to Biays, N 52 1/2 W 7.1 perches along Walker's land to the south-east side of a road, and along the road to the beginning: the same courses, call for call, as the Spear daughters' deed of May 30, 1801 (W.G. 67/447). Special warranty only. Mary was examined privately before Spencer Roane, a judge of Virginia's Supreme Court, at Richmond, and Philip gave a power of attorney to James A. Buchanan and John Hollins of Baltimore to acknowledge and record it, with Governor James Monroe's certificate. What it settles: (1) the 9 7/8 acres came to Biays from both lines of William Spear's family: the four daughters in May 1801 ($790) and, in October, his son John's only child for a share ($20), so Biays's title to the Spear piece was complete. (2) 'N 5.6 W' in the May deed is 5 degrees 6 minutes. (3) By October 1801 Biays already held the Gorsuch lot (Harkin's Rest, deeded to his trustees in 1803, W.G. 76/243) and Walker's parcel (Mar. 9, 1801, W.G. 66/519), and the Spear piece closes on both. What it does not settle: the size of the share (one fifth if William Spear died intestate with four daughters and a son, an inference), William Spear's own title (probably Job Garretson's 1781 deed of 46 acres, abstracted in the Bouldin papers; not recited here), and the recording date.

Lease, Baltimore County Court land records, Liber W.G. 84, folios 302 to 305 (MSA CE 66-134; read by a helper agent on the scan Jeff saved, the rent and execution checked). Dated and acknowledged Mar. 20, 1805 before James Carroll (Gough's son-in-law) and Geo. Gouldsmith Presbury, justices, who also witnessed it, Prudence examined apart; recorded Apr. 11, 1805 (Wm. Gibson, Clerk); marked 'Duplicate'. Harry Dorsey Gough and Prudence lease John Neale of Baltimore, for 99 years renewable forever (renewal fine one year's rent), at 59 pounds 14 shillings current money a year, due Mar. 1, tenant paying all taxes, 9 a 3 r 32 p of 'Huntingdon resurveyed': beginning on the south-west side of 'a private road laid out by said Harry Dorsey Gough leading from the York Turnpike to the grounds of Hugh Thompson and others for the accomodation of said lots', N 50 W and N 60 W 8 perches each along it to Samuel Vincent's lot, S 38 W 48.6 perches along Vincent's, S 50 E 43.6 perches to 'the road leading to Rutters Mill', N 40 E 28 perches along that road, N 50 W 28.6 perches and back (an L-shaped lot; the courses close within about 1 percent). Neale may buy the fee at any time for 995 pounds, the rent capitalized at 6 percent (100 pounds an acre). No title is recited and no building is required. What it settles: (1) the 'Gough to Neale lease' of Bouldin's abstract is read: the '59.14' is pounds and shillings, 6 pounds an acre, a redeemable ground rent. (2) By 1805 Gough was leasing Huntington in lots along a private road he had laid out from the York Turnpike to Hugh Thompson's, with Samuel Vincent already holding the next lot: the same road the McFadon trust deed of 1822 calls the road 'from the Land of Hugh Thompson unto the York Turnpike Road at or near the Gate', the lane at the first toll gate (probable: Bouldin filed the lease with the toll-gate papers; the lease itself names no gate). (3) The road to Rutter's Mill ran at right angles to it (Cope's plat envelope is docketed 'York Rd and Rutters Mill Road'). What it does not settle: where the lot lies along the lane (no distance from the turnpike), the later steps (Neale to John Mycroft, Mycroft to Philip B. Sadtler, Nov. 1815, per Bouldin), and whether the fee was ever bought.

Plat, in the Baltimore City Superior Court Survey Papers, envelope 'York Road No. 5' (MSA CE71-283, legacy C2843-283, pages 58 to 60 of the Archives' public PDF; item 1 of the envelope's index, 'A[u]lls Lot York Rd & Old York Rd'; found in the page-by-page sweep of Oct. 15, 2026, the courses checked on the page). An unsigned, undated pencil working plat of Jacob Aull's lot east of the Old York Road, at 30 feet to the inch: its seven courses are those of the 1848 Bowerman-to-Aull deed (A.W.B. 409/275: N 21 1/2 E 10.7, S 77 1/4 E 27.2, S 28 1/4 W 16.9, N 66 1/2 W 5.8, N 81 1/4 W 8.9, N 17 E 6.3, N 81 1/4 W 10.4 perches), with the Old York Road front re-measured at 10 9/20 perches (172 ft) and the long side converted to 448.8 ft; they close within 0.3 perch at 2 a 30 p, against the deed's 2 a 29 p. Inside the lot the surveyor drew a building at the corner on the Old York Road, strips measured in feet and a 'Street ... 40 feet', and beside it a sketch of a lot on the 'Old road' with a stable. What it suggests: the Aull lot was being laid off for building, with a new 40-ft street through it, at some date after 1848 (the docket's box number, 350, sits among the 1830s to 1880s papers of the same series). It is the first drawing of the Aull ground found. What it does not settle: the date, the surveyor, the client, and which present street (if any) the 40-ft street became; that is the handle for placing the 1848 lot on today's grid.

Lot description, in the Baltimore City Superior Court Survey Papers, envelope 'York Road No. 4' (MSA CE71-282, legacy C2843-282, pages 11 and 12 of the Archives' public PDF; item 10 of the envelope's index; found in the page-by-page sweep of Oct. 15, 2026 and checked on the page). Docketed 'Jno. W. Beall Lot, Bo't of Dd Mumma, York Road, County, 2 and 3 mile s[tones]': a lot bought by John W. Beall from David Mumma, beginning at a stone marked 'DM' and 'LH' on the EAST side of the York Turnpike, a corner of the part of the tract conveyed to Ludwig Herring, north 17.7 perches (292 ft) along the turnpike, S 82 E 17.1 perches to the west side of the Old York Road, S 4 1/2 W 17.2 perches along it to the end of Herring's second line, and back along that line (about S 83 E, computed): 1 a 3 r 2 p, closing within about 1 percent. The tract is not named and the paper is undated. What it suggests: David Mumma, who bought the Biays heirs' lot at the lane in 1844 (A.W.B. 354/374), also held ground in the wedge between the turnpike and the Old York Road, and sold it in lots: Ludwig Herring's to the south and Beall's north of it, each running the full width between the roads (260 to 280 ft here). 'County' dates it before the 1888 annexation, and 'between the 2 and 3 mile stones' puts it north of the 2-mile stone, which the 3013 and 3015 deeds place on the east side in front of the Waverly Methodist Episcopal Church lot, about 190 ft north of 3013: so in the wedge between the two roads north of the 3000 block's fork (probable from the milestone; the lot is not placed exactly). What it does not settle: Mumma's title to the wedge (not the 1844 deed, which is west of the turnpike), the dates and libers of the Mumma-to-Herring and Mumma-to-Beall deeds, and which modern lots they are.

Building-permit index card, Baltimore City Archives, Department of Housing and Community Development records (BRG48), Building Permits master index cards (the City's 1924 to 1961 cards, viewed as scanned images in the Archives; photographed by Jeff in the reading room on Oct. 14, 2026 and read from the photo). What it settles: the City's own record of the 1936 Provident Savings Bank building: permit 9660, $10,600, issued May 28, 1936, the same cost as the Sun's permit notice of May 29, 1936 (row 738:373828616: a 24 by 70 ft bank by John E. Building-permit index card, Baltimore City Archives, Department of Housing and Community Development records (BRG48), Building Permits master index cards, image bca677-0891 (photographed by Jeff in the reading room on Oct. 14, 2026 and read from the photo). The card for 3013 Greenmount Avenue (Division 9, Section 3, Block 4076-A, Lot 1/2) lists two permits: Sept. 23, 1954, permit 167771, 'Raze 1 sty store', completed Oct. 5, 1954; and Dec. 17, 1956 (issued Jan. 4, 1957), permit 196584, a certificate of occupancy, apparently 'for pet shop' (the words are partly illegible), dated Jan. 2, 1957. What it settles: a one-story store stood at 3013 until September 1954, when it was razed a month after the Silens bought the leasehold and the reversion (Aug. 24 and 25, 1954); and by January 1957 the lot was certified for a new use, probably a pet shop, which fits the animal-hospital use of the 3011 to 3015 group in later deeds (inference). What it does not settle: who razed it (the owner line is blank), what replaced it, and the card's reverse ('OVER'), not photographed. Update Oct. 15, 2026: the 3011-3013 card (720:bca-brg48-permit-card-3011-3013-greenmount-1945-1961) shows the new two-story building that replaced both stores, Oct. 1954 to Mar. 1955, built by Max Silen.

Building-permit index card for 2958 Greenmount Avenue (Block 3855, Lot 17), 1946 to 1961. The corner carried advertising structures in 1946 and an illuminated poster board in 1949 (BZA 510-49). In 1961 the house was converted to offices: a basement office doorway (Jan.), the Greenmount entrance closed and a new entrance made on the 30th Street side (Mar.), four side windows (Mar.) and the front porch enclosed (May, BZA 125-61, completed Oct. 25, 1961). What it settles: the porch enclosure the National Register dates 'ca. 1940' was permitted in 1961, with the office conversion. What it does not settle: anything before 1946 (no earlier entries). Transcribed Oct. 15, 2026 by helper agents from the Archives' scanned card (downloaded with the City Archives' permission), key entries checked on the card; front of the card only (each says OVER; no back was scanned).

Building-permit index card for 3010-3020 Greenmount Avenue (Block 3856, Lots 2-3), owner Edward Constanzo, 1937 to 1958. The ground held two-story frame dwellings: 3018-20 was re-sided with asbestos shingle in 1937 and 3020 fenced in 1945. Constanzo then rebuilt it piece by piece: a one-story masonry launderette store at 3010-16 (1953, $5,000), a one-story office at 3012 (1955, $8,500), both frame houses razed (Aug. to Sept. 8, 1955), an office at 3014 (1956, $7,000) and a finance company office at 3010-20 (1958, $10,000). What it settles: the present one-story row dates from 1953 to 1958, and the last 19th-century frame houses on the lot came down in 1955. What it does not settle: which frame house was which on the old deeds. Transcribed Oct. 15, 2026 by helper agents from the Archives' scanned card (downloaded with the City Archives' permission), key entries checked on the card; front of the card only (each says OVER; no back was scanned).

Building-permit index card for 3011-3013 Greenmount Avenue (Block 4076A, Lots 1-2), owner Max Silen of 4351 Park Heights Avenue, 1945 to 1961. The brick and frame store at 3011 was razed (permit 167612, Sept. 21 to Oct. 5, 1954), together with the one-story store at 3013 (its own card), and a two-story masonry store and office building for 3011-13 was permitted Oct. 1, 1954 ($12,000, plan 467) and completed Mar. 18, 1955. Later tenants show in the sign permits: a cleaning pickup store (1955), neon signs (1956) and a savings and loan at 3011 1/2 (1959). What it settles: (1) the present 3011-3013 building dates from 1954-55, built by Max Silen right after his family bought the leasehold and reversion (Aug. 1954); the National Register's 'originally 2-story brick commercial building built ca. 1900, altered ca. 1970' is wrong for the building, though right for the lot's age. (2) The 1847 'two Story Brick House' on the Leitzinger wedge did not survive past 1954 (inference: it was probably the brick and frame store razed). What it does not settle: the savings and loan's full name. Transcribed Oct. 15, 2026 by helper agents from the Archives' scanned card (downloaded with the City Archives' permission), key entries checked on the card; front of the card only (each says OVER; no back was scanned).

Building-permit index card for 3015-3017 Greenmount Avenue (Block 4076A, Lots 3-4), 1934 to 1958. A two-story brick dog hospital was erected at 3015 in Sept. 1934 ($5,000); in Aug. 1950 the two-story frame building at 3017 was razed and a brick and cinder-block animal-hospital addition built ($12,000); the sign was rehung in 1958. What it settles: the animal hospital (the use of 3011-3015 in later deeds) began here in 1934, in a new building, and spread to 3017 in 1950; the National Register's 'originally 2-story ca. 1900, expanded ca. 1940' should read 1934 and 1950. What it does not settle: who the 1934 owner was (not on the card). Transcribed Oct. 15, 2026 by helper agents from the Archives' scanned card (downloaded with the City Archives' permission), key entries checked on the card; front of the card only (each says OVER; no back was scanned).

Building-permit index card for 3028 Greenmount Avenue (Block 3856, Lot 5), 1925 to 1955. Mortgage, Baltimore County Court land records, Liber T.K. No. 280, folios 186 to 188 (MSA CE 66-330; read 2026-10-16 from the scans Jeff saved). Dated and acknowledged June 16, 1838 (Culver's 1915 article prints 1836). Eleanor Merryman, widow, and Nelson Merryman and Sarah his wife, Charles Merryman and Mary Ann his wife, Lewis, Eleanora, Joseph, George and Oliver P. Merryman mortgage to Samuel Brady of Baltimore City, to secure $2,000 lent that day for two years with interest half-yearly, "All that farm called Clover Hill" in Baltimore County near the City, about 200 acres, "on which Joseph Merryman late of said County deceased formerly resided and of which he died seized", descended to the widow and the seven children as his heirs at law. Witnesses Thomas W. Bond and William W. Waite. What it settles: Oliver P. Merryman, grantor of the 3224 ground to Sinclair about 1884, is one of Joseph Merryman's heirs to Clover Hill. What it does not settle: the deed gives no tract name and no bounds, so it cannot show whether Merryman land reached the York Road.

H. Hallman [?], and 475 ft south of the south side of Wilson Street, at the southeast corner of "lot number Seven as conveyed by the said parties ... to P. P. Pendleton"; west 200 ft along Pendleton's south line to the centre of a 20-ft alley kept open for all the trustees' lots; south 22 1/2 ft along the alley to the northeast side of Merryman's lane; southeast along the lane 30 ft more or less to where "the old division fence between Brown's [?] lot and said Wilsons land formerly stood"; southeast 175 ft along that line to the turnpike; north 44 1/2 ft to the beginning. Sinclair could redeem the rent for $800 within the year (then at 6 percent, $1,200), or pay $300 by Feb. 1, 1873 for a reduced rent; failing that he must build a house of at least $1,250 within six months. What it settles: the 3224 lot was Wilson-estate ground let by the trustees, next to Pendleton's Lot No. 7 of a numbered trustees' division, and its south line was the old fence between the Wilson land and Brown's [?] lot. No tract name, no plat cited. Update Oct. 16, 2026 (batch 3): the Pendleton deed read (E.H.A. 72/153, 768:mdlr-eha72-153-wilson-trustees-pendleton-lots-7-8-1871). 'Lot number Seven as conveyed ... to P. P. Pendleton' is one of Lots 7 and 8 on the Wilson sales plat filed in Wilson against Wilson and others (Circuit Court of Baltimore City), 50 ft by 200 ft each, together 375 to 475 ft south of Wilson Street; this lease's beginning at 475 ft south of Wilson Street makes Lot 7 the southern lot [inference]. The trustees conveyed Pendleton's lots in fee under James Wilson's 1848 will (N.H. 26/354), which fits their holding the fee of this lot too and selling Sinclair the reversion for $800 in 1873 (J.B. 84/387).

Deed of sale, Baltimore County Court land records, Liber B No. Q, folios 740 to 741 (MSA CE 66-36; read 2026-10-16 from the scan Jeff saved). Found in the Baltimore County Court Grantor Index 1655-1769 (MSA CE 33-1, p.107, 'En cont'd', Joseph Ensor's sales), pulled Oct. 16, 2026. The index dates it 1767; the deed is dated July 7, 1768. Joseph Ensor of Baltimore County, for 18 pounds current money, sells James Madewell (written also Madowell; the James Maidwell of the 1787 mortgage), of the same county, wheelwright, 'All that part of a Tract or Parcel of Land called Ensor's Inspection': beginning at a bounded white oak marked with three notches, being the second bounded tree of the part of Ensor's Inspection heretofore sold to Thomas Cole Speagle; N 36 1/2 E 35 perches to a stone marked M standing in the given line of the part sold by Ensor to Job Garrison; N 76 1/2 E 25 perches to the main Road; then bounding on and with the main Road and the part of Ensor's Inspection sold to Richard Dick, S 10 E 30 perches and S 35 W 14 perches to the beginning tree of Thomas Cole's part, a black oak standing by the road side marked with six notches; then a straight line to the beginning; nine acres more or less. General warranty. Witnesses Mark Alexander and Wm. Aisquith; receipt of 18 pounds the same day; alienation fine of 4 1/2 pence sterling received by Dan. Bowly for Lord Baltimore by order of Daniel of St. Thomas Jenifer; acknowledged July 7, 1768 before Wm. Aisquith and Benjamin Rogers, justices, with Mary Ensor's release of dower; recorded Jan. 2, 1769, examined by B. Bordley, Clerk. What it settles: the source of Maidwell's nine acres. The courses are those of his 1787 mortgage (W.G. AA/193) and 1795 release (W.G. S.S. 231); computed, the unstated closing line runs N 80 1/2 W 42.9 perches, as the chapter had computed from the mortgage, and the figure closes on about 8.2 acres. With the 1800 Maidwell deed to Biays (W.G. 67/62), the 2958 ground's chain now reaches Joseph Ensor, for whom Ensor's Inspection was surveyed in 1754 (S1190-1698) (the Biays-to-Wilson-to-Keelty link stays marked probable). The lot lies on the main road (the York Road) between Speagle's part, Garretson's line and Richard Dick's part. Update Oct. 17, 2026 (County grantor index, Dick and Gorsuch): the County grantor index runs for Di (CE 33-1 pp. 87-88 for 1655-1769, CE 33-2 p. 84 for 1770-86, CE 33-3 pp. 97-98 for 1787-97, CE 33-4 p. 99 for 1799-1803, the first Di page of that volume, p. 98, not held) show no Richard Dick as grantor in any form, and no Dick deed of Ensor's Inspection or of any land on the York road; the Dicks indexed (Thomas, James, Christian) are other men on other ground. No deed from Dick to Edwards is indexed before 1804, so how Edwards came by Dick's part is open: a will or descent, a deed entered under another first-named grantor or a variant spelling, an unrecorded deed, or a Dick deed of 1804 or later (CE 33-5 not held). Ensor's own deed to Dick was not among the Ensor lines found in CE 33-1 pp. 105-107 either. Next: the Grantee Index (MSA CE 32) under Dick, 1655-1769, for Ensor's deed to Richard Dick; and the Maydwell-to-Edwards deeds, W.G. 66/123 (1801) and 82/206 (1804), whose liber and folio are already known (row 46122). (714:index-ce33-1-p87-dick-richard-1765-1769 and its three siblings.)

Joseph Ensor of Baltimore County, for 10 pounds current money, conveys Thomas Cole Speigle (also Speagle), Rachel Cole Speagle and William Carter Junior, planters (the two added names interlined before signing), part of 'Ensors Inspection lying on the West Side of the main Road that leads from Baltimore Town to George Hailes': beginning at a bounded black oak of Mrs. Achsah Carnan's, with her land S 52 E 22 perches to the main Road; up the road N 14 E 29 1/2 perches to a black oak marked with six notches; on the road N 41 E 6 perches to a red oak marked with six notches; N 81 1/2 W 39 perches to a forked white oak marked with six notches; S 50 W 4 perches to Achsah Carnan's line, and with it to the beginning; 5 1/4 acres (the alienation-fine note says 5 1/2). Deed, Baltimore County Court land records, Liber B No. K, folios 84 to 86 (MSA CE 66-30; read 2026-10-16 by a helper agent from the scan Jeff saved, folios 81 to 85; folio 86, with the justices, the alienation fine and the recording, was not saved). Found in the Baltimore County Court Grantor Index 1655-1769 (MSA CE 33-1, p.107, 'En cont'd', Joseph Ensor's sales), pulled Oct. 16, 2026. The index cites folio 81; the deed opens on 84 (81 to 84 hold the end of Thomas Harrison's lease to John Sligh, recorded May 5, 1762). Dated May 5, 1762. Joseph Ensor of Baltimore County, for 66 pounds current money of Maryland, conveys Job Garison (Garretson in the clerk's margin and the index) 'all that Part of a Tract of Land Called and known by the Name of Ensors Inspection', 'Beginning for the same at a Bounded Red Oak Standing in an Old Field being a Bounded Tree of a Tract of Land Called Huntington', thence North East 276 perches, S 27 W 140 perches, S 7 W 37 perches, then a direct line to the beginning; fifty-five acres (the index and margin say 50; plotted, the calls enclose about 51 acres and the closing line runs about S 75 W 131 1/2 perches). Special warranty; receipt of 66 pounds; witnesses Walt. Tolley and John Hall. No recital of Ensor's title. What it settles: (1) the root of William Spear's land. The Bouldin abstract of Job Garretson's 1781 deed to Spear (46 acres, MSA C2843-15 p.68) begins at the same 'bounded oak in an old field, a bounded tree of Huntingdon' and repeats this deed's S 27 W and S 7 W courses, so Spear bought the south-west part of these 55 acres from Garretson, who had it from Joseph Ensor in 1762. Through Spear the ground runs to his heirs' 1801 sale to Biays (W.G. 67/447, beside 2958) and to John Foster about 1786 and on to Christopher Walker (1800) and Biays (1809), the 3010 corner. (2) The 276-perch north-east line has the length of the long north-east line of the 1754 Ensor's Inspection certificate (S1190-1698, surveyed for Joseph Ensor), so Garretson's land very probably runs along that line from a Huntington boundary tree (inference: the certificate's line starts 27 perches along Darley Hall's north line, and the deed names no Darley Hall). Maidwell's 1768 lot calls 'the given line' of this part. Update Oct. 16, 2026 (later): folio 86 read (MSA CE 66-30 p.00086, saved by Jeff). It completes the acknowledgment before Walt. Tolley and John Hall (of Swan Town [?]), justices; the alienation fine of two shillings sterling was received May 5, 1762 by B. Bordley by order of Lord Baltimore's agent Edward Lloyd; recorded May 5, 1762, B. Bordley, Clerk. Two shillings is the fine on 50 acres at the usual four shillings per hundred (the 1768 Maidwell fine, 4 1/2 pence, fits nine acres the same way), so the fine supports the index's 50 acres against the body's 'fifty five'.

Deed, Baltimore County Court land records, Liber A.L. No. L, folios 307 to 311 (MSA CE 66-47; read 2026-10-16 by a helper agent from the scan Jeff saved). Found in the Baltimore County Court Grantor Index 1770-1786 (MSA CE 33-2, p.103: 'Ensor, Joseph to Griffith and Gist, Hailes Folley 100 Acres Land', A.L. L 307). Dated May 24, 1774. Joseph Ensor, now of Cecil County, for 500 pounds current money of Pennsylvania, conveys Benjamin Griffith and Mordecai Gist of Baltimore County, as tenants in common, 'all that undivided Moiety or half part of a Tract of Land ... called or known by the Name of Hales Folly containing and laid out for one hundred Acres ... originally Surveyed for a Certain Nicholas Hale long Since Deceased', with houses and improvements. No courses and no recital of how Ensor held it. The warranty excepts any part found 'to lie within the Bounds of a Tract of Land called Salisbury Plains' (Salisbury Plains is, with Hailes Folly, a named bound of the 1757 Huntington resurvey). Witnesses George McCall and Owen Allen; acknowledged May 24, 1774 before Isaac Van Bibber and Wm. Spear, justices of Baltimore County; Mary Ensor released dower in 'the within mentioned fifty Acres' in Cecil County on Sept. 30, 1774, before John Veazey Jr. and Stephen Hyland, certified Oct. 3, 1774; no recording clause on these folios. What it settles: by 1774 the Ensor family that surveyed Ensor's Inspection (1754) held at least half of Hailes Folly, the tract whose 1742 courses fix Huntington's course 25; so Ensor's Inspection, Hailes Folly and Huntington were neighbouring holdings near the York Road. What it does not settle: how Ensor took Hailes Folly from the Boring line, who held the other half, and where Mordecai Gist and Benjamin Griffith's half went. Update Oct. 17, 2026 (County grantor index, Dick and Gorsuch): lead: the County grantor index for Gorsuch, CE 33-2 p. 133 (the 'Gi cont'd' page, read for the Gorsuch run), has 1781, Gist Mordecai &c to John McLure, 'Hailes Folly 50 Acres', W.G. G/108, which is very probably this moiety going on to McLure (INFERRED; the deed is not read).
